en: Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
The Recitation of the Moggallāna Sutta.
First Section: Perception, etc.
1. There are forty-three consonants (vaṇṇa). 2.
There are ten vowels (sara).
3. Each vowel has two corresponding semi-vowels (savaṇṇa).
4. The first [vowels] are short.
5. The latter [vowels] are long.
6. The consonants begin with *ka*.
7. There are five groups of five [consonants].
8. A nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*) is a *bindu*. 9.
The vowels *i* and *u* are *jhal* when they stand at the end of a noun-base (*nāmam*).
10. On the back.
11. Smell. 12.

(Perception) 13.
[The suffix] -anta follows the word *vidhi* when it is a qualifier. 14.
In the locative case, [the suffix -anta follows] the preceding word.
15. On the fifth day, it belongs to another.
16. Of the beginning.
17. Of that which ends in the sixth case.

18. [A root] having *v* as its suffixal marker (*anubandha*) [is termed a verb]. 19. [Roots] having *ṭ* as their suffixal marker (*anubandha*) consist of multiple phonemes (*ane-ka-varṇa*) and apply to the whole [of the base]. 20. [Roots] having *ñ* or *k* as their suffixal markers (*anubandha*) [are termed roots] when they occur at the beginning or the end [of a word].
21. A consonant that follows a vowel is called an *anubandha*.

22. [The term *anubandha* is used] in the sense of negation (*vippaṭisedha*). 23. A conventionally established (*saṅketa*) consonant that is not a constituent part (*navaya*) of a word is an *anubandha*.
24. By means of a following vowel, even a preceding vowel [is elided].
25. [The suffixes] -ntu, -vantu, -māntu, -āvatu, and -tuvat are related [to the base].
This is a paribhāṣā rule.
26. When a vowel follows a vowel, there is elision of the preceding vowel. 27. In some cases, the subsequent [vowel] is substituted. 28.
Or, there is no doubling [of the consonant].
29. One of the [two] semi-vowels is elided. 30. [The remaining semi-vowel] becomes *y* or *v* before a vowel. 31. [The same applies to] *e* and *o*.
32. [The vowel] *o* is called *gossāvaṅa*.
33. In consonants, there are long and short [vowels]. 34. After a vowel, [the following consonant] is doubled.
35. For the fourth and second [vowels], there is the third and first [consonants]. 36.
After *vī*, *tissē*, and *ve*, there is *vo*.
37. After *e* and *o*, there is *vaṇṇe*.
38. The nasalized vowel (niggahīta).
39. Elision (lopa). 40.
The substitution of the letter *sa* (parasara).
41. *vaga* becomes *vagga* at the end of a verse-quarter.
42. *ña* occurs in place of *ya* before vowels.
43. *saṃ* becomes *ssa* before *ye*.
44. *m* becomes *y* before *d*.
45. *c* and *g* become *y* and *v* respectively before *a*.
46. *ch* becomes *ḷ*.
47. *Ta*, *da*, *min*, and so forth.

48. For the *tavagga* (the *ta*-group), *vara* (the *va*-group), and *ṇa*, there are the *yavagga* (the *ya*-group), *ca* (the *ca*-group), and *ba* (the *ba*-group). 49. These [consonants] are [substituted] by the respective *vaggas* (groups) and *la*, *sa*.
50. The perversion of hatred (hassa-vipallāsa). 51.
Or those two (ve vā).
52. For the letters ta, tha, na, ra, ṭa, ṭha, ṇa, la.
53. There is elision of [the suffix] beginning with *saṃyoga*. 54. In the case of *viccha* and *abhikkhañña*, there is elision of two [vowels].
55. There is elision of *si* and so forth, preceded by *asse* and *kassa*.

56. [The substitution of the accusative case ending] occurs after *sabbā* and the rest in the sense of "exchange. 57. [The substitution of the accusative case ending occurs] in the sense of "confusion" up to the point of enlightenment. 58. [This application of the rule occurs] frequently (*bahulam*).
Thus ends the first chapter, on Nouns and so forth, in the Moggallāna Grammar.

I shall speak of the Saṅgha of the True Dhamma, the Māgadhī grammar of phonetics.
1. There are forty-three consonants beginning with *a*.

The forty-three syllables (*akkhara*) beginning with the vowel *a* and ending with the *niggahīta* (visarga) are called "consonants" (*vaṇṇa*). [The vowels are: *a*, *ā*, *i*, *ī*, *u*, *ū*, *e*, *o*, *o*.
ka kha ga gha ṅa, ca cha ja jha ñña, ṭa ṭha ḍa ḍha ṇa, ta tha da dha na, pa pha ba bha ma, ya ra la va sa ha ḷa aṃ. What is the purpose of this?
By the rule “e o na mavaṇṇe” (1.37), the mention of forty-three [vowels] indicates that in certain instances there is the elision of a vowel.
By this, forms such as *paṭisaṅkhā yoniso* are established.

2. Vowels (*sara*). Among these, the first ten sounds are called vowels (*sara*). What is the purpose of this? [It is for rules such as: “A vowel is elided before a vowel” (1.2.26), and so forth. 3. Homogeneous sounds (*savaṇṇa*).

Among those, every two vowels are called homogeneous (*savaṇṇa*). What is the purpose of this? [It is for rules such as: “A homogeneous sound may also [be substituted] for a consonant followed by another” (1.2.24).
4. Short (rassa).

Among those two [vowels], whichever is the first is designated as short (rassa). Among them, they appear only before the consonant clusters *e*, *o*, and *saṃ*. What is the purpose of that? [It is for the application of rules such as: “Or short” (2.62), etc. 5. Long (dīgha). The subsequent [vowel] is long.

Those very same [vowels] which are long elsewhere become short in this [context]. What is the purpose of that? [It applies] in such rules as: “A vowel (*lo*) before *pa*, *ni*, or *su* is short” (2.88), and so forth. 6.

**Consonants (*byañjana*):** The phonemes beginning with the letter *ka* and ending with the *niggahīta* (the nasal stop) are designated as consonants (*byañjana*). What is the purpose of that? [It applies] in such rules as: “Long and short [vowels] before a consonant” (1.33), and so forth.
7. Five groups of five.

The five groups beginning with *ka* are called "vaggas" (consonant groups). What is the purpose of this? [It is for rules such as: "In a *vagga*, the final letter of the *vagga* [is substituted]" (1.41), and so forth.
8. The nasal dot (*bindu*) is the *niggahīta*.

This vowel which consists of a single dot (*bindu*) is designated as *niggahīta*. What is the purpose of this? [It is used in rules such as: “*Niggahītaṃ*” (1.3.8), etc. The designation of it as *garu* (heavy) is for the sake of a designation that corresponds to its actual nature (*anvatthasaññatthaṃ*). 9. The vowels *i* and *u*, when occurring at the end of a noun (*nāman*), are designated as *jhal*.

A “noun” is that which begins with the first word; the vowels *i* and *u* occurring at the end of such a noun are designated as *jhal* respectively. What is the purpose of this? [It is used in rules such as: “*Jhalā vā*” (2.1.111), etc.
10. *Pitthiyaṃ*.

In the case of a feminine noun (*itthi*), the vowels *i* and *u* occurring at the end of the word are designated as *pasaññā*. What is the purpose of this? [It is for the application of rules] such as "ye passivaṇṇassa" (2.1.116), etc.

The final phoneme (*ākāra*) of a noun existing in the feminine gender is designated as *gha*. What is the purpose of this? [It is for the application of rules] such as “*ghabrahmādite*” (Pāṇini 7.3.60).
12. In addressing, *go* is designated as *si*.
In addressing, the word *go* is designated as *si*.
What is the purpose of that? [It is] "geva" (2,65), etc. (The section on) 13.
The suffixes of the optative and the specific endings.

Whatever is a qualifying term (*visesana*), the grammatical operation (*vidhi*) should be understood as applying to its final letter, as in the rule *ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe* (Pāṇini 7.3.41): *narānare*. 14. In the locative case, [the operation] belongs to the preceding [vowel].

In the description of the locative case, it should be understood that the grammatical operation applies only to what precedes: *saro lopo sare* (Pāṇini 6.1.93), as in *veḷaggaṃ*. Why does the rule *tama haṃ* not apply here? Because in that context, only a proximate substratum (*upasilesikādhāra*) is mentioned; it is stated there that "it applies only to what precedes, not to what follows."
15. Regarding the fifth [case], it belongs to another.

In the exposition of the fifth case, the grammatical operation (*kāriya*) belonging to another must be understood, as in: *ato yoṇaṃ ṭāṭe* (Pāṇini 7.1.13), as in *narānare*. Why does this not occur here in the phrase *‘jantuho anattā’*? Because of the rule of proximity (*osakkana*), a grammatical operation applies to what is immediately following and not to what is separated by an interval. 16. Regarding the first [case].

13. "Or it is reckoned as *ra*" (3.103): when a grammatical operation (*kāriya*) is prescribed for another [element], it should be understood as applying to the phoneme (*vaṇṇa*) beginning with that [element].

For example: "In the case of *rāja* before the suffix *ssi*" (2.23), as in *rājinā*. 17. "Of that which ends in the genitive": whatever grammatical operation is prescribed for what is indicated by the genitive case, it should be understood as applying to the phoneme ending in that [genitive element]. For example: "In the case of *rāja* before the suffix *ssi*" (2.23), as in *rājinā*.
18. *Ṅānubandho*.
That which has the letter *ṅ* as its *anubandha* (indicatory letter) occurs at the end [of a word], as in *gossā vaṅa* (from *go + assaṃ*) = *gavassaṃ*. 19.
Those polysyllabic [stems] that have *ṭ* as their *anubandha* undergo substitution for the whole.

That which has the letter *ṭ* as its *anubandha* is a multi-syllabic substitute for the whole [of the original element], as in the following examples: by the rule “*imassānitthiyaṃ ṭe*” (2.128), [the suffix] *ṭā* is applied; and by the rule “*nāmha-nimi*” (2.126), [the suffix] *ṭum* is applied. 20.

Those whose initial or final [consonants] have *ñ* or *ṇ* as their *anubandha* belong to the sixth case. Those whose initials or finals have *ñ* or *ṇ* as their *anubandha* apply to what is indicated by the sixth case, as in: by the rule “*brūto tissīña*” (6.36), [the suffix] *issīña* is applied after the root *brū*; and by the rule “*bhūssa vuka*” (6.17), [the suffix] *vuka* is applied after the root *bhū*, resulting in *babhūva*.
21. A consonant (*m*) followed by a vowel is a suffix (*anta*).

That which has *m* as its suffix is called a "vowel-suffix" (*sarānamantā*); when a vowel follows it, it becomes [a suffix]. For example, in the case of "mañca rudhādīnaṃ" (5-19), [the suffix *m*] appears in *rundhati*.
22. [The above rule applies] in the sense of negation (*vippaṭisedhe*).
When two disciples are mentioned together in a single context, the third person is used. For example, when two or three men set out together:
"He goes" (*so gacchati*), "you go" (*tvaṃ gacchasi*), and "you both go" (*tumhe gacchatha*). Or:
"He goes," "you go," and "I go" (*ahaṃ gacchāmi*), or "we go" (*mayaṃ gacchāma*).
23. A Conventional Term that is Not a Component is a Suffix (Saṅketo-navayavo-anubandho).
That which is a conventional term and is not a component should be known as a suffix, as in the rule: "after [roots] ending in *l* etc., when *āsi* follows" (2-57), where *kattā* is a suffix.

Why is the mention of "conventional term" (saṅketa) made? So that a collection such as *pakati* etc. does not become a suffix; for a collection is not a component... precisely because it is a composite form.

What is the purpose of including [the term] *anavayava* (without parts)? It is for the sake of [the rule]: “by that person” (*atena*). Since elision (*lopa*) is already understood by this very [term], the statement was not commenced for the sake of eliding a *anubandha* (phonetic marker).
24. *Savaṇṇa* (homogeneous) is also [included] when followed by *vaṇṇa*.

Since the word *vaṇṇa* follows, by it *savaṇṇa* is also grasped; thus the form *samāna* is [derived]. This is because it has been stated [in the rule]: “*e* and *o* [replace *i* and *u*] when *yuvaṇṇa* [vowels] are elided. (*yuvaṇṇānameo luttā* 1-29). Thus, *samāna*.
25. [The suffix] *vantu*, *mantu*, *āvantu*, and *tavantu* are related to [the suffixes] *vantu* and so forth.
Only that which is related to *vantu* and so forth is taken here; for example, in the rule "the *nto* of *nta*-suffixes when followed by *to* in the first case" (2-215), we have *guṇavanto*.
Why is it said "related to *vantu* and so forth"? [Consider: *jantū* and *tantū*.
(Paribhāsās. 26.
*Saro lopo sare*:
A vowel is to be elided when followed by a vowel. Examples: *tatrime*, *saddhindriyaṃ*, *nohetam*, *bhikkhuno vādo*, *sametāyasmā*, *abhibhāyatanaṃ*, *puttām-atthi*, *asantettha*.

27. *Paro kvaci*. Somewhere, a vowel following another vowel may be elided. As in: *so pi*, *sā va*, *yato dakaṃ*, *tato va*. Why "somewhere"? As in: *saddhindriyaṃ*. This heading [of rules] continues until the end of the section; therefore, there is no over-extension [of the rule]. 28. *Na dve vā*. [The elision does not occur] twice or optionally.
In some instances, both the preceding and following vowels are not elided, as in *latā iva*, *late-va*, and *latā-va*. 29.
When vowels are elided, the vowels *i* and *u* of the following [words] optionally become *e* and *o* respectively.

*Tasse-daṃ*, *vāte-ritaṃ*, *no-peti*, *vāmo-rū*, *ate-vaññehi*, *vo-dakaṃ*. How is it that [the sandhi] occurs in the case of *paccorasmi*? By means of the division of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*). Is it only in the case of *vā*? Yes; this applies to *tassa*.
Why [is the word] *lutta* mentioned? As in *latā iva*. 30. *Yavā sare*: [The substitution of *ya* for *ta* occurs] before a vowel.

In place of *i*-vowels and *u*-vowels, the letters *ya* and *va* optionally occur respectively before a vowel. As examples: *byākato*, *iccassa*, *ajjhiṇamutto*, *svāgataṃ*, *svāpanalānilaṃ*. Is it only in these cases? No; for example: *vātveva?* and *iti-ssa*. Is it only in certain instances? Yes; for example: *yānī-dha*, *sū-paṭṭhitaṃ*. 31. *Eonaṃ*:

In place of *e* and *o*, *ya* and *va* optionally occur respectively before a vowel. Examples: *tyajja*, *te-jja*, *svāhaṃ*, *so-haṃ*. Is it only in certain instances? Yes; for example: *puttāma-tthi*, *asante-ttha*.
32. *Gossāvaṅa*.

In the case of *go*, *avaṅ* is substituted [for the vowel]. *Gavāssaṃ*. “*Yatharīva, tatharive*” are particles; in “*bhusāmive*,” the word *iva* has the sense of *eva*. 33. *Byañjane dīgharassā*. [The substitution of] long and short vowels [occurs] before a consonant.
In certain instances, short vowels become long before consonants. In this regard, O wanderer of the sages, [the example] "mālabhārī" is indeed correct.
34. After a vowel, there are two.
In certain instances, after a vowel, a following consonant may have two forms. As in *paggaho*. Why "after a vowel"? [As in] *taṃ khaṇaṃ*.

35. In the fourth and second [vowels], for these [consonants], the third and first [vowels] [apply]. In the fourth and second [vowels], for the others [consonants], the third and first [vowels] become the third and first of their respective groups. Examples:
*paccāsatti*, *nigghoso*, *akkhanti*, *bojjhaṅgā*, *setacchattaṃ*, *daḍḍho*, *niṭṭhānaṃ*, *mahaddhano*, *yasatthero*.
*Apphuṭaṃ*, *abbhuggato*. [In these cases] what is the word *esa*? *Thero*. What is the word *esaṃ*? *Pattho*. 36. *Vitisseve vā*:
when followed by the word *eva*, *itissa* optionally becomes *vo*. *Itveva*, *icceva*. What is the word *eva*? *Iccāha*.
37. Regarding the word *vaṇṇe*.

In the word *vaṇṇe*, the suffix *a* optionally occurs after *eonaṃ*. Examples: *disvā yācaka māgate*, *akaramhasa te*, *esa attho*, *esa dhammo*, *aggamakkhāyati*, *svātanaṃ*, *hiyyattanaṃ*, *karassu*.
Is it only when expressing praise (*vātveva*)? When the beggar has arrived, this is the proper way (*eso dhammo*). Why [is it] "in the word *vaṇṇe*"? [Example: *so*.
38. *Niggahīta*.
A *niggahīta* may optionally be inserted (*āgama*) in certain instances. For example: *cakkhuṃ udapādi* becomes *cakkhuudapādi*; *purimaṃ jātiṃ* becomes *purimajātiṃ*; *kattabbaṃ kusalaṃ bahuṃ*.
In cases such as *avaṃsira*, it is obligatory; however, because the governing rule (*adhikāra*) is stated with a fixed option (*vavatthitavibhāsā*), [the insertion is not always required].
The rule of sammatthi (the elision of *m*) applies only when there is a short vowel (*rasa*); moreover, it occurs only before a short vowel, because that [elided *m*] follows a short vowel.
39. Elision (*lopa*).

There is optionally an elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra) in some instances. For example: *kyāhaṃ*, *kimahaṃ*, *sāratto*, *saṃratto*. However, in cases such as *salle kho-gantukāmo gantumano*, the elision is obligatory.

40. *Parassa*. The elision of a following *sa* may optionally occur after a nasalized vowel (*niggahīta*). Example: *tvaṃ si* becomes *tvamasi*. 41. *Vagge vagganto*. [In a consonant group, the final member of that group [is doubled].]
In the case of a *niggahīta*, when followed by a group of consonants (*vagga*), it becomes the final letter of that group according to proximity. Thus: *taṅkaroti* becomes *taṃ karoti*;
*tañcarati* becomes *taṃ carati*; *taṇṭhānaṃ* becomes *taṃ ṭhānaṃ*; *tandhanaṃ* becomes *taṃ dhanaṃ*; and *tampāti* becomes *taṃ pāti*.
Having always moved into the middle of a word, it sometimes remains even elsewhere.
42. *Ño* occurs for *ṇ*.
Indeed, when there are vowels, *ñ* is substituted for the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). Is it *yaññadeva*, *taññeva*, *tañhi*, or *vātveva*?
It is *yaṃ yadeva*. 43. *Ye* occurs for *saṃ*.
The *niggahīta* (anusvāra) that follows a consonant optionally becomes *ña* before the letter *ya*. For example: *saññamo* or *saṃyamo*. 44.
*Maya* [is substituted] for a vowel.

In some instances, *maya* is optionally substituted for *niggahīta* before a vowel. For example: *tamahaṃ*, *tayidaṃ*, *tadalaṃ*. Is it not also the case that the option applies? For example: *taṃ ahaṃ*.
45. *Vanataragā* and *cāgamā*.
These are also *mayadā* and *āgamā* [sandhi rules] occurring before a vowel (*sare*) or sometimes elsewhere.
*Tivaṅgikaṃ*, *ito nāyati*, *cinitvā*, *tasmātiha*, *nirojaṃ*, *puthageva*, *idhamāhu*, *yathayidaṃ*, *attadatthaṃ*. Or rather, *vā tveva*: *attatthaṃ*. "It is too early" (*atippago*).
*Kho tāvā* means "firstly. 46. *Chā ḷo*:
After the word *cha*, the letter *ḷ* optionally becomes an augment (*āgama*) for the following vowel. Examples: *chaḷaṅgaṃ*, *chaḷāyatanaṃ*. Is it only in these cases? No; for example: *chaabhiññā*.
47. *Tadaminādīni*. Words such as *tadaminā* are correct. *Taṃ iminā* becomes *tadaminā*; *sakiṃ āgāmī* becomes *sakadāgāmī*; *ekaṃ idha ahaṃ* becomes *ekamidāhaṃ*;
*saṃvidhāya avahāro* becomes *saṃvidāvahāro*; *vārino vāhako* becomes *valāhako*; [and so on] for *jīvanassa*.
*Jīmūta* is derived from *mūta*; *susāna* is the resting place (*sayana*) of the skin (*chavi*); *udukkhala* is that which is above (*uddhaṃ*) the sky (*kha*);

*pisāca* is one who eats what is crushed (*pisita*); *mayūra* is that which cries out on the earth (*mahiyam*). In this way, other words should also be understood through their application (*payoga*), just as *pisodara* and others are seen among outsiders.
48. For the groups *tavagga*, *varaṇa*, and *na*, there are the groups *cavagga*, *bayañña*.

In certain instances, when followed by the letter *y*, the *tavagga* (dental) and *vaggalasa* (guttural and labial nasals) are respectively replaced by the *cavagga* (palatal) and *bayañña* (labial) sounds. As in: *apuccaṇḍatāya*, *tacchaṃ*, *yajjevaṃ*, *ajjhattaṃ*, *thaññaṃ*, *dibbaṃ*, *payyosanā*, *pokkharañño*.
Is it only in some cases?
Yes. Rule 49: *Vaggalasehi te*. Following *vaggalasa* sounds, the *y* sound of a subsequent word is sometimes replaced by those same *vaggalasa* sounds.
*Sakkate*, *paccate*, *aṭṭate*, *kuppate*, *phallate*, *assate*. In some cases only? *Kyāhaṃ*. 50.
The substitution for *has*.
The substitution for *has* occurs before the letter *ya*. *Guyhaṃ*.
51. Or there is a substitution of *v* for *h*. Thus, *bahv-ābādho* becomes *bavh-ābādho*. 52.
Likewise, for the vowels *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, and *ḷ*, [the following consonants are substituted]: *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ṇa*, and *la*.

For *tatha* sounds, *ṭa*, *ṭha*, *ṇa*, and *la* may occur. Examples: *dukkaṭaṃ*, *aṭṭhakathā*, *gahaṇaṃ*, *paligho*, *palāyati*. Is it only after *vā*? *dukkataṃ*. Is it only in certain cases? *sugato*. 53.
Elision of the first member of a conjunct (*saṃyoga*).
There is optionally, in some instances, elision of that constituent which is the first member of a conjunct consonant cluster. Examples: *pupphaṃ*, *sā*, *jāyate*, *gini*.
54. Two [types of] repetition (*vīpsā*).

In the case of repetition (*vīpsā*) and non-repetition (*abhīpsā*), there are two forms for that which occurs. Repetition (*vīpsā*) is the desire to pervade a meaning that is differentiated by action (*kriyā*), quality (*guṇa*), or substance (*dravya*).
Examples: "He waters tree after tree" (*rukkhaṃ rukkhaṃ siñcati*); "Every village is delightful" (*gāmo gāmo ramaṇīyo*).
In every village there is water; in every house there is a master; he eats flavor after flavor; he undertakes action after action.
Indeed, even in a sequence (*ānupubbī*), there is a diversity: it is thick at the root, root after root, and fine at the tip, tip after tip.
For if there were no distinction between root and tip here, there would be no sequence either. [I shall give] to you, sirs, a penny after penny from this kahāpaṇa coin.

From the expression "give two māṣakas," the distributive suffix *vicchā* is understood as "one māṣaka and one māṣaka"; however, from another word, there is a restriction [to a specific unit], such as "this kahāpaṇa.
In the cases "they bloom one by one" (*pubbaṃ pubbaṃ*) and "they ripen one by one" (*paṭhamaṃ paṭhamaṃ*), the distributive suffix is likewise present.

In the case of "these two are wealthy; which of these two is wealthy? (*ime ubho aḍḍhā katarā katarā eṣaṃ dvinnamaḍḍhatā*), it refers to the wealthiness of these two. In the case of "all these are wealthy; which of these is wealthy? (*sabbe ime aḍḍhā katamā katamā imesaṃ*), [it refers to the wealthiness of] these.
The suffixes *aḍ* and *uta* are also elided here [after a prefix]. [Examples: *ābhikkhaṇṇaṃ*, *ponopuññaṃ*; *pacati pacati*, *papacati papacati*;
*lunāhi lunāhi*—thus he cuts; *bhutvā bhutvā gacchati*; *paṭapaṭā karoti*, *paṭapaṭāyati*. 55.
There is the elision of the first [element] when followed by a single consonant.

In the case of *vicchāya* (repetition for emphasis), there is the elision of the suffixes beginning with *si* (the nominative) after the first member. [This applies] to each individual instance. How is it that we have *matthakamatthakena*? It is due to the analysis of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) stating “there is elision of the suffixes beginning with *si* after the first member.

Because of this analysis of the rule, there is no over-extension (*atippasaṅga*), and the desired result is established. 56. **Of the words beginning with *sabba*, when used in the sense of reciprocity.** When words beginning with *sabba* are used in the sense of reciprocity, they take the dual number, and there is also the elision of the suffixes beginning with *si* after the first member. Examples: *aññamaññassa bhojakā* (reciprocal givers), *itarītarassa bhojakā* (reciprocal givers).
57. *Yāvabodhaṃ sambhame*.
In a state of agitation (*sambhama*), there is an urgent proclamation of words that serve as a cause for alarm;
when such a situation exists, as many sounds as are necessary for the intended meaning to be understood are employed. "Snake! Snake! Snake! "Wake up! Wake up! Wake up!"
"The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split! The Saṅgha of bhikkhus is split!

(58). [The word] *bahulaṃ* (frequently) serves as a heading (*adhikāra*) up to the completion of the section on "seated" (*āsatta*). By means of this, there is no over-extension (*atippasaṅga*), and what is intended is successfully established.
Thus ends the first section in the Vutti on the Moggallāna grammar. 2.
The second section (beginning with *si*, etc.).

1. From a noun (*nāma*), when it occurs in both singular and plural senses, there are two forms each for the following endings: *si*, *yo*, *nā*, *hi*, *sa*, *naṃ*, *smā*, *hi*, *sa*, *naṃ*, *smiṃ*, and *su*.

These occur in pairs because they function in both singular and plural meanings. Examples: Singular: *muni* (sage), *munayo* (sages); *muniṃ* (sage), *munayo* (sages); *muninā* (by the sage), *munīhi* (by the sages);

*munissa* (of the sage), *munīnaṃ* (of the sages); *munismā* (from the sage), *munīhi* (from the sages); *munissa* (to the sage), *munīnaṃ* (to the sages); *munismiṃ* (in the sage), *munīsu* (in the sages).
In this way, *kumārī* [is used for] girls, and *kaññā* for maidens. These seven pairs constitute the seven case endings (*vibhattiyo*), based on the principle that "division is *vibhatti*.
Here, the letters *si*, *am*, *itī*, *kā*, and *rā* are conventional symbols (*saṅketa*) for the purpose of indicating the endings, according to the rule "What is the meaning of *si-su*? (2,200). 2.
The second case is used for the object (*kamma*).

That which is performed (*karīyati*) by means of being connected with the action of an agent (*kattu-kiriyāya-abhisambandhīyati*) is called the object (*kamma*); the second case ending (*dutiyāvibhatti*) occurs in relation to that. For example: *kaṭaṃ karoti* (he makes a mat), *odanaṃ pacati* (he cooks rice), *ādiccaṃ passati* (he sees the sun).
In the expression *odano paccati* (rice is cooked), the status of being an object is not understood from the word *odana*; rather, it is understood from the verb (*ākhyātato*).

In the sense of “he makes a large, beautiful mat,” there is indeed the status of being an object for that which is endowed with qualities (*guṇayuttassa*). Furthermore, even in the case of what is desired (*icchita*), the second case is used precisely because of its status as an object.

"The Siddhas milk the cow," "He asks for a cow that has many calves," "He obtains a cow as a prize," "He asks the boy the way," "He begs for a cow that has many calves," "He gathers fruits from the tree," "He teaches the Dhamma to the pupil," "He instructs the pupil in the Dhamma.
Thus, even when not desired [as the object], one "leaps over a snake" or "consumes poison."

Even in cases where [the action] is neither desired nor undesired, the second case (accusative) is established there as well. For example: "While going to the village, he approaches the foot of a tree";

"he will lie upon the earth"; "he stands over the village"; "he sits upon the tree. In the usage of the prefixes *adhi*, *si*, *ti*, *tha*, and *āsa*, the object is intended as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*);
for grammatical factors (*kāraka*) arise from the speaker's intention. This is just as in the expression: "The lightning flashes from the cloud" (*valāhakā vijjotate*). From the cloud...
"It flashes," "the cloud flashes," "it flashes in the cloud," or "it flashes by means of the cloud.
One who is thus intent either intends toward a phenomenon (*dhamma*) or [intends] within phenomena.
Likewise, regarding the expressions for dwelling near, living with, eating, and departing: "he dwells near the village," "he lives with me."
"He dwells on the mountain" (*pabbatam adhivasati*), "he dwells in the house" (*gharam āvasati*). What is the example for the word expressing the cessation of eating (*abhojana-nivutti*)?

"He fasts in the village" (*gāme upavasati*); the meaning is that he performs the cessation of eating. Even in the case of the manner of drinking (*tappāna-ācāra*), the accusative may occur because it is an object:

"he drinks from the river" (*nadiṃ pivati*), "he wanders through the village" (*gāmaṃ carati*); likewise in such cases as "if he will address me" (*sace maṃ ālapissati*). The accusative is indeed prescribed in connection with a particle (*pati-dhā-yoge*).
"May the factors of enlightenment (bojjhaṅgā) occur to you, Cunda. The meaning is: "May the factors of enlightenment speak to you. When *pati* is joined with a noun, it expresses a relationship;
thus, due to that connection, the genitive case is used for the relation, as in "it does not occur to him" (*tassa na paṭibhāti*).

Regarding "he plays with dice" (*akkhe dibbati*), "he plays with dice" (*akkhehi dibbati*), or "he plays in the dice" (*akkhesu dibbati*), there is a desire to express the object, the instrument, or the locus.
3. *Kāladdhānamaccantasaṃyoge*.
Absolute connection (*accantasaṃyoga*) is the complete relationship of time (*kāla*) or distance (*addhāna*) with an action (*kiriyā*), a quality (*guṇa*), or a substance (*dabba*).

When such [connection] is understood, the second case ending occurs after words for time and words for distance. Examples: *māsam adhīte* (he studies for a month), *māsaṃ kalyāṇī* (she is beautiful for a month), *māsaṃ guḷadhānā* (jaggery-rice for a month).

He studies for a *kosa*; the crooked river [flows] for a *kosa*; the mountain [extends] for a *kosa*. Why say "in absolute connection" (*accantasamyoga*)? [Consider: "He studies for two days of the month";
"the mountain is in one part of the *kosa*.

In such cases as "having dressed at the time of forenoon" (*pubbaṇhasamayaṃ nivāsetvā*), "at one time the Blessed One," or "this night the four Great Kings," the accusative case is established simply because of absolute connection with the expression of time. Alternatively, it is due to the frequent application of a change in case endings (*vibhattivipallāsa*).

In the attainment of a result (*phalappatti*), there is the completion of an action (*kriyāparisamatti*). When that [completion] is understood, the third case (*tatiyā*) is intended for time (*kāla*) and distance (*addhāna*) when they are in absolute conjunction with the action (*accantasamyoga*), such as:
“The lesson was learned in a month” (*māsena anuvāko adhīto*) or “The lesson was learned in a *kosa*. This too is established simply by virtue of being an instrument (*karaṇa*).

However, where there is no attainment of a result, because the status of being the most effective means (*asādhakatama*)—that is, the status of being an instrument—is absent, only the second case (*dutiyā*) applies, as in: “He has studied the lesson for a month” (*māsam adhīto anuvāko*) or “He has not grasped it even after a month.”

Among the grammatical factors (*kāraka*), those which denote time or distance are intended to take the seventh and fifth case endings— as in “Having eaten today, Devadatta will eat in two days” (*ajja bhutvā devadatto dvihe bhuñjissati*), “He will eat after two days” (*dvīhā bhuñjissati*),
“The archer here pierces the target from the treasury” (*atraṭṭho-yamissāso kose lakkhaṃ vijjhati*), or “From the treasury he pierces the target” (*kosā lakkhaṃ vijjhati*). Thus,
these are established solely according to the speaker’s desire for the expression of their respective grammatical factors.

4. In the case of verbs signifying motion (*gati*), cognition (*bodha*), eating (*āhāra*), sound (*sadda*), those that are intransitive (*akammaka*), and [verbs] such as *bhajja*, the second case ending is used for the agent when they are employed causatively (*payojje*).
By virtue of the capacity [of the construction], it is understood that through the activity of the instigator (*payojaka-vyāpāra*), the status of an object (*kamma-tā*) accrues to this [agent].
He causes the boy to go to the village; he causes the boy to traverse the village; he causes the boy to understand the Dhamma;
he causes the boy to experience the Dhamma; he causes the boy to eat the sweetmeat; he causes the boy to lie down; he causes the boy to study the Veda;
he causes the boy to recite the Veda; he causes Devadatta to lie down; he causes [him] to taste.
He causes Devadatta to cook, to fry another, to pound another, or to spread out another. What is meant by "by these very [agents]"?
Yaññadatta causes Devadatta to cook rice. What is meant by "he employs"? Devadatta goes.
But when Yaññadatta causes Devadatta to go, and another person employs him (Yaññadatta), then it is expressed as: "Yaññadatta causes Devadatta to go."
It must be [understood as] *bhavitabbaṃ* ... because it has the sense of causing to go (*gamayati*).

5. Or, in the case of *hara*-type verbs: after the causative forms of *hara*-type verbs, the second case ending optionally occurs for the agent (*kattari*). For example: *hāreti bhāraṃ devadattaṃ* or *devadattena*.
Or, one consumes barley meal [thinking], "Devadatta [consumes it] by means of Devadatta"; or one has a mat made [thinking], "Devadatta [has it made] by means of Devadatta";
or one causes people to see a king [thinking], "the king [is seen] by means of the people"; or one pays homage to a teacher [thinking], "Devadatta [pays homage] to the teacher by means of Devadatta.
6. Not [in the case] of eating and so forth.
The second case ending does not occur for the agent when used with the verbs *khāda* (to eat), etc. He causes Devadatta to eat; he causes Devadatta to take; he calls, he causes Devadatta to call;
he makes Devadatta sound; he makes Devadatta cry; he causes Devadatta to lead. (1) With the verb *vaha* (to carry), [the second case is not used] when the agent is not a driver.
He causes Devadatta to carry the load—why say "when the agent is not a driver"? He causes the oxen to carry the load.

(2) *Bhakkhissāmi sāyam* (I shall eat in the evening). *Modake bhakkhayati devadattena* (He eats the sweetmeats by means of Devadatta). Why [is it] "for non-injury"? *Balīvadde bhakkhayati sassam* (He feeds the crop to the oxen).

7. Joined with *jhā* and so forth. When joined with *dhī* and so forth, the second case ending occurs. *Dhiratthu maṃ pūtikāyaṃ*, *antarā ca Rājagahaṃ antarā ca Nālandaṃ*, *samādhānam antarena*, *mucalindaṃ abhito saraṃ*, and so forth; this is an exception to the sixth case.

8. *Abhi* is used with the second case (*dvitīyā*) when it signifies characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*), and so forth. When joined with words meaning "characteristics" and the like, the second case ending is employed after [the noun]. Examples: "The lightning flashes toward the tree" (*rukkham abhi vijjotate vijju*); "Devadatta is kind toward his mother" (*sādhu devadatto mātaram abhi*); "He stands facing each tree" (*rukkhaṃ rukkham abhi tiṭṭhati*). 9. *Paṭi* and *pari* are used in the sense of "division" (*bhāga*) as well. When joined with these two, the second case is also employed. Examples: "He shares the food with the teacher" (*ācariyaṃ paṭi bhattaṃ deti*); "He distributes the wealth among the relatives" (*ñātike pari dhanaṃ deti*). When used in the sense of "repetition" (*āvutti*), they take the third case (*tatiyā*). Example: "He studies verse by verse" (*gāthaṃ gāthaṃ paṭi adhīte*). When used in the sense of "distribution" (*vikappana*), they take the fourth case (*catutthī*). Example: "He gives the almsfood to the teacher" (*ācariyassa paṭi bhattaṃ deti*). When used in the sense of "surpassing" (*adhika*), they take the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*). Example: "The ocean surpasses all rivers" (*nadiyo pari samuddo*). When used in the sense of "exclusion" (*apanayana*), they take the seventh case (*sattamī*). Example: "He excludes Devadatta from the assembly" (*devadattaṃ pari parisāya ṭhapeti*). When used in the sense of "repetition," they take the accusative (*accanta*) and the locative (*okāsa*). Example: "He studies verse by verse" (*gāthaṃ gāthaṃ paṭi adhīte*). When used in the sense of "distribution," they take the accusative. Example: "He distributes the almsfood to the teacher" (*ācariyaṃ paṭi bhattaṃ deti*). The second case ending occurs after words joined with *pati*, *pari*, *ā*, and *lakkhaṇa* (and others) when expressing the sense of "towards" (*bhāge catthe*). Examples: *Rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate vijjū* — The lightning flashes towards the tree.

*Anu*: When joined with *anu* in the sense of characteristics (*lakkhaṇa*) and so forth, the second case ending occurs after the word. Lightning flashes following the tree; following the act of truth (*saccakiriya*).
Rain fell; "hetu" (cause) and "lakkhaṇa" (characteristic) occur [with this particle]; "it is well that Devadatta followed his mother"; "he stands tree after tree";

When joined with *anu* in the sense of "nearby," the second case ending occurs. Example: *pabbatamanu senā tiṭṭhati* ("The army stands near the mountain").

12. In the sense of inferiority (*hīna*). When joined with *anu* in the sense of inferiority, the second case ending occurs. Example: *anu sāriputtaṃ paññavanto* ("Those possessing wisdom are inferior to Sāriputta").
13. *Upena*.

When joined with *upa* in the sense of inferiority (*hīnattha*), the second case ending occurs. Example: *upa sāriputtaṃ paññavanto* (inferior to Sāriputta in wisdom). 14. *Sattamyādhikye*. [The seventh case ending occurs when joined with *upa*] in the sense of superiority (*adhikya*).
The seventh case ending occurs after a word joined with *upa* in the sense of superiority. *Upa khāriyaṃ doṇo* ("A *doṇa* measure is superior to a *khārī*").
15. *Sāmitte-dhinā*:

The seventh case ending occurs after a word joined with *adhi* in the sense of ownership (*sāmibhāva*). *Adhi brahmadatte pañcālā* ("The Pañcālas belong to Brahmadatta"), *adhi pañcālesu brahmadatto* ("Brahmadatta belongs to the Pañcālas").
16. The third case ending occurs for the agent and the instrument.

The third case ending is used for the agent (*kattar*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*) among the grammatical factors (*kāraka*). Examples: "done by a man" (*purisena kataṃ*); "he cuts with a sword" (*asinā chindati*). [Examples of other uses:

The third case ending occurs precisely when [the word] denotes the instrument (*karaṇa*). Thus: "He runs on even ground," "He runs on uneven ground," "He buys grain for two *doṇas*," "He buys livestock for five.
17. With the hand (*sahatthena*).

The third case ending may occur after the word *saha* when it signifies "together with" (*yoge*). For example: *puttena saha gato* ("he went together with his son"), *puttena saddhiṃ āgato* ("he came together with his son").

The third case, like the sixth, occurs only when the term is subordinate (*appadhāne*). 18. Regarding the characteristic (*lakkhaṇe*): The third case ending may occur after a word expressing a characteristic. For example: *tidaṇḍakena paribbājakaṃ addakkhi* ("he saw the wandering ascetic by means of his triple staff"), *akkhinā kāṇo* ("blind in one eye"). 19. In the sense of "on account of" (*hetumhi*). The third case ending may be used for words suitable for reasoning (*takkiriyā*). Examples: *annena vasati* (he lives on account of food), *vijjāya yaso* (fame on account of knowledge).
20. Or the fifth case ending [may be used] in the sense of "on account of" (*ṇe*).
The fifth case ending optionally occurs after a word expressing a cause (hetu). For example: *satasmā baddho* or *satena baddho* (“bound because of a stake”). 21. *Guṇe*:

The fifth case ending optionally occurs after a word expressing a cause that functions as a subordinate factor (*paraṅga*). For example: *jaḷattā baddho* or *jaḷattena baddho* (“bound because of stupidity”), *paññāya mutto* (“released by means of wisdom”), *hutvā abhāvato aniccā* (“impermanent because of the non-existence of having been”), and *saṅkhāranirodhā viññāṇanirodho* (“with the cessation of volitional formations, there is the cessation of consciousness”).

22. The sixth case ending occurs after words expressing the sense of cause (*hetvattha*) when used in connection with [a word] signifying a cause. For example: *udarassa hetu*, *udarassa kāraṇā* (for the sake of the stomach).
23. After the group beginning with *sabba*, all case endings may occur.
When joined with words expressing the sense of cause (*hetvattha*), all case endings are used after the pronouns *sabba* and its synonyms.
For example: *ko hetu*, *kaṃ hetuṃ*, *kena hetunā*, *kassa hetussa*, *kasmā hetusmā*, *kassa hetussa*, *kasmiṃ hetusmiṃ*; *kiṃ kāraṇaṃ*, *kena kāraṇena*; *kiṃ nimittaṃ*, *kena nimittena*;

24. The fourth [case] is used for the recipient (sampadāna).

The fourth case may be used for that person to whom something is properly given. For example: *saṅghassa dadāti* ("He gives to the Saṅgha"). When expressing exclusion, the fifth case ending occurs in connection with *apa* and *pari*. For example: *apa sālāya āyanti vāṇijā* (the merchants come from outside the hall), *pari sālāya* (from around the hall).

28. In the case of *paṭinidhi* (substitute) and *paṭidāna* (giving back), [the suffix] *pati* [is used].
When *pati* is employed in the sense of a substitute or in the act of giving back, the fifth case ending occurs after a noun. For example:

*buddhassa pati sāriputto* ("Sāriputta is a substitute for the Buddha"), *ghataṃ assa tesaṃ pati dadāti* ("he gives a jar back to them"). Why say "in the case of substitute and giving back"? [Consider: *rukkhaṃ pati vijjotate* ("it flashes toward the tree").
29. *Rite* and *dutiya*.
When used in conjunction with the word *rite*, the second case (*dutiya*) and the fifth case (*pañcamī*) occur after a noun. Example: *rite saddhammaṃ*, *rite saddhammā*.
30. *Vinā* and *aññatra* [take] the third case as well.

In connection with *vinā* and *aññatra*, the third, second, and fifth case endings occur after a noun. *Vinā vātena*, *vinā vātaṃ*, *vinā vātasmā*; *aññatra ekena piṇḍapātanīhārakena*, *aññatra dhammaṃ*, *aññatra dhammā*.
31. With *putha* and *nānā*:
in connection with these, the third and fifth case endings occur. *Puthageva janena*, *puthageva janasmā*; *janena nānā*, *janasmā nānā*.
32. The Seventh Case in the Locative (Sattamī).
When there is a support for action—that is, a locus which supports the agent or the object—then the seventh case suffix occurs after a noun in that grammatical relation (kāraka). Examples:
*kaṭe nisīdati* (Devadatta sits on a mat), *thāliyaṃ odanaṃ pacati* (he cooks rice in a pot), *ākāse sakunā* (birds in the sky), *bhillesu*.

When the state of one thing serves as the characteristic of another state, the seventh case ending occurs.

36. [The locative is used] for specification (*niddhāraṇa*).

37. In the sense of the nominative alone:

when there is merely the name—that is, the thing to be designated—the first case ending occurs. For example, *rukkho* (tree). Gender (*liṅga*) also [functions as a factor], namely: feminine, masculine, and neuter.

When used in connection with the sense of equality, the sixth case ending may occur, or the third case ending; for example: *tulyo pitu*, *tulyo pitarā* (equal to the father), *sadiso pitu*, *sadiso pitarā* (similar to the father).
Why is the third case ending not used here in the following examples: *ajjunassa tulā natthi* (there is no equal to Arjuna) and *kesavassupamā na ca* (and there is no likeness to Keśava)?

The suffixes *net* and *tulya* do not have the same meaning; rather, *tulya* has the sense of comparison (*aupamya*). 41. *Ato yonaṃ ṭāṭe*: After a noun ending in the vowel *a*, the suffixes *ṭā* and *ṭe* occur respectively.

The letter *ṭ* serves as a marker for all case endings (*sabbadesattha*). Examples: *buddhā*, *buddhe*. Why [is the rule] "after *a*" (*ato*) stated? [To exclude cases like] *kaññāyo*, *itthiyo*, *vadhuyo*. Why does it not apply here in the case of *aggayo*? Because of the power of the specific grammatical formulation (*avidhāna-sāmatthiyā*).
42. *Ninam* or *Ṭā-ṭe*.

After a noun ending in *a*, *ninam* or *ṭā-ṭe* are substituted respectively [for the case endings *bhyām* and *bhis*]. Thus: *rūpā*, *rūpe*, *rūpāni*; and likewise *atoti* [for the neuter plural], as in *aṭṭhīni*. 43. *Smā-smim-nam*. [The suffixes *smā*, *smim*, and *nam* are substituted for the case endings *bhyas*, *bhyaḥ*, and *su* respectively.]

After a noun ending in short *a*, the suffixes *smā* and *smin* become respectively *ṭā* and *ṭe*. Thus: *buddhā*, *buddhasmā*; *buddhe*, *buddhasmiṃ*. Likewise, after [the word] *aggi*: *aggismā*, *aggismiṃ*. 44.
For the dative case, *āyo* optionally replaces *sassa*.

After [a noun] ending in short *a*, *āyo* optionally occurs in place of the dative suffix *sassa*. Thus: *buddhāya*, *buddhassa*. Furthermore, this *āyo* occurs only when expressing identity (*tādatthye*).

It is declined; in some places it is otherwise, such as *atoti eva isissa*. Why [is the word] "fourth case" (*catutthiyā*) mentioned? [In the example] *buddhassa mukhaṃ*, there is a compound with the word *attha* in *attatthaṃ*.

Even from the group beginning with *sabba*, the forms *smā*, *smiṃ*, and *sānaṃ* indeed become *ṭā*, *ṭe*, and *āya*... because this is accepted by the authors of grammatical treatises (*niruttikārā*) and is seen in the Buddha’s word (*buddhavacana*).

And in this regard, there is this example: "From this world and from the next, the man falls away from both," "I am arrogant regarding these mantras," and "For whatever purpose you have come, upon that very matter you should carefully attend.
45. As in the case of the rivers in the *Ghapateka* [Sutta].

In the singular of feminine nouns ending in *gha* or *pa*, the suffix *nādī* is applied according to the sequence [of the following words]: *kaññāya*, *rattiyā*, *itthiyā*, *dhenuyā*, *vadhuyā*. What is the purpose of saying "in the singular"? [To exclude the plural: *kaññāhi*, *rattīhi*. 46. *Ssā vā tetimāmūhi*:
After feminine nouns marked by the technical term *gha* or *pa*, the suffix *ssā* optionally occurs in the singular. [Examples: *tassā kataṃ*, *tassā dīyate*, *tassā...*

*Nissaṭaṃ*, *tassā pariggaho*, *tassā patiṭṭhitaṃ*, or *tāya vā*. Thus, for this [word], by this [instrumental], of this [genitive], with this [instrumental], or of that [genitive], with that [instrumental]—what is the example?
*Sabbāya* (of all). Is it only for rivers? *Sā* (she), only for a householder? *Tāhi amūhi* (by those women). 47.
After the twelve [words] ending in *-naṃ*, there is the suffix *-nuka* for seventeen [words].

The substitution of *nu* occurs for the numbers from twelve (*dvādīnaṃ*) up to seventeen (*sattarasannaṃ*) when followed by a case-ending (*naṃmhi*). [Examples: *dvinnaṃ*, *catunnaṃ*, *pañcannaṃ*, and so on up to *aṭṭhārasannaṃ*.

The letter *u* is for the sake of pronunciation (*uccāraṇattha*), and the letter *k* is for the sake of indicating the end of the word (*antāvayavattha*); therefore, there is no long vowel before the case-ending.
48. *Basukatinnaṃ*.
In place of *naṃ* [the suffix] following a word ending in *bahu*, *kata*, or *kati*, there occurs [the substitution of] *ṇṇaṃ* or *ṇṇannaṃ*.
49. *Ṇṇaṃ-ṇṇannaṃ* [is substituted] for *ti* when followed by *jhā*.

The term *jha* is a designation for the case-ending *naṃ* following the word *ti*; in its place, *ṇṇaṃ* or *ṇṇannaṃ* occurs. Examples: *tiṇṇaṃ*, *tiṇṇannaṃ*. Why "when followed by *jhā*"? [Because in] *tissannaṃ*, [the substitution does not occur].
50. *Ubhinnaṃ*.
The suffix *inaṃ* is substituted for the word *ubho*, [forming] *ubhinnaṃ*. 51.
*Suña sassa*. [The suffix *sassa* is substituted for the word *suṇa*.]

The form *nāmasmā* does not become *suñña* (empty/omitted) for the Buddha; although this could have been established by reading "dvisakāra" (two *s*-sounds), this [separate rule] is for the sake of brevity.
In the case of *ssaṃ*, *ssā*, and *ssā*, the substitute *kaññe* occurs before *abhi* and *māna*.
In the case of *ssam* and so forth, the substitute *itarādīnam* occurs for *itara* and so forth: *itarissaṃ*, *itarissā*, *ekissaṃ*, *ekissā*, *aññissaṃ*, *aññissā*.
*etissaṃ*, *etissā*, *etissāya*, *imissaṃ*, *imissā*, *imissāya*, *esvīti*—what [is the purpose]? *Itarāya*.
*Esantīti*—what [is the purpose]? *Sabbassaṃ*, *sabbassā*. 53. *Tāya vā*.
In the case of *sā* and so forth, does it become *tassā*, *tissaṃ*, *tissā*, *tassā*, *tissāya*, or *tassāya*—and likewise *ssaṃ*, *ssā*, *ssāyo*, and *ssāyesu*?
It becomes *tāya*. 54. After *ta*, *ti*, *mā*, and *imā*, the suffix *sassa* optionally becomes *ssāyo*. Thus: *tassāya* or *tāya*; *etissāya* or *etāya*; *imissāya* or *imāya*.
55. *Ratyādīhi ṭo smino*. After *rati* and other such words, *ṭo* optionally replaces *smin*.
[Examples: *ratte* (in pleasure), *rattiyaṃ*; *āde* (at the beginning), *ādismiṃ*. 56. *Suhisubhasso*. [The suffixes] *su*, *hi*, and *su* become *bha*.
*Ubho* becomes *suhi* before *sva*. [The forms] *ubhosu*, *ubhohi* [are derived from *ubha*].
57. *Ltuppitādinamā simhi*:

For those ending in the *ltu* suffixes and for *pitā* and the others, *ā* is substituted before the nominative (*si*) case ending. [Examples: *kattā*, *pitā*; *pitu*, *mātu*, *bhāvu*, *mītu*, *duhitu*, *jāmātu*, *nattu*, *hotu*, *potu*.
58. After *ge* and *ā*, [the forms] *a* and *ca* occur for words such as *ltu-pitā*; for example: *bho katta*, *bho kattā*, *bho pita*, *bho pitā*. 59.
Optionally, there is a long vowel for *ayu* and *naṃ*.
A, i, or u at the end of these [words] becomes long when followed by *ge* in all three genders. *Bho purisā*, *bho purisa*, *bho aggī*, *bho aggi*, *bho bhikkhū*, *bho bhikkhū*.
60. *Ghabrahmādite*:
After *gha* and after *brahma* etc., there is optionally *ga* before *e*. *Bhoti kaññe*, *bhoti kaññā*; *bho brahme*, *bho brahma*.
O khatte, O khatta; O ise, O isi; O sakhe, O sakha. The forms *sakhi* and *sakhī* are already established for the feminine.
This is an *ākṛtigaṇa* (an open class); thus it is also elsewhere. 61. [The suffix] after words beginning with *nam*.
The [particle] *ge* does not occur after *ammā* and so forth. [Examples: *bhoti ammā*, *bhoti annā*, *bhoti ambā*. 62. *Rasso vā*:
After *ammā* and so forth, the [final vowel] becomes short (*rassa*) optionally before *ge*. [Examples: *bhoti amma*, *bhoti ammā*.
63. *Gho* becomes short (*rassa*) before *ssam*, etc.
[That is,] in *tassam*, *tassā*, *tassāya*, *taṃ*, *sabhātiṃ*. Why say "before these"? [Because it does not apply] in *tāya* or *sabhāya*.
64. In the singular, [the suffixes] *-yosva-* become *-ghonaṃ*.
In the singular and in the *yosu* (locative plural), for nouns ending in vowels other than *gha* and *o*, the vowel becomes short in all three genders.
Examples: *itthim*, *itthiyā*, *itthiyo*; *vadhun*, *vadhuyā*, *vadhuyo*; *daṇḍin*, *daṇḍinā*, *daṇḍino*; *sayambhun*, *sayambhunā*, *sayambhuvo*.
Why does [the rule] say "other than *gha*"? [Consider: *kaññāya*, *kaññāyo*. The mention of *ogha* is for the sake of subsequent purposes.
65. *Ge* or *vā*:

After [a word ending in] *aghon*, the vowel becomes short before a consonant (*ge*) in all three genders: *itthi*, *itthī*; *vadhu*, *vadhū*; *daṇḍi*, *daṇḍī*; *sayambhu*, *sayambhū*. Only after [a word ending in] *aghon*? *Bhoti kaññā*, *bho go*. 66.
Before the suffix *si*, [the vowel becomes short] except in the neuter.

In the nominative singular (*sismiṃ*), the short vowel does not occur for a noun that is not neuter. For example: *itthī* (woman), *daṇḍī* (staff-bearer), *vadhū* (bride), *sayambhū* (self-existent). Why "in the nominative singular"? [Consider: *itthiṃ* (accusative singular). Why "not neuter"? [Consider: *daṇḍi kulaṃ* (the staff-bearing family). 67.

In the case of the word *go* (cow), when excluding the nominative plural (*sihi*) and the accusative singular (*naṃ*), there are the forms *gāva* and *gava*. In case-endings other than the nominative plural and the accusative singular, the word *go* becomes *gāva* or *gava*. (Examples: *gāvaṃ*, *gavaṃ*; *gāvo*, *gavo*.
*gāvena*, *gavena*, *gāvassa*, *gavassa*, *gāvasmā*, *gavasmā*, *gāve*, *gave*. Why [is it said] "except in the case of *bho* and *go*"?
[Examples: *bho go*, *go tiṭṭhati*, *gohi*, *gonaṃ*. 68.
Optionally before the suffix *su*.
The word *go* becomes *gāvagava* optionally. [Examples: *gāvesu*, *gavesu*, *gosu*.
69. *Gavaṃ sena*:
after *go*, the form *gavaṃ* optionally occurs before the suffix *se*. [Examples: *gavaṃ*, *gāvassa*, *gavassa*.
70. And for *go* [cow], *gunnaṃ*.
Together with the word *naṃ*, for *go*, there is *gunnaṃ* or *gavaṃ*. [Examples: *gunnaṃ*, *gavaṃ*, *gonaṃ*.
71. For *nā* [she], *assā*.
In place of *go*, *ā* optionally occurs [before the nominative singular ending]. Thus: *gāvā*, *gavā*, *gāvena*, *gavena*.
72. *Gāvumhi*:

In the case of the accusative singular (*am*-vacana), *gossa* becomes *gāvha* optionally. Thus: *vāvhaṃ*, *gāvaṃ*, *gavaṃ*. The substitution of *goṇa* for *go* was not made here because it would result in a different word-form (*saddantara*).
73. After the word *pasaññī*, there is either *yaṃ* or *aṃ* for the word *itthi*. [The forms are] *itthiyaṃ* and *itthiṃ*. Why say *pīta*? [Counter-examples: *daṇḍiṃ*, *rattiṃ*. 74.
After the word *jhī*, there is *naṃ*.

After a word ending in *jh*, the suffixes *naṃ* or *aṃ* may optionally replace *am*. Thus: *daṇḍinaṃ* or *daṇḍiṃ*. How is it that [the form] “*buddhaṃ ādiccabandhunam*” occurs? It is due to the resolution of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāvā*).

What is the purpose of specifying *jh*? [To exclude: *itthiṃ*. What is the purpose of specifying *ī*? [To exclude: *aggiṃ*. 75. *Yonaṃ none pume*: After a word ending in *jh*, the suffixes *no* and *ne* optionally replace *am* in the masculine gender, respectively. Thus: *daṇḍīno*, *daṇḍine*, *daṇḍī*. Why specify *jh*? [To exclude: *itthiyo*. Why specify *pu* (masculine)? [To exclude: *daṇḍīni kulāni*.
76. *Jhī* becomes *no* or *vā* when followed by a masculine noun. For example: *daṇḍino tiṭṭhanti*, *daṇḍino passa*, or *daṇḍī*.
77. *Smin* becomes *ni*.

The suffix *smin* optionally becomes *ni* after words ending in *jhī*, such as *daṇḍin* and *daṇḍi*: *daṇḍini*, *daṇḍismiṃ*; however, it remains *jhī* as well: *jhīto*. [It occurs] after *aggi*: *aggismiṃ*. 78. After *ambu* and so forth. The suffix *smin* optionally becomes *ni* after *ambu* and similar words:
*phalaṃ patati ambuni*, "the fruit falls into the water," just as a flower [falls] into the dust when placed in the sun; however, it remains *vā* (unchanged) as well: *ambumhi*, *paṃsumhi*.
79. From *kamma* etc.

The suffix *smin* optionally becomes *ni* after [the word] beginning with *kamma*. [Examples: *kammani*, *kamme*. [The words beginning with *kamma* are: *kamma*, *camma*, *vesma*, *bhasma* (*asma*), *brahma*, *atta*, *ātuma*, *ghamma*, *muddha*. Why say "from *kamma* etc."? [Counter-example: *buddhe*. 80. After *nāssa*, [the suffix *smin* becomes *ni*].

After words beginning with *kamma*, the suffix *ena* optionally replaces the nominative case ending (*nā*). For example: *kammena* or *kammanā*; *cammena* or *cammanā*. Why "after words beginning with *kamma*" (*kammādito*)?
Because [in that case] it would be *buddhena*. 81. *Jhalā sassa no*:

After a word ending in a *jhala* (consonant), the nominative case ending (*sassa*) is optionally replaced by *no*. For example: *aggino* or *aggissa*; *daṇḍino* or *daṇḍissa*; *bhikkhuno* or *bhikkhussa*; *sayambhuno* or *sayambhussa*.
How is it that [the phrase] "And whatever disciple of the Great Sage" occurs? (3) Regarding the rule "After *sassa*, *ṭā* is the suffix," there are readings such as "among Brahmā and others";

thus, *ṭā* is the suffix for *sassa*. 82. *Nā* optionally replaces *smā* after *jhal*. After a consonant (*jhal*), *smā* is optionally replaced by *nā*. Examples: *agginā* / *aggismā*; *daṇḍinā* / *daṇḍismā*; *bhikkhunā* / *bhikkhusmā*; *sayambhunā* / *sayambhusmā*.
83. *Lā yo naṃ vo pume*:

After *la*, the suffixes *ya*, *naṃ*, and *va* optionally become *vo* in the masculine. Examples: *bhikkhavo* (masculine plural nominative) and *bhikkhū*; *sayambhuvo* and *sayambhū*. Why [is it said] "in the masculine"? [Because] *āyūni* [is neuter]. 84. *Jantvādito no ca*:
After *jantu* and others, *no* does not [become *nāmo*].

After *jantu* and so forth, the suffix *no* optionally occurs for the nominative case in the masculine gender. Examples: *jantuno*, *jantavo*, *jantuyo*; *gotrabhuno*, *gotrabhuvo*, *gotrabhū*; *sahabhuno*, *sahabhuvo*, *sahabhū*. 85. *Kūto*:
After a word ending in the suffix *kūpa*, the suffix *no* optionally occurs for the nominative case in the masculine gender. Examples: *viduno*, *vidū*; *viññuno*, *viññū*; *sabbaññuno*, *sabbaññū*.

86. *Dhalāpo-musmā*. After the word *amu*, when it is not followed by the particle *sa*, there is elision (*lopa*) of the nominative plural suffixes in the masculine gender. Is it only in the masculine that [the forms] are *amū* and *pumā*? [No; they are also] *amuyo* and *amūni*. This is an exception (*vappavāda*) to the preceding rule. 87. *Na no sassa*. [The substitution of *na* for *no* does not apply] after the genitive singular suffix *sassa*.
"Amusmā sassa no na hoti": for "amussa," why is it "no"? [Answer: Because of "amuyā. 88. "Yolopanisu dīgho":

when there is elision of *ya* (yolope) and in the case of *nisu*, a long vowel (*dīgho*) occurs. For example: *aṭṭhi* becomes *aṭṭhīni*. Why "in the case of elision of *ya* and *nisu*"? [Counter-example: *rattiyo*.
89. In the case of *sunaṃhisu*, there is a long vowel for the noun [ending]. [Examples: *aggīsu*, *aggīnaṃ*, *aggīhi*.
90. For the fourteen [nouns] beginning with *pañca*, [the following applies].
The form *sunaṃhi* occurs for the fourteen [numerals] beginning with five. For five: *pañcasu*, *pañcannaṃ*, *pañcahi*; for six: *chasu*, *channaṃ*, *chahi*;
and so on up to eighteen. 91. *Yvādo ntussa*:
After *y*, *v*, or *ā*, the *ntu* suffix becomes *a*. Thus: *guṇavantā*, *guṇavantaṃ*, *guṇavante*, *guṇavantena*, and so forth. Why "after *y*, *v*, or *ā*"? [Observe: *guṇavā tiṭṭhati*.
92. *Ntassa ca ṭa vaṃse*.

In the case of the suffix *nta*, *ṭa* optionally occurs for both *nta* and *ntussa*. For whatever a king serves, whether it be virtuous or unvirtuous, he should perform his duty toward that person who fails to do what ought to be done, just as the Himavat mountain [provides water] even to one who is ill-born, provided he possesses good birth himself.

By means of the division of grammatical rules (*yogavibhāga*), [the suffix] also occurs elsewhere. Those who possess eyes are blind; however, the monks dwelling on the banks of the Vaggumudā are praised. 93. *Yosu jhissa pume*:

In the masculine gender, the suffix *ṭ* optionally replaces the *i* of a stem marked with the technical term *jha*, when followed by the nominative plural endings *yu* or *su*. Examples: *aggyo* (nominative plural) and *aggī* (nominative plural). Why is *jha* mentioned? To prevent *ṭ* from replacing the entire group ending in the vowel *i*; for example, *rattiyo* (nominative plural). Why is *i* mentioned? [To exclude cases like] *daṇḍino* (nominative plural). Why is "in the masculine" mentioned? [To exclude] *aṭṭhīni* (neuter nominative plural).
94. *Veevasu* [is substituted] for *lussa*.

For that which has the perception of *lasa*, *ṭa* is substituted for *ussa* when followed by *veevasu*. [Examples: *bhikkhave*, *bhikkhavo*, *veevasū*. What is the meaning of this? [They refer to] living beings (*jantuyo*). What is the apprehension? [It is] the Self-Existent Ones (*sayambhuvo*). 95.
Or, in some cases, it occurs in the locative case (*yomhi*).
In some instances, the suffix *ussa* becomes *ṭa* after a word marked with the *lasa* designation. For example: *hetayo*, *nandanti taṃ kurayo dassanena*, and *ajjeva taṃ kurayo pāpayatu*.
Why [is it] *vāti*? As in *hetuyo*. 96. *Pumālapane vevo*:

After a word marked with the *lasa* designation, the suffixes *ve* and *vo* optionally occur instead of *u* when addressing in the masculine (*puliṅge*). Examples: *bhikkhave*, *bhikkhavo*, *bhikkhū*. Why "in the masculine"? As in *āyūni*. Why "in addressing" (*ālapaneti*)? As in *jantuyo tiṭṭhanti*. Is it only *lu* that becomes *tu*? Yes: *dhenuyo*, *sayambhuvo*.
97. After *smā*, *hi*, *smā*, *hi*, *smiṃ*, *naṃ*, *mhā*, *bhimhi* [are substituted].

After *nāmā*, *smā*, *pare*, *saṃ*, *smā*, *hi*, *smiṃ*, *naṃ*, *mhā*, or *bhimhi* occur respectively. From *buddhamhā*, *buddhasmā*; by *buddhebhi*, *buddhehi*; in *buddhamhi*, *buddhasmiṃ*; and because of the rule of abundance (*bahulādhikāra*), even in cases of exception (*apavāda*), as in *dasasahassimhi dhātuyā*. 98. *Su*, *hi*, *sva*, and *sse* [are substituted].
The [suffix] *su* becomes *hi* after words ending in short *a*.
[Examples: *buddhesu*, *buddhehi*. 99. *Sabbādinam naṃmhī ca*:

After words ending in short *a* that belong to the *sabbādi* group, the [suffix] *e* occurs before the suffix *naṃ* as well as before *su* and *hi*. [Examples: *sabbesaṃ*, *sabbesu*, *sabbehi*; [the term] "of the *sabbādi* group" is used...
What? Of the Buddhas; is it only of them? No, not of those [only]. Regarding *sabba*, *katara*, *katama*, *ubhaya*, *itara*, *añña*, *aññatara*, *aññatama* (Pāṇini 1.1.27):
“The words *pubba*, *para*, *avara*, *dakkhiṇa*, *uttara*, and *adhara* are used in the sense of delimitation (*vavatthāya*)”;
and *ya*, *tya*, *ta*, *eta*, *ima*, *amu*, *kiṃ*, *eka*, *tumha*, *amha*.
100. *Saṃsānaṃ*.
For the word ending in *-naṃ* following *sabba*, *saṃsānaṃ* occurs [in place of *naṃ*]. [Examples: *sabbesaṃ*, *sabbesānaṃ*. 101. *Ghapā sassa ssā vā*.
After a word ending in *gha* or *pā*, *ssa* or *ssā* optionally [occur in place of *naṃ*].
After the word *sabba* and others ending in *gha*, *ssa* or *ssā* occurs [in place of the genitive suffix]. For example: *sabbassa* or *sabbāya*;

[the mention of *pagga* is for the sake of subsequent purposes]. 102. After *smin*, *ssaṃ* [occurs]. After *sabba* and others ending in *gha*, *ssaṃ* optionally occurs in place of *smin*. For example: *sabbassaṃ* or *sabbāya*; *amussaṃ* or *amuyā*.
after a word ending in *-gha*, there is *yaṃ* or *yaṃ*; for example, *kaññāyaṃ* or *kaññāya*, *rattiyaṃ* or *rattiyā*, *vadhuyaṃ* or *vadhuyā*, *sabbāyaṃ* or *sabbāya*, *amuyaṃ* or *amuyā*.
104. *Tiṃ* is used for *sabhāparisāya*.
After *sabhā* and *parisā*, *smin* optionally becomes *si*: *sabhātiṃ* or *sabhāya*, *parisātiṃ* or *parisāya*.
105. After *pada* and other such words, *si* is substituted for *smin*: *padasi* or *padasmiṃ*, *bilasi* or *bilasmiṃ*.
106. *Nāssa sā*.
With words such as *pada*, *nāssa sā* becomes *vā*: *padasā* for *padena*, *bilasā* for *bilena*.
107. With words such as *kodha*.
The suffix *nā* becomes *sā* when it follows *ehi*, as in *kodhasā* for *kodhena* and *atthasā* for *atthena*.
108. *Atena*:
The substitution of *enā* occurs for the word *nā* following a stem ending in short *a*; as in *buddhena*. Why say "ending in short *a*"? [Observe] *agginā*.
109. *Sissa*.

After a noun ending in short *a*, *sissa* becomes *o*; for example, *buddho*. Why [is it] not so in the case of *atoti*? [Example: *aggi*. 110. *Kvace vā*. Or, in some cases, [the substitution does not occur].

After a noun ending in short *a*, the suffix *si* optionally becomes *e* in some instances, as in "the forest thicket with its tops in bloom. Because the rule is frequently stated even in cases where it is an exception—such as in "pleasure" (*sukhe*) and "pain" (*dukkhe*)—one might ask: why say "optionally"? Why say "in some instances"?
So that it does not apply everywhere in other alternatives. 111. *Aṃ* in the neuter: After a noun ending in short *a*, the suffix *si* becomes *aṃ* in the neuter gender. Example: *rūpaṃ*.
112. *Yonaṃ ni*.

After a noun ending in *a*, *ni* is substituted for *yonaṃ* in the neuter gender. All forms [are thus established]; in the rule for the permanent [substitution], the fruit [is seen] in the nominative case of words such as *ekacca*, *sabba*, etc. 113. *Jhalā vā*. [The substitution of *ni* for *yonaṃ* occurs optionally] after a word ending in a consonant (*jhal*).
After a *jhal* [consonant], the suffix *yonaṃ* becomes either *vā* or is neuter: *aṭṭhīni*, *aṭṭhī*; *āyūni*, *āyū*. 114. *Lopa*:
After a *jhal*, there is elision (*lopa*) of *yonaṃ*: *aṭṭhī*, *āyū*, *aggī*, *bhikkhū*. Why does it not occur after *jhal* alone? Because of the internal nature (*antaraṅga*) of the vowel *a*.
115. Or [there is elision] after words ending in *jantu*, *hetu*, and *ī* (long *i*), as well as after those having the technical designation *gha*.

There is optionally the elision of the following *yōnaṃ* (the nominative plural suffix *-yo*). Examples: *jantū*, *jantuyo*; *hetū*, *hetuyo*; *daṇḍī*, *daṇḍiyo*; *kaññā*, *kaññāyo*; *rattī*, *rattiyo*; *itthī*, *itthiyo*; *dhenū*, *dhenuyo*; *vadhū*, *vadhuyo*.
116. *Ye* after a word ending in *i*.
There is optionally the elision of the vowel *i* (*ivaṇṇa*) when followed by the letter *y*, as in: *ratyo*, *ratyā*, *ratyaṃ*; or *pokkharañño*, *pokkharaññā*, *pokkharaññaṃ*.
Is it only thus? [No,] as in *rattiyo*. Why say "after a word ending in *i*"? [Observe: *daṇḍiyo*. Why say "of the vowel *i*"? [Observe: *dhenuyo*, *vadhuyo*.
How is it that "I am permitted by you"? [It is] through the analysis of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*) in the phrase "those who see.
117. *Gasīnaṃ*.
There is elision of the genitive case endings (*gasīnaṃ*) after a noun when there is no intervening vowel, as in: "O man," "this one," "the staff-bearer."
118. *Asaṅkhyehi sabbāsaṃ*.

There is elision of all case-endings (*vibhatti*) following numerals that do not possess a specific number (*asaṅkhya*). And because of this very indicative mark, it is inferred that the addition of case-suffixes (*syādi*) occurs after such numerals. 119. *Ekatthatāyaṃ*. [This rule applies] when there is identity of referent (*ekatthatā*).
In the state of becoming a single word (*ekatthībhāva*), there is generally (*bahulaṃ*) elision of all case endings (*vibhatti*):
*puttīyati*, *rājapuriso*, *vāsiṭṭho*. In some instances, it does not occur because of the general rule (*bahulaṃ vidhānā*):
*parantapo*, *bhagandaro*, *parassapadaṃ*, *attanopadaṃ*, *gavampati*, *devānaṃpiyatisso*, *antevāsī*, *janesuto*, *mamattaṃ*, *māmako*.
120. *Pubbasmāmādito*.
When a compound has the same referent (*ekattha*) as the word ending in *-amā*, there is elision of all case endings (*vibhatti*) following that compound. Examples: *adhitthi* (from *adhi-attani*).

This [elision] does not occur here frequently (*bahulaṃ*), according to the rule (*vidhānā*) and as required by the context (*yathāpatthīyā*), such as in *yathāparisāya*. Why say "preceding" (*pubbasmā*)? [Counter-example: *gāmagato* (gone to the village).
121. Not after the fifth case-ending.

When a compound ending in *am* (the accusative) precedes another word that ends in *am*, there is no elision of any of the case-endings that follow it—provided it is not the fifth case-ending (*pañcamī*). Examples: *antam* and *bhavatyapañcamiyā*. For instance: *upakumbham*. Why "not after the fifth case-ending"? Consider: *upakumbhā ānaya* ("Bring from near the jar"). 122.
Optionally, [there is no elision] of the third and seventh case-endings.

When a word ending in -a forms a compound with another word (ekattha), the suffix *aṃ* optionally replaces the third case ending (*tatiyā*) and the seventh case ending (*sattamī*) of the following words. For example: *upakumbhena kataṃ* (made near the jar) or *upakumbhaṃ kataṃ*; *upakumbe nidhehi* (place it near the jar) or *upakumbhaṃ nidhehi*.
123. *Rājasī nāmhi*:

In the case of the word *rājā* (king), the suffix *nām* optionally occurs before the sixth case ending (*chaṭṭhī*). For example: *sabbadattena rājinā* (by King Sabbadatta). Is it not so? It is: *raññā*.
124. In the case of *sunaṃhi*, there is optionally *ū* after *rāja*: *rājūsu* or *rājesu*; *rājūnaṃ* or *raññaṃ*; *rājūhi* or *rājehi*. 125.
In the locative singular (*aditthiyaṃ*), *ṭe* is substituted for *imassa*.

After the word *ima*, when it is not feminine, *ṭe* is substituted [for the nominative plural suffix], as in *ime* or *sunaṃhisu*; [the forms] *esu*, *imesu*, *esaṃ*, *imesaṃ*, *esi*, and *imehi* [are also formed]. Why say "not feminine"?

[Because in the feminine we have] *imāsu*, *imāsaṃ*, and *imāhi*. 126. *Nāmhi nimi*: After the word *ima*, when it is not feminine, the substitution *nimi* occurs for the locative singular suffix *nām*. Thus, [we have] *anena* or *imīna*. Why say "only when not feminine"? [Because in the feminine we have] *imāya*.
127. *Ayaṃ* [is substituted] for the neuter *imaṃ* in the locative case (*simhi*).
For the neuter form of the word *ima*, *ayaṃ* occurs in the locative: *ayaṃ puriso*, *ayaṃ itthī*. Why say "for the non-neuter"? [To exclude: *imaṃ*. 128.
*So* [is substituted] for *ta*, *tya*, and *eta* in the genitive case (*tassa*).

For those non-neuter [stems], *tassa* becomes *so* before the locative singular suffix *sim*. For the masculine, it is *syo*; for the feminine, *syā*. Thus: *so*, *sā*, *eso*, *esā*. Is this only for the non-neuter? Yes: *tyaṃ*, *taṃ*, *etaṃ*. 129. *Massāmussa*.
For the non-neuter, the *m* of *āmussa* becomes *s* before the locative singular suffix *sim*: *asu* (masculine), *asu* (feminine).

130. *Ke vā*: "Of whom is this? or "Whose is this?"—[referring to] such-and-such a person, such-and-such a woman, such-and-such a thing, or such-and-such things. 131. *Tatassa no tabbāsu*: "That belongs to him," or "It is not to be given to them."
For that *tad* [pronoun], there is optionally [the substitution] in all case-endings (*vibhatti*): *te* or *te*, *nāyo* or *tāyo*, *naṃ* or *taṃ*, *nāni* or *tāni*, and so forth.
132. In the case endings beginning with *sā* (i.e., *sā*, *smā*, *smiṃ*, *ssā*, *yassaṃ*, *ssā*, *saṃ*, *mhā*, *mhi*, *svi*), and for *massa*, the letter *ṭ* optionally replaces *ta* or *taṃ*.
Thus: *assa* or *imassa*; *asmā* or *imasmā*; *asmiṃ* or *imasmiṃ*; *assāya*... [and so on].

*imissāya*, *assaṃ*, *imissaṃ*, *assā*, *imissā*, *āsaṃ*, *imāsaṃ*, *amhā*, *imamhā*, *amhi*, *imamhi*, *assa*, *tassa*, *asmā*, *tasmā*, *asmiṃ*, *tasmiṃ*, *assāya*, *tassāya*, *assaṃ*, *tassaṃ*, *assā*, *tassā*, *āsaṃ*, *tāsaṃ*, *amhā*, *tamhā*, *amhi*, *tamhi*; [the mention of *ssāya* etc.
is so that it does not occur when there is a different substitution.]
133. *Ṭe* [is substituted] for *sissa* after *isi*.

After *isi*, *ṭe* optionally occurs in place of *sissa*, as in: “yo nvajja vinaye kaṅkhaṃ, atthadhammavidū ise” (he who today has doubt regarding the Vinaya, O seer who knows the meaning and the Dhamma). Or rather, it is simply *isi*. 134.
[The substitution of] *yossa* occurs for the second person pronoun (*yuṃ*).

After *isi*, when followed by a second [vowel], there is optionally *ṭe*: “I revere the ascetics and brahmins, the seers (*isī*) perfected in conduct. Why say “after a second [vowel]”? [Observe: “The seers (*isayo*) stand. 135. After *ekacca* and the like, *to* [is substituted].

After *ekacca* and other words ending in *a*, *to* is substituted for the feminine suffixes: “Some (*ekacce*) stand,” “See some (*ekace*). Why say “after [a word] ending in *a*”? [Observe: “Some women (*ekaccāyo). Thus this is the first [section].
136. *Na nissaṭā*.

After certain words such as *ekacca*, the suffix *nissaṭā* does not occur for another word; [examples include] *ekaccāni*. 137. *Sabbādīhi*. [The suffix *nissaṭā* occurs] after words beginning with *sabba*.
The suffix *nissa* does not occur after the words beginning with *sabba*.
[Example: *sabbāni*. 138. *Yona meṭa*:

After the words beginning with *sabba* that end in the vowel *a*, the suffix *meṭa* occurs. [Examples: *sabbe tiṭṭhanti*, *sabbe passa*. Why is it not simply *ato* (after *a*)? [Counter-example: *sabbāyo*.
139. *Nāññaṃ canāmappadhānā*:

That which has been stated by means of the words beginning with *sabba* when they function as names (*nāma*) or as non-prototypical (*appadhāna*), as well as any other grammatical operation belonging to the *sabba*-class, does not take place: *te sabbe*, *te piyasabbe*, *te atisabbe*. 140. *Tatiyatthayoge*: [The same applies] when used in the sense of the third case (*tatiyattha*).

In the case of a compound with the third sense (*tatiyatthena*), that which has been prescribed for the *sabba*-group and other such *sabba*-derivations does not occur; as in *māsena pubbānaṃ* or *māsapubbānaṃ*. 141.
Regarding the fourth-sense compound (*catthasamāsa*).

In the domain of the fourth-sense compound, that which has been prescribed for the *sabba*-group and other such *sabba*-derivations does not occur; as in *ikkhiṇuttarapubbānaṃ*. Why "in a compound" (*samāse*)? [Consider: *amusañca tesañca dehi*.

In this [section], the suffix *ya* is stated [to be applied] after *sabbādi* [words] following *yadha*; or it occurs after that [word] when followed by *pugga*, with the former and the latter [members] being compounded.
143. After the six beginning with *pubba*.

After these six words beginning with *pubba*, the suffixes *e* or *o* occur when referring to their own respective domains: *pubbe* or *pubbā*, *pare* or *parā*, *apare* or *aparā*, *dakkhiṇe* or *dakkhiṇā*, *uttare* or *uttarā*, *adhare* or *adharā*. What about after the six [words] beginning with *kiṃ*? [The suffixes are] *ye*. 144.
After words beginning with *mana*, the suffixes *si*, *smiṃ*, *sā*, *nā*, *smā*, and *naṃ* optionally become *si*, *so*, *sā*, *sā*, *sā*, and *sā* respectively:
after *manas*, *si* becomes *si* (locative) or *so* (genitive); after *manas*, *smiṃ* becomes *sā* (locative) or *sā* (genitive). Thus: *manasi* or *manasmiṃ*; *manaso* or *manassa*.

“*Mano*, *manaṃ*, *manasā*, *manena*, *manasā*, *manasmā*—how [is it that] ‘a son is born who is mindless, while the wise one departs, having abandoned [it], clad in pure upper garments, dressed in golden robes’?
[The answer is: they have the sense of the self (*sakattha*) and the sense of the arrow (*iṇattha*). [The following roots take these meanings:
*man*, *tama*, *tapa*, *teja*, *sira*, *ura*, *vaca*, *oja*, *rajaya*, *sa*, *paya* (6). [Also] in the cases of *saravayā*, *yavāsacetā*, *jalāsayā*, *akkhayalohapaṭamanesu*.
145. *Sato sabbaṃ bhe*.
After the word *santhā*, *sabba* becomes *saba* before the letter *bha*; [e.g.,] *sabbhi*. 146. *Bhavato vā bhonto gayonāse*.
Optionally, after *bhava*, it becomes *bhonta* when followed by a vowel or a nasal (*ya*).
In place of the word *bhavanta*, there is optionally the substitute *bhonta* when the suffix *gayona* (the vocative case ending) follows: *bhonta*, *bhavaṃ*, *bhonto*, *bhavanto*;
*bhotā*, *bhavatā*; *bhoto*, *bhavato*. The particle *bho* is used for addressing, as in: “From where indeed do you three people come, O sir?
This is established through the alternative form of the word *bhavanta*, namely *bhadda*, by means of the doubling of the letter *d* according to the rule of reduplication (*saddhantha*).
147. *Sissāggito ni*.
From *aggi* and *sissa*, the suffix *ni* is applied; thus, *aggini* means fire.
148. *Ntassaṃ*.
In the nominative singular (*simhi*), the suffix *aṃ* optionally replaces the ending of a word ending in *nt*. Examples: *gacchaṃ*, *gacchanto*.
149. *Bhūto*:
After the verbal root *bhū*, the suffix *aṃ* always replaces the nominative singular ending *nt*; this is stated again for the sake of repetition. Example: *bhavaṃ*.
150. For *mahant* and *arahant*, *ṭā* optionally [replaces the suffix].
In the locative singular (*simhi*), for *mahant* and *arahant*, the *nt* is optionally replaced by *ṭā*: *mahā* or *mahaṃ*; *arahā* or *arahaṃ*. 151.
[The same applies] for the suffix *ntu*.
In the nominative singular (*simhi*), *ntu* becomes *ṭā*, provided it has a *guṇa* vowel.
152. *Aṃ* and *ṅa* in the neuter:

in the nominative singular of the neuter, *ntu* becomes *aṃ* and *ṅa*. Examples: *guṇavaṃ kulaṃ* (the virtuous family), *guṇavantaṃ kulaṃ* (the virtuous family). Why specify "in the neuter"? [Consider: *sīlavā bhikkhu* (the virtuous monk).
153. *O* or *o* after *Himavant*.
The suffixes *ntu* and *o* optionally become *o* after *Himavant*; thus, *himavanto* or *himavā*.
154. By the rules for *rājādi* and *yuvādi*.
The suffix *ā* occurs after words such as *rājā* and *yuvā* when expressing the vocative case: *rājā*, *yuvā*.

(7) After *rājan*, *brahman*, *sakhi*, *ātman*, and *ātumana*, the suffix *a* is applied in the sense of another meaning (*aññatthe*), resulting in *daḷhadhamma*, *asma*. (8) After the word *ima* in the sense of a state (*bhāve*), the suffix *aṇ* is applied, yielding *aṇimā*, *mahimā*, *garimā*, and *laghimā*.
After *yuvan*, *susan*, *maghavan*, and *puman*, the suffix *ta* is applied.

155. *Vāmaṅa*. For words such as *rājan* and those beginning with *yuvan*, the substitution *ānaṅ* optionally occurs before the suffix *aṃ*; thus, *rājānaṃ* or *rājaṃ*, *yuvānaṃ* or *yuvaṃ*. 156. *Yonamāno*. [The suffix *ām* is substituted for the dual ending *au* after bases ending in *u* or *ū*.]
After *rāja* and so forth, and after *yuvan* and so forth, either *āna* or *ā* occurs [as a suffix]. Thus: *rājāno*, *yuvāno*; or simply *rājā*, *yuvā*. 157.
And after *sakhi*, *āya* [is added].
After *sakhi*, *āya*, *no*, and *no* occur optionally, as well as *āna*. Thus: *sakhāyo*, *sakhino*, *sakhāno*; or simply *sakhā*, *sakhe*.
158. *Ṭe* becomes *smino*.
*Ṭe* becomes *smino* after *sakha*; O friend, this undertaking has the sense of eternity. 159. [The substitution occurs] except before *no* and *asesu*.
In the case of *sakha*, the vowel *i* optionally occurs before the endings *smānaṃsu*: *sakhissa*, *sakhino*, *sakhinā*, *sakhissa*;
or [the original form remains]:

*sakhasmā*, *sakhasmā*, *sakhīnaṃ*, *sakhānaṃ*. 160. *Smānaṃsu vā*. In the case of *sakha*, the vowel *i* optionally occurs before the endings *smānaṃsu*: *sakhismā*, *sakhasmā*, *sakhīnaṃ*, *sakhānaṃ*.
161. *Yosvaṃhisu cāraṅa*.

In the case of the word *sakha* (friend), *āraṅ* is substituted for the final vowel (*o*) in the neuter forms (*smānaṃsu*) and in the locative plural (*yosvaṃhisu*). [Examples: nominative singular *sakhā*, nominative plural *sakhāro*, *sakhāyo*; locative plural *sakhāresu*, *sakhesu*; accusative singular *sakhāraṃ*, *sakhaṃ*; instrumental plural *sakhārehi*, *sakhehi*; ablative singular *sakhārā*, *sakhā*; genitive plural *sakhārānaṃ*, *sakhānaṃ*. 162. *Lthupitādīnamase*. [The substitution of *āraṅ* occurs] for words beginning with *lthu* and *pita*, except in the case of the neuter (*ase*).

The suffix *ānaṅ* occurs in place of stems ending in the *ltu*-suffixes and of words such as *pitṛ*, except when followed by the genitive case-ending (*sato*). For example: *kattāro*, *pitaro*; *kattāraṃ*, *pitaraṃ*; *kattārā*, *pitarā*; *kattari*, *pitari*. Why [is it said] "except when followed by the genitive"? [Because in that case: *kattuno*, *pituno*. 163. *Namhi vā*.

In the presence of the locative case-ending *nam*, *ānaṅ* optionally occurs for stems ending in the *ltu*-suffixes and for words such as *pitṛ*. For example: *kattārānaṃ* or *kattūnaṃ*; *ditarānaṃ* or *pitunnaṃ*.
164. After *ā*, the substitution of *ā* optionally occurs for *ltu*, *pit*, and so forth: *kattānaṃ* or *kattūnaṃ*; *pītānaṃ* or *pitunnaṃ*.
165. Elision of *s*.
The elision of *ltu*, *pi*, and so forth, occurs optionally: *katthu* / *katthuno*, *sakamantātu* / *sakamandhātuno*, *pītu* / *pituno*.
166. *Suhisvāraṅa*:
After *su* and *hi*, the suffix *āraṅ* optionally occurs for *ltu*, *pi*, and so forth: *kattāresu* / *kattūsu*, *pitaresu* / *pitūsu*; *kattārehi* / *kattūhi*, *pitarehi* / *pītūhi*.
167. *Najjāyo* [is formed] from *nadi*.
After the word *nadi*, the suffix *āmo* optionally becomes *āyo*; thus, *najjāyo* (the rivers).
168. *Ṭi* [is applied] after *kati*.
From which [numerals] does *ṭi* arise? How many remain? How many are seen? 169.
*Ṭa* [arises] after the fourteen beginning with five.

After the fourteen numerals beginning with five, *ṭa* arises: *pañca*, *pañca*, and so on up to eighteen. Why say "beginning with five"? [To exclude: *dve*, *tayo*, *cattāro*. Why say "fourteen"? [To exclude: *dve visatiyo*.
170. *Ubhago* becomes *ṭo*.

For the words *ubhaya*, *ubha*, *go*, and *gava*, the substitute *ṭo* occurs: *ubho*, *ubho*, *gāvo*, *gāvo*. How is it that one says, “We two dwell together for this single purpose” (*imekaratthiṃ ubhayo vasāma*)? In the case of *ṭo*, there is the augment *y*. 171. *Āraṅa smā*.
[The suffix *smā* is substituted for *āraṅa*.]
