After the substitute *āra*, the suffixes *ṭā* and *ṭo* become *sakhāro* and *kattāro*, [respectively], as in *pitaro*.
172. *Ṭoṭe vā*:
After the substitute *āra*, the suffixes *ṭā* and *ṭo* optionally become *sakhāro* and *sakhāyo*, respectively. The inclusion of *ṭo* is for the sake of brevity.
173. *Ṭā* replaces *nāsmānam*.
After a word ending in *āra*, *ṭā* replaces *nāsmānam*, as in *kattārā* or *kattarā*. Optionally, it may be *ṭi* due to the governing rule of *bayula*; such forms occur after words ending in *sakhā*.
174. *Ṭi* replaces *smino*.
After the verbal roots *āra* and *vada*, *ṭi* is substituted for *smin* when the agent (*kattar*) is expressed, provided that *vi* or *ti* follows.
175. From *div* and so forth:
after nominal stems beginning with *div*, *ṭi* is substituted for *smin*; as in *divi* and *bhuvi*. The augment *va* is always inserted.
176. *Rassāraṅa*.
In the case of *smi*, the vowel *ā* becomes short (*rassa*) before *kattari* and *nattari*.
177. [The same applies] to *pita* and so forth, and to *anata* and so forth.
In all case endings, the *ā* of words such as *pitā* (father) becomes short (*rassa*), with the exception of *nattā* (grandson) and others; for example: *pitaro*, *pitaraṃ*.

Why "with the exception of *nattā* and others"? [Answer: *nattāro*. 178. In the case endings *su* and *hi*, there is the substitution *ānaṅ* for words such as *yuvan* (young man). In *su* and *hi*, there is the substitution *ānaṅ* for words such as *yuvan*; for example: *yuvānesu*, *yuvānehi*.
179. *Nonānesvā*.

In these [cases], *ā* replaces the [suffixes] *yu*, etc., [in the nominative plural]: *yuvāno*, *yuvānā*, *yuvāne*. 180. *Smāsminnaṃ nāne*. [The suffixes] *smā* and *smin* become *naṃ* and *nāne* [respectively].

After the words beginning with *yuvan*, *asmin* and *anaṃ* become *nā* and *ne* respectively: *yuvānā*, *yuvāne*. 181. *Yonaṃ none vā*: After the words beginning with *yuvan*, *yonaṃ* optionally becomes *none* respectively:
*yuvāno*, *yuvāne*. Why is the word *vā* ("optionally") used? [To show: *yuve passa* ("look at the youth"). The inclusion of *noggahaṇaṃ* (the mention of *na*) is for the sake of brevity.
182. *Ito ññatthe pume*.

After a noun ending in *ī*, when it denotes another referent (*aññapadattha*) in the masculine gender, the suffixes *yonaṃ* and *none* optionally occur respectively; for example: *tomaraṅkusapāṇino*, *tomaraṅkusapāṇine*. [Is it] only when there is a *vā* [in the rule]? [Yes: *tomaraṅkusapāṇayo*. Why "when denoting another referent"? [Example: *pāṇayo*. 183. *Ne smino kvaci*.
[The suffix] *smin* becomes *ne* optionally in certain cases.

In the masculine gender, the suffix *smin* optionally becomes *ne* after a noun ending in long *ī*, provided it occurs in a sense other than its own base form (*aññapadatthe*), and when referring to a person who knows gratitude, one who is virtuous, noble, and of good conduct. Is it only in the sense of "noble conduct"?
Yes. Is it only in the masculine? Yes; [it is] *ariyavuttiyā*. 184. *Pumā*: That which was stated regarding the suffix *smin* after the word *pumā* optionally occurs as *yaṃ*; thus: *pumāne*, *pume*.
185. *Nāmhi*.

That which was stated [to occur] after a masculine [stem] ending in *-m* occurs [also] after a masculine [stem] ending in *-ā* or *-ena*. 186. *Sumhā ca*. [The same applies] after [a masculine stem] ending in *-su*.
That which was stated for the masculine [ending] *su* optionally becomes *ā* or *vā*: *pumānesu*, *pumasu*, *pumesuṃ*.
187. *Gaṃ*. After the word *puma*, *ga* optionally becomes *aṃ*: *bho pumaṃ*, *bho puma*; *bho ittipumaṃ*, *bho itthipuma*.
188. *Sā* becomes *ānaṅ* before *aṃse* and *ge*.
The word *sā* undergoes the substitution of *ānaṅ* before *aṃse* and *ge*: *sānaṃ*, *sānassa*, and *cabhā sāna*. 189. *Vattahā* [is the substitute] for *sanaṃ* and *naṃ*;
[the substitutes] *no* and *nā* [are used] for *naṃ*.
For the forms *vatta* and *sana*, *u* is substituted for the final vowel in the genitive plural according to the respective order: *vattūnaṃ*, *sanūnaṃ*.

For *vatta*, the forms are *vattassa*, *vattānaṃ*. 190. Or *u* for *brahma*. In the genitive plural *sanaṃsu*, *u* optionally replaces the final vowel of *brahma*: *brahmuno* or *brahmassa*; *brahmūnaṃ* or *brahmānaṃ*.
191. *Nāmhi* occurs after *brahmā* as *brahmaṇo* and *brahmaṇā*. 192.
[The substitution of *u* occurs] after masculine nouns, after words denoting action, power, or time, and after those ending in *-as* or *-m*.
The forms *pumādinam* occur in the genitive plural (*sasmāsu*) and the locative singular (*nāmhi*);
*pumano*, *pumassa*; *pimunā*, *pumnā*; *pimunā*, *pumnā*; *kammuno*, *kammassa*; *kammunā*, *kammasmā*; *kammunā*, *kammanā*;
*thāmuno*, *thāmassa*; *thāmunā*, *thāmasmā*; *thāmunā*, *thāmena*; *addhuno*, *addhassa*; *addhunā*, *addhasmā*; *addhunā*, *addhanā*.
193. *Yuvā* [is substituted] for *sassin*.
It becomes *yuvā* for *sassa*, or *yuvino* for *yuvassa*.
194. Not [substituted] for *ttā* or *tumam*.
For *attā* and *ātumā*, there is optionally [the substitution of] *attan-* for *attā* and *ātuman-* for *ātumā*. 195. Regarding *suhīsu*, the suffix *naka* does not occur.

For *attānaṃ*, *attesu*, *ātumānaṃ*, *ātumesu*, *attanehi*, *attehi*, *ātumanehi*, and *ātumehi*, [the suffix *naka* is not used]. How is it [applied] in the case of “*verinesu*” (among enemies)? It is because of the division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*) stating “*naka*.”
196. *Smā* is the substitute for *nā*, *brahmā*, and *ca*.
And *svā* is the substitute for *assa*, *nā*, *hoti*, *brahmunā*, *attanā*, and *ātumāna*.
197. These [substitutes] occur in the second case (*dvitīyā*) when there is a subsequent reference (*anvādesa*).

In the context of repeating what has been said regarding these words ending in *eta*, the substitution of *ena* occurs in place of the second case ending: "Instruct this monk (*imaṃ bhikkhuṃ*) in the Vinaya;
furthermore, instruct him (*enaṃ*) in the Dhamma"; "Instruct these monks (*ime bhikkhū*) in the Vinaya;
furthermore, instruct them (*ene*) in the Dhamma"—in this way, it should be applied to this as well.
198. *Kissa* in all [cases].
In all case-endings (*vibhatti*), what does *kissa* become? It becomes *ko*, *eko*, *kā*, *kāyo*, *kaṃ*, *kāni*, and *kena*, etc.
199. *Ki* in the locative plural (*sasmiṃsu*) when not feminine.

In the case of *anitthiyaṃ*, what [form] occurs after *kiṃ*? [The forms are] *kissa*, *kassaṃsu*, *kissa*, *kassa*, *kismiṃ*, *kasmiṃ*. What is meant by *anitthiyaṃ* (non-feminine)? [It refers to] *kassā* and *kassaṃ*. 200.
*Kiṃ* becomes *kiṃ* before the neuter endings *aṃ* and *su*.

When the neuter endings *aṃ* and *su* follow, the word *kiṃ* becomes *kiṃ* in the neuter. What is meant by "in the neuter"? [The forms are] *kiṃ* and *kiṃ*. What is meant by "neuter"? [It refers to] *ko* and *kaṃ*.
201. *Imassa idaṃ vā*.
After the word *aṃsi*, when it means "together with that," the form *idaṃ* becomes *imassa*; thus, in the neuter, one says *idaṃ imaṃ* or *imaṃ idaṃ*.
202. *Amussāduṃ*. [The suffix *duṃ* is applied] after *amu*.
In the locative plural (*aṃsu*), together with those [forms], *aduṃ* becomes *amu* or *napuṃsaka* (neuter) in the nominative singular;
that is, *aduṃ* or *amuṃ*. 203. *Sumhāmussāsmā*:
In the locative singular (*sumhi*), *amha* optionally becomes *asmā*; for example, "the devotion which is toward us" (*bhattirasmāsu yā tava*). Or simply: "in us" (*amhesu*).
204. *Naṃ* becomes *tissā* and *catassā* for the words *ti* and *cattāri* respectively when followed by the feminine suffix *naṃ*.

For *ti* and *cattāri*, *tissā* and *catassā* occur respectively when followed by the feminine suffix *naṃ*, as in *tissannaṃ* and *catassannaṃ*. Why say "feminine"? [To exclude: *tiṇṇaṃ*, *catunnaṃ*. 205.
*Tisso* and *catasso* occur before the suffix *yaṃ* when they possess case endings.
For the forms *ti* and *cattāri* when accompanied by case endings, there are *tisso* and *catasso* respectively in the feminine; that is, *tisso* and *catasso*.
206. In the neuter, *tīṇi* and *cattāri*:
for the forms *ti* and *cattāri* when accompanied by case endings, there are *tīṇi* and *cattāri* respectively in the neuter; that is, *tīṇi* and *cattāri*.
207. *Tayo* and *cattāro* [are substituted] for *ti* and *catu*.
In the masculine gender, for the forms *ti* and *catu* together with their case endings, *tayo* and *cattāro* occur respectively: *tayo*, *cattāro*. 208.
Or *caturo* [is substituted] for *catussa*.

When the word *catus* is accompanied by a case ending and followed by the suffix *-o*, it optionally becomes *caturo* in the masculine gender, as in *caturo janā saṃvidhāya*. How then [is it explained] in the phrase “*kathaṃ caturo nimitte nāddassāsī*” (How will you not see the four signs)?

It is due to a transposition of genders (*liṅgavipallāsa*). 209. *Mayam* and *asmāmhassa*: When the pronoun *yo* is accompanied by a case ending and followed by the suffix *-amha*, it becomes *mayam* or *asmā* respectively; [the forms are] *mayaṃ*, *asmā*, and *amhe*.
210. *Naṃse* replaces *asmākam* and *mamam*.
*Naṃse* replaces *tassa* when it has its case endings; *asmākam*, *amhākam*, *mamam*, and *mama* occur respectively.
211. *Simha* and *haṃ*.
In the case of *amha* when accompanied by a case ending, *ahaṃ* becomes *ahaṃ*.

212. In the case of *tumha*, when accompanied by a case ending, *tuvaṃ* and *tvaṃ* become *amhi* and *simhi* respectively; thus, for *tumha* with its case endings, *tuvaṃ* and *tvaṃ* occur in their respective order: *tuvaṃ*, *tvaṃ*.
213. *Tayātayīnaṃ* or *tassa*.

In the forms *tumha*, *tayā*, and *tayīnaṃ*, the letter *ta* optionally becomes *tv*; thus: *tvayā* or *tayā*, *tvayi* or *tayi*. 214. *Smāmhi tvamhā*. [In the locative singular of the second person pronoun, the forms are] *smāmhi* or *tvamhā*.
Is it that from *tvam* with its case-ending (*savibhatti*) there arises *tvamhā*, or *tvamhā* [arises] directly from *tvam*, or indeed *tvayā*?
215. For stems ending in *-nt*, the *-nt* optionally becomes *-o* in the nominative singular.
In the nominative singular, for stems ending in *-nt* with their respective case-endings, the substitution of *-o* for *-nt* optionally occurs: *gacchanto*, *gacchantā*; *guṇavanto*, *guṇavantā*.
216. For *taṃ*, *naṃ*, and *mi*:
for the forms ending in *nta* and *ntu* when accompanied by case endings, *taṃ* optionally occurs; as in *gacchataṃ* or *gacchantānaṃ*, and *guṇavataṃ* or *guṇavantānaṃ*.
217. For *to*, *tā*, *ti*, *tā*, *sā*, *smā*, *smiṃ*, and *nā*.

In the case of *sādī* (the present participle), for nouns with case endings, *to*, *tā*, *ti*, and *ta* occur respectively; as in: *gacchato* (of one going), *gacchantassa* (of one going); *guṇavato* (of one possessing virtue), *guṇavantassa* (of one possessing virtue); *gacchatā* (from one going), *gacchantamhā* (from one going);

*guṇavatā* (from one possessing virtue), *guṇavantamhā* (from one possessing virtue); *gacchati* (in one going), *gacchante* (in one going); *guṇavati* (in one possessing virtue), *guṇavante* (in one possessing virtue);
*gacchatā* (by one going), *gacchantena* (by one going); *guṇavatā* (by one possessing virtue), *guṇavantena* (by one possessing virtue).

218. Before a following *ge*, the substitutes *ṭa*, *ṭā*, and *aṃ* occur for nouns ending in *-ntu* when they bear case endings: *bho gaccha*, *bho gacchā*, *bho gacchaṃ*; likewise *to guṇava*, *bho guṇavā*, *bho guṇavaṃ*. 219.
When the suffix *yo* follows, the forms *duve* and *dve* occur for the two [numbers].
In the case of *dvi* with its case-ending (*savibhatti*), when it is in the nominative-accusative (*yoṃhi*), it becomes *duve* and *dve* respectively;
thus: *duve*, *dve*. 220. In the case of the genitive (*naṃmhi*), *dvi* with its case-ending optionally becomes *duvinnaṃ*; thus: *duvinnaṃ*, *dvinnaṃ*. 221.
In the case of the genitive (*naṃmhi*), *rāja* with its case-ending optionally becomes *raññaṃ*; thus: *raññaṃ*, *rājānaṃ*.

222. *Raññā* [is used] for us. For the word *rāja*, when it possesses a case ending, *raññā* is substituted [in the instrumental]; as in *raññā kataṃ* (done by the king) and *raññā nissaṭaṃ* (escaped from the king).
223. *Rañño*, *raññassa*, and *rājino* are [the forms] for *se*. For the word *rāja*, when it possesses a case ending, *se* becomes *rañño*, *raññassa*, and *rājino*;

as in *rañño*, *raññassa*, and *rājino*. 224. *Raññe* and *rājini* are [the forms] for *smimhi*. For the word *rāja*, when it possesses a case ending, *smimhi* becomes *raññe* and *rājini*; as in *raññe* and *rājini*.

225. *Samāse vā*. In the domain of compounds, these substitutions optionally occur for *rāja*: *kāsiraññā* or *kāsirājena*, *kāsiraññā* or *kāsirājasmā*, *kāsirañño* or *kāsirājassa*, *kāsiraññe* or *kāsirāje*.

226. *Smimhi tumhāmhānaṃ tayimayi*. In the locative singular (*smimhi*), the forms *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ*, together with their case endings, become *tayi* and *mayi* respectively: *tayi*, *mayi*. 227. *Aṃmhi taṃ maṃ tavaṃ mamaṃ*.
In the accusative singular (*aṃmhi*), [the forms become] *taṃ*, *maṃ*, *tavaṃ*, and *mamaṃ*.
In place of the words *tumha* and *amha*, along with their case endings, *taṃ*, *maṃ*, *tavaṃ*, and *mamaṃ* occur respectively: *taṃ*, *maṃ*, *tavaṃ*, *mamaṃ*.
(228) *Nāsmāsu tayāmayā*:

In place of the words *tumha* and *amha*, along with their case endings, *tayā* and *mayā* occur respectively: *tayā kataṃ* (done by you), *mayā kataṃ* (done by me); *tayā nissaṭaṃ* (escaped from you), *mayā nissaṭaṃ* (escaped from me).
229. *Tava*, *mama*, *tuyhaṃ*, *mayhaṃ*:
these forms—*tava*, *mama*, *tuyhaṃ*, *mayhaṃ*—respectively arise from the words *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ* along with their case endings.
230. *Ṅaṃ*, *ṅā*, *kaṃ*, *naṃ*, *mhi*.

In place of the words *tumha* and *amha*, together with their case endings, the suffixes *ṅa*, *ṅā*, *ka*, and *am* occur respectively: *tumhaṃ*, *tumhākaṃ*, *amhaṃ*, *amhākaṃ*. Here, the respective order is not intended to be strictly observed. 231.

In the second person (*dutiye*), when the suffix *yo* follows, [the suffixes] are optionally [used]. In place of the words *tumha* and *amha*, together with their case endings, the suffixes *ṅa*, *ṅā*, *ka*, and *am* occur optionally when the second person suffix *yo* follows: *tumhaṃ*, *tumhākaṃ*, *tumhe*; *amhaṃ*, *amhākaṃ*, *amhe*.
232. *Apādādo padatekavākye*.

This should be understood as a governing rule (*adhikāra*). A "word" (*pada*) is that by which a meaning is reached; it consists of forms ending in case-suffixes such as *si* (nominative) or those ending in personal endings such as *ti* (present indicative). A "sentence" (*vākya*) is a collection of words. 233. *Yonaṃ hisvapañcamyā vono*.
[The suffixes] *va*, *na*, *hi*, *su*, and *paṃcamī* [are replaced by] *vo* and *no*.

In a single sentence, for the words *tumha* and *amha* with their case endings that follow a word standing at the beginning of a line (*pādādi*) other than the fifth [case], the substitutes *vo* and *no* optionally occur respectively; for example: *tiṭṭhatha vo*, *tiṭṭhatha tumhe*;
*tiṭṭhāma no*, *tiṭṭhāma mayaṃ*; *passati vo*, *passati tumhe*; *passati no*, *passati amhe*; *dīyate vo*.
"It is given to you," "it is given to us," "it is given to me"; "wealth for you," "wealth for you (plural)," "wealth for us," "wealth for me";
"done by you," "done by you (plural)," "done by us," "done by me. Why say "except for the ablative"? [Because of examples like:
"It was escaped by you," "it was escaped by us. Why say "only when it is not the ablative case" (*apādādo*)? [Because of examples like: "And strength was bestowed upon the monks by you..."
"Is it 'merit well-performed, not small'? "Only with *padato*? "You stand, while Devadatta stands in the village;
you stand in the city—is it only with the case endings (*savibhattīnam*)? "The Dhamma is worthy for those like you;
the Dhamma is worthy for those like us."
234. *Teme* and *nāse*:

In a single sentence, the forms *tume* and *nāse* optionally take the place of the words *tumhaṃ* and *amhaṃ* respectively—provided they possess case endings and follow a word ending in the ablative case (*apādāda*)—when these words stand [in apposition] to those [forms].
For example: *kataṃ te*, *kataṃ tayā*; *kataṃ me*, *kataṃ mayā*.
"It is given to you," "it is given for you," "it is given to me," "it is given for me"; "wealth for you," "wealth for you," "wealth for me," "wealth for me.
235. In the case of *anvādesa* (subsequent mention):

in the context of repeating what has already been stated, the substitutes for the words *tumha* and *amha* always occur when there is a further specification, as in: "The village is your domain, and furthermore, the province is your domain."

236. *Sapubbā paṭhamantā vā*. The substitutes for the words *tumha* and *amha* optionally occur after those ending in the nominative case that are preceded by something else, even in subsequent reference (*anvādesa*). For example:

"In the village the cloth is yours" (*gāme paṭo tumhākaṃ*), or "Furthermore, in the city the blanket is yours" (*atho nagare kambalo vo*), or "Furthermore, in the city the blanket is yours" (*atho nagare kambalo tumhākaṃ*). [The rule applies] when preceded by something else.

What? "The cloth is yours, and furthermore the blanket is yours" (*paṭo tumhākaṃ, atho kambalo vo*). What about "firstly"? "The cloth is yours in the city, and furthermore the blanket is yours in the village" (*paṭo nāgare tumhākaṃ, atho kambalo gāme vo*).
237. *Na ca vā hā he* [are used] in connection with *yoga*.
When connected with *ca* and so forth, the substitutes for the words *tumha* and *amha* do not occur: "The village is your possession and my possession" (*gāmo tava ca pariggaho, mama ca pariggaho*).
"The village is your possession" or "the village is my possession"; "the village is indeed your possession" or "the village is indeed my possession";
"the village is yours alone as possession" or "the village is mine alone as possession"—in this way it should be illustrated in all instances.
What is the purpose of the particle *yo*? [It is used for emphasis: "The village is your possession, and the city is my possession."
238. In the sense of seeing (*dassana*), excluding the sense of perceiving (*ālocana*).

When used in senses of seeing other than perceiving, the substitutes for the words *tumha* and *amha* do not occur: "The village has come for you" (*gāmo tumhe uddissāgato*), "The village has come for us" (*gāmo amhe uddissāgato*). Why "excluding the sense of perceiving"? [Because in that case: "The village perceives you" (*gāmo vo āloceti*), "The village perceives us" (*gāmo no āloceti*).

293. An address (*āmantaṇaṃ*) preceding [the word] is as if non-existent. An address occurring before [the word] is, within the scope of the substitutes for the words *tumha* and *amha*, as if it were not present.
"Devadatta, your possession"—what is the purpose of the vocative address? "A blanket is your possession"—what is the purpose of the word *pubba* (before)?

"All this has been explained to you, O best of the twice-born. For if the other [the possessor] were not present, the prohibition regarding the ablative (*apādāda*) would not apply. What is the purpose of *iva*?
It is so that there may be hearing (*savana*).
240. A general term [does not remain] when there is co-referentiality (*ekattha*).

When followed by a word in grammatical apposition (*samānādhikaraṇa*), a general term used as an address (*āmantaṇa*) becomes as if it were non-existent; for example: *māṇavaka jaṭilaka te pariggaho* ("O young man, O matted-hair ascetic, this is your inheritance").
Even though the subsequent form is not present, the substitution occurs by taking the preceding form as the basis; thus it is called a "general term."

What [is the example]? “Devadatta, young man, your retinue is one and the same” (*ekattha*)—what does this mean? “Devadatta and Yajñadatta, your retinue is one and the same. 241. Or, when there are many:

an address occurring in reference to many persons may, as it were, not exist as a common term (*sāmaññavacana*) when there is a single referent; for example: “The virtuous brahmins are your retinue,” or “The virtuous brahmins are your retinue.”
Thus ends the second chapter, beginning with *syāt*, in the commentary on the Moggallāna grammar.
(3) The third chapter: Compounds (*samāsa*).
1. *Syādi* (words ending in case-suffixes) forms a compound with another *syādi* word.

It should be understood that this [rule] is an addition [to the general principle]: "That which ends in a case-suffix forms a single-meaning unit (*ekattha*) with another word ending in a case-suffix. Furthermore, this state of becoming a single meaning from words that originally had distinct meanings is called a "compound" (*samāsa*).

2. [The following types of words form compounds: numerals (*asaṅkhyā*), case-suffixes (*vibhatti*), excellence (*sampatti*), proximity (*samīpa*), totality (*sākalya*), absence (*abhāva*), "according to" (*yathā*), "after" (*pacchā*), "simultaneously" (*yugapad*), and their respective meanings.
An indeclinable (asaṅkhya) ending in a case-suffix, occurring in the sense of case-suffixes and so forth, forms a compound with another word ending in a case-suffix;
in that regard, first, concerning the sense of case-suffixes: "discourse regarding women" is *itthīsu kathā*, which becomes *adhitthi*.

Prosperity (*sampatti*) is twofold: personal prosperity (*attasampatti*) and abundance (*samiddhi*). "The Licchavis are endowed with Brahman" is *sabrahmaṃ licchavīnaṃ*; "abundance for the monks" is *subhikkhaṃ*.

*Upakumbham*: near the jar (*kumbha*). *Sātiṇamajjhoharati*: he swallows everything, including the grass. *Sāgyadhīte*: she studies everything, including the *agya*. Non-existence (*abhāva*) is manifold due to the distinctions of its correlates; therein: In the case of non-existence of power (*iddhi*):

"devoid of power" (*vigatā iddhi*), [as in] *saddikānam dussaddikam* (of those with wealth, that which is devoid of wealth). In the case of non-existence of meaning (*attha*): "absence of flies" (*abhāvo makkhikānam*), [as in] *nimmakkhikam* (flyless).

In the case of non-existence of approach (*ahikkama*): "grass that has gone beyond" (*atigatāni tiṇāni*), [as in] *nittiṇam* (grassless). In the case of non-existence of attainment (*sampatti*): "gone beyond" (*atigatam*).
"Light covering" means an extremely light covering; the meaning is that this is not the time for its enjoyment.
Just as there are many kinds here, so too in those [categories]: in "appropriateness," one wears what is suitable; in "splendor," every half-month;
in "not exceeding the purpose," according to one's ability; in "similarity," a *kikhi* garment is similar to a *sakikhi*; in "sequence," according to seniority.
Place [the word] *pacchā* when it means "behind," and *yugapat* when it means "simultaneously"—that is, with wheels. 3.

Regarding "not when it has the sense of equality": the word *yathā*, when expressing the sense of equality, does not form a compound with a word ending in a *syādi* (case) suffix, as in: "Devadatta is like Yajñadatta."

4. *Yāva* in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*). When the word *yāva* is used in the sense of restriction, it forms a compound with a form ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*); restriction means limitation or delimitation. Examples:
*yāvāmattaṃ brāhmaṇe āmantaya* (address the brahmin only to that extent), *yāvajīvaṃ*. Why "in the sense of restriction"? [Consider: *yāva dinnaṃ* (as far as given).
"I have eaten that much; I do not determine exactly how much was eaten by me.
(5) *Pari*, *apa*, *bahi*, *tiro*, *pure*, and *pacchā* optionally form a single unit with a word ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*).
For example: *paripabbataṃ vassi devo* or *paripabbatā* ("the rain fell around the mountain").
The rain fell away from the mountains, not upon the mountains; it fell up to Pāṭaliputta, not beyond Pāṭaliputta;

outside the village, not within the village; across the mountains, not upon the mountains; before the meal, not after the meal; after the meal, not before the meal. This is the section on "vetā" (the suffix -ta). 6. *Samīpa* (nearness), *āyāma* (extent), and *anu* (along/after) [are used as limits].

The word *anu*, when used in the senses of proximity (*sāmīpya*) or extension (*āyāma*), optionally forms a compound with a word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) to express a single meaning (*ekattha*). Examples: *anuvanamaṃ asani gatā* (the thunderbolt went along the forest), *anugaṅgaṃ Bārāṇasī* (Vārāṇasī is along the Ganges).

Why specify "in the senses of proximity and extension"? [Counter-example: *rakkhaṃ anu vijjotate vijju* (the lightning flashes along the fence). 7. *Tiṭṭhagū*-type compounds. Words beginning with *tiṭṭhagu* are treated as indeclinables (*nipāta*) in the domain of forming compounds that express a single meaning. For example: *tiṭṭhagu* (the time at which cows stand). This refers to the time when cows are standing.
*Kālo*, *vahaggu kālo*. *Āyatīgavaṃ*, *khaleyavaṃ*, *lūnayavaṃ*, *lūyamānayavam*, and so forth.
Here too, *kesā* becomes *kesi*; *daṇḍā* becomes *daṇḍi*. Likewise, there is also the meaning of "time" (*velā*) and "manifestation" (*pabhāva*):
*pāto nahānaṃ* becomes *pātarahānaṃ*; *sāyaṃ nahānaṃ* becomes *sāyanahānaṃ*; *pātakālaṃ* becomes *sāyakālaṃ*; *pātameghaṃ* becomes *sāyameghaṃ*; *pātamaggaṃ* becomes *sāyamaggaṃ*.
8. *Ora*, *pari*, *pati*, *pāra*, *majjha*, *heṭṭhā*, *uddha*, *adho*, and *anta* are optionally compounded with a word ending in the genitive case.

Because they are taught as monosyllabic (*ekāranta*) by way of grammatical convention (*nipātana*), the following examples are formed: *oregaṅgaṃ* (on this side of the Gaṅgā), *parisikharaṃ* (around the peak), *paṭisotaṃ* (against the current), *pāreyamunaṃ* (on the far side of the Yamunā), *majjhegaṅgaṃ* (in the middle of the Gaṅgā), *heṭṭhāpāsādaṃ* (below the palace), *uddhagaṅgaṃ* (above the Gaṅgā), *adhogaṅgaṃ* (below the Gaṅgā), and *anthopāsādaṃ* (inside the palace).
Furthermore, there are also alternative forms such as *gaṅgāora* and so forth. 9.

That is neuter. Whatever has been explained above regarding the formation of compounds (ekatttha), that should be understood as having the neuter gender; it has been illustrated accordingly. Alternatively, in some instances, due to the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*), we have *yathāparisaṃ*, *yathāparisāya*, meaning "according to one's own respective assembly" (*sakāya sakāya parisāya*).
10. Amādi.

An item ending in a case-suffix (syādyanta) frequently forms a compound with another item ending in a case-suffix (syādyanta) in the sense of "oneness of meaning" (ekattha). Examples: *gāmaṃ gato* becomes *gāmagato* ("gone to the village");

*muhuttaṃ sukhaṃ* becomes *muhuttasukhaṃ* ("momentary happiness"). In the case of a dependent compound (*upapadasamāsa*), it is restricted to the following: *kumbhakāro* ("potter"), *sapāko* ("one who cooks together"), *tantavāyo* ("weaver"), *varāharo* ("boar-hunter").
The phrase *ntamānaktavantū* is itself a sentence. [Examples include: "listening to the Dhamma," *dhammaṃ suṇanto*, *dhammaṃ suṇamāno*;

"having eaten rice," *odanaṃ bhuttavā*; "killed by a king," *raññā hato rājahato*; "cut with a sword," *asinā chinno asicchinno*; "like a father," *pitusadiso*, *pitusamo*; "accompanied by pleasure," *sukhasahagataṃ*;

"food mixed with curds," *dadhinā upasittaṃ bhojanaṃ dadhibhojanaṃ*; "rice mixed with sugar," *guḷena misso odano guḷodano*. This is because the action of mixing and so forth is expressed by the very word for the state (*vuttipada*).

There is no state of having a connected meaning (*ayuttatthatā*). In some cases there is only a compound (*vutti*), as in *uraga* (snake) and *pādapa* (tree). In other cases there is only a sentence (*vākya*), as in *pharasunā chinnavā* (cut by an axe) and *dassanena pahātabbā* (to be abandoned by vision).

*Buddhassa deyyaṃ* is *buddhadeyyaṃ* (a gift for the Buddha); *yūpāya dāru* is *yūpādāru* (wood for a sacrificial post); *rajanāya doṇi* is *rajanadoṇi* (a vat for dyeing). Here, however, it does not occur as *saṅghassa dātabbaṃ* (to be given to the Saṅgha). How is it that [the word] "for this purpose" (*etadattha*) becomes "for this purpose" (*etadatthā*) and "for this purpose" (*etadattha*)? It will occur when another word-meaning (*aññapadattha*) follows.

*Śabarabhayam* means fear of the Śabaras; [this applies to one] who has gone out from a village, having been led away for sexual intercourse. In some cases, it refers only to activity, whether born of karma (*kammaja*) or born of mind (*cittaja*).
Here, it does not exist [as a cause], such as when one has fallen from a tree. A "king’s man" (*rājapurisa*) is a person belonging to the king.

Due to the predominance of the frequent usage (*bahulādhikāra*), there is no elision of the *m* in *mamānukubbam* or *mamānukurumāno*. Among cows, the black ones are the most excellent in milk; among students, the fifth.
Regarding the whiteness of a cloth, there is indeed the sense of proximity to the present tense (*vattamānasāmīpya*). How then is it that one says, “The Brahmin’s teeth are white”?

Because of the presence of a dependent relationship (*sāpekkhatā*), it does not apply here. However, in this case, it certainly does apply: “the scent of sandalwood,” “the sound of a river,” “the beauty of a maiden,” “the touch of the body,” and “the taste of fruit.
[Examples include: “satiated by fruits,” “refreshed by fruits,” and “satisfied by fruits.”
In the expression “the high house of the brahmin,” [the genitive] does not occur because of the presence of expectation (*sāpekkhatā*).
In the case of the genitive expressing a connection with wealth, as in “the wealth of the king of Pāṭaliputta,” it will not occur because there is no connection with Pāṭaliputta.

In the case of “the king’s cow, horse, and man,” it is merely a sentence because the meanings are distinct. In the cases of “the king’s cows, horses, and men” or “the king’s cow-horse-men,” [the compound is formed].
The grammatical function (vutti) occurs only when there is a state of unity.

One who is greedy for giving is "dānasoṇḍo"; one who delights in the Dhamma is "dhammarato," one who delights in giving is "dānābhirato. In some cases, the function occurs even when [the parts] are separate: as in *kucchisaya* (lying in the womb), *thalaṭṭha* (standing on dry land), *paṅkajaṃ* (born from mud), and *saroruhaṃ* (growing in water).
Here, however, there is no moderation in eating, no guarding of the sense doors, and no [restraint] regarding the seat.
"Sitting" [is used] when one ought to sit on a seat.
11. Compound by Coalescence (*ekattana*).

A qualifier ending in the locative case (*syānta*) forms a compound by coalescence with a qualificand ending in a case suffix (*syādyanta*), provided they share the same grammatical referent (*samānādhikaraṇa*); for example, "blue" (*nīlaṃ*)...

*Taṃ uppalañca* means "that blue lotus" (*nīluppala*). *Chinnañca taṃ paruḷhañca* means "cut and grown again" (*chinnaparuḷha*). *Satthīva satthī* means "a knife indeed is a knife"; *satthī ca sā sāmā ca* means "she who is both a knife and a woman" (*satthisāmā*).
*Sīhova sīho* means "like a lion, a lion"; *muni ca so sīho ca* means "he who is both a sage and a lion" (*munisīho*).

*Sīlameva dhanaṃ* is "virtue itself is wealth" (*sīladhana*). In some cases it is the sentence itself that is full, such as "Mantāṇiputta Puṇṇa" or "the householder Citta. In some cases it is the compound itself, such as "black snake" (*kaṇhasappo*) or "red rice" (*lohitasāli*).

What is the purpose of the term *visesana* (qualifier)? [To show: "The snake is a woodcutter" (*tacchako sappo*). What is the purpose of the phrase *ekatthena* (in the sense of identity)? [To show: "One who is other than black" (*kāḷamhā añño*).
How is it that [expressions such as] *pattajīviko*, *āpannajīviko*, and *māsajāto* [are formed]? They will occur in the sense of a different word-meaning (*aññapadatthe*). 12. *Nañ*.

When this negative particle *nañ* ending in a case-suffix (*syādyanta*) is combined with another word ending in a case-suffix (*syādyantena*), it forms a single compound (*ekattha*). For example: *abrāhmaṇo* (a non-Brahmin). Due to the application of the rule of "frequently" (*bahulādhikārato*), this occurs with certain words expressing incapacity:
*apuna-geyyā gāthā* (a verse not to be sung again), *anokāsaṃ kāretvā* (having made no room), *amūlā mūlaṃ gantvā* (having gone from rootless to the root).

Also, *īsaṃ-kaḷāro* (slightly tawny) and *īsaṃ-piṅgalo* (slightly reddish-brown) are compounds formed by the rule "*syādi syādine*" (a word ending in a case-suffix [with a word] ending in a case-suffix); otherwise, it would remain merely a sentence, as there would be no over-extension (*atippasaṅgābhāvā*).
13. *Kupādayo* [are used] always (*niccam*) in the context of the *syādi* suffixes.
The word *ku* and those beginning with *pa* form a single meaning with a word ending in a *syādi* suffix, always, except in cases other than the scope of the *syādi* suffix rules:
*kucchito brāhmaṇo* = *kubrāhmaṇo* (a contemptible Brahmin); *īsakaṃ uṇhaṃ* = *kaduṇhaṃ* (slightly warm); *panāyako*, *abhiseko*, *pakaritvā*.
(9) *Pakataṃ*, *duppuriso*, *dukkataṃ*, *supuriso*, *sukataṃ*, *abhitthutaṃ*, *atitthutaṃ*, *ākaḷāro*, *ābaddho*.
“*Pādayo* [are used] with the first case (*paṭhamā*) in the sense of ‘gone to,’ etc.”: *pāgato ācariyo* = *pācariyo* (a teacher who has gone away), *pantevāsī* (a resident disciple).

(10) “*Accādayo* [are used] with the second case (*dutiyā*) in the sense of ‘exceeded,’ etc.”: *atikkanto mañcaṃ* = *atimañco* (one who has exceeded the bed), *atimālo* (one who has exceeded the garland).

(11) “*Avādayo* [are used] with words such as *kuṭṭha* in the sense of ‘covered by,’ with the third case. For example: *avakokilaṃ* (“a forest covered by cuckoos”) and *avamayūraṃ* (“covered by peacocks”).

(12) “*Pariyādayo* [are used] with words such as *gilāna* in the sense of ‘inclined toward’ or ‘devoted to,’ with the fourth case. For example: *pariyajjheno* (“inclined toward study”) and *parigilāno* (“inclined toward illness”).
(13) “*Nyādayo* [are used] with words such as *kantā* in the sense of ‘distressed by’ or ‘longing for,’ with the fifth case.”
"Having departed from Kosambī, even while departing, he shines upon the tree"—in what sense [is this] "in the manner of an action" (*asyādividhimhi*)?
14. *Cī* with words expressing action:
A word ending in the suffix *cī* becomes a single unified meaning (*ekattha*) when combined with words ending in *syādi* that express an action, such as *malinīkariya*.
15. *Bhūsanā-dara-anādara-svalam-āsā-sā*.

In the case of *bhūsanā* (adornment) and the like, words such as *svalam* and others become compound with words ending in the *syādi* (case endings) when they have the sense of an action (*kiriyattha*). Examples: *alaṃkariya*, *sakkacca*, *asakkacca*. Why is it said "in the case of *bhūsanā* and the like"?
[Consider these counter-examples: *alaṃ bhutvā gato* (having eaten sufficiently, he went), *sakkaṭvā gato* (having honored, he went), *asakkaṭvā* (not having honored).
*Gato*: the meaning is that the study (*pariyattaṃ*) has become beautiful or not beautiful. 16.
*Aññe ca* ("And others"):

other words also frequently form compounds with words ending in case suffixes (*syādyanta*) that express an action (*kiriyattha*), such as: *purobhūya*, *tirobhūya*, *tirokariya*, *urasikariya*, *manasikariya*, *majjhekariya*, *tuṇhībhūya*.
17. *Vānekaññatthe*.
Several [words] ending in case-suffixes may become unified in meaning with another word; for example: one who has much wealth is *bahudhana*;
one whose ears are hanging down is *lambakaṇṇa*; one who has a thunderbolt in his hand is *vajirapāṇi*; those who are intoxicated are many.
O Mātaṅgas, here is a forest with many rutting elephants; the tree which a monkey has climbed is "one climbed by a monkey";
he by whom the sense-faculties are conquered is "one of conquered faculties"; he to whom food has been given is "one to whom food is given";
that cloth from which blackness has departed is "one from which blackness has departed"; those to whom ten have approached are "approached-by-ten," meaning "near-ten."
*Adūradasā* (those not far from ten), *adhikadasā* (those exceeding ten), and *tidasā* (those whose measure is three tens).
How does the word *dasa* function in the sense of a number? It is due to its proximity to a word denoting a measure (*parimāṇa*);

just as *pañcaka* refers to those whose measure is five, so too *dvattaya* refers to those whose measure is two or three—the word *vā* having the sense of "or"—meaning either two or three, or two-and-three.

The intermediate direction between the southern and eastern directions is the southeastern direction; it is called "southeast" because it is both southern and eastern. "With son" (*saputta*) means one who has come with a son;
"with hair" (*salomaka*) means one for whom hair exists—the meaning being that [the suffix] *ka* denotes existence. Likewise, "with wings" (*sapakkhaka*).

In the expression "the Brahmin woman who has milk" (*atthi khīrā brāhmaṇī*), the word *atthi* is a particle used in the sense of existence. In some cases, when its meaning is already established, other words are not employed.
One whose neck is black is *kaṇṭhekāḷo*; one whose face is like that of a camel is *oṭṭhamukho*; one whose mass of hair is a crest is *kesacūḷo*;
one whose ornament is made of gold is *suvaṇṇālaṅkāro*; one whose leaves have fallen is *papatitapaṇṇo* (or *papaṇṇo*);
one whose sons do not exist is *avijjamānaputto*; one for whom sons do not exist is *aputtako*.

In the case of *aputte*, [the suffix] does not occur anywhere; for although there are five who have eaten, the word *putto* (son) exists as the son of his brother, according to the rule of frequent occurrence (*bahulādhikārato*).

18. Regarding that: having taken [a word] ending in the seventh case and a word ending in the third case which are similar in form (*sarūpa*), and having struck with it in battle—this refers to another nominal base (*aññapadatthe*) where multiple similar forms occur.
It has a single referent (*ekattha*): a battle that proceeds by seizing hair against hair is called *kesākesi*;

a battle that proceeds by striking with staffs against staffs is called *daṇḍādaṇḍi*; [and] *muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi*. Regarding the rule “*ci vītiyāre*” (Pāṇini 2.4.51), the suffix *ci* occurs when there is a compound;
regarding the rule “*cismiṃ*” (Pāṇini 7.3.66), the vowel *a* is substituted. In that context, what is meant by “by that”? It is “body against body.”
"Having seized, a battle took place. "Having seized and struck? "The battle took place with each standing in his own chariot.
"Regarding 'battle'? "Friendship took place with each grasping the other by the hand.
"Regarding 'identical form'? "A battle took place with sticks and clubs."
19. *Catthe*.

When there is a sense of "and" (*ca*), that which consists of multiple words ending in case-suffixes may become a single word. The meanings of the word *ca* are: conjunction (*samuccaya*), subsequent mention (*anvācaya*), mutual connection (*itarītarayoga*), and collective aggregate (*samāhāra*).
Among these, the state of becoming a single meaning (*ekatthībhāva*) is not possible in the cases of conjunction and subsequent mention; for in those two, conjunction (*samuccaya*)...

Accumulation (*aññamaññanirapekkhānamattappadhānānaṃ katthaci kiriyāvisese cīyamānatā*) occurs when several items, each being the primary factor independently of the others, are combined toward a particular action, as in:

"Cut the *dhava*, the *khadira*, and the *palāsa* trees. And accumulation by repetition (*anvācaya*) occurs where one item is enjoined as the primary factor and another as a subordinate attribute, as in:
"Go for alms and bring the cows. However, these two [types] are possible in the other two cases [of conjunction and disjunction].
For among these, *itaretarayoga* (mutual conjunction) follows the distinction between the members of the compound when they are mutually dependent, as in "Sāriputta and Moggallāna";
because the individual members are predominant here, the plural number is used.

*Samāhāra* (aggregation), on the other hand, is the predominance of the collective whole when the mutual dependence of the members remains but their individual distinctions are obscured, as in "umbrella and sandals"; because the collective whole is predominant here, the singular number is used.
And these compounds, through their frequent application of mutual conjunction (*itarītarayoga*), are generally restricted to specific domains;

herein is the classification of those domains as found in the *Niruttipiṭaka*: [the domain] of living beings, musical instruments, parts of a chariot, constant enemies, numerals and measures, names of small creatures, outcaste cooks, common branches of conduct, single recensions of the scriptures, and distinctions of gender.

There is a constant unification of various opposing directions and rivers; or likewise, of grass, trees, domestic animals, birds, wealth, grain, condiments, and human beings, as well as other things through their mutual conjunction.
[Examples of such conjunctions include:
the limbs of a living being—eye and ear, mouth and nose, jaw and neck, skin, flesh, and blood; and name-and-form, aging, and death.
For the factors of the fourth [jhāna]: the drum, the *gomukha* drum, the conch, the *deṇḍima* drum, the soft-sounding *pāṇava* drum, singing and instrumental music, and the rhythmic beat.
For the factors of yoga: the plowshare, the cooking vessel, the yoke, and the plow. For the factors of the army:
the sword, the spear, the javelin, the club, the sword-and-shield, the bow-and-quiver, and the weapons and armor. For those who are eternal enemies: the snake and the mongoose, the cat and the mouse.
The crows and owls; the nagas and supaṇṇas. Of numbers and measures: the single and the pair, the pair and the triad, the triad and the tetrad, the tetrad and the pentad, the ten and the eleven.
Of small creatures: the insects and moths, the ants and termites, the gadflies and mosquitoes, the flies and ants.
Of butchers and outcasts: the sheep-slaughterers and pig-butchers, the fowlers and hunters, the deer-trappers and cow-killers.
The outcaste who cooks with fire, the bamboo-worker and the chariot-maker, the scavenger and the cremator of corpses;
among those who share the same conduct—Atisabha, Rādha, and Jāta; ethical discipline and wisdom, serenity and insight, and the knowledge of the way;
among the recitations of the single study—the Dīgha, Majjhima, Aṅguttara, Saṃyutta, Khandhaka, and Vibhaṅga; among the distinctions of gender—the female organ.
Slaves, male and female; robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick; grass, wood, branches, and foliage.
It is also seen [in the texts] that "he is a recipient of robes, almsfood, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. [He understands] the various opposites:
the wholesome and the unwholesome, the blameworthy and the blameless, the inferior and the superior, the dark and the bright, the clever and the wicked.
The directions: east and west, south and north, southeast, northeast, southwest, northwest.
Rivers: the Gaṅgā and Yamunā, the Mahī and Sarabhū.
Specific types of grass: *kāsakusa* and *kāsakusa*, *usīra* and *bīraṇa*, *muñja* and *pabbaja*.
*Muñja* and *pabbaja*. Among specific trees: *khadira* and *palāsa* are "khadirapalāsas"; *vossaka* and *kaṇṇa* are "dhavāssakaṇṇas";
*pilakkha* and *nigrodha* are "pilakkhanigrodhas"; *assattha* and *kapittha* are "assatthakapitthanas";
*sāka* and *sāla* are "sākasālās. Among specific animals: *gaja* and *gavaja* are "gajagavajas"; *go* and *mahisa* are "gomahisas"; *eṇeyya*, *go*, and *mahisa* are...
A pair of antelopes, a cow and a buffalo; a pair of antelope-boars, antelope-boars; a pair of goats and sheep, goats and sheep; a pair of dogs and pigs, dogs and pigs;
a pair of elephants, cows, horses, and mules, elephants, cows, horses, and mules. Among specific birds—a pair of swans and ducks, swans and ducks;
a pair of *kāraṇḍava* ducks and ruddy geese, *kāraṇḍava* ducks and ruddy geese; a pair of cranes and crows, cranes and crows. Among riches—a pair of silver and gold.
Gold and bullion; gems, conch-shells, pearls, and beryl—gems, conch-shells, pearls, and beryl; native gold and silver—native gold and silver. Of grains: rice and barley—rice and barley;
sesame, mung beans, and black gram—sesame, mung beans, and black gram; niṣpāva and horse-gram—niṣpāva and horse-gram. Of condiments: potherbs and greens—potherbs and greens;
products of cows and buffaloes—products of cows and buffaloes; products of antelopes and wild boars—products of antelopes and wild boars.
The compound of animals: *eṇeyyavārāha* (the black antelope and the boar), *migamāyūra* (the deer and the peacock), *migamāyūrā*. The compound of countries:

*kāsikosala* (Kāsi and Kosala), *vajjimalla* (Vajji and Malla), *cetivaṃsa* (Ceti and Vaṃsa), *macchasūrasena* (Maccha and Sūrasena), *kurupañcāla* (Kuru and Pañcāla). The compound of mutual connection (*itaretarayoga*) is, for example:
*candimasūriyā* (moon and sun), *samaṇabrāhmaṇā* (ascetics and brahmins), *mātāpitaro* (mother and father), and so forth.
In this section on the formation of single-word compounds (*ekatthībhāva*), whatever was stated previously is placed first, because there is no purpose for deviating from the sequence.
In some cases, however, there is an inversion due to the influence of frequent usage (*bahulādhikāra*); for example, *dantānaṃ rājā* becomes *rājadanta*.
In certain instances, disregarding the sequence, that which belongs to the prior time is placed last; for example: *littavāsita*, *naggamusita*, *sittasammaṭṭha*, and *bhaṭṭhaluñcita*.

In the *Catthasadda*, regarding those instances where a single compound is formed, it should be understood that some authorities restrict the preceding member (*pubbapada*) in various ways; however, such restrictions are not stated here because they would demonstrate inconsistency (*byabhicāra*).
20. In a collective sense (*samāhāre*), the neuter gender is used.

In a compound of aggregation (*samāhāra*) where there is a single referent (*ekattha*), that [compound] takes the neuter gender (*napuṃsakaliṅga*); this has been illustrated accordingly. However, in some cases it does not occur, as indicated by the examples: *sabhāparisāya*, *ādhipaccaparivāro*, *chandapārisuddhi*, and *paṭisandhipavattiyaṃ*. 21. Numerals, etc. (*saṅkhyādi*).

In a compound of aggregation where there is a single referent, numerals and so forth take the neuter gender: *pañcagavaṃ* (five cows), *catuppathaṃ* (four roads). Because the aggregation is a single entity, the singular number alone is used. Only in the case of aggregation [do we have]: *pañcakāpālo pūvo* (a cake made of five cups) and *tiputto* (one who has three sons).
22. And in some cases, the neuter gender occurs with the genitive case in a single sense.
In certain instances, the neuter gender is used for the genitive when it expresses a single sense: *salabhānaṃ chāyā* becomes *salabhacchāyaṃ*;
likewise, *sakuntānaṃ chāyā* becomes *sakuntacchāyaṃ*, *pāsādacchāyaṃ* becomes *pāsādacchāyā*, and *gharacchāyaṃ* becomes *gharacchāyā*.
In the case of non-human assemblies, the neuter singular form occurs: *brahmasabhaṃ*, *devasabhaṃ*, *indasabhaṃ*, *yakkhasabhaṃ*, *sarabhasabhaṃ*.

However, in the case of human assemblies, there are forms such as *khattiyasabhā* and *rājasabhā*. Why [is it said] "in some cases"? [Because in other instances] there is *rājapuriso*. 23. In the presence of [suffixes] beginning with *si*, [the final vowel] is shortened.
In the neuter gender, when occurring before the *sy*-suffixes and so on, the [final vowel] becomes short. Example: *salabhacchāyaṃ*. Why "before the *sy*-suffixes and so on"?
Example: *salabhacchāye*. 24. Of a *gha*-suffix that is final and non-emphatic.

When a *gha*-suffix is final and non-emphatic, it becomes short before the *sy*-suffixes and so on. Examples: *bahumālo poso*, *nikkosambi*, *ativāmoru*. Why "that which is final"? Example: *rājā kaññāpiyo*. Why "non-emphatic"? Example: *rājakumārī brahmabandhū*.
25. *Gossu*.

For the word *go* (cow), when it is subordinate (*appadhāna*) and final in a compound, *u* is substituted for the vowel before case endings beginning with *sy-*. Why “when subordinate”? *Cittagu* (a clever cow). Why “final in a compound”? *Sugo* (a good cow). *Gokulaṃ* (a herd of cows). 26. *Itthiyam atvā*. [The substitution occurs] when the feminine suffix *-ī* follows.

The suffix *āp* occurs after a feminine noun ending in the vowel *a*. Example: *Dhammadinnā*. 37. **Nadādito vī**: The suffix *vī* occurs after [words] beginning with *nadī* when expressing femininity.

Examples: *nadī*, *mahī*, *kumārī*, *taruṇī*, *vāruṇī*, *gotamī*. (14) **“Gotovā”**: [In the word] *gāvī*, [the suffix *vī* is applied] optionally after *go*. This is a class-based (*ākati*) group. Regarding the rule *“ntantūnaṃ vīmhi to vā”* (3-36), the mention of *to* is for the purpose of specification.

28. And [the suffix] *inī* follows *yakkha*, etc., when a female is denoted, with the elision of the intermediate vowel (*vī*). Thus: *yakkhinī* (female spirit), *yakkhī*; *nāginī* (female serpent), *nāgī*; *sīhinī* (female lion), *sīhī*. 26.
[The suffixes] follow *ārāmika*, etc.

The suffix *nī* occurs after [words ending in] *ārāmika*, etc., when denoting a woman: *ārāmikinī*, *anantarāyikinī*, *rājinī*. (15) After the word *mānusa* in the sense of a "perception," *nī* is added: *mānusinī*; otherwise, it is *mānusī*. 30. **Yuvaṇṇehi nī**:

After words ending in the vowels *i* or *u*, the suffix *nī* is generally applied in the feminine. Examples: *sadāpayatapāṇinī*, *daṇḍinī*, *bhikkhunī*, *khattabandhunī*, *paracittavidunī*. Why is it not applied after *mātu* and others? Because even without the feminine suffix, they express the state of being female (*itthatta*).
31. *Kti* from another meaning.

After a word ending in *kti*, the suffix *nī* is frequently applied in the feminine when the meaning is indeed other than that [of the base]. For example: *sāhaṃ ahiṃ sāratinī* ("I am one who delights in snakes"), *tassā muṭṭhassatiniyā* ("of her who is forgetful"), *sā gāvī vacchagiddhinī* ("that cow is greedy for her calf"). Why "from another meaning"? [Answer: *dhammarati* ("delight in the Dhamma"). 32. *Gharaṇī* and others.
[The words] *gharaṇī* and so forth are [feminine bases formed by this rule].

The words *gharaṇī* and so forth are formed with the addition of the suffix *ānī*. *Gharaṇī*, *pokkharaṇī*, and *īsattaṃ* are irregular forms (*nipātanā*). According to the rule “*ācariyā vā ya-lopo ca*,” there are *ācariyā* and *ācarinī*. 33. Regarding the suffixes beginning with *mātula*:

the suffix *ānī* is applied after words beginning with *mātula* when referring to a wife. Thus, *mātulānī*, *vāruṇānī*, *gahapatānī*, and *ācariyānī*. According to the rule “*abhariyāyaṃ khattiyā vā*,” there are *khattiyānī* and *khattiyā*. However, because of its inclusion in the list of words beginning with *nada*, it is also *khattiyī* when referring to a wife.
34. When preceded by *upama*, *saṃhita*, *sahita*, *saññata*, *saha*, *sapha*, *vāma*, *lakkhaṇa*, and so forth, the word *ūru* becomes *ū*.

Words beginning with *ūru* followed by these prefixes undergo this change. Examples: *karabhorū*, *saṃhitorū*, *sahitorū*, *saññatorū*, *sahorū*, *saphorū*, *vāmorū*, *lakkhaṇorū*. Due to the separation of the rule (*yogavibhāga*), *ū* [is also applied] as in *brahmabandhū*.
35. The word *yuvā* [is also included].
From the word *yuvan*, the feminine suffix *ī* occurs: *yuvati*. 36.
After words ending in *nt* or *t*, the suffix *ī* optionally occurs.
After words ending in *nt* or *t*, the suffix *ī* optionally replaces *t*: *gacchantī* (from *gacchatī*), *sīlavantī* (from *sīlavatī*).
37. *Bhavato* becomes *bhoto*.
Optionally, the substitution of *bho* for *bhava* occurs. [Examples: *bhoti*, *bhavantī*. 38. *Go* becomes *āvaṅ*.
There is doubt regarding the word *gosadda*. [The forms] *gāvī* [and others arise]. 39.
Regarding *puthussa*, there are the forms *pathava* and *puthavā*.
There is doubt regarding *puthussa*; there are the forms *pathava* and *puthavā*. [Examples include] *pathavī*, *puthavī*, and *ṭhe pathavī*.
40. *Samāsanta*: "At the end of a compound" (*samāsanta*) is also added as a governing rule (*adhikāra*). 41.
[The suffixes] *pāpa* and so forth [are applied] to the ground (*bhūmi*).
When the word *bhūmi* follows words such as *pāpa*, the compound ending becomes *-a*. For example: *pāpabhūmaṃ*, *jātibhūmaṃ*.
42. With numerals:
when the word *bhūmi* follows numerals, the compound ending becomes *-a*. For example: *dvibhūmaṃ*, *tibhūmaṃ*.
43. *Nadīgodāvarīnaṃ*.

When *nadī* and *godāvarī* follow numerals, the suffix *a* is applied in a compound: *pañcanadaṃ* (five rivers), *sattagodāvaraṃ* (seven Godāvarīs). Why "after numerals"? [Counter-example: *mahānadī* (great river). Why "of *nadī* and *godāvarī*"? [Counter-example: *dasitthi* (ten women). 44. *Asaṅkhyehi cāṅgulyānaññāsaṅkhyatthesu*.
[The suffix *a* is also applied] after non-numerical words when *aṅgulī* follows, provided the sense is not that of a specific number.

When combined with numerals (*asaṅkhyā*) and numbers (*saṅkhā*), the prefix *parā-* becomes *pa-* in a compound, provided that the compound does not express another word-meaning (*aññapadattha*) and the compound expresses a non-numerical sense (*asaṅkhyattha*).
Examples: *niraṅgulaṃ* (without fingers), *accaṅgulaṃ* (beyond the fingers); *dvaṅgulaṃ* (two fingers joined together). Why is it said "not when expressing another word-meaning or a numeral"?
Consider: *pañcaṅguli hattho* (a hand with five fingers), *upaṅguli*. How then is [the term] *dvaṅgulimāna* (having the measure of two fingers) formed?

Regarding the term *dvaṅgula*: here, it does not function [as a compound] when the suffixes such as *-matta* have been elided, as is prescribed for the meaning of a word distinct from the members of the compound.
Alternatively, the word *aṅgula* is another term denoting a measure, as in the expressions “a hundred fingers full by the measure of a finger-army” (*senaṅgulappamāṇena*) or “fourteen fingers.”
45. After words such as *dīgha* ("long") and so forth, including *asaṅkheyya* ("innumerable") and numerals, when combined with *ratti* ("night"), the suffix *a* is added [to form a compound].
Examples include: *dīgharattaṃ*, *ahorattaṃ* (*tto*), *vassārattaṃ* (*tto*), *pubbarattaṃ*, *apararattaṃ*, *aḍḍhurattaṃ*; and [the form] *atikkanto*.
At night: *atiratto*; two nights combined: *dirattaṃ* (or *dvirattaṃ*); in some cases, by virtue of the rule for frequent usage (*bahulādhikāra*), [it is] *ekarattaṃ* (or *ekaratti*);

[is this only] in the sense of "not another number"? Long night: *dīgharattihemanto*; cessation: *uparatti*; in some cases, because of the frequent application of the rule, it occurs even as *yathārattaṃ*.

46. And when *go* is elided, [the suffix] *a* occurs at the end of a compound following the word *go*, provided it does not denote a number (*cattha*) and the compound has another word as its referent (*aññapadattha*), except for the sense of a numeral (*asaṅkhyattha*). Examples:

*rājagavo* (king-bull), *paramagavo* (supreme bull), *pañcagavadhano* (one who possesses five bulls), *dasagavaṃ* (ten bulls). Why say "when there is elision"? [Consider: *pañcahi gohi kīto* (bought for five cows).
Why [is it] *pañcagu* and not *acatthu*? Only in the sense of "belonging to" (*anañña-saṅkhya-atthe*)?
As in *cittagu*, *upagu*. 47. *Rattindiva-dāragava-caturassa*:

these words ending in *-anta* are formed as indeclinables (*nipacca*). *Rattañca divā ca* = *rattindivam*; *ratti ca divā ca* = *rattindivam*; *dārā ca gāvo ca* = *dāragavam*; *catasso assiyō assa* = *caturasso*.
48. *Āyāmenugavam*.
The term *anugava* is derived from the sense of "length" (*āyāma*) when it is being traversed. An example is *anugavaṃ sakaṭaṃ* ("a cart [as long as] a cow's length"). Why "length"?

[Because in the case of] *gunnaṃ pañchā anugu* ("behind the cows"), it does not apply. 49. *Akkhismāññatthe*. The suffix *a* occurs after *akkhi* at the end of a compound, provided that the compound conveys a meaning other than its constituent parts. Examples: *visālakkho*, *visālakkhī*.

50. *Dārum-aṅgulyā*. When *aṅguli* (finger) is the final member of a compound denoting a different referent (*aññapadattha*) and refers to wood (*dāru*), the suffix *a* is applied. Examples: *dvaṅgulaṃ dāru*, *pañcaṅgulaṃ*.

This refers to a piece of wood used for scattering grain and so forth, having parts resembling fingers; however, when it denotes a measure (*pamāṇa*), it is established as before, like the words *sakha* and *raja*.
First, regarding those ending in *a*: even the suffix *si* is not seen [here], as it is established by another rule (*pakatantarena*) that *gāṇḍī* and *vadhanvā* [are formed].

51. *Ci* occurs in the sense of mutual exchange (*vītihāra*). The suffix *ci* occurs after a word denoting something other than the base itself (*aññapadatthe*), when a mutual exchange of floods (*oghābyatihāra*) is implied. Examples are *kesākesi* ("hair-for-hair") and *daṇḍādaṇḍi* ("stick-for-stick"). The letter *c* is for the purpose of specification (*visesanattha*) in the rule "in *ci*" (3.66). Usage such as *sugandhi* and *duggandhi* is not seen [as examples here].

52. *Ko* [is added] after feminine bases ending in *ltu* suffixes and those ending in *ī* or *ū*. The suffix *ka* frequently occurs in the sense of another word (*aññapadattha*). Examples: *bahukattuko*, *bahukumāriko*, *bahubrahmabandhuko*. Why "frequently" (*bahulaṃ*)? As in: *subbhū*. 53. Or otherwise than that (*vāññato*).
In the sense of "another" [expressed] by another [word], what [suffix] occurs frequently? It is *ka*. Examples:
*bahumālaka*, *bahumāla*. 54. In the subsequent word (*uttarapada*). This should be understood as the governing rule (*adhikata*). 55. Of this, this.
When the word *uttarapada* (subsequent member of a compound) follows, this [pronoun] becomes *idaṃ*. Thus: *idamaṭṭhitā*, *idappaccayatā*;

[here] there is the elision of the *niggahīta* and the doubling of the following consonant. 56. *Puṃ*: optionally for *pumassa*. Optionally, *puṃ* is substituted for *pumassa* when a subsequent member follows. Thus: *pulliṅgaṃ*, *pumaliṅgaṃ*. 57. *Ṭantantūnaṃ*.

In these cases, *ṭa* optionally becomes *u* when followed by a following word (*uttarapada*). Examples: *bhavampatiṭṭhāmayaṃ*, *bhagavaṃmūlakā no dhammā*. Because of the rule regarding frequency (*bahulādhikāra*), this applies even to words beginning with *tara*, let alone to those beginning with *mahat*:
*rattaññumahattaṃ*. 58. A. In these cases, *a* becomes *o* when followed by a following word. Example: *guṇavantapatiṭṭho-smi*. 59.

For *manas* and so forth, as well as for *āpas* and so forth, *o* is substituted before a following word and before the suffix *maya*. For *manas* and so forth, and for *āpas* and so forth, *o* occurs before a following word and before *maya*. Examples: *manoseṭṭhā*, *manomayā*; *rajojallaṃ*, *rajomayaṃ*; *āpogataṃ*, *āpomayaṃ*; *anuyanti disodisaṃ*.
60. In the case of numerals.

When numerals follow as the second member of a compound, the final vowel of the preceding word becomes *o*. Examples: *parosataṃ* (more than a hundred), *parosahassaṃ* (more than a thousand). Why "in the case of numerals"? [Counter-example: *paradattūpajīvino* (those who live on what is given by others).
61. In the case of *jane*, when followed by *puthu*.
The substitution *u* occurs for *pu* when followed by the word *uttara*. Thus, "this person is distinct from the Noble Ones" (*ariyehi*) is called a *puthujjana* (worldling). 62.
Or, when *cha* precedes the word *āyatana*, the *cha* may optionally become *sa*. Thus: *sāhaṃ*, *chāhaṃ*; *saḷāyatanaṃ*, *chaḷāyatanaṃ*.
63. *Āraṅ* and *araṅ* after *ltu*, *pitā*, etc.

After suffixes ending in *ltu* and after words such as *pitā*, *āraṅ* or *araṅ* may optionally occur when followed by a subsequent word (*uttarapada*). Examples: *satthāradassanaṃ* (the seeing of the Teacher), *kattāraniddeso* (a description of the agent); [in the alternative] *mātarapitaro* (mother and father). Why is it stated "only *vātu*"? [To show: *satthudassanaṃ* (the seeing of the Teacher), *mātāpitaro* (mother and father). 64.
*Ā* occurs in the sense of "there" (*tatra*) after words denoting connection through knowledge (*vijjā*) or birth (*yoni*).

The substitution of *ā* occurs for the words *ltu*, *pitā*, and so forth—which denote relations by learning (*vijjā*) and relations by birth (*yoni*)—when they appear as the second members of compounds with those same words *ltu*, *pitā*, etc., provided they denote the fourth case (*catthavisaye*).
Examples: *hotāpotaro* (father and son), *mātāpitaro* (mother and father). Why "of *ltu*, *pitā*, and so forth"? [Counter-example: *puttabhātaro* (son and brother).

Why "therein" (*tatra*)? [Counter-example: *pitupitāmahā* (father and grandfather). Why "the fourth case" (*cattheti*)? [Counter-example: *mātubhātā* (mother’s brother). Why "relations by learning and by birth"? [Counter-example: *dātubhattāro* (teacher and student).
65. *Putte*.

When *putta* follows as a subsequent word (*uttarapada*) in the sense of "son," the suffix *ltu* is substituted for words such as *pitā* and others when they denote a relationship arising from learning or birth. Examples: *pitāputtā*, *mātāputtā*. 66. *Cismiṃ*. [The suffix *ltu* is also applied] before the word *cismiṃ*.
When the suffix *cippa* occurs at the end of a compound, *ā* is substituted for the final vowel of the preceding member.
For example: *kesākesi* (hair-for-hair), *muṭṭhāmuṭṭhi* (fist-for-fist). 67.

When a feminine word (*itthiyam*) expressing a single meaning (*ekatthe*) is compounded with another word that is its coreferential (*samānādhikaraṇe*) subsequent member (*uttarapade*), and that subsequent member is a word whose masculine form has been stated (*bhāsitapumā*), the feminine word becomes masculine (*pumeva*).

[The following examples illustrate: *kumārabhariyo*, *dīghajaṅgho*, *yuvajāyo*, [and] *itthī*. What is the purpose of [specifying] *itthī*? [As in: *kalyāṇīpadhānāmesaṃ* (those for whom a beautiful woman is the primary object).

What is the purpose of [specifying] *bhāsitapuma* (masculine when spoken)? [As in: *kaññābhariyo*. What is the purpose of [specifying] *itthī*? [As in: *gāmaṇikulaṃ* (the family of a village headman); *diṭṭhi assa gāmaṇidiṭṭhi* (his view is that of a village headman).
What is the purpose of [specifying] *ekattha* (in the same sense)? [As in: *kalyāṇiyā mātā* (the mother of a beautiful woman) = *kalyāṇimātā*.
68. Regarding certain suffixes (*paccaya*):

When a word has been expressed as masculine or feminine, it remains masculine when a certain suffix follows. For example: *byattatarā*, *byattatamā*. 69. Words such as *sabba* remain in their original gender only when they function as mere adjectives (*vutti-matte*).

All words denoting females, such as *itthī* and others, become masculine in form when expressing only the grammatical function (*vutti*). For example: *tassā mukhaṃ* becomes *tammukhaṃ*; *tassaṃ* becomes *tatra*; *tāya* becomes *tato*; and *tassaṃ velāyaṃ* becomes *tadā*.
(70) The substitution of *jayaṃ* for *jāyā* occurs before the word *pati*.
When *pati* follows, *jāyā* becomes *jayaṃ*, as in *jayampatī*. This is established by another traditional rule (*pakatantarena*) as *jānipatī*; likewise, there are the forms *dampatī* and *jampatī*.
71. *Ud* is the substitute for *udaka* when it occurs as the second member of a compound. For example: *udadhi*, *udapānaṃ*. 72.
Optionally so in the case of *kumbha* and other such words.

In compounds beginning with *kumbha* and others, there is optionally the substitution of *uda* for *udaka*. Thus: *udakumbho* or *udakakumbho*, *udapatto* or *udakapatto*, *udabindhu* or *udakabindhu*; this is a class of words formed by convention (*ākati-gaṇo*).
73. Elision in the case of *sota* and others:
In compounds beginning with *sota* and others, there is the elision of the *u* of *uda*. Thus: *dakasotaṃ*, *dakarakkhaso*.
74. *Ṭa* replaces *nañ* before a following word (*uttarapada*).

The substitute *ṭa* occurs for the word *nañ* when it precedes another word. Example: *abrāhmaṇo*. Why is the letter *ñ* mentioned? It is so that it does not apply to the word alone, as in *pāmanaputto*. 75. *Ana* is the substitute [for *nañ*] before a vowel (*sare*).
When *uttarapada* follows, the word *nañ* becomes *ana*. [This is] *anakkhātaṃ*. 76. *Nakhādayo*.

Words such as *nakha* and others are derived through the substitution of *ana* for *an*. That which does not endure (*khamati*) is *nakha*; that which does not endure otherwise [is *anakha*]. These are technical terms (*saññā-sadda*).
And [the word] *nakula* means "one for whom there is nothing that must be done in any way whatsoever," being derived from *na-kulam-arthi*;
*akula*, *añña*, *nakha*, *nakula*, *napuṃsaka-nakkhatta*, *nāka*, and so forth.
77. *Naga* means "without living beings."

The word *naga* is derived from *na* (not) and *gacchati* (goes), or it is derived from *nipacca* (to go). Thus, *nago* means a tree; *nago* means a mountain. [Conversely,] *ago* means a tree; *ago* means a mountain. Why say "from *appaṇini*" (not moving)? [Example: *ago vasalo sītena* (the outcaste does not move because of the cold). 78. *Sahassa so-ññatthe*:

In a compound where the resultant meaning is something other than the constituent members themselves, when the subsequent member (*uttarapada*) follows, the *sahassa* becomes *so* optionally. [Examples: *saputto*, *sahaputto*. Why say "in another meaning" (*aññatthe*)? [Counter-examples: *saha katvā* (having done together); *saha yujjhitvā* (having fought together).

79. In the case of a noun (saññā), when followed by the word *uttara*, the suffix *sa* occurs to form a noun; for example, *sāssatthaṃ* and *sapalāsaṃ*. 80. [The suffix *sa* occurs] when not referring to something directly perceived (*appaccakkhe*).

When the sense of "together with" (*saha*) is not directly perceived, the substitution *so* occurs before the word *uttara-pada*, as in: *sāggi* (with fire), *kapoto* (a dove), *sapisācā* (accompanied by spirits), *vātamaṇḍalikā* (a whirlwind). 81. Regarding the word *sakattha* (meaning "one's own"):

when the word *saha* has the sense of "one's own" as its primary meaning, the substitution *so* occurs before an *uttara-pada* that does not denote time. Examples: *sabrahmaṃ* (one’s own sacred knowledge), *sacakkaṃ nidhehi* (place the wheel together with it), *sadhuraṃ pājehi* (drive the chariot together with the yoke). Why "not denoting time"? Because in *saha pubbaṇhaṃ* (together with the forenoon) and *sahāparaṇhaṃ* (together with the afternoon), the substitution does not occur.

82. In the sense of "at the end of a book" (ganthanta) and "in excess" (ādhikya). When [a word] ending in *sahassa* occurs before these two, it becomes the subsequent member (*uttarapada*). Examples: *sakalajotimadhīte* ("he studies the entire Joti"), where the meaning is "beginning from" (*ārambha*) in the sense of time; *sadoṇā khārī* ("a khārī with an extra doṇa") in the sense of excess; *samāsako kahāpaṇo* ("a kahāpaṇa with an extra āsaka"). This rule is begun for the purpose of expressing constancy (*nicca*).
83. Optionally, when *samāna* occurs before *pakkha* and so forth.
In the secondary suffixes beginning with *pakkha*, the substitute *sa-* optionally occurs for *samāna-*. Examples: *sapakkho* (having the same side), *samānapakkho* (having the same side);
*sajoti* (having the same light), *samānajoti* (having the same light). Why "beginning with *pakkha*"? [Counter-example: *samānasīlo* (of similar character). The suffixes are:
*pakkha*, *joti*, *janapada*, *ratti*, *pattinī*, *pattī*, *nābhi*, *bandhu*, *brahmacārī*, *nāma*, *gotta*, *rūpa*, *ṭhāna*, *vaṇṇa*, *vayo*, *vacana*, *dhamma*, *jātiya*, *ghacca*.
84. In the case of *udara*, [the suffix] *iya* is applied.

In the case of *udara*, when it is used in the sense of "equal" (*samāna*) with respect to another, the suffix *so* or *vā* occurs. Examples: *sodariyo*, *samānodariyo*. Why is *iya* mentioned? [To exclude: *samānodaratā*. 85.
In the case of *rī* and *rikka*, [the suffix *iya* is applied].
For one who is equal (*samāna*) among these, there is *so* [as a suffix]. [The forms are] *sarī*, *sarikkho*, *sariso*.

86. For *sabba* and the others, *ā* [is the substitute] before *rī*, *rikka*, and *ka*. For *sabba* and the others, *ā* occurs before *rī*, *rikka*, and *ka*. [The forms are] *yādī*, *yādikkho*, *yādiso*.
87. *Ṭākīṭī* replaces *nta*, *kiṃ*, and *ima*.

In the case of words ending in *nta*, the substitutes *ṭā*, *kīṭī*, and *imasadda* replace *nta*, *kiṃ*, and *ima* respectively. Examples: *bhavādī*, *bhavādikkho*, *bhavādiso*; *kīdī*, *kīdikkho*, *kīdiso*; *īdī*, *īdikkho*, *īdiso*. 88.
*Tā* replaces *tumha* and *amha* when referring to a single person.

In the case of *rī* and *rikkha*, when there is a single [person] among you or us, the forms *tumha* and *amha* become, respectively, *tādī*, *tādikkho*, *tādiso*; and *mādī*, *mādikkho*, *mādiso*. What is the purpose of "in the case of a single [person]" (*ekasmiṃ*)? [Examples: *tumhādī*, *amhādī*; *tumhādikkho*, *amhādikkho*; *tumhādiso*, *amhādiso*. 89. *Taṃ mamaññatra*:

Following that, when there is another word as the following member (*uttarapada*), *taṃ* and *maṃ* replace *tumha* and *amha* respectively when there is a single [person]. [Examples: *taṃdīpā*, *mandīpā*; *taṃsaraṇā*, *maṃsaraṇā*; *tayyogo*, *mayyogo*—here the *bindu* (anusvāra) is elided.
90. *Vetasseṭa*:
After *rī*, *rikkha*, and *kesa*, the suffix *ta* becomes *eṭ*. [Examples: *edī*, *etādī*, *edikkho*, *etādikkho*, *ediso*, *etādiso*.
91. In the case of *vidha* and other such words, *dvi* becomes *du*.
*Du* becomes *du* before suffixes such as *vidha*: *dvividho*, *dupaṭṭaṃ*, and so forth.
92. *Di* occurs before *guṇa* and the like.
Before *guṇa* and similar terms, *du* becomes *di*: *dviguṇaṃ*, *diratti*, *digu*, and so forth.
93. *Tīsva*.
In the three [cases], *dvi* becomes *ahū*. Examples: *dvattikkhattuṃ*, *dvittipattapurā*. 94. *Ā saṅkhyāyāsatādo-naññatthe*.
Up to the number *asata*, [the substitution occurs] except in the sense of negation (*nañ*) or other meanings.

When a numeral is followed by a subsequent word, the substitution of *ā* for *dvi* occurs, provided it does not mean "a hundred" (*sata*) or the like, and provided the meaning is not something other than that [of the numeral]. Examples: *dvādasa* (twelve), *dvāvīsati* (twenty-two), *dvattiṃsa* (thirty-two). Why "when a numeral"? Example: *dirattaṃ* (two nights). Why "provided it does not mean 'a hundred' or the like"? Examples: *disataṃ* (two hundred), *disahassaṃ* (two thousand). Why "provided the meaning is not something other than that"? Example: *dvidasā* (the two sets of ten). 95. *Tisse*:

When a numeral is followed by a subsequent word, the substitution of *e* for *ti* occurs, provided it does not mean "a hundred" or the like, and provided the meaning is not something other than that. Examples: *terasa* (thirteen), *tevīsa* (twenty-three), *tettiṃsa* (thirty-three). Why "when a numeral"? Example: *tirattaṃ* (three nights). Why "provided it does not mean 'a hundred' or the like"? Example: *tisataṃ* (three hundred). Why "provided the meaning is not something other than that"? Example: *ticatukā* (three sets of four).
96. Or from *cattālīsādo*: there is *cattālīsādo* for *tisso*;

*tecattālāsaṃ* and *ticattālīsaṃ* for *tecatālīsaṃ*; *tepaññāsaṃ* and *tipaññāsaṃ* for *tepaṇṇāsaṃ*; *tesaṭṭhi* and *tisaṭṭhi* for *tesaṭṭhi*; *tesattati* and *tisattati* for *tesattati*; *teasīti* and *tiyāsīti* for *teasīti*; *tenavuti* and *tinavuti* for *tenavuti*. Is it only *asatādo*? It is *tisataṃ*. 97. And from *dvissā*.

In the sense of "other than" (aññattha), when the word *catālīsā* follows *dvi*, it optionally becomes *ā*. Thus: *dvecattālīsaṃ*, *dvācattālīsaṃ*, *dvicattālīsaṃ*; *dvepaññāsaṃ*, *dvāpaññāsaṃ*, *dvipaññāsaṃ*, and so forth. 98. *Bācattālīsādo*:

In the sense of "other than" (*aññattha*), when the word *acattālīsā* follows *dvi*, *dvi* optionally becomes *bā*. Thus: *bārasa*, *dvādasa*; *bāvīsati*, *dvāvīsati*; *battiṃsa*, *dvattiṃsa*. Why say "other than *acattālīsā*"? [Because it does not apply here: *dvecattālīsaṃ*.
99. In the [groups of] twenty and ten, for the fifth, there are fifty-five.
In the subsequent [groups of] twenty and ten, for the fifth, there are fifty-five respectively. For the twenty, it is twenty-five; for the fifteen, it is fifteen. 100.
For the four, there are four in the ten.
Before the word *dasa*, the letter *c* becomes *cu* when followed by *da*. Thus: *cuddasa*, *coddasa*, *catuddasa*.
(101) For the letter *ch*, there is the substitution of *so* when followed by the word *dasa*. Thus: *soḷasa*.
102. *Eka-ṭṭhāna-mā*.
When followed by ten [suffixes], *eka-aṭṭhānaṃ* becomes *ā*: *ekādasa*, *aṭṭhārasa*.
103. *Ra* may optionally be substituted for *saṅkhyāta*.

In the case of the number *saṅkhyā* followed by *para*, *daśa*, and *ra*, there is an option (*vibhāsā*). [The forms are] *ekārasa* or *ekādasa*, *bārasa* or *dvādasa*, *pannarasa* or *pañcadasa*, *sattarasa* or *sattadasa*, *aṭṭhārasa* or *aṭṭhādasa*.
In the cases of the substitutes *panna* and *bā*, it is always [the former]; here [in the case of *catu*], it does not occur as *catuddasa*.
104. After *cha*, *ti*, and *tī*, there is also *ḷ*.
In the words *chatīhi*, *parassa*, *dasassa*, *ḷo*, *ro*, *soḷasa*, *sorasa*, *teḷasa*, and *terasa* [the substitution rules apply].
105. Regarding the fourth and third [vowels], there is *maḍḍhuḍḍhatiyā*.

The half (*aḍḍha*) of the following fourth and third vowels becomes *uḍḍhatiya* respectively. The fourth with a half is *aḍḍhuḍḍha*; the third with a half is *aḍḍhatiyo*. How is *aḍḍhateyyo* formed? By adding the suffix *ṇya* in its own sense (*sakatthe*), there is a strengthening (*vuḍḍhi*) of the subsequent syllable.
106. For the second [element], together with *diyaḍḍha* and *divaḍḍha*.
When combined with the word *aḍḍha*, the second element becomes *diyaḍḍha* or *divaḍḍha*. The second [element] preceded by *aḍḍha* becomes *diyaḍḍha* or *divaḍḍha*.
107. Before a vowel, *ka* is substituted for *ku* when it follows another word.

When *ku* occurs before a word beginning with a vowel as its second member (*uttarapada*), the substitute *ka-* takes the place of *ku*. Examples: *kadannaṃ*, *kadasanaṃ*. Why "before a vowel"? Witness: *kuputto*. Why "as a second member"?
Witness: *kuaḍḍho rājā*. 108. *Kāppatthe*:
When *ku* occurs in the sense of "insignificant" (*appa*), *kā* is substituted for it when followed by a second member; e.g., "insignificant salt" is *kālavaṇaṃ*.

109. *Purise vā*. [The suffix] *vā* occurs after *kussa* when it refers to a person (*purisa*). *Kāpuriso*, *kupuriso*: this is an instance where the alternative explanation (*vibhāsā*) has not been reached; however, when the sense is "bad" (*appattha*), the suffix always precedes [the word], as in *īsaṃ puriso* = *kāpuriso*.
110. After words ending in *pubba*, *apara*, *ajja*, *sāya*, *majjha*, *hi*, and *aha*, the suffix *ṇha* is applied.
The substitution of *ṇha* for the *aha* of the second member occurs after *pubba* and other such words: *pubbaṇho*, *aparaṇho*, *ajjaṇho*, *sāyaṇho*, *majjhaṇho* (also *paṇho*).
Thus ends the third section, the Section on Compounds, in the Vutti of the Moggallāna Grammar.
4. The Fourth Section (on the suffix *ṇa*, etc. 1. *Ṇo vā pacce*.

The suffix *ṇa* optionally occurs after a noun ending in the sixth case when the meaning "except" (*apacca*) is not to be expressed; the letter *ṇ* serves the purpose of causing vowel strengthening (*vuddhi*), and likewise for other [purposes].

*Vāsiṭṭha* [is formed] from *vasiṭṭha*, and likewise *vāsiṭṭhī*; *opagava* from *opagava*, and likewise *opagavī*. The particle *vā* is for the purpose of providing an option regarding the formation of a compound or a sentence;
its governing authority extends up to the end of the section on *sakattha*. 2. From *vaccha* and so forth, the suffixes *ṇa*, *āna*, and *āyana* [are applied].
The suffixes *ṇa* and *ṇāya* are optionally applied to words such as *vaccha* and others that do not already end in a suffix, as well as to words denoting lineage (*gotta*) and the like;
when they are not applied, the forms are *vacchāno*, *vacchāyano*, *kaccāno*, *kaccāyano*, with the augment *kā* added, *kātiyāno*, *moggallāno*, *moggallāyano*,
*sākaṭāno*, *sākaṭāyano*, *kaṇhāno*, *kaṇhāyano*, and so forth.

3. From *kattika* and so forth, and from *vidhavā* and so forth, the suffixes *ṇeya* and *ṇera* respectively become *apacca*, as in *kattikeyya*, *venateyya*, *bhāgineyya*, etc., and *vedhavera*, *bandhakera*, *nālikera*, *sāmaṇera*, etc.
4. From [stems ending in] *ṇya* and so forth.
After *diti* and so forth, the suffix *ṇya* optionally occurs when not forming a patronymic (*apacca*): *decca*, *ādicca*, *koṇḍañña*, *gaggya*, *bhātabba*, and so on.
After a word ending in long *ā*, the suffix *ṇi* optionally occurs when not forming a patronymic: *dakkhi*, *datthi*, *doṇi*; *vāsavi*, *vāruṇi*, and so on.

6. After *rāja*, [the suffix] *ña* occurs in the sense of lineage, provided that it is something other than *rāja* itself, when the offspring of the king is understood; e.g., *rājañño*. Why say "in the sense of lineage"? [Observe: *rājāpaccaṃ* (the king's descendant). 7.
After *khatta*, [the suffix] *iya* occurs.
Regarding the word *khatta*, when applied to a caste (*jāti*) that is not a secondary derivative (*apacca*), the forms *khatto*, *khattiyo*, and *khatti* are used specifically for the caste.

8. From the word *manu*, the suffixes *-ssa* and *-saṇa* occur when applied to a caste that is not a secondary derivative: *manusso*, *mānuso*; in the feminine, *manussā*, *mānusī*; specifically for the caste, *mānavo*.
9. From the name of a country, [the suffix] *ṇo* is applied to denote a Kṣatriya descendant and a king.

Whatever the name of a country is, that same name becomes [the name of] a Kṣatriya descendant and a king, provided it is not [already] a [proper] name. For example: Pañcāla, Kosala, Māgadha, Okkāka. [Question: Why is it "from the name of a country"? [Answer:

Because the son of a Brāhmaṇa from Pañcāla is called a Pañcāli. [Question: Why is it "a Kṣatriya"? [Answer: Because the son of a Brāhmaṇa from Daśaratha is called a Dāsarathi. [Question: Why is it "and a king"? [Answer: Because the son of a Brāhmaṇa from Pañcāla is called a Pañcāli.
10. The suffix *ṇya* is applied after the words *kuru* and *sivi*.
It occurs in the sense of offspring and also in the sense of a king. [Examples: *Koravyo*, *Sebyo*. 11.
The suffix *ṇa* is applied after the word *rāga* in the sense of "colored by that."

The suffix *ṇo* occurs after a verbal root denoting "coloring" (*rāga*) when the sense of "colored" (*ratta*) is intended; for example, *kāsāvaṃ* (ochre), *kosumbhaṃ* (safflower), or *yāliddaṃ* (red lead).
Why [is it not used] in the case of *devadattena rattaṃ vatthaṃ* (a cloth colored by Devadatta)?
Because here [the words] *nīlaṃ* (blue) and *pītaṃ* (yellow) are quality-denoting terms (*guṇavacana*), and thus they express the state of being colored even without the suffix *ṇo*.
12. *Nakkhatteninduyuttena kāle*:
