At a time marked by a lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*) from the third case ending, the suffix *ṇo* occurs if that lunar mansion is conjoined with the moon (*indu*).

Examples: *phussī ratti*, *phussaṃ ahaṃ*. Why say "by a lunar mansion"? [Answer: *gurunā lakkhitā ratti* (a night marked by Jupiter). Why say "conjoined with the moon"? [Answer: [To exclude cases where it is not so conjoined.]
What [is meant]? A *muhutta* (hour) is characterized by *Kattikā*; what does "in time" mean? The accomplishment of one's purpose (*atthasiddhi*) is characterized by *Phussa*.
In the expression "today is *Kattikā*," the word *kattikā* refers to the moon when it is in conjunction with the *Kattikā* constellation.
13. That full-moon day is its presiding deity.
The suffix *ṇo* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*chaṭṭhyatthe*) after words ending in the nominative singular (*paṭhamantā*).

Whatever ends in the nominative, if that is a deity (*devatā*) [and it is] a full-moon day (*puṇṇamāsī*), then [the suffix applies]. For example: *sugato devatā assā ti sugato*, "Sugata is its deity"; *māhindo*, *yāmo*, *vāruṇo*.
[If] the full moon (*puṇṇamāsī*) is related to [a deity], then [the suffix applies]: *phusso*, *māso*, *māyo*, *phagguno*, *citto*, *vesākho*. *Jeṭṭhamūlo*, *āsaḷho*, *sāvaṇo*, *poṭṭhapādo*.

Regarding *assayuja*, *kattika*, *māgasira*, and *puṇṇamāsī*: what is [the meaning]? [The term] *phussī* is derived from the fifth [lunar day], and the full moon (*puṇṇamāsī*) does not belong to a month that involves wages (*bhataka*).

[The form] is analyzed as "may it not be full" (*puṇṇo mā assa*); therefore, by this very irregular derivation (*nipātana*), there is the suffix *-ṇo* and the augment *s*. Precisely because of the mention of "month" (*māsa*), the rule for the fifteen nights and so forth does not apply.

14. *Tam adhīte tam jānāti kaṇikā ca.* From the second [word] onwards, in the sense of "he studies that" or "he knows that," the suffix *ṇa* is applied, as well as *ṇika*. For example: one who studies or knows grammar (*vyākaraṇa*) is a *Veyyākaraṇo*;
likewise, a *Chandaso*, a *Kamako*, a *Padako*, a *Venayiko*, and a *Suttantiko*. The inclusion of the word "second" (*dutiya*) is for the purpose of restriction.

This is for the purpose of showing that [the suffix] is applied separately for the sake of the rule (*vidhānatta*), for the purpose of demonstrating that it is the object of study (*ajjhenavisayabhāva*) for one who knows, and for the purpose of including established conventions (*pasiddhūpasaṅgaha*).
15. *Tassa visaye dese*:

after a word ending in the sixth case, when the sense is "region" (*desa*), the suffix *ṇo* occurs; for example, *vāsātīnaṃ visayo deso vāsāto* ("the region which is the domain of the Vāsātīs is Vāsāta"). Why say "region"? [Counter-example: *cakkhussa visayo rūpaṃ* ("form is the domain of the eye"), *devadattassa visayo-anuvāko* ("the recitation is the domain of Devadatta").
16. Regarding the name of the residence.

The suffix *ṇo* occurs after a word ending in the sixth case when it denotes the name of a country that is the residence of [a people]; for example, *sebyo*, meaning "the country which is the residence of the Sivi people," from the word *vāsa*. 17. Regarding proximity. [The suffix *ṇo* occurs] when denoting that which is not far from [something].

The suffix *ṇo* does not occur after a word ending in the sixth case (*chaṭṭhī*) when it denotes a place not far from that [referent] and shares its name; for example, *vedisā* (Vedisā) means "not far from Vedisa.
18. *Tena nibbatte*:

The suffix *ṇo* occurs after a word ending in the third case (*tatiyā*) when it denotes a place produced by that [instrumental factor] and shares its name; for example, *kusambena nibbattā kosambī nagarī* ("the city of Kosambī produced by *kusamba*"), *kākandī*, *mākandī*, and *sahassena nibbattā sāhassī parīkhā* ("a moat produced by a thousand [pieces]"). In the sense of the agent (*hotumhi kattari*) and the instrument (*karaṇe*), the third case is used as appropriate.
19. *Tam-īdha-atthi*.

The suffix *ṇo* occurs after a word ending in the nominative case *tam*, when it signifies a place (*idha*) in the locative sense (*sattamī*), provided that the nominative form *atthi* (is) follows; for example, "there are *udumbara* trees in this place" becomes *odumbaro*, *bādaro*, *babbajo*. 20. *Tatra-bhave*. [The suffix *ṇo* occurs] in the sense of "originating there" (*tatra-bhave*).

The suffix *ṇa* occurs after words ending in the seventh case (*sattamyanta*) in the sense of "being there" (*bhavattha*). For example: *udake bhavo* = *odaka* ("aquatic"); *orasa*, *jānapada*, *māgadha*, *kāpilavatthava*, *kosamba*. 21.

From *ajja* and other such words, the suffix *tana* is used. In the sense of "being there," the suffix *tana* occurs after *ajja* and others: *ajje bhavo* = *ajjatana* ("of today"); *svātana*, *hiyyattana*.
22. *Purā* with *ṇo* and *ca*.

After the word *purā*, when it occurs in the sense of "being" (*bhavatthe*), the suffixes *ṇo* and *tano* are applied: *purāṇo*, *purātano*. 23. *Amā* with *tvacca*. [The suffix *tvacca* is applied after *amā*.]
The suffix *acca* occurs after the word *amā* in the sense of "being" (*bhava*), as in *amacca* ("minister"). 24.

The suffix *ima* occurs after words beginning with *majjha* when they end in the locative case, in the sense of "being. Examples: *majjhima* ("middlemost"), *antima* ("last"). [The bases are: *majjha*, *anta*, *heṭṭhā*, *upari*, *ora*, *pāra*, *pacchā*, *abbhantara*, *paccanta* (as well as *purattha* and *bāhira*).
25. *Kaṇa*, *ṇeyya*, *ṇeyyaka*, and *iya*:
These suffixes occur in the sense of "originating from" (*bhava*) after words ending in the locative case. *Kaṇa*: Originating from Kusinārā is *Kosināraka*;
[originating from] Māgadha is *Māgadhaka*; an Āraññaka monastery. *Ṇeyya*: *Gaṅgeyya*, *Pabbateyya*, *Vāneyya*. *Ṇeyyaka*: *Koleyyaka*, *Bārāṇaseyyaka*.
*Campeyyaka*, *mithileyyaka*—thus [ending in] *-eyyaka*. *Ya-gamma*, *dibba*.
*Iyagāmiya*, *udariya*, *diviya*, *pañcāliya*, *bodhipakkhiya*, *lokiya*.

The suffix *ṇika* occurs after a word ending in the seventh case (*sattamyanta*) in the sense of "belonging to that" (*bhavattha*). For example: *sāradiko divaso* (an autumn day), *sāradikā ratti* (an autumn night). 27.

When [the suffix] denotes a craft (*sippa*), character (*sīla*), merchandise (*paṇya*), weapon (*paharaṇa*), or purpose (*payojana*), the suffix *ṇika* occurs after a word ending in the nominative (*paṭhama*) that expresses such a craft or other category, provided it stands in a genitive relationship (*asseti chaṭṭhiyatthe*). For example: *vīṇāvādanaṃ sippam assa veṇiko* (lute-playing is his craft; he is a lute-player).

One who uses a drum is a *modaṅgika*; one who uses a flute is a *vaṃsika*; one whose habit is wearing rags from dust-heaps is a *paṃsukūlika*, as is one who possesses only the three robes; one whose merchandise is perfume is a *gandhika*;

one who deals in oil is an *telika*; one who deals in balls is a *goḷika*; one whose weapon is a bow is a *cāpika*; one who uses a lance is a *tomarika*; one who uses a club is a *muggarika*; that which has the acquisition of material things as its motive is "pertaining to acquisitions" (*opadhika*), such as [the attainment] with a cart (*sātika*) or with a thousand coins (*sāhassika*).
28. The suffix *ṇika* occurs in the sense of "one who kills," as in such expressions as "he goes to kill" (*hantv-ara-hati*) or "he moves about killing" (*gacchatuñ-chati carati*).

From the second [root] *han*, in these senses beginning with "he kills," the suffix *ṇika* is applied. For example: one who kills birds with birds is a *pakkhika*, a *sākunika* (fowler), or a *māyūrika* (peahunter).
One who kills fish is a *macchika* or a *menika*. One who kills deer is a *māgavika*, a *hāriṇika*, or a *sūkarika* (hunter of boars).

*ika*: *satam arahati* means *sātika*; it is *sanditthika* (visible here and now); it is *ehi-passika*, meaning it deserves the method of "come and see" (*ehi-passa-vidhi*); it is *sāhasika*. *Sahassiyo* becomes *iya*.
One who goes to another's wife is a *pāradārika*; [one who goes] on a path is a *maggika*; [one who goes] fifty *yojanas* is a *paññāsayojanika*. One who gleans badara fruits is a *bādarika*;
one who gleans *sāmāka* grain is a *sāmākika*. One who practices the Dhamma is *dhammika*; one who practices what is not the Dhamma is *adhammika*.

29. The suffix *ṇika* occurs after words ending in the third case when used in the sense of "done by," "bought for," "bound by," "prepared by," "mixed with," "struck by," "kills," "conquers," "shines," "digs," "crosses," "moves," "carries," or "lives.
Done by the body: *kāyikaṃ*; by speech: *vācasikaṃ*; by mind: *mānasikaṃ*.
A disease caused by wind: *vātiko*. Bought for a hundred: *sātikaṃ*; for a thousand: *sāhassikaṃ*. [Bought] from the very root; by Devadatta...
The term *kīta* is not used here for the sake of conveying that specific meaning. One bound by a leather strap is a *vārattika*; one bound by iron is an *āyasika*; one bound by a snare is a *pāsika*.
That which is prepared with or mixed with curd is *ghātika*, as are *goḷika*, *dādhika*, and *māricika*. One who kills with a net, or is killed by a net, is a *jālika*;
so too is a *bālīsika* (a fisherman). That which is won by dice is *akkhika*, as is *sālākika*. Or, one who wins or plays with dice is an *akkhika*.
*Akkhiko* (one who works with an axle). One who digs with a spade is *khāṇittiko*, meaning a digger or one with a hoe. "Victory was won by Devadatta" (*devadattena jitam*).
One who digs with a finger is not [called] *aṅguliko*, because the meaning of that [suffix] is not understood [in that context]. One who crosses by means of a raft is *oḷumpiko*;

"oḷumpiko" [is formed] with the suffix *-ika* as in *gopucchiko* and *nāviko*. One who travels by cart is *sākaṭiko*; "rathiko" and "parappiko" [are also formed] with the suffix *-ika*. One who carries on his shoulder...
The suffix *-ika* occurs in *khandhika*, *aṃsika*, and ‘*sīsika*’. One who lives by means of wages is a *vetanika*;
the suffix *-ika* also occurs in ‘*bhatika*, *kayika*, *vikkayika*, and *kayavikkayika*’. 30.
It conduces to that.

The suffix *ṇika* occurs in the sense of "it leads to" (*saṃvattati*) when preceded by a word ending in the fourth case. Thus, "it leads to renewed existence" (*punabbhavāya saṃvattati*) becomes *ponobhaviko*;
in the feminine, it is *ponobhavikā*. "It leads to the world" (*lokāya saṃvattati*) becomes *lokiko*. "Sagga" means a very excellent (*suṭṭhu aggo*) state;
"it leads to heaven" (*saggāya saṃvattati*) becomes *sovaggiko*, according to the reading beginning with *sassovaka*. "It leads to wealth" (*dhanāya saṃvattati*) becomes *dhaññaṃ*, [ending] in *-yo*.
31. *Tato sambhūtam āgatam*.

The suffix *-ṇika* occurs after words ending in the fifth case (*pañcamī*) in the senses of "originated from that" (*sambhūtam*) or "come from that" (*āgatam*). For example: *mātṛkaḥ* (originated from or come from the mother), *mātṛkam* (the same);

*paitṛkaḥ* (originated from or come from the father). The suffixes *-ṇya*, *-riya*, and *-na* are also seen [in this sense]: *surabhitah sambhūtam* becomes *saurabhyam* (originated from fragrance); *stanataḥ sambhūtam*...
*Thaññaṃ*, *pitito sambhūto*, *pettiyo*, *mātiyo*, *mattiyo*, *macco vā*. 32.
*Tattha vasati*, *vidito*, *bhatto*, *niyutto*.
After a word ending in the seventh case, the suffix *-ika* occurs in such senses as "dwelling there," and so forth. For example: one who dwells at the foot of a tree is a *rukkhamūlika*.

A forest-dweller (*āraññika*); one who frequents charnel grounds (*sosānika*). Known in the world, he is worldly (*lokika*). Those whose food is among the Four Great Kings are the Cātummahārājika devas.

One appointed at the gate is a gatekeeper (*dovārika*); from such readings as *dassoka*, there are also *bhaṇḍāgārika* (treasurer), *navakammika* (superintendent of works), *kiyojātikiya*, and *andhakiya*. 33. This belongs to that [category].
The suffix *ṇika* occurs after words ending in the sixth case in the sense of "belonging to this.
For example: *saṅghassa idaṃ* becomes *saṅghikaṃ*; *puggalikaṃ*, *sakyaputtiko*, *nātiputtiko*, *jenadattiko*, *kiye-sakiyo*, *parakiyo*, *niye-attaniyaṃ*, *kesako*, *rājakaṃ bhaṇḍaṃ*.

The suffix *ṇo* occurs after words ending in the sixth case in the sense of "belonging to this. For example: *kaccāyanassa idaṃ* = *kaccāyanaṃ* (this grammar of Kaccāyana); *sogataṃ sāsanaṃ* (the teaching of the Sugata); *māhisaṃ maṃsādi* (beef, etc.). 35. *Gavādīhi yo*. The suffix *yo* occurs after the group of words beginning with *go*.

The suffix *ya* occurs after words ending in the sixth case, such as *go*, etc., in the sense of "belonging to this. For example: *gavyam* (belonging to cows), such as meat and so forth; *kavyam*; *dabbaṃ*. 36.
*Reyyaṇa* [is added] after *pitṛ* in the sense of "brother.
The suffix *reyyaṇa* occurs after the word *pitṛ* when meaning its brother: *pitu bhātā* = *petteyyo* (father's brother).
37. From the mother’s side, [the suffix] *cha* is used for a sister.

From both the mother’s and the father’s sides, the *cha* suffix is used for their sisters: the mother’s sister is *mātucchā*, and the father’s sister is *pitucchā*. How is it that the word *mātula* (“maternal uncle”) is formed? It is by means of the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātanā*) known as “*mātulāditvāni*” (those beginning with *mātula*). 38. For the mother and father, [the suffix] *maha* is used.

In relation to their own parents, they have the status of *āmaha* (grandchild) toward those [parents’] parents: the mother’s mother is the maternal grandmother (*mātāmahī*), the mother’s father is the maternal grandfather (*mātāmaho*), the father’s mother is the paternal grandmother (*pitāmahī*), and the father’s father is the paternal grandfather (*pitāmaho*). These are not to be understood according to the numerical order [of the preceding list], as they are connected individually.
39. Regarding welfare (*hita*), the suffix *-eyyaṇa* is applied after "mother" and "father": thus, *matteyyo* (one who honors his mother) and *petteyyo* (one who honors his father).
40. Regarding *nindā*, *aññāta*, *appaṭibhāga*, *rassa*, *sadayā*, and *asaññā*:

what [suffix] occurs after these? The suffix *ko* occurs after words such as *nindā*. For example: *nindāyaṃ muṇḍako* (a shaveling who is contemptible), *samaṇako* (a wretched ascetic). After *aññāta*: *kassāyaṃ asso ti assako* ("whose horse is this? thus "one whose horse is unknown").
Through the power of the construction (*payoga*), the specific relationship is understood even though it is not explicitly stated. After *appa*: *telakaṃ* (a little oil), *ghatakaṃ* (a little ghee).

In the sense of resemblance: *hatthiko* (an elephant-like thing), *assako*, *balībaddako*. In the sense of a small animal: *mānusako* (a humanling), *rukkhako* (a little tree), *pilakkhako* (a little wood-apple tree).
In the sense of compassion: *puttako* (a dear son), *vacchako* (a dear calf). In the sense of a designation: *morako* (a peacock-like thing). 41.
The suffix *ṇika* is also used to denote measure.
The suffix *ṇika* (or *ka*) occurs after a word ending in the nominative case in this sense [of "belonging to"], provided that such first-case ending is a measure (*parimāṇa*).

A measure is that by which something is measured. For example: rice for which a *doṇa* is the measure is called *doṇika*; *khārasatika* (worth a hundred measures of salt); *khārasahassika* (worth a thousand measures of salt); *āsītiko vayo* (eighty years of age);
*upaḍḍhakāyikaṃ bimbohanaṃ* (a bolster half the size of the body); *pañcakaṃ* (consisting of five); *chakkaṃ* (consisting of six).
42. *Yattakehi* and *ettake*.

After [words] ending in the nominative case (*paṭhamantehi*), the suffix *ttaka* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*chaṭṭhiyatthe*), provided that the nominative form is a measure (*parimāṇa*). Whatever the measure of that [thing] may be—be it *yattaka*, *tattaka*, *ettaka*, *āvataka*, *yāvataka*, or *tāvataka* (and *etāvataka*)—[these suffixes are applied]. 43. And *sabbā* and *cāvantu*. [The suffixes *ttaka* and *ttika* also occur after these two words.]

After all words ending in the nominative case (*paṭhamantehi*), the suffix *āvantu* occurs in the sense of the genitive (*chaṭṭhiyatthe*), provided that the word ending in the nominative is a measure (*parimāṇa*). For example: "all is its measure" = *sabbāvantaṃ*;
*yāvantaṃ*; *tāvantaṃ*; *etāvantaṃ*. 44.

After the word *kiṃ* ending in the nominative, the suffixes *rati*, *īvarīvata*, *karitta*, and *kā* occur in the sense of the genitive, provided that the word ending in the nominative is [a measure].
There is "measure" (*parimāṇa*). What is their numerical measure? How many are these? How much? How great? How small?
As for how many there are by way of intrinsic nature, they are incalculable (*asaṅkhyo*).
[The suffix] *-ita* is applied after *tāraka*, etc., in the sense of "arisen from. (45)

The suffix *ita* occurs after words beginning with *tāraka* ending in the nominative case to express the sense of the genitive (*chaṭṭhī*), provided that those things have arisen [in the subject]. For example: "the sky has stars arisen in it" is *tārakitaṃ gaganaṃ*; "a tree has flowered" is *pupphito rukkho*; "a creeper has put forth shoots" is *pallavitā latā*. 46.

*Matta* [is used] after a word denoting measure (*māna*) ending in the nominative. The suffix *matta* occurs after a word expressing a measure ending in the nominative to express the sense of "having this much. For example: "this has a measure of one *pala*" is *palamattaṃ*.

Examples: *gāmato āgacchati* (he comes from the village) / *gāmasmā āgacchati*; *corato bhāyati* (he fears the thief) / *corehi bhāyati*; *satthato parihīno* (fallen away from the caravan) / *satthā parihīno*.
96. *Ito*, *etto*, and *kuto*.

The suffix *ṭi* is substituted for *ima* [in the ablative case], and for this [suffix] *ṭa* is substituted; furthermore, *kutta* is substituted for the word *kiṃ*. *Ito* means "from this"; *ato*, *etto* mean "from that" (this);
*kuto* means "from what. 97. By means of *abhi* and others. The suffix *to* occurs after *abhi* and other such words. *Abhito*, *parito*, *pacchato*, *heṭṭhato*.

98. *Ādyādīhi*. After the words beginning with *ādi*, the suffix *to* optionally occurs: *ādo* (from the beginning), *āditō* (from the beginning), *majjhatō*, *antatō*, *piṭṭhitō*, *passatō*, *mukhatō*; *yatōdakaṃ tadādittaṃ* means "the water where it is, that very [place] is set on fire," i.e., "that very water is set on fire.

99. *Sabbādito sattamyā trattā*. After words beginning with *sabba* ending in the locative case (*sattamī*), the suffixes *tra* and *tā* optionally occur. Examples: *sabbatra* (in all), *sabbattha* (in all); *yatra*, *yattha*, *yasmiṃ* (where). Due to the rule of diversity (*bahulādhikāra*), they do not occur after *tumha* and *amha*.
100. *Katthettha kutrātra kvehidha*. [The forms] *kattha*, *ettha*, *kutra*, *atra*, *kva*, and *iha* [are used].
The forms *eta* and *sa* are declined [as follows]: *kasmiṃ*, *kattha*, *kuttra*, *kva*, *etasmiṃ*, *ettha*, *atra*, *asmiṃ*, *iha*, *idha*.
101. *Dhi* optionally after all [forms]. After every form ending in the locative case, the suffix *dhi* may optionally be used.
[Examples: *sabbadhi*, *sabbattha*. 102. *Hiṃ* after *yā*. After a form ending in the ablative case derived from *yā*, the suffix *hiṃ* may optionally be used. [Examples: *yahiṃ*, *yata*.
103. From the seventh case ending, *haṃ* and *tato* become *haṃ* and *hiṃ* respectively; thus: *tahaṃ*, *tahiṃ*, [and] *tatra*.
104. *Kuhiṃ* and *kahaṃ*.

The words *kiṃ* and *saddā*, when ending in the locative case, undergo the suffixes *hiṃ* and *haṃ*, and *kiṃ* becomes *kukā*. [Examples: *kuhiṃ*, *kahaṃ*. As for *kathaṃ kuhiñcananti*: *canaṃ* is another particle (*nipāta*), just like the word *ci* in the expression *kuhiñci*.

105. After *sabba*, *eka*, *añña*, and *yata*, the suffix *dā* occurs when expressing time. The suffix *dā* follows these words when they end in the locative case to denote time. [Examples: *sabbasmiṃ kāle* → *sabbadā*; *ekadā*; *aññadā*; *yadā*; *tadā*. Why say "when expressing time"? [Counter-example: *sabbattha dese* ("in every place"). 106.
After *kadā*, *kudā*, *sadā*, *dhuna*, and *idāni* [the suffix *dā* occurs].
These words are derived through grammatical derivation (*nipacca*). At what time? *kadā* (when); at all times, *sadā* (always); at this time, *adhunā* (now) or *idāni* (now). 107.
*Ajja*, *sajju*, *parajju*, *etarahi*, and *karahā*:
these words are derived through grammatical derivation. All of this—the base form, the suffix, the substitute, and the specific time—is obtained through conventional usage (*nipātana*).

The suffix *jja* is substituted for *idaṃ* when it refers to the current day: *ajja* (today). The suffix *ju* is substituted for the inherent form (*sabhāva*) of *samāna* when referring to the same day:
*sajju* (on the same day). From *apara*, the suffix *jju* is used: *aparajju* (yesterday). The suffix *rahi* is added to *imaṃ* to denote time: *etarahi* (now).
For the word *kiṃ*, the suffix *raha* is used to denote a time other than the present: *karaha* (when?).
108. *Thā* occurs after *sabba* and other words when expressing a manner.

A specific distinction that differentiates a general category is "manner" (*pakāra*). When these words such as *sabba* are present [in the sense of manner], the suffix *thā* is applied. For example: *sabbathā* (in every way), *yathā*, *tathā*.
109. *Katham* and *ittham*.

These suffixes are added after words expressing manner (*pakāra*). What is the function of these [suffixes]? They are the *thaṃ* suffix, and *ka*, *ita*, and *ca* follow them respectively: *kathaṃ* (how?), *itthaṃ* (thus). 110. *Dhā* follows numerals.
After words expressing numbers, the suffix *dhā* occurs in the sense of manner. For example: "in two ways" or "he acts in two ways" is *dvidhā karoti*.
He makes many; he makes one heap into five kinds, making it fivefold; he makes the five kinds into one kind, making it single.
111. Vekā jjhaṃ.
From *eka*, *pakāra* becomes *jjha*. One makes into one; [the suffix] *dhā* becomes *ekadhā*.
112. From *dvi*, *tī* and *edhā*.
From *dvi*, *tī* or *edhā* occurs. Thus: *dvedhā*, *tedhā*, *dvidhā*, *tidhā*.
113. *Jāti* (classes).
Words that denote a class through its various modes (*pakāra*) are *jāti*; for example, "sharp classes" (*paṭujātiyo*) and "soft classes" (*mudujātiyo*).
114. *Kkhattum* (times) is used after a word expressing a turn or a number.

The word *kkhattum* is used after a numeral connected with a "turn" (*vāra*). For example: *dvikkhattum bhuñjati* (he eats twice), meaning he eats two turns during the day. Why include the term "turn"? [To exclude cases such as: *pañca bhuñjati* (he eats five times).

Why include the term "numeral"? [To exclude cases such as: *pahūte vāre bhuñjati* (he eats many turns). 115. From what [word] does it follow? The word *kkhattum* occurs after the numeral *kati* when it is connected with a "turn": *kati vāre*, *katikkhattum bhuñjati* (how many times does he eat?).
116. *Bahumhā* [the suffix] *dhā* occurs after the numeral *bahu* when there is proximity of turns (*vāra*).

That is, *dhā* occurs after the numeral *bahu* when it relates to turns, and also *kkhatthuṃ*, provided there is proximity of the turns. Examples: *bahudhā divasassa bhuñjati* (he eats many times a day), *bahukkhattuṃ bhuñjati*. Why say "when there is proximity"? [Observe: *bahuvāre māsassa bhuñjati* (he eats many times a month). 117. Or *sakiṃ*. [The suffix *dhā* occurs after *sakṛt* to express frequency.]

The suffix *sakim* is used once in the sense of "once" (*ekavāram*) or "at once" (*sakiṃ*). For example: *ekavāraṃ bhuñjati* (he eats once) or *sakiṃ bhuñjati* (he eats at once). What is the meaning of *vā*? It means *ekakkhattuṃ bhuñjati* (he eats one time).
118. Regarding the suffix *so*:
it occurs frequently in the senses of distribution (*vicchā*) and manner (*pakāra*). In the sense of distribution: *khaṇḍaso*, *bilaso*. In the sense of manner: *puthuso*, *sabbaso*.

119. In the sense of "becoming what it was not" (*abhūtatabbhāve*), when there is a connection with the suffixes *ka*, *ra*, *sa*, or *bhū*, the suffix *cī* is used after words denoting a modification (*vikāra*). When that which has not existed in a certain state comes into being in another state through that very state, provided there is a connection with *ka*, *ra*, *sa*, or *bhū*, the suffix *cī* expresses the modification. For example:
*adhavalaṃ dhavalaṃ karoti* (he makes what is not white white) becomes *dhavalīkaroti*; *adhavalo dhavalo siyā* (what is not white may become white) becomes *dhavalī*.

It may be that what is not white becomes white, it turns into white. What is it that brings about that state which was previously non-existent? "He makes a pot," "there is curd," "the pot comes into being.
Why specify "in connection with the root *kar* (to make)"? [Because] "what was not white becomes white" [does not require this]. Why specify "modification"?
[Because] "he makes gold into an earring" [is a modification, but the gold remains gold by its original nature].
120. Other conditions are also seen.

Conditions other than those already mentioned are also seen among the meanings stated and unstated. *Vividhā mātaro* means "various mothers"; *vimātaro* means "stepmothers"; their sons are *vemātikā*.
*Pathaṃ gacchatīti pathāvino* means "one who goes on a path. *Issā assa atthīti issukī* means "one who has envy. *Dhuraṃ*... [the rest of the text follows].
It carries, thus it is a *dhorayha* (draft animal)—this is the suffix *-yha*.
121. In another sense.

The suffixes mentioned are seen even in meanings other than those already stated. One who rules over the Magadhas is a *māgadha*—this is the suffix *-dha*. A *kāsi* is worth a thousand; that which is worth this is a *kāsiya*—this is the suffix *-iya*.
122. In the sense of "own" (saka).
Suffixes are also seen in the sense of "own": *hīnako*, *potako*, *kiccayaṃ*.
123. Elision (*lopa*).

The elision of suffixes is also observed. In the examples "Buddhe ratanaṃ paṇītaṃ" (the Buddha is a sublime jewel) and "cakkhuṃ suññaṃ attena vā attaniyena vā" (the eye is empty of self or of what belongs to self), there is the elision of the abstract suffix (*bhāvappaccaya*).
124. *Sarānamādissāyuvaṇṇassāeo ṇānubandhe*. For vowels beginning with *a*, *i*, or *u*, the substitutions *ā* and *e* occur respectively when followed by a suffix having *ṇ* as its *anubandha*.

When *a*, *i*, or *u* are the initial vowels of a word, they become *ā* and *e* respectively when a suffix with *ṇ* as its *anubandha* follows. Examples: *rāghavo* (descendant of Raghu), *venateyyo* (son of Vinatā), *meniko* (made of mṛdanga wood), *oḷumpiko* (belonging to a raft), *dobhaggaṃ* (misfortune). Why specify "when followed by a suffix with *ṇ* as its *anubandha*" (*ṇānubandhe*)? [Counter-example: *purātano* (ancient).
125. In certain instances of a consonant cluster (*saṃyoga*).

When *i* and *u* vowels are preceded by a vowel and occur at the beginning [of a word], they become *e* and *o* respectively, but only in certain instances within the scope of a consonant cluster that has *ṇ* as its *anubandha*. Examples: *decco*, *koṇḍañño*. Why say "in certain instances"? [Answer: *kattikeyyo*. 126. In the middle [of a word].
In some instances, when the *y*-vowels (*i* and *u*) occur in the middle [of a word], they become *ā*, *e*, and *o*. Examples: *aḍḍhateyyo*, *vāseṭṭho*. 127.

*Kosajja*, *ājjava*, *pārisajja*, *sohajja*, *maddava*, *ārissāsa*, *bhājañña*, *theyya*, *bāhusacca*: these words are derived by adding the suffix *-ya* with the elision of the final vowel (*anubandha*).
The state of being lazy (*kusīta*) is *kosajja*; the state of being upright (*ujju*) is *ājjava*; among the assemblies (*parisāsu*)...
"Sādhu" refers to a member of the assembly; "suhadayo" means a friend, and the state of being such is "sohajjaṃ";
the state of being mild is "maddavaṃ"; that which belongs to a sage (isi) is "īsibhāva" or "ārissaṃ"; that which belongs to a bull (usabha) is "āsabhaṃ";
the state or quality of a well-bred horse (ājānīya) is "ājaññaṃ"; the state or action of a thief (thena) is "theyyaṃ"; and the state of one who has heard much is "bāhusaccaṃ."

Among these, that which has *yamal* as its characteristic is due to *nipātana* (irregular formation). 128. *Saka* is substituted for *mana* and other [bases] when followed by a suffix with *ṇ* as its *anubandha*.
That which exists in the mind (*manas*) is *mānasa*; the state of having a troubled mind is *domanassa*; [the state of having a happy mind is] *somanassa*.
129. *Uvaṇṇassa avaṅ sare*.

After a vowel (*sara*), *avaṅ* is substituted for *uvaṇṇa* when followed by a vowel that is not an *anubandha*. Examples: *rāghavaḥ*, *jambavam*. 130. *Yamhi gośca*. [The substitution of *avaṅ* for *go* occurs] also before the suffix *yam*.
Before an affix beginning with *y*, *avaṅ* is substituted for both *go* and *suvaṇṇa*.
Examples: *gabyaṃ*, *bhātabyo*. 131. *Lopo-vaṇṇivaṇṇānaṃ*:

Before an affix beginning with *y*, there is the elision (*lopa*) of vowels (*avaṇṇa* and *ivaṇṇa*). Examples: *dāyajjaṃ*, *kāruññaṃ*, *ādhipaccaṃ*, *deppaṃ*. Due to the rule being formulated as "mostly" (*bahulaṃ*), this operation does not occur in some instances, such as *kiccayaṃ*.
132. *Rānubandhe-nta sarādissa*:
When a suffix has *r* as its consonantal ligature (*anubandha*), the final vowel of that constituent which begins with a vowel is elided. Examples: *kittakaṃ*, *petteyyaṃ*. 133.
*Kisamahatamime kasa mahā*: For *kisa* and *mahata*, [the suffixes] *ima* and *ika* become *kasa* and *mahā* respectively.
Of *kisa* and *mahat*, these [forms]—*kasamahā* and so forth—occur in their respective order: *kasimā* and *mahimā*.
134. Regarding the substitution of *āya* for *āyu* in the *mantu* suffix:
the replacement of *āyu* with *āya* occurs when the *mantu* suffix follows. Thus: *āyasmā*.
135. *Jo* for *vuddha* when followed by *iya*, *iṭṭha*, or *esu*.
When *jo* occurs before *iya*, *iṭṭha*, or *esu*, it becomes *jeyya* or *jeṭṭha*.
136. For *bāḷha*, *antika*, and *pasattha*, [the suffixes] *sā* and *dha* are substituted for *ne* and *sa*.

In the case of the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha*, applied to words meaning "near" (*nedīya*) and "praised" (*pasattha*), the forms *sādhi*, *sādhiṭṭha*, *nedi*, and *nediṭṭha*, as well as *seyya* and *seṭṭha*, arise respectively.
137. Regarding *kaṇa*, *kanā*, and *yuvan*:
in the case of the suffixes *iya* and *iṭṭha*, applied to words meaning "young" (*appayuva*), *kaṇa* and *kanā* arise respectively. Thus: *kaṇiya*, *kaṇiṭṭha*; *kaniya*, *kaniṭṭha*.
138. *Lopo vī mantu vantūnaṃ*.

There is elision (*lopa*) of the suffixes *-vī*, *-mantu*, and *-vantu* before the [suffixes] *-iya*, *-iṭṭha*, and so forth. For example: one who is exceedingly wise is *medhiya*, *medhiṭṭha*; one who is exceedingly mindful is *satiya*, *satiṭṭha*; one who is exceedingly virtuous is *guṇiya*, *guṇiṭṭha*. 139. *Ḍe satissa tissa*.
[In the dative case (*ḍe*), there is the substitution of *tissa* for *satissa*.]
In the word *sattha*, there is the elision of the letter *t* when followed by *ti*. Thus: *vīsati-sataṃ* (twenty hundred), *tiṃsati-sataṃ* (thirty hundred).
140. *Etasseṭa ttake*:
When *ttaka* follows, *eṭ* is substituted for this [word-final *a*]. Thus: *ettakaṃ* (so much).
141. Or *ṇikassiya*.
After *ṇika*, *iya* optionally occurs; thus, *sakyaputtiya* or *sakyaputtika*.
142. For a word ending in *adhātu*, *gha* is substituted for *kā* and *syādi*.

In the case of a non-feminine suffix (*adhātu*), the letter *k* that follows [a vowel], the *a* preceding it frequently becomes *i*, provided that the feminine suffix (*syādi*) does not intervene after it. Examples: *bālikā*, *kārikā*. Why "non-feminine suffix"? Example:
*sakā* (where the suffix is feminine). Why "the letter *k*"? Example: *nandanā* (where the suffix begins with *n*). Why "provided the feminine suffix does not intervene"?
Example: *bahuparibbājakā mathurā*, *bahucammikā*; these are established because they are separated from the feminine suffix by the letter *k*. Thus ends the section on *gha*.
What [is it]? "Bālako," he says; what [is it]? "A hall for many activities.
Thus ends the fourth section, beginning with *Ṇa*, in the *Vutti* on the *Moggallāna-vyākaraṇa*.
5. The Fifth Chapter (Khādi) 1. Regarding the roots *tij*, *mā*, and *kha*:
*sa* and *kha* occur as suffixes in the senses of endurance (*khanti*) and investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).

In the sense of endurance, *tij* and in the sense of investigation, *mā* take the suffix *kha* respectively, as in *titikkhā* (endurance), *vīmaṃsā* (investigation), *titikkhati* (he endures), and *vīmaṃsati* (he investigates). What is the meaning of the root *kham* in the sense of investigation? It is *tejanaṃ* (sharpening), *tejo* (heat/energy), and *tejayati* (to sharpen); likewise, *mānanaṃ* (measuring), *māno* (pride), and *māneti* (to measure).
2. *Kit* becomes *cho* when used in the senses of healing (*tikicchā*) and doubt (*saṃsaya*).

When occurring in the sense of healing or doubt, *kit* becomes *cho*. Examples: *tikicchā*, *vicikicchā*, *tikicchati*, *vicikicchati*. With the exception of *niketa*, *saṃketa*, *ketanaṃ*, *keto*, and *ketayati*.
3. In the sense of censure (*nindā*), *gup*, *badh*, and *vas* become *bho*.

When *nindā* (blame) is being expressed, *gu* and *badha* become *cho* and *bassa*, respectively. [Examples: *jigucchā*, *bībhacchā*; *jigucchati*, *bībhacchati*; except for the sense of "concealing," *gopanaṃ*, *gopo*, *gopeti*, and *badhako*.
4. Regarding the elision after *tum*:

in the sense of desire (*icchā*), after a word ending in the suffix *tum*, the suffixes *kha* and *sa* frequently occur with the suffix *cha*, and there is an elision of the *tum* suffix because it has already been heard [in the preceding form].

*bubhukkhā*, *jigīsā*, *jighacchā*; *bubhukkhati*, *jigīsati*, *jighacchati*. Why is it not [formed] here as ‘*bhottum icchati*’ (desires to eat)? Because it is expressed by another word (*padantara*).
What is the purpose of [the condition] *tuṃ-smā*? [Example: *bhojanam icchati* (he desires food). What is the purpose of [the condition] *icchāyaṃ*? [Example: *bhuñjitum gacchati* (he goes to eat).
How is [the form] ‘*kūlaṃ vipatī satī*’ (being about to fall into the bank) explained? Just as in the case of ‘*kūlaṃ patitum icchati*’ (he desires to fall into the bank).
When there is a sentence (*vākya*), there will likewise be a derivative form (*vutti*). But how indeed does a sentence become a discourse (*katha*)?

It is through the world’s desire for such expression. 5. *Īya* as the object. From the sense of desiring an object, the suffix *īya* occurs in the meaning of "desire. One desires a son: *putthīyati*. Why "object"? (To exclude cases where no object is intended.)

[He] desires a horse (*asinecchati*). Why is it that [the same form] does not occur here in the sense of “he desires the king’s son” (*rañño puttam icchati*)? Because of the requirement of expectancy (*sāpekkhattā*);

for one who is expectant of one thing cannot simultaneously undergo a state of identity with another. But then, would it not also fail to occur here in the sense of “he desires his own son” (*attanō puttam icchati*)?
It certainly should not occur here either; for there is no such expression as “he desires his own son” (*attanō puttīyati*). How, then, regarding the son...
How is self-dependence understood? Because it is not heard of in relation to another, and because desire has that as its object.
6. Regarding the sense of behaving like:

after a word denoting an object of comparison, the suffix *īya* occurs in the sense of behaving. One behaves like a son: *puttīyati māṇavakaṃ* (he treats the young student as a son). Why "object of comparison"? [Example: He behaves like a son (*puttamācarati*).
7. Ādhāra (Locative).

The suffix *īya* is used in the sense of location (*ādhāratthe*) when the object of comparison serves as the locus. For example: *kuṭīyati pāsāde* (“he behaves as if in a hut while in a palace”), *pāsādīyati kuṭiyaṃ bhikkhu* (“the monk behaves as if in a palace while in a hut”). 8. Kattutāyo (Instrumental). [The suffix *tā* is used] in the sense of the agent (*kattutā*).
The suffix *āya* occurs after a noun in the sense of behaving like that [noun]. For example: *pabbatāyati*, meaning "he behaves like a mountain. 9. In the sense of becoming (*yattha*).

The suffix *āya* frequently occurs after a noun in the sense of the transition from not having been to being so (*abhūtatadbhāve*). Examples: *bhusāyati*, *paṭapaṭāyati*, *lohitāyati*. Why does it not occur here in the case of "he becomes intense" (*bhusī bhavati*) when derived from "he makes intense" (*bhusaṃ karoti*)? Because the meaning has already been expressed [by the verb itself].
10. *Saddādīni karoti*.

The suffix *-āya* occurs in the sense of “he acts with” when [words] such as *sadda*, ending in the accusative case, are used. Examples: *saddāyati*, *verāyati*, *kalahāyati*, *dhūpāyati*. 11. *Numotvasso*. [The suffix *-āya* is applied] after [words] ending in *-nu* or *-m*.
In the sense of "he acts toward this [person] with *namo*," the suffix *assa* occurs. He pays homage to the Tathāgata. 12. Regarding the meaning of a verbal root (*dhātu*), the suffix *nāma* occurs.
After a word ending in *nāma*, the suffix *iha* occurs diversely in the sense of a verbal root.
From *hatthinā* (by means of an elephant), one derives *atihatthayati* (he passes by); from *vīṇāya* (with a lute), one derives *upagāyati* (he sings along).
He plays the lute; he makes discipline firm, he strengthens it; the night becomes pure, it is purified; he asks about the wholesome, he makes it wholesome.
13. Also by means of truth and so forth.

The suffix *āpi* occurs after verbal roots (*dhātu*) in the sense of "causing to be" (*sacca-ādi*). Examples: *saccāpeti*, *atthāpeti*, *vedāpeti*, *sukkha-peti*, *sukhāpeti*, *dukkhāpeti*. 14. *Kriyatthā*: This is a governing heading (*adhikāra*) extending until the end of the treatise.
A root (*dhātu*) is called *kriyattha* (meaning-action) because action (*kriyā*) is its meaning (*attha*).
15. *ṇi* after *cur*-beginning [roots].

After roots beginning with *cur* when they have the sense of "doing" (*kriya*), the suffix *ṇi* is generally added in the sense of the root itself (*sakattha*). The letter *ṇ* is for the purpose of causing *vṛddhi*; this applies elsewhere as well. Thus: *corayati*, *lāḷayati*. How is it that one says “he causes the kingdom to be ruled” (*rajjaṃ kāreti*)? By means of a division of the rule (*yogavibhāga*). 16.
And also *ṇa* and *api* in the sense of the activity of an instigator (*payojaka-byāpāra*).
When one employs an agent, the affixes *ṇi*, *ṇā*, and *pī* generally occur in place of the verbal root (*kriyattha*) to express that agent's activity: *kāreti*, *kārāpeti*.

But surely, since the agent himself is the employer of instruments and other factors, shouldn't these affixes also apply to his activity? They do not, because this is precluded by the force of the specific mention of "employer" (*payojaka*) [in the rule], and also by the force of the separate statement regarding the *cur*-class verbs.
Beyond this, there is only *ṇā* and *pī*; from the vowel *u* there is only *ṇi*; and the other two [affixes] are from the other vowels.

17. *Kyo* [is the suffix] after verbal roots (*kriyattha*) when followed by endings beginning with *māna*, *anta*, etc., which are prescribed for the passive (*bhāva*) and the object (*karman*), excluding the aorist (*parokkhā*).
The mention of *anta* is for the sake of subsequent rules; the letter *k* is for the purpose of preventing vowel strengthening (*avuddhi*), as it is also in subsequent cases.
Examples: *ṭhīyamānaṃ*, *ṭhīyate*; *sūyamānaṃ*, *sūyate*. [The rule applies] "when followed by endings beginning with *māna*, *anta*, etc., excluding the aorist."

What [is the case]? In the examples "The deity was present by means of Devadatta" (*babhūva devadattena*) and "The husk split" (*bibhida kusulaḥ*), the status of the object (*karmatā*) is understood from the hearing of the word "splits" (*bhijjate*), and the status of the agent (*kartṛtā*) is understood from the hearing of the word "by itself" (*sayameva*).

However, when there is a desire to express the agenthood, it becomes "the husk splits itself" (*bhindati kusulaḥ ātmānam*); in this way, other cases should also be followed according to the scriptures. [This applies] "to the roots *mān*, *tan*, etc., when they are not perceptible."

This is the governing rule up to [the sūtra] *atanādito* (5.26). Furthermore, since these suffixes beginning with *kya* are prescribed when the suffixes beginning with *tya* follow—being those prescribed for the agent (*kartṛ*), the object (*karman*), and the abstract state (*bhāva*)—they are to be understood as occurring only in those very cases.

Thus, they occur with intransitive roots in the sense of the agent, with transitive roots in the sense of both the agent and the object, and in the sense of the object and the abstract state when there is a desire to express the object. Of which...

Furthermore, it should be understood that an action (kriyā) which depends upon an object (karman) is "with an object" (sakarmaka), whereas an action which depends merely upon an agent (kartṛ) is "without an object" (akarmaka).
18. [The suffix] *lo* [is used] in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*).

The suffix *lo* occurs in place of the personal endings beginning with *āna* and *anti*, which are prescribed for the agent (*kattṛ*) when they follow verbal roots denoting action (*kriyārtha*) and are not separated [by other elements]. The letter *l* is for the purpose of distinguishing it from the suffix *ñi* (as per rule 5.1.63). Examples: *pacamāno*, *pacanto*, *pacati*. 19. *Maṃ ca rudhādīnaṃ*:

After roots belonging to the *rudhādi* class, the suffix *ma* is substituted for the agent-prescribed endings beginning with *āna* and *anti*; furthermore, the vowel following the final consonant (*anta-sara*) becomes *m*. The letter *m* is a phonetic marker (*anubandha*), and the letter *a* is for the purpose of pronunciation (*uccāraṇattha*). Examples: *rundhamāno*, *rundhanto*, *rundhati*.

20. After [causative] suffixes ending in -ṇi, -ṇāpi, or -āpi, the substitution of *lo* for the suffix *āna* prescribed when the agent is expressed occurs optionally before the endings beginning with *ti*. Thus: *orayanto*, *corento*;
*kārayanto*, *kārento*, *kārāpayanto*, *kārāpento*; *saccāpayanto*, *saccāpento*; *corayati*, *coreti*; *kārayati*.
*kāreti*, *kārāpayati*, *kārāpeti*, *saccāpayati*, *saccāpeti*. This particle *vā* has the sense of expressing a fixed alternative;
by it, [the suffix] *māna* is used invariably: *corayamāno*, *kārayamāno*, *kārāpayamāno*, *saccāpayamāno*. 21. After roots beginning with *div*, the suffix *yaka* [is added].
The suffix *yaka* occurs after roots beginning with *div-* in the sense of the present participle (*la*). Example:
*dibbanto*, *dibbati*. 22.
After roots beginning with *tud-*, the suffix *ko* occurs in the sense of the present participle (*la*). Example: *tudamāno*, *tudanto*, *tudati*.
23. *Knā* after *ji* and others.

The suffix *knā* occurs after roots beginning with *ji* when the object (*la*) is present. Examples: *jinanto*, *jināti*. How is it that “*jayanto*,” *jayati*? Because of their inclusion in the *bhūvādi* class.
24. *Kṇā* after *ky* and others.
After roots beginning with *kī*, the suffix *kṇa* occurs when the object is a *la*-ending word. [Examples: *kiṇanto* (buying), *kiṇāti* (he buys). 25.

After roots beginning with *su*, *kṇa* occurs when the object is a *la*-ending word. [Examples: *suṇamāno*, *suṇanto*, *suṇoti*. How is it that there is *suṇāti*? Because it is included in the list of roots beginning with *kī*.

26. *Tan-ādito*. After roots beginning with *tan*, *o* is substituted for *l* when the suffix *a* follows. *tanoti*. 27. *Bhāva-kammesu tabbā-nīyā*. The suffixes *tabba* and *nīya* occur after verbal roots in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*).

The *tabba*, *aniya*, and *ya* suffixes, when following verbal roots, frequently occur in the senses of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the object (*kamma*). For example: *kattabbaṃ*, *karaṇīyaṃ*, *kattabbo kaṭo*, *karaṇīyo*.

Due to the application of the rule of "frequently" (*bahula*), they also occur in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*) and other cases: *sinānīyaṃ cuṇṇaṃ* (bathing powder), *dānīyo brāhmaṇo* (a Brahmin worthy of gifts), *sammāvattanīyo guru* (a teacher who should be properly attended to), *pavacanīyo upajjhāyo* (a preceptor who should be spoken to respectfully), and *upaṭṭhānīyo sisso* (a student who should be served).
28. Ghyana.

After a verbal root meaning "to do" (kriyārtha), the suffix -ghyaṇa is frequently applied in the sense of the bhāva (action/state) and kamma (object). Examples: vākyaṃ, kāriyaṃ, ceyyaṃ, jeyyaṃ. 29. And after the root ās (to sit/remain), [the suffix -ghyaṇa is applied].

The suffix *ghyaṇ* occurs after verbal roots in the sense of the abstract action (*bhāva*) or the object (*karman*), and for this [suffix], *e* is substituted for *a*. Example: *deyyaṃ* (that which is to be given). 30. After the group of roots beginning with *vad*, the suffix *ya* occurs frequently in the sense of the abstract action or the object when expressing the meaning of the action itself.

Examples: *vajjaṃ* (that which is to be spoken), *majjaṃ* (that which is to be drunk), *gammaṃ* (that which is to be gone to). (42) Regarding the rule "after *bhuj*": *bhojjo odano* (rice that is to be eaten), *bhojjā yāgu* (gruel that is to be eaten), *bhoggaṃ aññaṃ* (other things that are to be enjoyed).

The time for making has arrived. In this way, even when [the time] is "more than a moment" (*uddhamohuttika*), they are established as being understood from the verbal roots *kar-* (to do) and so forth.

Likewise, when the agent (*kattar*) is understood as distinguished by capability (*satti*) and distinguished by the necessity (*āvassaka-dhamma*) of the action, they are established from the abstract state (*bhāva*):
"More than a moment ago, it must be done by you; the kingdom must be ruled by you. You are worthy; by you..."

"Sāra" (the essence) must be carried; "bhavaṃ sakko" (the venerable Sakka); "bhotā" (by the master), "avassaṃ kaṭo kattabbo" (a mat must certainly be made); "bhotā nikkho dātabbo" (a coin must be given by the master). 33.

*Ltuṇaka* suffixes occur after verbal roots when there is an agent (*kattari*). When there is an agent as the factor of action, *ltuṇaka* suffixes occur frequently after verbal roots. Examples: *paṭhitā*, *pāṭhako*. Is it only "frequently"? [Yes.]

One who is carried away by the feet is a *pādahāraka*; one who seizes by the throat is a *galecopaka*. The suffix *-ta* is established here because it is prescribed as a general rule for those worthy of, or excellent in, moral virtue and the like;
thus: "You, indeed, are one who has been chosen (*pariggahitā*) by a maiden," meaning "you are worthy of this. Furthermore, regarding virtue and so forth:
"the taker of the boy," "the goer of the spittle," and "the shavers of the bride who has already been chosen" [are examples of such usage].

[The suffix] *-aka* is generally used in the sense of the agent (*kattari*) when it denotes something manifest (*āvī*). [As in: “one who sees danger” (*bhayadassāvī*). The separation of the compound (*bhinnayogakaraṇa*) is for the purpose of indicating a restricted scope (*appavisayatā*); because it is prescribed as a general rule (*sāmaññavihitattā*), it occurs even in the case of “virtue” (*sīla*) and so forth. 35. *Āsiṃsāyam-ako*. [The suffix] *-aka* is used in the sense of wishing (*āsiṃsāya*).

The suffix *aka* occurs after a verbal root (*kriyāttha*) when expressing a wish (*āsīsā*) or an action currently being performed (*gamyamāna*), provided it denotes the agent (*kattari*). For example: "May he live" (*jīvatūti*) results in *jīvaka*; "May he rejoice" (*nandatūti*) results in *nandaka*; "May he become" (*bhavatūti*) results in *bhavaka*. 36. After the root *kar*, the suffix *ṇana* occurs.

The suffix *ṇana* occurs after the root *kar* when denoting the agent. For example: "He does" (*karotīti*) results in *kāraṇaṃ*. Why "when denoting the agent"? [Because] *karaṇaṃ* (the instrument) is not so formed.

37. *Hāta* [is used] in the sense of "in the time of rice" (*vīhikālesu*) and also in the sense of "rice" (*vīhismiṃ*). Furthermore, the suffix *ṇa* occurs when the agent (*kattari*) is expressed. *Hāyana* means "harvest," and *hāyana* means "year. Why say "in the sense of the time of rice"? [Answer: [To show that it is not used otherwise, as in] *hātā*. 38. *Vidā* [takes the suffix] *kū*.
The suffix *kū* is added after the root *vid* when it means "one who knows" (*kattar*).
Examples: *vidū*, *lokavidū*. 39. *Vito ñāto*:
The suffix *kū* is added after the root *jñā* preceded by the prefix *vi-* when it means "one who knows. Example: *viññū*. Why is it said "preceded by *vi-*"? [To exclude: *paññā* (wisdom).
40. *Kammā*.

After the word *kamma*, the suffix *ñāiccasmā* becomes *kū* when expressing the agent (*kattari*). Examples: *sabbaññū* (all-knowing), *kālaññū* (knowing the right time). 41. *Kvacaṇa*. [The suffixes *kvaci* and *caṇa* are used in the sense of "somewhere" or "at some time"].

The suffix *aṇ* sometimes occurs after verbal roots meaning "to do" when used with an object, provided the agent is expressed. [Examples: *kumbhakāra* (pot-maker), *saralāva* (grass-cutter), *mantajjhāya* (Veda-reciter).

Because of the rule of frequent occurrence (*bahulādhikāra*), it does not occur here: *ādiccaṃ passati* (he sees the sun), *himavantaṃ suṇoti* (he hears the Himalayas), *gāmaṃ gacchati* (he goes to the village). Why say "sometimes"? [Counter-example: *kammakāra* (laborer). 42. *Gamā rū*.
After the word *kamma* (object), when used in the sense of the agent (*kattari*), the suffixes *ru* and *ha* occur. Examples: *vedagū*, *pāragū*. 43.
After the words *samāna*, *añña*, *bhavanta*, *yādi*, and *upamāna*, the suffixes *disa*, *kamme*, *rī*, and *rikkhaka* occur.

After the words *samāna* and so forth, after the words beginning with *yādi*, and after words expressing comparison (*upamāna*), the suffixes *disa*, *kamme*, *rī*, and *rikkhaka* occur in the sense of the object (*kammakārake*). Example: *samāno viya*.
*Sadī* means "appearing like," *sadikkho*, or *sadiso*. *Aññādī* means "appearing as another," *aññādikkho*, or *aññādiso*. *Bhavādī* means "appearing as existence," *bhavādikkho*, or *bhavādiso*.

*Yādī* means "appearing as which," *yādikkho*, or *yādiso*. *Tyādī* means "appearing as that," *tyādikkho*, or *tyādiso*. [Question: Why [is it said] "from *samāna* and so forth"? [Answer: It appears like a tree (*rukkho*). [Question:

Why [is it said] "a standard of comparison" (*upamāna*)? [Answer: He appears. [Question: Why [is it said] "in the sense of the object" (*kamma*)? [Answer: He sees like him. The letter *ra* serves the purpose of eliding the final vowel and the following consonant.
The letter *ka* signifies the absence of the vowel *e*. 44. Regarding the suffixes *a*, *ghaṇ*, and *gha*:
in the sense of a state (*bhāva*) or an agent (*kāraka*), the suffixes *a*, *ghaṇ*, and *gha* frequently occur after verbal roots meaning "to do" (*kriya*). [Examples: *appaggaḥa*, *niggaha*, *kara*.
*Garō*, *cayō*, *jayō*, *ravō*, *bhavō*, *pacō*, *vacō*, *annadō*, *purindadō*, *īsakkarō*, *dukkarō*, *sukarō*. In the sense of becoming (*ghana-bhāve*): *pāko*, *cāgo*, *bhāvo*.

Also, in the sense of an agent (*kārake*), by way of a derivative suffix (*saññāya*): first, that which one goes forth by means of it is a *pādo*; that which breaks is a *rogo*; that which enters is a *veso*;
that which remembers a later time is a *sāro*, meaning a firm part; those by which things are split apart are... [the rest of the text follows].
*dārā* (wife); *jīryati anena iti jāraḥ* (one by whom one ages); even in the sense of non-perception (*asaññā*), *dāyaḥ* is given; *lābhaḥ* (gain), *labdhaḥ* (obtained);
*ghavakaḥ*, *nipakaḥ*, *kapiyaḥ*, *khipaḥ*, *bhujah*, *āyudham*.
45. From the root *dā*.
The suffix *atha* occurs after the roots *dā*, *dhā*, and *bhū* when expressing the sense of the agent (*kāraka*) or the action itself (*bhāva*).

Examples: *ādatha*, *nidhatha*, *vālatha*. 46. *Vam-ādīhi athu*: The suffix *athu* occurs after the roots *vam* and others when expressing the sense of the agent or the action itself. Examples: *vamathu*, *vepathu*, (*avathu*, *sayathu*).

The suffix *kvi* occurs frequently in the sense of the abstract state (*bhāva*) and the agent (*kāraka*). The letter *k* serves the purpose of causing the *kā*-suffixation. Examples: *abhibhū*, *sayambhū*, *bhattaggaṃ*, (*dānaggaṃ*), *salākaggaṃ*, *sabhā*, *pabhā*.

From verbal roots (*kriyattha*) expressing action, there arise feminine nouns denoting the state (*bhāva*) or the agent (*kāraka*). [Examples of such nouns are: going (*gamana*), giving (*dāna*), recipient (*sampadāna*), source (*apādāna*), locus (*adhikaraṇa*), moving (*calana*), burning (*jalana*), being angry (*kodhana*), provoking anger (*kopana*), adorning (*maṇḍana*), and decorating (*bhūsana*).
49. *Itthiyamaṇa tti ka yaka yā ca*:

In the feminine gender, for the state and the agent, suffixes beginning with *a* (such as *a*, *ti*, *kkhā*, *vīmaṃsā*) and *ana* are frequently applied to verbal roots. [Examples are: endurance (*titikkhā*), investigation (*vīmaṃsā*).
Jigucchā, pipāsā, puttiyā, īhā, bhikkhā, āpadā, medhā, godhā, ṇakārā, hārā, tārā, dhārā, ārā, kti-iṭṭhi,
siṭṭhi, bhitti, bhatti, tanti, bhūti, ka-guhā, rujā, mudā, yaka-vijjā, ijjā, ya-seyyā,

50. After *jāhā* and *ni*, the suffix *ni* occurs in the feminine. [Examples: *jāni*, *hāni*. 51.
After *karā*, the suffixes *ri* and *riya* occur.

The word *karato* becomes *ririyo* when followed by a feminine suffix. *Karaṇaṃ* means action (*kiriyā*). How is it called "action" (*kriyā*)? It is due to the grammatical rule of irregular derivation (*nipātanā*) from the form "kriyāyaṃ. 52. *Iki-tī* [are substituted] for a root of similar form.

When a word expressing an action (*kriyattha*) follows another word expressing an action that is identical in form (*sarūpe*), the affixes *iki* and *tī* are applied. This occurs in cases such as *vaci*, *yudhi*, and *pacati*. In examples like "the letter *a* [is] the letter *ka*" (*akāro kakāro*), there is a compound with the word *kāra*; this is just as in the case of *evakāro*.

53. The suffix *ṇī* occurs after words such as *sīla*, *abhikkhañña*, and *vassaka* when they function as verbal nouns (*kriyattha*). Examples: *uṇhabhojī* (one who eats hot food), *khīrapāyī* (one who drinks milk), *avassakārī* (one who acts necessarily), *satandāyī* (one who gives regularly).
54. [The suffix *ṇī* also occurs after] *thāvara*, *ittara*, *bhaṅgura*, *bhidura*, *bhāsura*, and *bhassara*.
These suffixes are applied when virtue (*sīla*) is being understood. 55.
*Ktavantu* and *ktāvī* [are used] in the sense of the agent (*kattari*) and the past (*bhūte*).

When expressing a past meaning, the suffixes *ktavantu* and *ktāvī* occur after verbal roots (*kriyattha*) in the sense of the agent. Examples: *vijitavā*, *vijitāvī*. The governing rule "in the past" (*bhūte*) applies up to the rule "having the sense of food" (*āhāratthā*; 5.60).
56. Regarding the past tense, the state, and the object:

the suffix *kta* occurs in the sense of the past, the state (*bhāva*), and the object (*karman*). Example: "It was sat by you" (*āsitaṃ bhavatā*); "A mat was made by you" (*kato kaṭo bhavatā*). 57. And [the suffix *kta* occurs] in the sense of the agent (*kartṛ*) when there is a commencement [of an action].

The suffix *kta* occurs after a verb root when the agent (*kartṛ*) is expressed, according to the specific rules. For example: *pakato bhavaṃ kaṭaṃ* (the venerable one has made the mat), *pakato kaṭo bhavatā* (the mat was made by the venerable one); *pasutto bhavaṃ* (the venerable one has slept), *pasuttaṃ bhavatā* (sleeping was done by the venerable one). 58.
After the roots *ṭhā*, *sav*, *vas*, *silis*, *sī*, *ruha*, *jara*, and *janī*, the suffix *kta* occurs when the agent is expressed, according to the specific rules.
For example: *upaṭṭhito guruṃ bhavaṃ* (the venerable one has attended upon the teacher), *upaṭṭhito guru bhotā* (the teacher was attended upon by the venerable one).
You have attended upon the teacher; the teacher has been attended upon by you. You have served the teacher; the teacher has been served by you.
You have embraced the teacher; the teacher has been embraced by you. You have supported the bedstead; the bedstead has been supported by you.
You have climbed the tree; the tree has been climbed by you. You have overcome the outcaste woman.
Devadatta; the outcaste woman was followed by Devadatta; the young man was born after the young woman; the young woman was born after the young man. 59.

The suffix *kta* occurs after verbal roots meaning "to go" (*gamanattha*) and after intransitive roots (*akammaka*), when used in the sense of a locus (*adhāra*), as well as in the sense of the agent (*kattar*), according to the rules. This belongs to them...

In a question: "Would the Venerable One master the Vinaya, or rather the Dhamma? or "Should I go to the Uposatha, or should I not go? In a wish:

"May I see you receive full ordination; may I see you remain free from illness for a hundred years; may your honor cook having attained the proper method; may your honor perform meritorious deeds;
may your honor eat here; may your honor sit here; may your honor teach the young brahmin.

Even at the times when permission has been granted, [the action] is indeed accomplished... because even there, it is due to the completion of the formal procedure; regarding the permission: 'You should do it in this way.'"
"You should do what is appropriate at the proper time; the time has come for you to perform what is appropriate. If it is appropriate for the Saṅgha, let the Saṅgha perform the Uposatha.
O Blessed One, this is the time; O Sugata, this is the time for the Blessed One to lay down a training rule for his disciples.
They even send a message, saying: 'O man, you should go to the village.'"
10. *tu*, *antu*, *hi*, *tha*, *mi*, *ma*, *taṃ*, *ssu*, *vho*, *e*, *āmase*—these [suffixes] occur after verbal roots (*kriyātthato*) in interrogative sentences and the like.
[Examples: *gacchatu*, *gacchantu*; *gacchāhi*, *gacchatha*; *gacchāmi*, *gacchāma*; *gacchataṃ*, *gacchantaṃ*;
*gacchassu*, *gacchavho*; *gacche*, *gacchāmase*. In an interrogation: *kinnu*...?
Indeed, sir, study the grammar; in a request: "Grant this to me"; in a benediction: "May your honor live long"; in an injunction: "May your honor perform the rite";
"May your honor perform a meritorious deed"; "May your honor eat here"; "May your honor sit here"; in an instruction:
"Venerable Sir, may the Blessed One recite the Pātimokkha for the monks"; in a sending: "Go to the village, O messenger"; in a consent: "So be it."
"Act! This is the time for you, O Great Hero; it is the time to arise in the mother's womb.
(11) *Satti*, *araha*, *veyya*, etc.:

after verbal roots (*satti*), the suffixes *ara* and *hattha* are used with the meanings of the verb (*kriyattha*), and the optative (*eyya*) and other suffixes follow. "May Your Majesty indeed rule the kingdom; may Your Majesty be capable and worthy. (11)

12. *Sambhāvane vā*. When there is a sense of possibility (*sambhāvana*) understood, and the verbal root expresses that possibility, the suffixes *eyya* and so forth occur optionally. "Even one might split a mountain with one's head" (*api pabbataṃ sirasā bhindeyya*); however, in the case of the non-occurrence of the action (*kriyātipatti*), [the form] begins with *ssā*:
"Even if struck by a thunderbolt, he would not have fallen" (*asaniyāpi hato nāpatissā*). I consider it possible; I believe it.
I consider that you might eat; you will eat, sir; you have eaten, sir; you did eat, sir. But in the case of the past conditional (kriyātipatti), [the suffix] *ssādī* is used:
I do not believe that you would not have eaten, sir. 13. In connection with the prohibitive particle *mā*, [the suffixes] *ī* and *ā* and so forth are used.

When there is a connection (*yoga*), the *ī*-class vowels and the *ā*-class vowels may optionally [be substituted]. "May you not do such a thing again," "May your lordship not go to the forest"—is this not so?
"May your mind not wander among the strands of sensual pleasure," "May you not do it," "May you not have done it"—this undertaking refers to the sense of the past;
however, through its connection with other words, such as "he will become a Buddha," its status as the future tense is understood.
"Thus the mat will be made tomorrow;
the task was already underway"—in such cases, "lunāhi lunāhi" (reap, reap) and "lunassu lunassu" (reap, reap) are the repeated dual forms of the second person singular imperative.
This means: "Just as one who is himself in haste also urges others on, so too does he perform the action."
In this way: "He cuts," "he indeed cuts"; "you two cut," "you two indeed cut"; likewise in other tenses: "he cut," "he indeed cut"; "he has cut," "he indeed has cut"; "he cut," "he indeed cut";
"he will cut," "he indeed will cut"—thus it should be applied to the optative as well. Likewise in the case of conjunction:
"He wanders from monastery to monastery," "he indeed wanders from monastery to monastery"; "may you two wander from monastery to monastery," "you two indeed wander from monastery to monastery."

However, when there is a difference in activity (*byāpāra*), because the word denoting the commonality (*sāmānyavacana*) itself is pervasive, there is no separate application [of the suffix]; for example:
*odanaṃ bhuñja, yāguṃ piva, dhānā khāda*—this person consumes [all of these] together. 14.

For the six preceding and following [suffixes], whether they refer to one or many, and for the substitutes *tumha* and *amha*, the two [sets] correspond respectively to the second, first, and third persons.

When there are agents—whether singular or plural—that are expressed by the words *tumhaṃ* and *amha*, as well as those expressed by other words (*tadañña*), two forms each of the first six case-endings (the *pubbacchakka*) and the last six case-endings (the *paracchakka*) are used respectively for the middle and the highest persons; these denote the action (*kriyattha*).
This word "highest" (*uttama*) is conventionally established (*ruḷha*) by its own nature (*sabhāvato*) in the third dual; [examples are: *tvaṃ gacchasi*, *tumhe gacchatha*, *tvaṃ gacchase*, *tumhe*.

*gacchavhe*, *ahaṃ gacchāmi*, *mayaṃ gacchāma*, *ahaṃ gacche*, *mayaṃ gacchāmhe*, *so gacchati*, *te gacchanti*, *so gacchate*, *te gacchante*—these forms occur even when the second person pronouns (*tumhaṃ*, *tumhe*, etc.

are not explicitly employed, because they are obtained through their inherent capacity (*sāmatthiya*). [Examples: *gacchasi*, *gacchatha*, *gacchase*, *gacchavhe*, *gacchāmi*, *gacchāma*, *gacche*, *gacchāmhe*.
*gacchati*, *gacchanti*, *gacchate*, *gacchante*.
15. *Āīssādīsvaña vā*.

After a verbal root (*kriyattha*) beginning with *ā*, *ī*, or *ssā*, the suffix *añ* optionally occurs. The letter *ñ* is an *anubandha*. [Examples: *agamā*, *gamā*, *agamī*, *gamī*, *agamissā*, *gamissā*.
16. *Ādīsvāho brūssa*. After the root *brū*, *āho* is substituted [for *bru*] when followed by initial vowels (*ādi*). [Examples: *āha*, *āhu*. 17. *Bhūssa vuka*.
[The suffix] *vuka* is added after the root *bhū*.
In the case of *bhū* and others, *vuka* is substituted. The letter *k* is a suffix (*anubandha*), and the letter *u* is for the purpose of pronunciation;
thus, *babhūva*. 18. *Pubbassa a*:
In the case of *bhū* and others when doubled, *a* is substituted for the preceding *bhū*; thus, *babhūva*.
19. Or *ussaṃ* becomes *vā*. In place of the following *ussa*, there occurs either *aṃ* or *su*. [Examples: *ahaṃsu*, *āhu*. 20.
For *tya* and *tīnaṃ*, there is *ṭa* or *ṭū*.

When *ti* and *anti* follow, they become *ṭa* and *ṭu*. The letter *ṭa* serves the purpose of indicating all substitutions; thus [we have] *āha*, *āhu*, and for this very reason as an indicator, *brū* becomes *ssa* and *ho* in the cases of *ti* and *anti*.

21. *Īādīsu vacassoma*: after the word *vaca*, *oma* occurs when *ī* and so forth follow. The letter *m* is an *anubandha*; thus [we have] *avoca*. Why say "after *ī* and so forth"? [Observe: *avacā*.
22. For the word *dā* [ending] in *da*, there is optionally *daṃ* or *mi* when it occurs after *advi*.

When occurring after *advi*, for the word *dā* [ending] in *da*, there is optionally *daṃ* or *mi*. Examples: *dammi*, *demi*; *damma*, *demo*. Why say "after *advi*"? [Counter-examples: *dadādhi*, *dadāma*. 23.
For the word *kar* [ending] in *sa*, there is *kuṃ*.
In place of the *sa*-vowel of the root *kar*, there is optionally *ku* before the suffixes *mi* and *mhe*. Thus: *kummi*, *kumma*; *karomi*, *karoma*. 24. Regarding *kā* and so forth.
In place of the *sa*-vowel of the root *kar*, there is optionally *kā* before the suffixes beginning with *ī*. Thus: *akāsi*, *akari*; *akaṃsu*, *akariṃsu*; *akā*, *akarā*.

25. For the roots *kar-* (to do), *hā-* (to abandon), and *ah-* (to go), there is the suffix *ssena* along with *āhaṅ* or *vā*. [Examples: *kāhati*, *karissati*; *akāhā*, *akarissā*; *hāhati*, *hāyissati*; *ahāhā*, *ahāyissā*. 26.
For the roots *labh-* (to obtain), *vas-* (to dwell), *chid-* (to cut), *bhid-* (to split), and *rud-* (to weep), there is the suffix *cchaṅ*.
In the case of *labha* and the others, there are six [forms] with the suffixes *-cha* and *-na*, together with *-ssa*. [Namely: *alacchā* and *alabhissā*; *lacchati* and *labhissati*;
*avacchā* and *avasissā*; *vacchati* and *vasissati*; *acchecchā* and *acchindissā*; *checchati* and *chindissati*; *abhecchā* and *abhindissā*;
*bhecchati* and *bhindissati*; *arucchā* and *arodissā*; *rucchati* and *rodissati*. This also applies to other [roots].
Alternatively, due to the separation of the grammatical rule (*yogavibhāga*) for *chid*, there are the forms *acchecchuṃ* and *acchantiṃsu*;
and for others, *gacchaṃ* and *gacchissaṃ*. 27.
For *bhuja*, *muc*, *vaca*, and *vis*, there is optionally *kkhaṅ* together with *ss*. Thus: *abhokkhā* and *abhuñjissā*; *bhokkhati* and *bhuñjissati*.
*Amokkhā* means *amuñcissā*; *mokkhati* means *muñcissati*; *avakkhā* means *avacissā*; *vakkhati* means *vaccissati*; *pāvekkhā* means *pāvisissā*; *pavekkhati* means *pavisissati*.

[The suffix] *-ssā* may also occur after *vi-* due to the analysis (*yogavibhāga*) of the rule for *kkhaṅ*: *pāvekkhi*, *pāvisi*. 28. After roots beginning with *ā*, there is *-sā* [in place of *-ssā*].
In the case of *ā* and *ī*, the augment *a* optionally precedes the root *hṛ*. Thus: *ahā* and *aharā*;
*ahāsi* and *ahari*. 29.
In the case of *gam*: the augment *a* optionally precedes the root *gam*. Thus: *agā* and *agamā*; *agā* and *agamī*.

30. After *ḍam*, there is optionally *chaṅ* for both *ḍam* and *gam* before vowels beginning with *ā*. [Examples: *aḍañchā*, *aḍaṃsā*; *aḍañchi*, *aḍaṃsī*; *agañchā*, *agacchā*; *agañchi*, *agacchī*. 31.
After *hū*, there is *he*, *hi*, *hi*, or *ho* before suffixes beginning with *ss*.
The forms *hussa*, *he*, and so forth occur after *ssat* and similar suffixes. [Examples: *hessati*, *hehissati*, *hohissati*.
32. Shortening before *ṇā* and *nā*:
In the case of verbal roots (*kriyattha*), shortening occurs before the suffixes *ṇā* and *nā*. [Examples: *kiṇāti*, *dhunāti*.
33. For *ā*, *ī*, *ñu*, *mhā*, *ssā*, and *ssamhā*, there is optionally [the short vowel].
There is optionally a short vowel for these: *gama* / *gamā*, *gami* / *gamī*, *gamu* / *gamū*, *gamimha* / *gamimhā*, *gamissa* / *gamissā*, *gamissamha* / *gamissamhā*.
34. After *ku*, *sa*, and *ruhe*, there is *chi* for *issa*.
And *kusā* becomes *rūhā*, and *parassa* becomes *īssā*. [The forms] *akkocchi*, *akkosi*, *abhirucchi*, and *abhiruhi* [are examples].
35. *A-ī-ssā-ādīnaṃ byañjanassa iña*:
Optionally, for the consonants *a*, *ī*, *ssa*, and so forth, which follow verbal roots (*kriyatthā*), there is the substitution of *i* for the consonant. [Examples: *babhuvittha*.

[The suffix] *tā* is applied after [the verbal root] *bhū* when preceded by *a*, *anu*, *pa*, *pari*, *saṃ*, or *upa*. Examples: *abhavitha*, *anubhavissa*, *anubhavissati*, *anubhossati*, *harisati*, *hassati*.

What is the purpose of saying "of these"? [To exclude cases like: *bhavati*. What is the purpose of saying "after the phoneme" (*byañjanassa*)? [To exclude cases like: *babhūva*. 36. After [the root] *brū*, there is *ti* and *ssī*.
The suffix *īna* optionally occurs after the root *brū* when another person is the object. [Examples: *bravīti*, *brūti*.
37. *Kyassa*:
The suffix *īna* optionally occurs after the root *ky* when it has the sense of the action (*kriyārtha*) and another person is the object. [Examples: *pacīyati*, *paccati*.
38. *Eyyātha*, *sse*, *a*, *ā*, *īthānaṃ*, *o*, *a*, *aṃ*, *ttha*, *ttho*, *vhoka*.
For *eyyātha* and the following, *o* and the other suffixes optionally occur in their respective order. [Examples: *tumhe bhaveyyātho* or *bhaveyyātha*; *tvaṃ abhavissa* or *abhavisse*;
*ahaṃ abhavaṃ* or *abhava*; *so abhavittha* or *abhavā*; *so abhavittho*; *abhavī*; *tumhe*...

*Bhavatha* and *bhavatha*: the letter *a* is taken here as if it were accompanied by *ā*; however, because they are taught at the end [of this section], they relate only to *tvā* and the others, or because they depend on those very [forms].
For it is the practice of the authors of the Suttas to provide a basis [for a rule] even when that basis is not explicitly stated.
39. *Uṃssiṃ svaṃsu*.
The augment *um* has been or is [applied]. They came; they went; they went. 40.
*Suṃ* after *e* and *o*.

After the substitution of *e* and the substitution of *o*, the augment *suṃ* optionally occurs before the augment *um*. They led; they caused to lead; they heard; they were. The inclusion of the letter *t* is for the purpose of indicating that it is a substitute.
41. *Hū* becomes *resuṃ*.
*Hū* becomes *resuṃ* for another person’s [subject] in the past tense (*atīta*). [Examples: *ahesuṃ*, *ahavuṃ*. 42.
For *ossa*, there are the substitutes *a*, *i*, *ittha*, and *ittho*.
The suffix *o* becomes *ā* and so forth. *Tvaṃ abhava*, *abhavi*, *abhavittha*, *abhavittho*, *abhavo*.
The suffix *o* optionally becomes *si*. *Ahosi tvaṃ ahuvo*.
44. *Dīghā īssa*.
After a long vowel, the suffix *īssa* optionally becomes *si*. For example: *akāsi* becomes *akā*; *adāsi* becomes *adā*.
45. *Mhātthānamuña*. [The suffix *uña* is applied] after the sounds *m*, *h*, and *tth*.
The suffixes *mhā* or *ña* are substituted for *mha*. *Agamhamhā*, *agamimhā*; *agamuttha*, *agamittha*. 46.

*Si* and *ña* are substituted for *issa* and *ica*. For the endings *issa* and *ica*, *si* and *ña* are frequently substituted; as well as *mhā* and *ña*. *Akāsiṃ*, *akariṃ*; *akāsimhā*, *akarimhā*; *akāsittha*, *akarittha*.
47. For *eyyuṃsuṃ*, the suffix *ñam* optionally occurs after *eyyum*. [Examples: *gacchuṃ*, *gaccheyyuṃ*. 48.
There is elision (*lopa*) of the suffixes *hi* and *ssa-to*.
Therefore, there is optionally the elision of *hi* after *ataḥ*. [Examples: *gaccha*, *gacchāhi*.

Why say "after *ataḥ*"? [Counter-example: *karohi*. 49. *kyassa sse*: There is optionally the elision of *ky* before *sse*. [Examples: *anvabhavissā*, *anvabhūyissā*; *anubhavissati*, *anubhūyissati*.
50. *Atthi* followed by *eyya*, etc., and *icchānaṃ*, *sa-su-sa-satha-saṃ-sāma*.
After *asa* (the root *bhū*), the suffixes *eyya* and so forth become *sāda* and so forth respectively. [The forms are: *assa*, *assu*, *assa*, *assatha*, *assaṃ*, *assāma*. 51.
*Ādi* and the following two [suffixes] become *iyā* and *iyuṃ*.
In the case of the two [words] beginning with *atthi* and *teyya*, the forms *iyā* and *iyuṃ* occur respectively: *siyā*, *siyuṃ*.
52. *Tassa tho*:
The letter *tha* replaces the following letter *ta* after *atthi*; thus, *atthi*, *atthu*.
53. *Sihisvaṭa*.

After [the particle] *si*, there is *aṭ* for these [words]; *ṭ* has the purpose of being a universal substitute (*sabbādesa*). *Asi ahi*. 54. *Mimānaṃ vā mhimhā ca*. [After the particle *si*,] there is optionally *mhi* and *mhā* for *mi* and *mānaṃ*.

The suffix *aṭ* is added to the root *atthi* (to be) when it follows *amhi*, *vā*, or *taṃsanniyogena*. Thus: *amhi*, *asmi*; *amha*, *asma*. 55. *Esu si*: In these [suffixes] beginning with *e*, the letter *s* is substituted for the *s* of *atthi*.
Thus: *asmi*, *asma*; this is for the purpose of preventing the application of the *pararūpa* rule.
56. *Īādo dīgho*.

After *atthi*, a long vowel occurs before suffixes beginning with *ī* or *ā*. [Examples: *āsi*, *āsuṃ*, *āsi*, *āsittha*, *āsiṃ*, *āsiṃ* (we were). 57. *Himimesvassa*. [The long vowel occurs] before *hi*, *mi*, and *me*.
The vowel *a* becomes long before the suffixes beginning with *him*. [Examples: *pacāhi*, *pacāmi*, *pacāma*, *muyhāmi*.
58. *Sakā ṇāssa kha īādīsu*:
After the root *sak*, the substitute *kha* occurs for *ṇā* before suffixes beginning with *ī*. [Examples: *asakkhi*, *asakkhiṃsu*.
59. *Ssa* or *sse*:
After *sakka*, [the suffix] *kṇa* becomes *sse*. [Examples: *sakkhissā*, *sakkuṇissā*; *sakkhissati*, *sakkuṇissati*. 60.
Among those [suffixes], after *suta*, *roṭa* replaces *kṇa* and *okṇa*.
Among those [roots] beginning with *ī*, *suta* becomes *suṇoti* for others. *Assosi*, *asuṇi*; *assossā*, *asuṇissā*; *sossati*, *suṇissati*. 61. *Ñāssa sanāssa nāyo timhi*:
For *sanā* and *ñā*, *nāyo* optionally occurs before the suffix *ti*. *Nāyati*, *jānāti*. 62. *Ñāmhi jaṃ*: [The substitute] *jaṃ* [occurs] for *ñā* before the suffix *mhi*.
In place of *ñā*, the substitute *jaṃ* optionally occurs for the *ñā* of *sanā*. [Examples: *jaññā* (*jāneyya*). 63.
*eyyā*, *ssi*, *yā*, or *ñā*:
*eyyā*, *ssi*, *yā*, and *ñā* optionally occur in place of *ñā*. [Examples: *jāniyā*, *jaññā*, *jāneyya*.
64. In the case of *īsati* and so forth, there is the elision of *kn*.
After *ī* and so forth, and after *ssati* and so forth, the elision of *kn* optionally occurs when *ñāta* follows. [Examples: *aññāsi*, *ajāni*; *ñassati*, *jānissati*. 65.
In the case of the passive (*kamme*), there is the substitution of *hi* for *ss*.
In the case of another person's action, *ñāta* becomes *ñātassa* or *ñātassa*. *Paññāyihiti* becomes *paññāyissati*.
66. From *eti*:
after *eti*, *s* becomes *ss* or *s* for another person; [examples are] *ehiti* and *essati*.
67. *Hanā chakhā*.
There are six cases for the root *han*: "I strike," "I shall strike," "I ward off," and "I shall ward off.
68. From *hata* comes *ha*.
The *s* of the following [suffix] becomes *h*, or it is dropped. It is said that it "will abandon" (*jahissati*) because it "abandons" (*jahati*). 69.
There is optionally elision (*lopa*) of the *s* of the following [suffix] after substitutes such as *dakkha*.

After the substitutes *dakkha* and so forth, there is optionally elision of the *s* of the following [suffix]. Thus: *dakkhati* (he will see), *dakkhissati*; *sakkhati* (he will be able), *sakkhissati*; *hehiti* (he will be), *hehissati*; *hohiti* (he will be), *hohissati*.
70. *Kayireyya* and so forth for the optative (*eyya*) endings;

*kayirā* and so forth for the optative (*eyya*) endings of another person (*para*), there is elision of the *eyya*. [Examples: *kayiruṃ*, *kayirāsi*, *kayirātha*, *kayirāmi*, *kayirāma*. 71. *Ṭā*. [The suffix] *ṭā* [is added].
One should do for another who is dear; he should do it.
72. *Ethassā*:
one should do for another who is near; one should do it. *Kayirātha*.
73. *Labha* [becomes] *iṃ*, *īnaṃ*, *thaṃ*, or *thā*.
After the root *labh*, these forms—*iṃ*, *ī*, *icce*, and *saṃ*—optionally become *thaṃ* and *thā*. [Examples: *alatthaṃ*, *alabhiṃ*; *alattha*, *alabhi*. 74.
When preceded by a heavy syllable (*guru*), a short vowel (*rassa*) becomes *re* before endings that end in *-nti*.

After a short vowel preceded by *gu* or *ru*, the suffixes *nt* and *nti* optionally become *re*. Examples: *gacchare* (they go), *gacchanti*; *gacchare* (they were going), *gacchante*; *gamissare* (they will go), *gamissanti*; *gamissare* (they will be going), *gamissante*. Why "preceded by *gu* or *ru*"?
Example: *paca* (cook). Why "after a short vowel"? Example: *honti* (they are). 75. *Eyya*, *eyya*, *āsa*, and *eyya* optionally become *ṭe*.
The suffixes *eyya* and so forth optionally become *ṭe*. Examples: *so kare* (he may do), *kareyya*; *tvaṃ kare* (you may do), *kareyyāsi*; *ahaṃ kare* (I may do), *kareyyaṃ*.
76. In the case of the *o*-vowel replacement, when followed by a subsequent group of six vowels, *u* occurs in place of the *o*. [Example: *tanute*. 77.
Optionally, in some instances, when followed by a preceding group of six vowels.
In some instances, the vowel *u* optionally occurs in place of the *o* of the vikaraṇa within the preceding sixth case (the optative).
Thus: *vanuti*, *vanoti*. 78.
In the case of *eyyāma* and *emu*, there is optionally *u* as well. Thus: *bhavemha*, *bhaveyyāmu*, *bhaveyyāma*.
Thus ends the sixth chapter, beginning with *ty-ādi*, in the *Vutti* commentary on Moggallāna’s grammar. 7.
The seventh chapter (*ṇv-ādi*).
The terms *bahulaṃ* (1.58) and *kriy-atthā* (5.14) apply everywhere. 1.
The roots *cara*, *dara*, *kara*, *raha*, *jana*, *sana*, *tala*, *sāda*, *sādha*, *kasāsa*, *caṭāya*, *vāhi*, and *ṇu*.
*Car* in the senses of moving and eating; *dar* in splitting; *kar* in doing; *rah* in abandoning; *jan* in producing; *san* in acquisition.
The root *tala* means "to fall"; *sāda* means "to taste" or "to enjoy"; *sādha* means "to accomplish"; *kasa* means "to scratch" or "to scrape"; *asa* means "to throw"; *caṭa* means "to break.
The root *aya* is a *daṇḍaka* root meaning "to go," while *vā* means "to move" or "to blow. Through these meanings of the action (*kriyārtha*), the suffix *ṇu* is frequently applied.
According to the rule "When *ṇ* is not a follower, *ā* replaces *u*" (5.84), the *u* of the suffix becomes *ā*. Thus, that which moves within the heart by way of being agreeable is [called] *cāru*.

*Cāru* means beautiful or lovely. *Dāra* refers to wood, as it is that which is split (*darīyati*). *Kāru* refers to a craftsman, a generous person (*maghavā*), and one who performs good deeds (*visukamma*).

*Rāhu* is the lord of the asuras, so called because he seizes (*rahati*) and destroys the special splendor of the moon and other luminaries. *Atijānu* refers to the joint of the shanks and thighs, by means of which coming and going (*jāyati*) occurs.
*Sānu* is a mountain ridge, so called because it inspires devotion (*saneti*) within oneself. *Tala* refers to that upon which things stand firmly (*talanti*).
Herein, *danta* refers to a part of the palate or the mouth. That which is given (*diyati*) or tasted (*assādīyati*) is *sādu*, meaning sweet.

That which accomplishes one’s own and others’ welfare is *sādhu*, meaning a virtuous person. That which is ploughed (*kasīyati*) is *kāsu*, meaning a furrow or pit; that which exists by way of swiftness is *āsu*, meaning quickly.
