That which breaks or destroys unpleasantness is *cāṭu*, meaning pleasant. That by which beings go forth or proceed is *āyu*, meaning life.
“*Assā ṇāpimhi yuka*,” thus [it is said]. *Yuka* means that which goes; hence *vāyu* is the wind (*vāta*). 2.

*Bhara mara cara tara ara gara hana tana mana bhama kita dhana baṃha kambamba cakkha bhikkha saṃkindanda yaja paṭāṇāsa vasa pasa paṃsa bandhā u*. *Bhara* in the sense of supporting; *mara* in the sense of abandoning life;
*cara* in the senses of moving and eating; *tara* in the sense of crossing over; *ara* in the sense of going; *gara*... [and so forth].
The letter *a* [is used] in the sense of sprinkling water on a house (*ghara-secana*), or in the sense of falling down (*girati-nipātana*).

[Roots ending in *a* include: *hana* in the sense of harming; *tana* in the sense of extension; *mana* in the sense of knowing; *bhama* in the sense of instability; *kita* in the sense of dwelling; *dhana* in the sense of sound; *baṃha*, *braha*, and *brūha* in the sense of growth;

*kamba* in the sense of covering; *amba* in the sense of sound; *cakkha* and *ikkha* in the sense of seeing; *bhikkha* in the sense of begging; *saṃka* in the sense of suspicion; and *inda* in the sense of supreme sovereignty.

In the sense of binding (*anda-bandhana*), in the sense of sacrifice and worship of deities (*yaja-devapūjā*), in the sense of wandering and moving about (*aṭa-paṭa-gamana*), in the sense of sound (*aṇa-saddattha*), in the sense of casting forth (*asa-khepana*), in the sense of dwelling (*vasa-nivāsa*), in the sense of pressing (*pasabādha*), and in the sense of binding (*paṃsa-nāsana*)—after these roots meaning "to do" (*kriyattha*), the suffix *u* occurs.

He supports (*bharati*) [them], thus *bhara* = supporter (*bhattā*). He dies together with his material body (*rūpakāya*), thus *maru* = deity (*deva*) and a waterless region (*nijjaladesa*). It is moved about (*carīyati*).
It is called *caru* because it is eaten; it is a sacrificial offering (*havya-pāka*). It is called *taru* because one crosses over by means of it; it is a tree (*rukkha*).

It is called *aru* because it rises upward due to its state of being raw (*sūna-bhāva*); it is a wound (*vaṇa*). It is called *garu* because it swallows (*garati*), sprinkles (*siñcati*), or vomits (*girati*)—it cherishes (*sinehati*) its disciples;

it is a teacher (*ācariya*). It is called *hanu* because it destroys (*hanati*) the specific color in rice and other foods; it is a part of the face (*vadanekadeso*). It is called *tanu* because it stretches out the suffering of *saṃsāra*.
*Tanu* means a slender body. *Maññati* (he conceives) the welfare and non-welfare of beings, thus *manu* = *pajāpati*.
It wanders and moves, thus *bhamu* = the eye (*nayana*) as its foundation. It shines upward or dwells above, thus *ketu* = a banner (*dhaja*).
It makes a sound, thus *dhanu* = a bow (*cāpa*). From the grammatical rule "in *baṃha*, there is always the elision of the *um* [vowel]," it increases (*baṃhati*), thus growth.

It goes (*gacchati*), thus it is *bahu* (much) or *anappaka* (not little). It moves (*kambati*) and performs restraint (*saṃvaraṃ karoti*), thus *kambu* is a bracelet (*valaya*) and a conch (*saṅkha*).

It makes sound (*nādaṃ karoti*), thus *ambu* is water (*vāri*). It sees form (*rūpaṃ*), thus *cakkhu* is the eye (*nayana*). He begs (*bhikkhati*), thus *bhikkhu* is a recluse (*samaṇa*). It pierces (*saṃkirati*), thus *saṃku* is a stake (*sūla*).
It exercises supreme sovereignty over the constellations (*nakkhattānaṃ paramissariyaṃ pavatteti*), thus *indu* is the moon (*canda*).
It is called *andu* (a chain) because beings go (*andanti*) and are bound (*bandhanti*) by it. It is called *yajurvedo* (the Yajur Veda) because one sacrifices (*yajanti*) by means of it.

It is called *paṭu* (clever) because it moves (*paṭati*), that is, it attains proficiency. It is called *aṇu* (subtle) because it exists (*aṇati*) in a subtle state; it also refers to a type of grain.

It is called *āsavo* (a taint) because beings exist (*asanti*) and proceed (*pavattanti*) by means of them. It is called *vasu* (wealth) because beings dwell happily (*sukhaṃ vasanti*) by means of it.

It is called *pasu* because it is bound (*pasīyati*) and oppressed by its owners; it is a four-footed animal. It is called *paṃsu* (dust) because it scatters (*paṃsati*) and destroys a particular beauty.
It is called *bandhu* (relative) because it is bound (*bandhīyati*) by the state of affection. 3.
[The suffixes] *ū*, *bandha*, and *vadha*.

In the word *bandha*, the suffix *timas* becomes *ū*, and there is a substitution of *vadhu* for *bandha*. One who binds herself to the five strands of sensual pleasure (*pañca-kāmaguṇa*) by means of a husband is called *vadhū*—that is, a daughter-in-law—and also a woman.
4. *Jambu* and others:

Words such as *jambu* and so forth are derived as nouns with secondary suffixes (*upaccaya*); "nouns" (*nipāta*) mean the bringing about of what has not yet been reached and the negation of what has already been reached.

From the root *jan* (to be born), with the augment *buk*, the nasal *n* becomes a *niggahīta* (anusvāra) according to rule 5.96 (*manānaṃ niggahītaṃ*); then, by rule 1.41 (*vagge vagganto*), the *niggahīta* becomes *m*. Thus, that which is born or is produced is *jambū*, the *jambu*-tree.
From the root *bham* (to wander/to tremble), there is the elision of the suffix *ama*; it wanders or trembles, thus *bhū* = *bhamu* (the brow).

From the root *karoti* (to do), with the suffix *ū* and the replacement of *t* by *ndhūñ*, [the form is *kandhu*]; then, by the rule "in the case of a consonant following *a*, the subsequent form occurs" (*pararūpamayakāre byañjane*).

(5.95) A consonant at the end of a verbal root undergoes substitution with the following vowel (*pararūpa*): *kakkandhū* is *badarī* [the jujube tree], because it causes the production of blood (*rudhiruppāda*).

*Lamb* means to hang down; preceded by *ā*, with the elision of the first member of the conjunct and the shortening of the long vowel, *ālambati* (it hangs down) becomes *alābū* = *tumbī* [the bottle gourd].
*Sar* means to go, to injure, or to think; with the suffix *ū*, there is the substitution of *abhuka* and *abuka*; *sarati* (it goes) becomes *sarabhū*, a certain great river.

*Sarabū* is a specific kind of small insect, derived from the root *sar*, meaning "to move" and *hiṃs*, meaning "to injure. *Camū* is an army; it is derived from the root *cam*, meaning "to eat," as in eating fodder.
*Tanu* is the body; it is derived from the root *tan*, meaning "to extend," as in extending the suffering of *saṃsāra*. In this way, other words should also be understood according to their usage.
5. *Tapusa, vidha, kura, putha, muda, ku.*
The prefix *ku-* is applied to these roots: *tapa* (to heat), *usa* (to burn), *vidha* (to pierce), *kura* (sound), *putha* (to spread on the earth), and *muda* (to rejoice).
The letter *ka* is an *anubandha* (indicatory letter) for the purpose of preventing elision by the rule "there is no elision of a consonant when followed by another consonant" (5.85).
Its vowel *i* is established by the very fact of its being taught as *tapa*. That which is heated is *tipu*, a specific type of metal. That which burns, i.e., causes burning, is *usu*.

*Usū* means an arrow. *Vedhati* means it trembles with rays; *timiraṃ ti* means darkness; *vidhu* means the moon. One who performs what ought to be done and what ought not to be done is called a *kuru-rājā*;

*kuravaḥ* is a country. *Puthati* means he spreads out by way of greatness or he desires; thus *puthu* means extensive. *Modanaṃ* means delight; or, because one is gladdened (*mudīyati*), *mudu* means soft or pliant. 6. *Sindhu* and others.
Words such as *sindhu* and others are derived with *kup*-class suffixes (*nipaccayanta*). [The root] *sand* means to flow;

its vowel becomes short (*itta*), and by the rule of elision of the final part, *dhoca*, the word *sindhu*—meaning "river"—is formed from the sense of "flowing" (*sandati*) or "pouring forth" (*passavati*).

In the case of [the root] *vah*, which ends in a *sup*-suffix, the vowel becomes long, etc., and through the substitution of the final part of *bādh*, *bāhu* is formed, meaning "that by which one carries" (*vahanti anena*). Alternatively, from *bādh* in the sense of warding off calamity, *bāhu* means "arm" (*bhuja*). [The root] *raṅgh* means to go.
There is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). One who moves (*raṅghati*) according to the royal duties (*rājadhamma*) is a *raghu*, meaning a king.
*Vid-* in the sense of obtaining: there is the augment *na*; *va* becomes *ba*; that by which one finds joy (*nandana*) is a *bindu*, meaning a drop or a small circle.

*Man-* in the sense of knowing: *na* becomes *dha*; that which is thought of and known as sweet is *madhu*, i.e., honey made by bees; *rapa*, *lapa*, *japa*, *jappa* in the sense of speaking: the suffix *assa-it-taṃ* is applied; he speaks (*rapati*).

*jappati* (he speaks) with the prefix *mant-* becomes *mantī*; *ripu-paccāmitto* (enemy and adversary). From *sasati* (he breathes), with the suffix *-gati*, [it means] among living beings; its vowel is lengthened (*assa uttaṃ*), and since he breathes (*sasati*) and lives, *sasu* = young man (*yuvā*).

From *ara* (in the sense of going), with the suffixes *-assa* and *-utta*, and with the change of *m* to *n*: he goes to a state of greatness (*mahantabhāvaṃ gacchati*), thus *uru* = great (*mahā*); by means of this *ara*, it is the thigh (*ūru-satthi*).
From *khaṇa* (in the sense of digging), preceded by *ā* and without the elision of the nasal (*analopa*): he digs (*ākhanati*), thus *ākhu* = rat (*undūro*).
*Tarataraṇe*: *tha* is [the suffix] *thu*; *tarati* means "to cross," hence *tharu* = a part of a sword.

In *laṅgha*, which has the senses of "leaping" (*gati*) and "drying" (*sosana*), the *gha* becomes *ha* and the *niggahīta* is elided; it leaps (*laṅghati*) or proceeds by way of lightness, thus *laghu* and *lahu* are synonymous.

(*Bhañja* means "to break" or "to crush"; with the prefix *pa-*, the *j* becomes *g*; it breaks specifically, thus *pabhaṅgu* = fragile. *Ṭhā* is used in the sense of "stopping motion" (*gatinivatti*).

The prefix *su-* is present when the root *ṭhā* occurs in the sense of proceeding in a beautiful manner; thus, *suṭṭhu* = "beautiful" (*sobhana*). The prefix *du-* is present when the root *ṭhā* occurs in the sense of proceeding in an unbeautiful manner;
thus, *duṭṭhu* = "unbeautiful" (*asobhana*). In this way, others [of such compounds] are also to be understood. 7. I.

The suffix *i* frequently occurs after verbal roots (*kriyattha*) in various senses, excluding the sense of shaking (*abha-khepane*). *Asi*: from the root *as*, meaning "to throw" (*khipati*), *asīyati khipīyati* = *asi* (a sword).
*Kasi*: from the root *kas*, meaning "to scratch" (*vilekhane*), *kasīyate* = *kasi* (plowing). *Masi*: from the root *mas*, meaning "to touch" (*āmasane*), *masīyati* = *masi* (soot/ink).

*Kavi*: from the root *ku*, meaning "sound," with *o* and *ava* substituted for the vowel; *kavati kathehi* = *kavi* (a poet). *Ravi*: from the root *ru*, meaning "sound"; *ravati gajjati* = *ravi* (the sun). *Sappi*: from the root *sapp*, meaning "to go" (*gamane*), *sappati*.

*Pavattati* means "it flows"; thus *sappighataṃ* (clarified butter in a jar). From the root *gantha* (to tie): according to the rule “*ta tha na rānaṃ ṭa ṭha ṇa lā*” (1.25), the *na* and *tha* become *ṇa* and *ṭha*;
that which ties together is a *gaṇṭhi*, meaning a knot or a joint. From the root *rāja* (to shine): it shines and proceeds, thus *rāji*, meaning a line or row.
From the root *kala* (to count): it is counted or measured, thus *kali*, meaning evil or misfortune. From the root *bala* (to breathe or live): they live...
*Jīvanti anena* means "they live by this," thus *balikara*. Regarding the word *dhana*: *dhanati nadati* means "it sounds," thus *dhani* is the sound. *Acca* is used in the sense of worship;

*acciyyati pūjiyyati* means "it is worshipped," thus *acci* is flame. *Vala* and *valla* mean "to cover"; *valanaṃ saṅkocanaṃ* means "folding or contraction," thus *vali* refers to wrinkles on the belly and so forth.
*Vallīyanti saṃvarīyanti sattā etāya* means "beings are covered or concealed by it," thus *valli* is a creeper. From *vi*, there are also the forms *valī* and *vallī*.
The word *soyeva-attha* [is formed] in this way; others are likewise. 8. *Dadhi*-class and others.

Words such as *dadhi* and so forth are derived with the suffix *ip*. From the root *dhā* (in the sense of "holding"), there is reduplication by virtue of a grammatical rule (*nipātanā*); thus, "he places a pot" (*ghaṭam ādadhāti*).
*Dadhi* becomes *gorasa* with the addition of *viśeṣa*. In *aṃha-gamana*, there is the elision of the nasal (*niggahīta*); because it goes (*gacchati*) into distress (*aṃha*), *ahi* means "snake.
In *kampa* (to shake), there is the elision of the first member of the conjunct; because it shakes (*kampati*) or moves, *kapi* means "monkey. In *mana* (to know), *utta* is added;

because he knows (*manati*) or understands, *muni* means "ascetic" (*samaṇa*). In *nassa*, there is the substitution of *ṇa*; because it goes to a state of great value (*mahagghabhāva*), *maṇi* means "jewel" (*ratana*).
*Ikṣ* means "to see"; that by which one sees oneself is *akṣi*, namely the eye (*nayana*). *Kam* means "to move about" or "to disperse"; its state is *itta*;

that which moves or goes is *kimi*, a specific kind of small creature. *Tṛ* means "to cross over"; with the substitution of *tittira*, that which crosses over swiftly is *tittiri*, a specific kind of bird.
*Kīḷ* means "to sport"; its state is *etta*; sporting is *keḷi*, namely play (*kīḷā*). [The suffix] *us* replaces *is*.
*Khaluñja* (a frying pan) burns when heated; the same applies to other vessels as well.
9. *Yuvaṇṇupantā ki*:

After suffixes ending in *i-vaṇṇa* (i, ī) and *u-vaṇṇa* (u, ū), the suffix *ki* is frequently applied when expressing the sense of the action (*kriyattha*). The letter *ka* is an *anubandha* (indicatory letter); [it serves to denote] *isa*...

In *sisa-icchā*, one who desires peace (*siva*) is an *isi*—an ascetic. In *gira-nigiraṇe*, that which swallows or produces medicinal herbs consisting of the essence of skin and flesh is a *giri*—a mountain.
In *suca-socane*, sorrowing is *suci*—purity; in *ruca-abhilāse*, that by which things are desired is *ruci*—desire, and so on for others as well.
10. *Vapa*, *vara*, *vasa*, *rasa*, *nabha*, *hara*, *hana*, *paṇa*—with these, *iṇa* occurs. In *vapa* (sowing), *bījanikkhepe* (the placing of seeds);

in *vara* (choice), *varasambhattīsu* (in the acts of choosing); in *vasa* (dwelling), *nivāse* (residence); in *rasa* (taste), *assādane* (enjoyment); in *nabha* (injury), *hiṃsāyaṃ* (harming); in *hara* (taking), *haraṇe* (carrying away); in *hana* (killing), *hiṃsāyaṃ* (injuring);
in *paṇa* (trade and praise), *byavahārathutisu* (in commerce and eulogy)—with these, *iṇa* is formed. [The root] *vap* is used in the sense of "they sow by means of this."

*vāpī* means a reservoir of water (*jalāsayo*). It is called *vāri* because they flow (*vārenti*) by means of it; thus *vāri* is water. It is called *vāsi* because they work with it (*vasanti*); thus *vāsi* is a carpenter’s tool.

It is called *rāsi* because it is heaped together (*rasīyati*) and gathered (*samu sarīyati*) by way of tasting or enjoying; thus *rāsi* is a collection. It is called *nābhi* because it strikes or injures (*nabhati hiṃsati*);

thus *nābhi* is a part of the body. It is called *hāri* because it carries away or captivates (*hāreti*); thus *hāri* is charming. According to the rule “*hanassa ghāto ṇānubandhe*” (5.99), there is a substitution of *ghāta* for *hana*; they strike (*hananti*).

By this [root *han*], *ghāti* means "striking" (*paharaṇa*). From *paṇati*, meaning "to trade" (*voharati*), comes *pāṇi*; or alternatively, that by which one trades is *pāṇi*, namely the hand (*karo*). 11. *Bhū-gam-ā-īṇa*.

From the root *bhū* (existence) and *ama* (from *gam*, motion), the suffix *īṇa* occurs in the sense of the future tense. That which will be is *bhāvī*—meaning "one who will come to be. That which will go is *gāmī*—meaning "one who will go."
12. *Tanda-lakkhā ī*.

From the roots *tand* [meaning] indolence (*ālasiya*) and *lakkh* [meaning] seeing or numbering, the suffix *ī* occurs. *Tandanam* is *tandī*, meaning indolence; *lakkhī* means prosperity (*sirī*), because beings are marked (*lakkhīyanti*) by it. 13. *Gamā ro*. [The suffix *ro* occurs after the root *gam*.]
The suffix *mā* becomes *ro*. By the rule “*rānubandhentasarādissā*” (4.132), there is elision of the vowel; thus, that which goes (*gacchati*) is a *go* = an animal.
(Thus ends the section on the prescription of *sara*-suffixes.
14. *I*, *bhī*, *kā*, *karāra*, *vaka*, *saka*, *vāhi*, *ko*.

The suffix *ka* occurs after these roots: *i* in the sense of going; *bhī* in the sense of fear; *gā* in the sense of sound; *kara* in the sense of doing; *ara* in the sense of going; *kuka* and *vaka* in the sense of seizing;
*saka* in the sense of power; and *vā* in the senses of blowing, binding, and going. One who goes (*eti*) or proceeds (*pavattati*) is *eto*—meaning "without companion.

One from whom they fear (*bhāyanti etasmā*) is *bheko*—meaning "a frog. One who cries out (*kāyati*) or makes a sound is *kāko*—meaning "a crow. One who does (*karoti*) what is beautiful (*vaṇṇaka*) is... [the remainder of the passage is omitted].
*Kakka* is a particular color, as well as flesh and a substance. *Akka* is that which goes with aversion; thus it means a hero, as well as a particular tree.
*Vakka* is that by which one carries or takes rice; thus it means a particular part of the body. *Sakka* is that which honors; thus it means the Lord of Devas, as well as one who is capable.
*Vāka* is that by which one binds; thus it means bark.
15. *Ñukādayo* (The *ñuka*-class).
Words ending in the suffix *-añ* are derived as *nipātas*. In the root *ūh* (to think), there is the elision of *h* by way of *nipātana* (irregularity);

thus, "that which is pondered (*ūhiyati*) or investigated" is *ūkā*, meaning "a well. In the root *und* (to moisten), there is the elision of the initial conjunct and the substitution of *aka*; thus, "that which makes wet (*undati*)" or "makes liquid" is *udakaṃ*, meaning "water."
*Bhī* (in the sense of fear): the state of being afraid; that from which they fear is *bhīka*, i.e., *bhīru* (one who fears).
*Saka* (in the sense of power): it is able to hold; thus *sikkā* is a particular kind of vessel or implement. *Hā* (in the sense of abandoning): it is abandoned by the virtuous, it is left behind;
thus *hāka* is anger. *Samba* (in the sense of ornamenting): with the suffix *uñ* added to *kasa*; it ornaments the water; thus *sambuka* is a particular kind of aquatic creature. *Putha*...
In the detailed explanation of the roots: from *ott* in the sense of "to be," with the suffix *uṇ*, and *puthati* meaning "to spread out" one's own foolishness, thus *puthuka* = a fool.
From *suc* in the sense of "to grieve," that by which they grieve is *sukkaṃ* = birth, and it is white (*seta*).

From *ci* in the sense of "to accumulate," preceded by *upa*, with the elision of *ettā*, those who accumulate are *upacikā* = anthills (makers of mounds). From *kamp* in the sense of "to shake," with the suffix *paṃ*, that which shakes or moves is *paṅko* = mud.

*Usa* means "to burn"; *usati* thus refers to a firebrand (*ukkā*) or a flame. *Kassa* means "of whom"; *muñcati*, "it burns," thus *ummukaṃ* is a firebrand or a glowing coal. *Vama* means "to vomit" or "to eject"; *kassa* means "of whom";

*vamīyati*, "it is vomited," thus *vammiko* is an anthill, a heap of earth built by termites. *Masa* means "to touch"; with the suffix *-tthaṅa*, *masīyati* means "it is touched with affection," thus *matthakaṃ* is the head.
In this way, other words are also to be understood.
16. *Bhītvā nako*.

From the root *bhī* (to fear), with the suffix *ānaka*, it becomes *bhī-ānaka*. They fear from this; thus, *bhayānaka* means "one who produces fear. 17. *Siṅghā āṇikāṭakā*. [The word *siṅghāṇika* is derived from] *siṅghā* (snot) and *āṇika* (emission).
[Thus, *siṅghāṇika* means nasal mucus.]

*Siṅghāṇikā*: from the root *siṅgh*, these [words] are derived. Regarding "having smelled a woman" (93.260): it smells, that is, it exudes; thus *siṅghāṇikā* = nasal discharge. *Siṅghāṭaka*: it goes to a state of union; thus *siṅghāṭaka* = a crossroads (a place where four roads meet).
18. The group beginning with *kara*. *Kara* = doing; *sara* = going, harming, and thinking; *nara* = leading; *tara* = crossing over; *vara* = choosing and sharing.

The suffix *aka* occurs in such words as: *jana-janane* (in the sense of producing people), *kara-ditti-gatikantīsu* (in the senses of hand, light, going, and beauty), *kaṭa-mandane* (in the sense of decorating the head), *kura-sadde* (in the sense of the sound "kura"), and *thu-abhitthave* (in the sense of praise).

It is called *karaka* because it is made (*karīyati*); thus, *karaka* = a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*). It is called *karakā* because it causes to act (*karoti*); thus, *karakā* = hailstones. It is called *saraka* because water flows (*sarati*) therein; thus, *saraka* = a drinking vessel.
It is called *naraka* because beings (*sattā*) reach (*naranti*) it; thus, *naraka* = hell (*niraya*). It is called *taraka* because one crosses (*taranti*) by means of it.

*Taraka* means crossing (*taraṇa*). *Varaka*—from "he wards off" (*vāreti*)—is a fence (*varaṇa*), as well as a particular kind of grain. *Janaka*—from "he begets" (*janeti*)—is a father. *Kanaka*—from "it shines" (*kanati*) or "it is seen" (*dibbati*)—is gold (*suvaṇṇa*).
*Kaṭaka*—from "it crushes" or "it grinds enemies" (*kaṭati maddati ripavo*)—is a city (*nagara*). *Koraka*—from "it is curved" or "it buds" (*kuratīti*)—is a bud (*kalikā*).
*Thavaka*—from "it is praised" (*thavīyati*)—is a cluster (*guccha*).
19. *Āka* is added after *bala* and *pata*.

With the roots *bal* (to live) and *pat* (to go), *āka* occurs. That which lives is *balākā*—a specific kind of bird. That which flies or goes is *patākā*—a banner. 20. *Sāmākā* and others [are formed in this manner].
*Ākanta* [words] ending in *sā*, *tanu*, *karaṇa*, and *avasāna* undergo the *nipatta* suffix. *Sā* + *muka*: "That which makes its body thin" (*sāssa tanuṃ karoti*) is *sāmāka*, a type of grain.
*Pā* (to drink) + *inaṅ*: That by which one drinks repeatedly is *pināka*, the bow of Maheśvara. *Gu* (sound):
By the rule "for *yu* and *vaṇṇa*, *miyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* before a vowel" (5.136), *uvaṅ* is substituted; that by which one roars (*gavati nadati*) is *guvaka*, the betel nut.
The roots *paṭ* and *ga* have the sense of going; that which goes or moves is *paṭākā*, meaning a banner (*vejayantī*). The roots *sal*, *pil*, *pal*, and *hul* have the sense of going;
that which glides or moves is *salākā*, meaning a medicinal implement. The root *vid* means to know; one who knows or understands is *vidāko*, meaning a wise man.
The roots *paṇ* (in the senses of trade and praise) and *ūka* have the sense of being praised; that which is traded or dealt with is *piññāko*, meaning sesame cake, and so too for others.
21. *Vicchā-laga-musa-kika*.
In *vicchā* (to move), *ala* (to bind), *ama* (to go), and *musa* (to steal), the suffix *kika* occurs.
That which moves or wanders is a *vicchika*—a worm (*kīṭa*). That by which one binds is *alika*—untruth (*asacca*). One who goes is a *gamika*—a traveler.
The vowel is long due to the rule *musāti niddesā*. Because it steals (*musati*) or robs (*theneti*), it is a "mouse" (*mūsika*);
[this refers to] a rat. 22. *Kiṃkaṇikādayo*:
Words such as *kiṃkaṇikā* are derived from the root *kik*. The suffix *kaṇa* is added; the verbal root *kaṇ* has the meaning "to sound. There is reduplication (*dvitta*) of the syllable *ka*.
From the root *ass* with the suffix *-ita*, there is the insertion of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra); *kiṅkaṇikā* means that which makes sound, i.e., a small bell.
From *mud* meaning "to rejoice," there is the doubling of the consonant; *muddikā* means that by which one rejoices, i.e., a finger-ring, or a specific kind of fruit.

From *mah* meaning "to be honored," *mahikā* means that which is honored, i.e., mist or frost. From *kal* meaning "to count," *kalikā* means that which is counted or measured, i.e., a bud. From *sapp* meaning "to go,"...
*Assa* means "it moves. That which moves (*sappati*) is called *sappikā*, a specific kind of aquatic creature; other [words] are likewise formed.
23. *Isā-kīko*.
From the root *isa*, meaning "desire" (*siṃsa*), the suffix *kīko* is added. That which is desired (*icchīyati*) is *isīkā*, the stalk of cotton.
24. *Kama* and *pada* take the suffix *ṇuka*.

*Kama* means desire; *pada* means going. With these [roots], *ṇuka* occurs. By the rule "ṇi-ṇā-pīna" (5.160), through a division of the grammatical connection (*yogavibhāga*), there is the elision of *ṇi*. One who desires is *kāmuka* = a desirer. That by which one goes or moves is *pādukā* = a foot-ornament (shoe).
25. *Maṇḍa* and *salā* take the suffix *ṇūka*.

In *maṇḍa-bhūsane*, the root *daṇḍ* has the sense of moving gracefully; with these [prefixes], the suffix *ṇūka* is applied. That which adorns (*maṇḍeti*) and beautifies the water is *maṇḍūka* = a frog. That which moves (*salati*) and enters its feeding ground is *sālūka* = the rootstock of a lotus.

26. *Ulūkādayo*: Words beginning with *ulūka* are derived with the suffix *ṇūka*. In the root *ula* (meaning "to seek"), the change to *o* occurs by way of a grammatical rule (*nipātanā*). That which seeks (*ulati*) is [thus called].
*Ulūka* is *kosiya*. *Mana* is *ñāṇa*; that which has its essence (*dhatta*) gone is *nassa-dhatta*, and because it conceives (*maññati*), it is *madhūka*, the tree.
*Jala* is in the sense of shining; that which shines (*jalati*) is *jalūkā*, the blood-sucker (leech), and other such words are likewise.
27. *Kasā* is *saka*.
From *kas* and *vilekhana*, the suffix *itima* is applied; thus it becomes *kassaka*. *Kasati* means "he plows," hence *kassaka* = a plowman or cultivator.
28. *Karā* is a triplet.
From *karoti*, the suffix *tika* is applied. Because they perform (*karonti*) play (*kīḷa*) here, it is *kattika* = the month of Bāhula.
29. *Iṣa* with the suffix *ṭhakan*.
From the root *iṣ*, meaning "to desire," the suffix *ṭhakan* occurs. That which is desired is *iṭṭhakā*—a derivative of clay (*mattikā*). 30.
*Samā* is indeed [the same].
Regarding the words *sama*, *upasama*, and *kheda*: it is from this [root] that they arise. Because it "calms" (*sameti*) and "completely calms" (*upasameti*), it is called *saṅkha* (conch).

31. *Mukha* and others: words beginning with *mukha* ending in *kh* are declined. The root *mu* means "to bind"; the absence of the vowel *o* occurs by way of a grammatical convention (*nipātanā*); thus, *munanti* means "they bind."

By this [prefix], *eti* means "to go toward," which is synonymous with "speaking" (*lapana*). In the word *sikhā*, *si* denotes service (*sevā*); through the rule of irregular derivation (*nipātanā*), the suffix *ūka* is added, and because flowers and the like rest (*sayanti*) upon it, it is called *sikhā* (crest) or *cūḷā* (tuft).

In the word *visikhā*, the *si* is either from *vipubba* (with *vi* as the prefix) or from *visatissa*; they rest (*sayanti*) there in a distinguished manner (*visesena*), or they enter (*pavisanti*) there, thus it is *visikhā* (street).
In the root *kana*, meaning "to shine," "to move," or "beauty," with *ni* as the prefix, there is an elision of the non-initial portion; it shines (*kanati*) or is radiant, thus [it is *nikanikā*].
*Nikkha* is a gold ornament. *Maya* is a verbal root meaning "to go"; with the suffix *-daṇḍaka*, the vowel *a* becomes *ū*, and because it goes (*mayati*), it is *mayūkha*, meaning a ray of light.
*Lū* means "to cut"; with the change of *o* to *u*, *lunāti* (he cuts) means he shines;
thus *lūkhā* means ungreasy. *Ara* means "to go"; that by which they go is *akkha*, meaning a part of a chariot or a die. *Yasa* means "to strive"; one strives (*yassati*).
"One who strives for the purpose of bringing an offering" is a *yakkha* (a non-human being). "That which grows, that which is born" is a *rukkha* (a tree, a plant).
"That which burns, that which consumes the fire of desire" is an *ukkho* (an ox). In the sense of enduring together, there is the elision of the suffix *-ha-*;
"one who endures, who forgives an offense committed against oneself" is a *sakhā* (a friend). Other examples are to be understood in the same way.
32. *Aja*, *vaja*, *muda*, *gada*, *gama*, *aga*.
In the sense of "going" (*aja-vaja-gamane*), "satisfaction" (*muda-tose*), "speech" (*gada-vacane*), and "going to the state of immortality" (*amagama-gamane*), these [terms] become *gaka* [nouns].

He goes to the state of excellence (*seṭṭhabhāva*) by not being born (*ajāti*)—thus he is *agga* (foremost) or *seṭṭha* (best). He goes to the state of being a collection (*samūhatta*)—thus *vagga* is a collection (*samūho*). They rejoice (*mudanti*).

By this [rule], *mugga* is a specific type of grain. *Gadati* means "he speaks," thus *gagga* is a sage (*isi*). According to the rule "the *man* becomes *niggahīta*" (5.96), the *man* of *maga* becomes *niggahīta*;
*gacchati* means "she flows," thus *gaṅgā* is the river that flows to the sea.
33. *Siṅga* and so forth.
Words such as *siṅga* are derived from verbal roots ending in *-ga*. From the root *sī* (to lie down), with the insertion of the nasal (*niggahīta*) and shortening of the vowel:

*sayati* (it lies down) or *pavattati* (it exists) at the head (*matthaka*), thus *siṅgaṃ* = a horn (*visāṇa*). From the root *phura* (to move), with the suffix *limuṅ*: *phurati* (it moves), thus *phuliṅgo* = a spark of fire (*jalitaṅgāra-āvayava*).

From the root *cala* (to shake), preceded by the prefix *upa*, with the substitution of *cāliṃ* for *cala*: *uccalati* (it moves upward) or *kampati* (it shakes), thus *uccāliṅgo* = a white insect (*sukkakīṭo*).
*Kala* means sound; *imuka*, [it] utters a cry (*abhinādaṃ karoti*) because of its great passion (*bahurajjatāya*), thus *kaliṅgo* = the Southern Region (*dakkhiṇāpatho*).
*Bhama* means instability; its state is such that it wanders (*bhamati*), thus *bhiṅgo* = a bee (*bhamaro*).
*Paṭa* and *aṭa* mean to go; for *paṭi*, there is *amuka* and *aka*. It flies and goes while falling, thus *paṭaṅgo*; *paṭago* = a moth (*salabho*); and so too others.
34. *Agā gi*.
The suffix *gi* occurs after the root *aga*, meaning "to go crookedly. Because it goes in a crooked manner (*kuṭila*), it is called *aggi* (fire), that is, *pāvaka*.
35. *Yāvalā gu*.

In the sense of reaching (*yā-pāpuṇane*) and in the sense of restraining or covering (*vala-vala-saṃvaraṇe*), the suffix *gu* occurs. That which goes (*yāti*) is *yāgu* (gruel); that which is restrained or covered (*valīyati saṃvarīyati*) is *vaggu* (pleasing).

36. *Pheggādayo*: Words beginning with *pheggu* ending in *gu* are derived as nouns. In the sense of the production of fruit (*phala-nipphattiyaṃ*), there is this [suffix]; it bears fruit, that is, it reaches its completion (*niṭṭhānaṃ*).
It moves, thus *pheggu* = that which lacks essence (*asāra*). In the root *bhara* (to support), there is the elision of *ra*. It supports, thus *bhagu* = a sage (*isi*).

In the root *hi* (motion), there is the insertion of the nasal (*niggahīta*); it proceeds as "low" (*hino*), thus *hiṅgu* = that produced from *rāmaṭha* (asafoetida). In the root *kama* (desire), it is desired, thus *kaṅgu* = a specific type of grain; other such [derivatives] are also [to be understood] in this way. 37. *Janā gho*.

The word *jaghaneti* becomes *jaṅghā*. According to the rule “the elided [nasal] of *man* is a *niggahīta*” (5.96), the *n* of *jan* becomes a *niggahīta*; thus, that by which going (*gamana*) is produced is *jaṅghā*, a specific part of the body.

38. *Meghādayo* (Clouds, etc.). Words beginning with *megha* are derived from the root *gha*. From the root *miha* (to sprinkle), there is the elision of the suffix; it sprinkles, hence *megha* = a cloud.
In *muha* (to faint), there is the elision of *ha*; beings faint therein, thus *mogha* means empty or vain. In *sī* (to lie down), there is the absence of *tta*;
it lies down, that is, it proceeds lightly, thus *sīgha* means swift. In *aha* (to reduce to ashes), preceded by *ni*, with the elision of *ha* and lengthening of the vowel;

it burns up, thus *nidāgha* means the summer heat. In *mahī* (earth), there is the elision of *ha*; it is honored (*mahīyati*), thus *maghā* is a lunar mansion. Other examples are to be understood in the same way.
(Thus ends the section on the prescription of the *ca*-group suffixes. 39. *Cusaravarā co*.

From the roots *cu* (to move), *sar* (to go, to injure, to think), *vara* (to choose, to obstruct), and *var* (to choose, to obstruct)—after these, the suffix *co* occurs. [The root] *cu* means to move.
*Rukkha* means *coca*, a specific type of fruit that has been consumed. *Sacca* means "truth," so called because it remembers (*sarati*) future suffering and destroys (*hiṃsati*) it;
thus it is non-false (*avitatha*). *Vacca* means "excrement," so called because it wards off (*vāreti*) happiness. 40. *Marā* and *cuīcī*.

In the case of *mara-pāṇa-cāga*, there are three [suffixes]: *cu*, *ī*, and *ī*. *Maraṇa* means death; it is *maru*. It kills (*māreti*) and destroys darkness, thus it is *marīci*, meaning a ray of light or a mirage. One who dies (*marati*) is a mortal (*macca*), meaning a living being (*satta*).

41. With the roots *kusa* and *pasa*, the suffix *chika* occurs. *Kusa* means to revile (*akkosa*); *pasa* means to oppress (*bādhana*). From these, *chika* arises. One is reviled (*kusīyati*) or insulted (*akkosīyati*), thus *kucchi* means the belly (*udara*). One is oppressed (*pasīyati*) or confined therein, thus *pacchi* is a particular kind of vessel (*bhājanaviseso*).
42. *Kasa*, *usa*, and *chuka*.

From *kasa* (to scratch) and *usa* (to burn), *chuka* is formed. That which they scratch (*kasanti*) and scrape (*vilekhanti*) is *kacchu* = scabies. That which burns (*usati*), consumes (*dahati*), and causes heat (*santāpeti*) is *ucchu* = sugarcane.
43. *Asa*, *masa*, *vada*, *kuccha*, *kaca*, and *cho*.
The suffix *cha* occurs after the roots *as* (to throw), *mas* (to lick), *vad* (to speak), *kuc* (to contract), and *kac* (to bind).
*Asati chippatīti accho* = a bear (*bhallūka*). *Masati jalanti maccho* = a fish (*mīna*). *Vadatīti vaccho* = a calf (*nelaka*).
*Kucīyati saṃkocīyatīti koccho* = a folding chair (*bhaddapīṭṭha*). *Kacīyati bandhīyatīti kaccho* = a region of the body, and a marshy place (*tanupadeso*, *anūpo*).

44. *Gucchādayo* (The group beginning with *guccha*). Words such as *guccha* and others are derived from verbal roots (*dhātu*). From the root *gup* in the sense of protecting: the state of being protected; that which is protected is a *guccha*, namely a cluster or bunch (*thavaka*). From the root *tus* in the sense of satisfaction:

that by which they are satisfied is *tuccha*, namely falsehood (*musā*). From the root *pus* in the sense of nourishing: that by which they nourish their bodies is a *puccha*, namely a tail (*vāladhi*). Other words are to be understood in the same way.
45. *Ara-ju-ñaṭa-ca*.

After the [verbal root] *ara*, there is the suffix *ju*; and after *ari*, there is *uṭa* as well. The letter *ṭ* serves the purpose of indicating a universal substitution (*sabbādesa*). Because it proceeds without crookedness, it is straight (*uju*)—that is, not bent. 46. *Rajjādayo*. (The group beginning with *rajju* follows).

The suffixes *ju* and others are added after verbal roots. From the root *rudh* (in the sense of "obstructing"), with the suffix *ussa* and the augment *atta*, we have *rujjhu-yottaṃ* (a rope), meaning "that by which they obstruct. From the root *man* (in the sense of "knowing"), from the form *amaññittha*, we derive *mañju* = *mañjulaṃ* (graceful);

other examples are to be understood in the same way. 47. *Gidhā jhaka*. After the root *gidh* (in the sense of "desiring intensely"), the suffix *jhaka* occurs. That which desires intensely is *gijjho*—a specific kind of bird.
48. *Vaṃjhādayo*.

Words such as *vañcha* and others are derived as *nipātā* (irregular formations) ending in the suffix *-jhaka*. From the root *vana* (to beg), *vanoti*—meaning "he begs to experience himself"—is *vañjha*, which refers to a fruitless tree;
*vañjhā* refers to a woman who has no offspring; *viñjha* refers to a mountain (*pabbata*), meaning its very nature. From the root *saṃja* (to bind): [the following forms are derived].

There is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra). That which is acquired (*sañjiyati*) is called *sajjhaṃ*, meaning silver (*rajataṃ*); other examples are to be understood in the same way. 49. After the roots *kama-* and *yaja-*, the suffix *ña* occurs. *Kama-* is used in the sense of desire;

*yaja-* is used in the senses of worshiping a deity, joining together, and giving. After these, the suffix *ña* occurs, with the substitution of the nasal class for the final *m*. That which is desired is a *kaññā*, meaning a young girl (*kumārī*). There is the substitution of the following form for the *j*. That by which one sacrifices is a *yañño*, meaning a sacrifice (*yāgo*).
50. *Puñña*.

It purifies (*punāti*), or it has been purified (*puṇitasmā*); the suffix *ña* is added and the root vowel is shortened. Or, because it makes something beautiful (*sundarattaṃ karoti*), it is *puñña* = wholesome (*kusala*).
51. *Ara*, *hāñño*, *hāssa*, and *hira* [are also suffixes].

In *ara-gamana* and *vā-cāga*, there is another [suffix] after these; for it (*assa*), there is the substitution of *hirañña*. That which is gone to or approached is *arañña* = forest. That which abandons the lowness of beings is *hirañña* = wealth and gold.
(Thus ends the rule for the application of the *ca*-group suffixes.
52. *Kira*, *tarā*, *kīṭo*.

In *kira* (to scatter) and *viki* (to scatter), and in *tara* (to cross), from these [roots] *kīṭa* arises. Because jewels are scattered here to beautify it, *kirīṭaṃ* = a crown (*makuṭaṃ*). From the grammatical rule *taraiti*, its suffix is *-ita*; because they cross over by means of this beautiful form, *tirīṭaṃ* = a turban (*veṭṭhanaṃ*).

53. From *saka* and others, the suffix *aṭ* [is applied]. *Saka* is in the sense of power; *kasa* is in the sense of going; *kara* is in the sense of doing; *makka* is a verbal root in the sense of playing; *deva* is in the sense of sporting; *kama* is in the sense of desire.

The suffix *aṭ* occurs after these and others. It carries a burden (*bhāraṃ vahituṃ*), thus *saṅkaṭo* = a vehicle (*yāna*). It has become sapless (*nirojattaṃ agamī*), thus *kasaṭaṃ* = sapless (*niroja*).
It acts in an unpleasant way (*amanāpaṃ karoti*), thus *karaṭo* = a crow (*kāka*). It rubs and moves (*makkati calati*), thus *makkaṭo* = a monkey (*vānara*).
He plays like a god and is worshipped (*devīyati pūjīyati*), thus *devaṭo* = a sage (*isi*). He moves, desires, and climbs up (*kamati icchati ārohati*), thus *kamaṭo* = a dwarf (*vāmana*).
54. *Makuṭa*, *āvāṭa*, *kavāṭa*, and *kukkuṭa*—these words are derived as follows.

From the root *maṅki* (to adorn), the suffix *uṭa* is added and the final nasal (*niggahīta*) is elided; it adorns (*maṅketi*) or beautifies, thus *makuṭa* = *kirīṭa* (a crown). From the root *ava* (to go), the suffix *āṭana* is added;

one goes into or is dug (*avyate khaññati*), thus *āvāṭa* = *kāsu* (a pit). From the word *ku* (bad/evil) and the root *itima* (to go), the suffix *āṭa* is added, with the appropriate substitution of *o* for *ava*.
It covers and it sounds, thus *kavāṭaṃ* = a door-panel. From the roots *kuka*, *vaka*—meaning "to take"—comes *kuṭaka*; from *kukati*, meaning "it takes its range," comes *kukkuṭo* = a cock.
55. With the suffixes *ṭha* after *kamu*, *kusa*, and *kasa*:
*kamu* means desire, *usa* means burning, *kusa* means reproaching, and *kasa* means going; with these, the suffix *ṭha* occurs, [provided they end] in a nasal or a labial group (*niggahīta-vagga*).

It desires rice and so forth; thus, *kaṇṭho* = *galo*. [The following are examples of] *okkapa-rūpa* and other such forms: it is heated by heat among rice and the like, thus *oṭṭho* = *dantacchado* (lip) and *karabho*.
It is pierced or tormented, thus *koṭṭho* = *dhaññanilayo* (granary). It is cut, goes, or perishes, thus *kaṭṭhaṃ* = *dāru* (wood).
56. *Kuṭṭha* and others.
The words *kuṭṭha* and others are derived from verbal roots with the suffix *-tha*. From the root *kus* (to revile), there is the substitution of *ṭha* and the elision of the vowel *o*;

thus, it is called *kuṭṭha* because one is reviled (*kusīyati*) or reviled excessively (*akkosīyati*), meaning a skin disease. From the root *kuṇ* (sound), there is the absence of the *pararūpa* sandhi and the elision of the vowel *o*; thus, it is called *kuṇṭha* because it makes a sound (*kuṇati*) or cries out, meaning extremely dull;

or because it is reviled (*kuṇīyati*) or reviled excessively, meaning one whose hands and feet have been severed, etc. From the root *daṃs* (to bite), there is the substitution of *dā*; thus, it is called *daṃsa* because one is bitten by it (*daṃsati*).

*dāṭhā* is a specific kind of tooth. From the root *kam*, with the suffixes *aka* and *a*: that which is desired (*kāmīyati*) or longed for (*dīneti*) is *kamaṭha*, meaning an alms-bowl, a dwarf, and a tortoise.
From the root *phass*, with the suffix *i*: that which is touched (*phuṭṭho*) is *phuṭṭha*, meaning contact (*phassa*);
other [derivatives] are likewise formed. 57. *vara*, *kara*, *aṇḍa*.

In *vara* (to choose) and *kara* (to do), the suffix *-aṇḍa* occurs. That which wards off (*vārayati*) phlegm (*pephaṃ*) within oneself is a *varaṇḍa*, a disease of the mouth. That which is done (*karīyati*) is a *karaṇḍa*, a particular kind of container. 58. The suffix *-aṇḍa* follows roots ending in *man*.

The suffix *-aṇḍa* frequently occurs after roots ending in *ma* or *na* when they have the sense of "action" (*kriyattha*). In *sama* (to calm), *samanaṃ* is a *saṇḍa*, meaning a collection (*samūho*).
*Kama* (to move): that which moves or goes is *kaṇḍa*, meaning an arrow or a section. *Dama* (to tame):
that by which one tames is *daṇḍa*, meaning restraint. *Ama* (to go): that wherein things arise is *aṇḍa*, meaning an egg or a sheath. *Gaṇḍa*:
that which goes toward a state of suppuration is *gaṇḍa*, meaning a disease or a part of the face. *Ramu* (to sport): that wherein they sport is... [raṅga].

*Ruṇḍā* means a widow. Regarding *mana-ñāṇa*: it is called *maṇḍa* because they think (*maññanti*) by means of it; it is the scum of rice-gruel and so forth. Regarding *khaṇa-khaṇa* in the sense of splitting:

it is called *khaṇḍa* because it is split (*khaññati*); it is a specific preparation of sugarcane. Regarding *lama* in the sense of harming: it is called *laṇḍa* because it soils (*lamati*) and harms the state of purity;
it is excrement. Other [words] are likewise [to be understood].

59. *Kuṇḍa* and others. Words beginning with *kuṇḍa* are derived as nouns ending in *-a*. From the roots *kama*, *mana*, and *tanā*, the suffix *assa-utta* is applied: that which is desired (*kāmīyati*) is *kuṇḍa* = a vessel.

One who conceives of what is beneficial and harmful (*maññati hitāhitaṃ*) is *muṇḍa* = one whose hair is shorn. That by which one stretches (*tanoti etena*) is *tuṇḍa* = the mouth. [The root] *īra* is used in the sense of throwing.

The substitution of *era-* [for *īra-*]. That which moves or trembles is an *eraṇḍa*—the castor-oil plant (*vyagghapuccha*). [The suffix] *si* is used in the sense of service (*sevā*); the *si* becomes *khamuka*.
That which serves what is fragrant is a *sikhaṇḍa*—a crest (*cūḷā*).
Other examples are to be understood in the same way. 60. [The roots] *tija*, *kasa*, *tasa*, *dakkhā*, *kiṇo*, *jassa*, and *kho*.

In *tija* (sharpening), *nisāna* (whetting), *kasa* (plowing/acting), *gamana* (going), *tasa* (fear), *pipāsā* (thirst), and *dakkha-vuddhi* (skillful growth)—with these [suffixes] *kiṇo* occurs, as well as *jassa* and *kho*.
That which has been sharpened is *tikhiṇaṃ* = *nisitaṃ* (whetted). That which plows or proceeds is *kasiṇaṃ* = *asesaṃ* (entirety). The state of fearing is *tasiṇā* = *taṇhā* (craving).
That by which one sees or attains growth is *dakkhīṇā* = *kusalaṃ* (wholesome).
61. The suffix *ṇi* occurs after the following roots: *vī* (to weave), *si* (to serve), *sū* (to bring forth), *du* (to go), *kī* (to buy), and *sā* (to finish).
Thus: *veṇi* is a braid of hair (*kesakalāpa*), derived from *vīyati*. *Seṇi* is a group of artisans of the same caste, derived from *sevanaṃ* (service).
It is approached and used, thus *niseṇi* = stairs (*sopānaṃ*). It flows and exudes, thus *soṇi* = the hip (*kaṭi*).
It runs and carries, thus *doṇi* = a wooden water-carrier and a boat; because it is read in the list beginning with *nada*, it also becomes *soṇī* and *doṇī*.
Buying, or that by which one buys, is *keṇi* = purchase. It makes suffering thin, thus *sāṇi* = a curtain (*tirokaraṇī*); other [words] are likewise.
62. Gahādīhyaṇi.
From roots such as *gaha* (to seize), *ara* (to go), *dhara* (to hold), *sara* (in the senses of movement, seeking, and thought), and *tara* (to cross), the suffix *-aṇi* occurs.
That which seizes is *gahaṇi* = the fire that digests food and so forth. That which is gone to or approached is *araṇi* = the wood used for churning fire.

*Dhāreti* means "it supports," thus *dharaṇī* is the earth (*mahī*). *Sarīyati* means "it is traversed," thus *bharaṇī* is the path (*magga*). *Taranti anena* means "they cross by means of this," thus *taraṇī* is a boat (*nāvā*) and also the sun (*sūriya*).

63. *Rīvībhāhi ṇu*: From the roots *rī* (to flow/emit), *vī* (to go), and *bhā* (to shine), the suffix *ṇu* occurs. *Rīyati* means "it flows/is emitted," thus *reṇu* is dust (*raja*). *Veti* means "it moves," thus *veṇu* is bamboo (*veḷu*). *Bhāti* means "it shines," thus *bhāṇu* is a ray (*raṃsi*).
64. *Khāṇu* and others.
Words beginning with *khāṇu* are derived as nouns ending in the suffix *-ṇu*. From the root *khaṇ* (or *khan*) in the sense of "digging" or "excavating," the vowel *a* is replaced by *ā*;

thus, that which is dug out or excavated is a *khāṇu*—a tree whose branches have been cut off. From the root *jan* in the sense of "birth" or "arising," the vowel *a* is optionally replaced by *ā*; thus, that by which one is born or produced is a *jāṇu* (the knee).

*Jaṇṇu* is the joint of the shank and thigh. *Hara* means "taking away"; from the root *hṛ*, with the suffix *enu*, we get *hareṇu*, meaning a fragrant substance (musk), and other such words as well. 65.

The suffix *ṇo* occurs after the roots beginning with *ku*. *Ku* means "sound," *su* means "hearing," *du* means "going," *vara* means "choosing," *kara* means "doing," and *paṇa* means "transaction" or "praise."
The suffix *ṇa* occurs after roots such as *tā-* (to protect), *lī-* (to cling), and others. That in which one cries out (*kavati*) or sounds (*nadati*) is a *koṇa*:

namely, the handle of a lute or other musical instrument. That which hears (*suṇoti*) is a *soṇa*: namely, a dog or a man. That which plays or moves about (*davati*) is a *doṇa*: namely, a specific measure of capacity.

That which wards off deformity (*virūpatta*) is *vaṇṇa*: namely, blue and other colors. That which performs hearing (*savanaṃ karoti*) is *kaṇṇa*: namely, the sense of hearing. That which is traded or bartered (*paṇīyati*) is *paṇṇa*: namely, a leaf.
*Tāṇaṃ* means protection, because it protects (*lāyati*). *Leṇaṃ* means a place of concealment, because beings hide (*nilīyanti*) therein.

66. The suffix *ṇaka* follows the roots *su-* (to hear) and *vī-* (to weave). From these, *ṇaka* is applied. One who hears is a *suṇo*, which is a dog (*sunakha*). That which is woven is a *vīṇā*, which is a lute (*vallakī*).
67. *Tiṇādayo* (Grass, etc.).

Words beginning with *tiṇa* are derived as nouns ending in the suffix *-ṇa*. From the root *tija* (to sharpen), there is the elision of *ja*; that by which one sharpens is *tiṇa*, such as *bīraṇa* grass and the like.
From the roots *lī* (to cling) and *lih* (to lick), there is the substitution of *lo* for *la* and *vā*; it clings to everything through its moisture, thus it is *loṇa* or *lavaṇa* (salt).
It is called *loṇa* (salt) because it is licked (*lehīyati*), it is called *loṇa* (salt) because it is tasted (*sādīyati*), and it is called *loṇa* (salt) because it moistens (*kledeti*).

From the root *gam*, with the suffix *issa*: it goes (*gacchati*), thus *goṇo* = *go* (ox). From *hara* in the sense of taking away (*haraṇe*), with the suffixes *ṇa* and *sañji*: it is carried away (*harīyati*), thus *hariṇo* = *migo* (deer).

From *īra* in the sense of shaking (*kampane*), with the shortening of the vowel (*rassattaṃ*), the suffix *ṇa*, and the addition of *ñi*: when its own dry state is reached, it shakes (*īrati*) or trembles, thus *iriṇaṃ* = *ūsaraṃ* (saline soil).
In *thu-abhitthave*, "it is praised at length" (*dīgho abhitthavīyati*), thus *thūṇaṃ* = city;
*thūṇo* = house-pillar; and so too others. 68. *Ravaṇa-varaṇa-pūraṇādayo*.

Words such as *ravaṇa*, *varaṇa*, and *pūraṇa* are established by means of the suffix *-aṇa*. One who cries out is *ravaṇo* = the cuckoo. One who wards off is *varaṇo* = the rampart. That by which one is filled is *pūraṇo* = fulfillment.
(Thus ends the section on the application of the *ṭa*-group suffixes.
69. *Pā* and *vasa* take *ati*.

The roots *pā* (to protect) and *vasa* (to dwell) take the suffix *ati*. There is elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbasaralopa*). That which protects is *pāti* = *pati* (lord/master); that in which they dwell is *vasati* = *gehaṃ* (house).
70. *Dhā* is in the sense of holding; *hi* in the sense of moving; *tana* in the sense of expansion; *jana* in the sense of producing;
*jara* in the sense of the decline of age; *ama* in the sense of going; and *saca* in the sense of conjunction—by these [roots], the suffix *tu* occurs.
That which holds is a *dhātu*, such as red ochre (*geruka*) and so forth. That by which one moves toward or brings about a fruit is [also a *dhātu*].

*Hetu* means cause (*kāraṇa*); it is called *setu* because people resort to it (*sevīyati*), which is to say, it binds (*bandhati*)—this refers to a path (*paddhati*). *Taṇṇateti* means thread (*tantu*), that is, yarn (*sutta*). It is called *jantu* because it is produced by kamma and defilements (*janīyate*);

or, it is called *jantu* because it is born from kamma and defilements—thus *jantu* means a being (*satta*). It is called *jattu* because it decays (*jīrati*)—thus *jattu* means a shoulder joint (*aṃsasandhi*).

It is called *gantu* because it goes (*gacchati*)—thus *gantu* means a traveler (*gamika*). It is called *sattu* because it is scattered or comes together (*sacati*, *sameti*)—thus *sattu* means the flour of barley and other grains.
71. *Arissuṭa ca*.

After the word *ari*, there is the substitution of *uṭ* [for the final vowel], and furthermore, *uṭ* is the substitute for *ari*. That which proceeds as aversion is *utu*—namely, the winter season and so forth. 72. *Pitvādayo*. [The suffixes] *pitva* and others [are applied].

The words *pitu* and so forth are derived as nouns ending in *-tu* and *-anta*. From the root *pā* (to protect), there is the substitution of *i* for *ā*; one who protects (*pāti*) is a father (*pitā*), meaning "the progenitor.

From the root *pā* (to drink) and others, there is the substitution of *m* for *ā*; she who causes to drink (*pāyeti*) is a mother (*mātā*), meaning "the progenitress. From the root *bhā* (to shine), one who shines (*bhātī*) is a brother (*bhātā*), meaning "one born from the same womb.

From the root *dhā* (to hold), there is the substitution of *ī* for *ā*; she who is held (*dhārīyati*) is a daughter (*dhītā*), meaning "a female child. From the root *duha* (to fill), there is the elision of *o*, and the substitution of *ñchi* for *tu*; she who milks (*duhati*) is...
She who gives birth and fills [the lineage] is *duhitā* = *puttī*. From the root *jan*, meaning "to produce," with the suffix *atta*; there is no substitution of *mā* for *ca*.

He who produces a son-in-law (*paputta*) is *jāmātā* = *duhitupati*. From the root *nah*, meaning "to bind," he is bound by affection; thus *nattā* = *paputta*. From the root *hu*, meaning "to invoke," he invokes and honors;
thus *hotā* = the performer of sacrifice (*yaññaka*). From the root *pū*, meaning "to purify," he purifies and makes future existence purified; thus *potā* = he himself.

73. *Jana* [is used] in the sense of being born (*janane*), and *kara* in the sense of doing (*karaṇe*); with these, the suffix *-tu* occurs. The letter *r* has the function of causing the elision of the final vowel and the following consonant. That which is born is *jatu* = lac. That which is done is *katu* = a sacrifice accompanied by a sacrificial post.
74. After the root *sak*, the suffix *-un* occurs.
From the root *sak* (to be able), *sakuṇṭa* becomes *sakunto*, meaning "a bird" (*pakkhī*). 75. From the root *kap* (to cover), *ota* is the suffix.
From *kapatīti* (he covers), *kapoto* is formed, meaning "a pigeon" (*pārevata*). Alternatively, *ṭo* may replace it, resulting in *kapoṭo*, which is the same word.
76. *Vasādīhyanto*.

In the sense of dwelling (*vasa-nivāse*), arising (*ruha-janane*), auspiciousness (*bhadda-kalyāṇe*), prosperity (*nanda-samiddhiyaṃ*), and sustaining life (*jīva-pāṇadhāraṇe*), and so forth—the suffix *-anta* occurs.
They dwell during this season, being intent on play, thus *vasanto* = the season (*utu*). It arises and grows, thus *ruhanto* = a tree (*rukkho*).

And there is the deer-king named [so-and-so]. In *Bhaddissa*, there is the elision of the suffixes beginning with *-saṃ* (the genitive). One who possesses auspicious qualities (*kalyāṇadhamma*) is a *bhadanta*—that is, one who has gone forth (*pabbajita*).
That by which one rejoices is *nandantī*—a female friend (*sakhī*); the vowel *ī* is used because it is listed among the words beginning with *nada*, and so it is in the following cases as well.

That by which they live is *jīvantī*—a medicinal herb (*osadhi*). It flows, thus it is *savantī*—a river (*nadī*). It causes to weep, thus it is *rodantī*—a medicinal herb (*osadhi*). It protects, thus it is *avantī*—a province (*janapada*).

77. *Hi* and *sī*: after these [roots], the suffix *-anta* occurs, and there is also the augment *muk*. The letter *k* is for the purpose of indicating the final portion of the suffix. *Himaṃ hinoti pavattati etasmin* = *hemanto* (the season); *sayanti ettha ūkā kusumādayo ca* = *sīmanto* (the hairline).
78. After *hara*, *ruha*, and *kulā*, the suffix *-ita* occurs.
In the words *hara-haraṇe*, *ruha-janane*, and *kula-patthāre*, the suffix *ita* occurs after these roots.

That which carries away (*harati*) its own moisture is *harita*—a particular color. That which grows (*ruhati*) is *rohita*—a particular kind of fish. That which spreads through the body by way of pervasion is *rohita*;
when the vowel is shortened, it becomes *lohita*—blood. That which gathers (*kulati*) and extends its own quality is *kolita*—the second chief disciple.
And likewise for [words] ending in -a such as *maru*. 79.

From roots ending in -a, such as *bhara*, *rañja*, *yaja*, *paca*, etc., the suffix *-ta* occurs. *Bharati* (he bears) becomes *bharato* = an actor (*naṭo*). There is the elision of the nasal (*niggahīta*). *Rañjanti ettha* (they color here) becomes *rajataṃ* = silver (*sajjhaṃ*). *Yajitabbo* (should be sacrificed to) becomes *yajato* = fire (*aggi*). *Pacati* (he cooks) becomes *pacato* = a cook (*sūpakāro*).
80. *Ātaka* [is added] after *kira*, *ala*, *cila*, and so forth.

From *kirati* (he scatters), *kirāta* = a Śabara; by the shortening of the vowel, *kilāta* = gold. From *alati* (it takes), *alāta* = a firebrand. From *cilati* (he wears), *cilāta* = a type of impurity.
81. *Atta* [is added] after *ama* and so forth.
But it is not so that he is afflicted by the arts (*kalā*). It moves for a period of time, thus *amattaṃ* = a vessel (*bhājana*); there is the elision of the preceding vowel (*pubbasaralopa*).

*Mānaṃ* becomes *mattaṃ*, meaning measure (*pamāṇa*) and delimitation (*pariccheda*). "By means of the excellent cord" (*varantunena*): *varattā* = a rope (*yotta*). It delimits (*kalati*), thus *kalattaṃ* = a wife (*bhariyā*). 82. [The suffix] *to* follows verbal roots (*vādīhi*).

The suffix *to* occurs after roots such as: *vā* (to blow), *tā* (to protect), *tan* (to extend), *dam* (to subdue), *am* (to go), *si* (to serve), *su* (to hear), *pū* (to purify), *gup* (to protect), *yuj* (to restrain), *gah* (to seize), *at* (to go continuously), and *khip* (to throw). For example:
*vāyatīti vāto* = wind (*vāyu*). *tāyatīti tāto* = father (*pitā*). *tanuteti tantaṃ* = thread (*tantavo*).

*Damatī* means "one who has tamed [his] teeth" (*anto-dasano*). *Amati yāti* means "that which goes to the end," thus *anto-osānaṃ*; it also refers to a part near the end or a division. *Sevīyati* means "it is served," thus *seto* = white.

*Suṇantunenā* means "by hearing," thus *sotaṃ* = hearing. *Savatī* means "it flows," thus *soto* = a flow of water. *Punīyati* means "it is purified," thus *poto* = a young child. *Gopīyati* means "it is protected," thus *gotthaṃ* = a fraction and so forth.
*Yojanti anenā* means "they yoke by means of this," thus *yottaṃ* = a rope. *Mamāyantehi gayhati* means "it is grasped by those who possess a sense of 'mine'."

*gatta* = body (*sarīra*). That which moves (*atati*) continuously (*nirantaraṃ*) toward itself (*abādhaṃ*) is *attā* = mind, etc. (*manādi*). That into which things are scattered (*khipīyati*) is *khettaṃ* = a field (*kedāraṃ*).
83. The suffix *taka* is added after *ghara* and others.
[The roots] *gara* (to sprinkle), *ghara* (to sprinkle), *si* (to serve), *dū* (to torment), *mida* (to be oily), *cita* (to perceive), *pusa* (to nourish).

In the sense of obtaining life (*vida-lābhe*), there is a *taka* suffix [forming] these and other words: it is held (*gharati*) and poured (*siñcati*), thus *ghataṃ* = clarified butter (*sappi*). It is served (*sevīyati*), thus *sito* = white (*seto*).

Because of being ill-spoken of, one is tormented (*dūyati*) and afflicted; thus *dūto* = a messenger (*pesarakāro*). He greets (*mijjati*) and shows affection (*sinehati*), thus *mitto* = a friend (*suhadayo*).
He thinks (*cinteti*), thus *cittaṃ* = consciousness (*viññāṇaṃ*) and painting (*cittakamma*) etc. He is nourished (*posīyati*), thus *putto* = a son (*attajo*). They find joy (*vindanti pītiṃ*).

*Manena* means *vitta*, which is wealth (*dhana*). Regarding *vara-va-raṇa-sambhattīsu*: *varaṇa* refers to conduct (*vatta*), such as the holy life (*brahmacariya*) and so forth. 84. *Nettādayo*. Words beginning with *netta* are formed by adding the suffix *taka*.

From the root *nī* (to lead), the form *etta* is used, and *taka* is added by way of grammatical derivation (*nipātanā*). Thus, it is called *netta* because it leads (*nayati*) or causes one to reach [the goal].
*Netta* means "eye" (*nayana*) and also "leader" (*netā*). In the sense of "making" (*kara-karaṇe*), *assu* is [the suffix]; the instrument (*karaṇa*) is called *kutta*, which is "action" (*kiriyā*).

In the sense of "going" (*kamissa assu*), that which goes or moves is a *kunta*, a specific type of weapon. In the sense of "sporting" (*rama-kīḷāyaṃ*), preceded by *su*, the long vowel is always substituted for *su*;

one who sports well or sports excellently is *sūrato*, meaning "easy to live with. In the sense of "urinating" (*mihissa assu*), that which sprinkles or emits is *muttaṃ*, meaning "urine" (*passāvo*).
In the root *pāl* (meaning "to protect"), there is shortening of the vowel due to the suffix *ñi*. That which protects is *palitaṃ*, meaning the whiteness produced by aging in the hair and body hair.

Through the addition of the suffix *ta* after the vowel *ā*, one who possesses that [whiteness] is *palito* (masculine) or *palitā* (feminine). In the root *mhi* (meaning "to smile"), the suffix *ta* is applied;
*mhitam* means a gentle smile (*mandahasita*). *Mhitam* is also *mihitam*, meaning the same thing. In the root *kus* (meaning "to revile"), the suffix *īña* is applied; thus, *kusīyati*.

"Akkosīyati" means *kusīta*, which is "lazy"; the root *si* means "binding," and it is lengthened [to *sī*]. They lie down (*sentī*) or bind themselves to the household life by means of this, thus it is *sītā*, meaning a furrow of a plow;
other examples are likewise. 85. *Samādīhyatho*.

The prefix *ā-* occurs with such words as *sama* (calm), *upasama* (tranquility), *dara* (fear), *daratha* (distress), *dama* (taming), *upāsama* (restraint), *kilama* (fatigue), *klama* (exhaustion), *gelañña* (sickness), *sapā* (swearing), *akkosa* (abuse), and *vāsa-nivāsa* (dwelling).

It is calm because it calms, thus *samatha* = concentration (*samādhi*). Distressing is distress (*daratha*), which means oppression (*pīḷā*). Taming is taming (*damatha*), which means self-restraint (*dama*).

Fatiguing is fatigue (*kilamatha*), which means exhaustion (*parissama*). Swearing is an oath (*sapatha*), which means making a solemn declaration (*saccakaraṇa*). They dwell... (*āvasanti*)... [in] dwelling.
*Ettha* means a dwelling or a house. 86. *Upavasā vasso ṭa ca*:

from the root *vas* preceded by *upa*, the suffix *tha* occurs, and furthermore, there is the substitution of *vassa* for *vas* and *ṭa*. That wherein they dwell near [the observance] is *uposatha*—meaning a specific lunar day (*tithi*) and the lineage of the nine great elephants.
87. *Ramā-thaka*.

After the root *ram*, the suffix *tha* occurs; due to its capacity to cause the elision of the following consonant, there is also the elision of the letter *a* even after the [augment] *at*. That by which they delight and sport is a *ratha*—that is, a chariot (*sandana*). 88. *Titthādayo*.
[The group beginning with *tittha* follows.]
Words such as *tittha* and others are formed with the suffix *-tta*. *Tara* means "to cross"; its abstract form is *taraṇa*.

With the substitution of the subsequent form (*pararūpa*), that by which one crosses—such as a river—is called *tittha*. *Sica* means "to sprinkle"; that which sprinkles is *sitta*, namely honeycomb (*madhucchiṭṭha*). *Hasa* means "to laugh";
that by which one laughs is *hattha*, meaning "hand," and also a certain lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*). *Gāyati* means "to sing"; that which is sung is *gāthā*, a specific type of verse.
The meaning is: "They flow by means of this," thus it is *dhana* (wealth). It pierces and afflicts disease, thus it is *tuttha* (medicine). The root *yu* means to mix;
with a long vowel, that which is mixed is *yūtha* (a herd), a collection of animals of the same species. The root *gup* means to protect; with a long vowel, it is *palopa*;
because it is to be protected due to its repulsiveness, it is *gūtha* (excrement), and other such words are formed in the same way.
89. *Vasa*, *mama*, *kusa*: after these, *thu* occurs.

After *vasa* in the sense of "dwelling," *mama* in the sense of "touching," and *kusa* in the sense of "reviling," *thu* is used. That which they dwell in is the meaning of the word *vatthu*. That which touches curd is *matthu*, namely the whey of curd (*dadhimanda*). That which is reviled, cursed, or called a beast is *kotthu*, namely a jackal (*sigāla*).
90. *Saka*, *vasā*: after these, *thi* occurs.

The suffix *thi* occurs after the roots *sak-* (in the sense of ability) and *vas-* (in the sense of dwelling). That by which one is able to go is *satthi*, meaning "the thigh. That in which one dwells—that is, that which covers—is *vatthi*, meaning "below the navel.
91. *Vī-* takes the suffix *thika*.
The suffix *thika* occurs after the root *vī-* in the sense of going. That by which they go—that is, they proceed—is *vīthi*, meaning "a row" or "street."
92. *Sārismā* becomes *rathi*.
After a root ending in *sāri*, the suffix *rathi* occurs. One who impels (*sāreti*) is a *sārathi*, that is, a chariot-driver (*ratha-vāha*). 93. *Tā-tā* becomes *ithi*.
After the suffix *tā*, the suffix *ithi* occurs.

The suffix *ithi* occurs after the roots *tā-* (in the sense of protecting) and *ata-* (in the sense of moving continuously). That which protects (*tāyati*) or guards is *tithi*, namely the lunar days such as the first day of the waxing moon (*paṭipadādi*). That which moves or goes (*atati*) is *atithi*, namely a guest (*abbhāgato*).
94. *Isā* [the suffix] *thī*.
After the root *is-* (to wish), the suffix *thī* occurs. That which wishes (*icchati*) or is wished for (*icchīyati*) is *itthī*, namely a woman (*nārī*).
95. *Ruda*, *khuda*, *muda*, *mada*, *chida*, *sūda*, *sapa*, *kamā*, *daka*.
By these [suffixes] it becomes a noun (*daka*). *Rudatīti ruddo* = Umāpati (the Lord of Umā). By the substitution of *ra* for *la*: *luddo* = a hunter. *Khudati asahatīti khuddo* = lowly.
*Modanti etāyāti muddā* = a coin (a small piece of metal used for gambling). *Majjanti asminti maddo* = a country (in which people delight).
*Chijjati* means it is pierced; thus, *chiddaṃ* is a hole or flaw. *Ū* becomes *ra*; one who serves (*sūdati*) by working for wages for his masters is a *suddo*, that is, a *vasala*.
*Sapantunena* means sound, which is the object of the sense of hearing. That which is desired (*kāmīyati*) is a *kanda*, a specific type of root.
96. *Kunda* and others.

The words beginning with *kunda* and ending with *uda* are derived through the *nipacca* (gerundive) suffix. From the root *kami*, *assu* [is added]: that which is desired is *kunda*, a type of flower. From *mani*, *a* [is added]:
it is thought of (*maññati*) as *manda*, meaning dull-witted. From *vuṇāti*, *una* [is added]: it is woven (*vuṇīyati*) or enclosed, thus *bunda*, the region of the root.

*Nindi* is used in the sense of censuring; there is the elision of *na*: it is censured (*nindīyati*), thus *niddā*, meaning sleep. *Undi* is used in the sense of moistening; there is the elision of *na*: it moistens (*undati*).

It is said that *kiledati* means "to play"; thus, *uddo* is a water-cat (*jalabiḷālo*). Because of the prefix *sam-* and because *undati* (from the root *undi*) means "to moisten" or "to play," *samuddo* is the ocean (*sāgaro*).

In the sense of greatness, abundance, and knowledge, there is the suffix *-ima*; thus, *pulati* (from the root *pula*) meaning "to strike" or "to harm" gives *pulindo*, a mountain-dweller (*savaro*). Other such forms exist as well. 97. *Dadā* [is used] in the sense of giving.
The suffix *dā* occurs after the roots *da*, *dān*, and *atim*. *Daddu*—meaning a specific type of leprosy (*kuṭṭha*)—is derived from the root *duddh* (to give pain), as it gives pain.
98. The suffix *dha* occurs after the roots *khan*, *dam*, and *ram*.

*Khan* is used in the sense of digging; *an* in the sense of breathing; *dam* in the sense of calming; and *ram* in the sense of sporting. By these [roots], *dha* is applied. [This applies] by means of knowledge (*ñāṇena*).

*Dhaññatā* means a heap or mass (*khandho*). *Andho* means one who does not see or live by means of it; that is, one without eyes. *Dandho* means one who is to be tamed; that is, one who is dull-witted or slow.
*Randhaṃ* refers to those such as snakes and other creatures that take delight therein;
thus, it means a hole or opening. 99. *Muddhā* and so forth.

Words beginning with *muddha* ending in *dha* are declined as follows: from the root *muda* (to rejoice), by the absence of the *t* sound, *modanti ettha ūkā* [they rejoice here in the body], thus *muddhā* = the head (*matthaka*).
From the root *ara* (to go), because they go (*aranti*) or proceed (*yanti*) there, *addhā* = a path (*magga*) and time (*kāla*), and *addhaṃ* = half (*upaddha*).

From the root *gidha* (in the sense of longing), with the prefix *abhi*, by the substitution of *i* for *a*, that which desires (*gedhati*) is *gaddho* = a vulture (*gijjha*). From the root *vidha* (to pierce), by the absence of the *e* sound, that which is avoided (*parivajjhati*)... [is *viddha*].
*Viddhaṃ* means pure; other [words] are likewise.
100. *Sīto dhuka*:
after *seti*, the suffix *dhuka* occurs. Because they settle (*sayanti*) by means of it, it is *sīdhu*—a specific kind of liquor.
101. The syllable *ku* arises from these [consonants]:

*va* (excellent), *rā* (to perish), *ka* (hand), *ta* (crossing), *da* (tearing), *ra* (passion), *ya* (Yama), *ma* (cessation), *jj* (yoked), *a* (going), *mi* (mutual), *tha* (place), *sa* (own), *kā* (power).

It occurs in the sense of excellence (*vara*), choosing (*varaṇa*), devotion (*sabbhatti*), going (*gamanā*), doing (*karaṇa*), crossing (*taraṇa*), tearing apart (*vidāraṇa*), Yama (*yama*), cessation (*uparama*), being yoked (*ajjana*), mutual encounter (*mithasaṅgama*), and one’s own power (*sakasatti*). [The rule] “*rā* becomes *ṇa*” applies here.
(5-171) *Nassa* means "to perish. *Varuṇa* means "one who wards off" (*vāreti*); thus it refers to a sage of that name, the king of the gods (*devarāja*), and a tree.

*Aruṇa* means "one who goes toward" (*arati gacchati*); thus it refers to the sun and its charioteer. *Karuṇā* means "compassion" (*dayā*), so called because it performs a task for the hearts of the virtuous when there is suffering in others.

*Taruṇa* means "one who has crossed beyond" (*atarī*) the state of childhood; thus it refers to a youth. [The suffix -uṇa is applied] by the rule of splitting the yoga (*yogavibhāga*) from "Ṇiṇāpina" (5.160).
The elision of *ṇi* [occurs]: that which tears apart (*vidāreti*) is *dāruṇo*—meaning cruel or harsh. That which leads away (*yāmeti*) evil is *yamunā*—the name of a great river.

That which drives together (*ajjati*) a collection of wealth is *ajjuno*—the name of a king and a specific type of tree. Mutual union is *mithunaṃ*—a pair consisting of male and female. That which is able (*sakkoti*) is *sakuno*—a bird.
From the list beginning with *nada*, the feminine suffix *vīm* is applied: *sakunī*. According to the rule "For *tatha*, *nara*, etc., the suffixes *ṭa*, *ṭṭha*, *ṇa*, and *la*" (1.27).
Or *ṇatta* = *sakuṇo*, *sakuṇī*. 102.
*Aja* takes *ino*.
From the root *aja* (to go, to move), *ino* occurs. Because it goes to the market (*vikkaya*), it is called *ajinaṃ* = hide.
103. *Vipinādayo*.
Words beginning with *vipina* are derived as nouns ending in *-in*. From the root *vapa* (to sow seeds), with the suffix *ittha*, we have *vapanti ettha* = *vipinaṃ* = forest (*vana*).

From the root *supa* (to sleep), *supanti etena* = *supinaṃ* = sleep (*niddā*), as well as that which is seen by one who sleeps. From the root *tuda* (to pierce/distress), [with the suffix *ittha*], the *da*...
*Ho*: it strikes and oppresses beings, thus *tuhina* = snow (*hima*). *Kappa* means capability; one who is capable of conquering enemies is *kappino* = a king. *Kama* means to step;
that which is stepped upon, where fish and other creatures enter, is *kumina* = a specific type of fishing net.
*Dā* means giving; that which they give therein is *dinaṃ* = a day. Other [roots] are to be understood in the same way.
104. *Kira* becomes *kana*.
After the root *kira*, *kana* is substituted. By the rule *nassa ṇo*, [it becomes] *kiraṇā* = rays, because they scatter (*kiranti*) or spread about (*vikiranti*).
105. After *dī* and roots ending in *ī*, *naka* is added.

In the roots *dī* (to perish), *ji* (to conquer), *i* (to go) with the prefix *adhi*, and *mī* (to injure), the suffix *naka* is applied. One who has gone to destruction (*khaya*) is *dīna*: one who is destitute.

One who has conquered (*ajinī*) the five Maras is *jina*: the Buddha. One who has gone to lordship (*issaratta*) is *ina*: a master. That which perishes (*mīyate*) or is injured (*hiṃsīyati*) is *mīna*: a fish.
106. *Sidhāvīvāhi no*.
From the roots *si* (to bind), *dhā* (to hold), and *vī* (to go), the suffix *no* occurs. That which binds (*seti*) is *sena* = that which lies down; *senā* = an army.
That which holds (*dhāreti*) is *dhānā* = parched barley. That which goes forth (*veti*) or proceeds (*pavattati*) is *vena* = one of low birth among beings.
It blows or proceeds, thus it is *vāna*—namely, craving (*taṇhā*).

107. *Ūna* and others. Words beginning with *ūna*, ending in the suffix *-na*, are derived from the root *nī*. From the root *ūh* (in the sense of thinking), there is the elision of the consonant *h*; *ūhanaṃ* is *ūna*, meaning incomplete or deficient. From the root *hi* (in the sense of going), there is lengthening of the vowel.

"He went to a state of inferiority" means *hīna* = degraded. In the root *ci* (to collect), there is lengthening: "treasures are collected here," thus *cīna* = a country. In the root *han* (to strike), there is *jagh*:
"it is struck," thus *jaghana* = the hips. In the root *ṭhā* (to stand), there is *the*: "it stands" or "proceeds," thus *thena* = a thief. In the root *und* (to moisten), there is *oda*:
"it is moistened," thus *odana* = cooked rice; that is, food. In the root *rañj* (to color), there is elision of the nasal (*niggahīta-lopa*) and the suffix *aka*: "it colors."
*Anena* + *rajanam* = *rāgo* (passion). *Rañjanti ettha* = *rajanī* (night). *Padissa* + *junuka*, *pajjati gacchati* = *pajjunno* (Indra, and also a cloud).
*Gamissa* + *gaṅa*, *gacchanti ettha vihaṅgādayo* = *gaganam* (the sky, the atmosphere); and so too for others. 108.
*Vī* + *patā* + *tano*.

The root *vī* means "to go," and *pata* means "to go on a path"; from these, the suffix *tanaka* is applied. That by which one moves (*veti*) or proceeds (*pavattati*) is *vetanaṃ* = wages. That wherein they fall (*patanti*) is *pattanaṃ* = a city. 109. *Rama-tanaka*.

From the root *rama*, meaning "to play" or "to delight," the suffix *tanaka* is applied. According to the rule "the final *r* of roots beginning with *gama* is elided" (5.109), the *m* is dropped; that wherein they delight (*ramanti*) is *ratanaṃ* = a gem and so forth, as well as the span of a cubit.

110. After the roots *bhā* ("to shine") and *sū* ("to bring forth"), the suffix *nuka* occurs when followed by *pasava*, *bhā*, and *ditti*. That which is brought forth (*pasavīyati*) is *sūnu* = son. That which shines (*bhāti*) or gleams (*dibbati*) is *bhānu* = the sun. 111. Also after the root *dhā* ("to place") and [the aforementioned roots].
The suffix *ani* is added after the roots *dhā*, *dhṛ*, *i*, *mas*, *nu*, and *ka*. Regarding *dhāretīti dhenu*: it means "she who nourishes" (*dhāreti*), thus *dhenu* = a cow (*gāvī*). 112.

The suffix *ani* is added after the roots *vatt*, *ṭhā*, *vam*, *as*, *hi*, *ani*, *vatt*, *aṭ*, *gam*, *ava*, *rakkh*, *dham*, *sad*, *as*, and *khip*. *Vatt* in the sense of conduct (*vattana*); *aṭ* in the sense of going; *ava* in the sense of protecting; *dham* in the sense of sound; *as* in the sense of throwing. After these, the suffix *ani* is applied.

*Vattani*: that by which one moves; thus *vattani* means a shuttle-rod (*tasa-ra-daṇḍa*). With the prefix *vi-* it becomes *vattanī*, meaning a path (*pantho*). *Aṭani*: that upon which one moves or goes; thus *aṭani* means a bedstead part (*mañcaṅgo*).
*Avani*: that which protects or guards beings; thus *avani* means the earth (*mahī*). *Dhamani*: that by which lutes and other instruments resound; thus *dhamani* means a vein (*sīrā*). *Asani*:
that which is hurled or thrown for the sake of a staff; thus *asani* means a thunderbolt (*kulisaṃ*).
113. Regarding *yuta*:
*yu* means "to go. That which beings (*sattā*) go toward or enter into is *yoni*, meaning "birth" (*bhaga*), as well as the various modes of birth such as egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) and so forth.
(Thus ends the rule for the suffix *tavagga*).
114. *Cam*, *ap*, *pā*, and *vapa* take the suffix *po*.

*Cam* means "to eat," *ap* means "to reach," *pā* means "to protect," and *vapa* means "to sow seeds. From these, *po* occurs. Because they eat (*camanti*) and consume (*adanti*) there, it is *campā* = a city.
Because he went only a little (*īsaka-mattaṃ*), it is *appaṃ* = not much. He protects from misfortune (*apāyaṃ pāti*).
*Rakkhati* means "he guards"; thus *pāpa-kibbisaṃ*. *Vapanti ettha* means "they sow here"; thus *vappa* = a field. 115.

After the roots *yu*, *thu*, and *kūna*, there is the suffix *-po*, and these [roots] undergo lengthening. Because of the power of the rule prescribing lengthening, [the vowels become long]. *Yu* in the sense of mixing, *thu* in the sense of praise, and *ku* in the sense of sound—after these, *-po* occurs, and there is lengthening of these [vowels]. Due to the force of the prescription for lengthening...
The state of being burnt (*ottābhāva*). That wherein things exist together is a *yūpa*—a sacrificial post—and a palace (*pāsāda*).
It is praised (*thavīyati*) as a *thūpa*—a shrine (*cetiya*). Wherein they cry out (*kavanti nadanti*) is a *kūpa*—a well (*udapāna*).
116. [Roots: *khip*, *sup*, *nīs*, *pū*, *pak*.
In *khipa* (to throw), *supa* (to sleep), *nī* (to lead), *sū* (to bring forth), and *pū* (to purify), the suffix *-pa* occurs.
It is thrown away, it goes to destruction—thus *khippaṃ* means "quickly. Dogs and others sleep upon this—thus *suppaṃ* means "a bolster" (*papphoṭana*).
They lead [fruit] from this—thus *nīpo* means "a protective tree. It brings forth flavor; thus *sūpo* means "a specific kind of sauce" (*byañjanaviseso*). It is purified (*pavīyati*).
That which is made pure with *marica*, cumin, and so forth is called *pūpa*—that is, a snack or sweetmeat.
117. *Sippādayo*.
The group beginning with *sippa* is derived from verbal roots. It belongs to one (*assa ittaṃ*); by means of this one purifies (*sapati*), thus *sippaṃ*—an art or craft. [The root] *vapi*...
One who sows knowledge (*vijjā*) is a *vippo*—that is, a *brāhmaṇa*. *Vassa* means "tears" (*bappa*); it is so called because one sows [them], that is, they go out from the heart due to grief.
*Chupa* means "to touch" (*samphasse*); with the suffix *-usse*, that by which one touches is *cheppa*—that is, the tail. *Rupa* means "being affected" (*ruppane*);

with the elision of *pa* and lengthening of the vowel, that which is affected, that is, undergoes transformation, is *rūpa*—namely, the primary elements and their derivatives—and so it is for others as well.
118. *Sāsāpo*.
Because it is a command (*sāsa*) that is to be followed (*anu-siṭṭhiya*), it is called *apo*; thus, *sāsāpo* is a specific type of grain.
119. *Viṭapādayo*.
*Viṭapa* and other such words are derived from roots ending in *p*. From the root *vaṭ* in the sense of "encircling" (*veṭṭhane*), with the suffix *itta*, one says *vaṭati* or *veṭṭhati*;

that by which [something] is encircled is *ativiṭapo*, a particular kind of thicket. From the root *kuth* in the sense of "putrefaction" (*pūtibhāve*), with *tha* changed to *ṇa*, one says *akuthi*, meaning "it went to putrefaction";
