thus it is *kuṇapo*, a corpse. From *maṇḍa* in the sense of "adornment" (*bhūsane*), one says *maṇḍeti* (he adorns) people, or it is *maṇḍīyati* (is adorned) by people; thus it is *maṇḍapo*, a hall for people. In this same way, others are also formed.
120. *Gupā* becomes *pho*.
From the root *gup*, the word *pho* arises. That which is to be protected (*gopīyati*) is called *goppho*—the ankle.
121. After *gara*, *sara*, and so forth, the suffix *bo* is applied.
It arises from the roots *gar*, *sar*, and others. Because one torments others by means of it, it is *garba* = conceit (*abhimāna*). Because it moves and proceeds, it is *sabba* = whole (*sakala*).
It is approached and gone to by people desiring fruit; thus it is *amba* = the mango tree (*cūta*). She is approached and gone to by her son; thus she is *ambā* = mother. 122. The *nimba* and others.
The *nimba* and other such trees are derived from verbal roots. *Namissa assī*: it bends (*namati*) under the weight of its fruit, thus *nimbo* = *ariṭṭho*.
*Vamissa vassa bittaṃ*: it vomits or ejects bile (*pitta*) and so forth, thus *bimbaṃ* = the body (*sarīraṃ*).
*Kusissa amuka*: it is made bitter (*tittena kusīyati*) or reviled, thus *kosambo* = the tree. *Kadatissa amuka*: they open (*kadanti*) the gates and so forth by means of it.
*Kadamba* becomes *rukkha* (tree). From *kuṭi*, by means of the suffix *-umuka*, it becomes *kuṭumba*; it is so called because it is "struck" (*koṭīyati*) or set in motion by people;

thus *kuṭumba* refers to the four-footed [livestock], fields, houses, wives, and slaves. From *kaṇḍi*, *kuḍu* arises. Because rice and other grains are "pounded" (*kaṇḍanti*) or measured by this, *kuḍuba* is a measure; and so it is with others as well.
123. *Dara* means "tearing.
From this root *dara*, there arises the word *dabbi*. Because it tears apart boiled rice and other foods, it is called *dabbi* (a spoon) or *kaṭacchu*; in the Vedic language (*vīmhi*), it is *dabbī*.
124. *Kara*, *sara*, *sala*, *kala*, *valla*, *vasā*, and *abho*.

The suffix *abha* occurs after these roots: *kṛ* in the sense of making (*karaṇe*), *sṛ* in the senses of going (*gati*) and harming/considering (*hiṃsā-cintāsu*), *sal* in the sense of going (*gamana*), *kal* in the sense of counting (*saṅkhyāne*), *val* and *vall* in the sense of covering (*saṃvaraṇe*), and *vas* in the sense of dwelling (*nivāse*).
One makes, thus *karabha*: the lip and the region of the hand. One moves/goes, thus *sarabha*: a particular kind of deer.
One moves/goes, thus *salabha*: a moth. One is counted/measured according to age, thus... (the word *kalabha* follows).

*Kalabha* is a young elephant (*hatthipotaka*). From this root *kal*, etc., in the *ḷatta* dialect, *kaḷabha* is the same [word]. *Vallabha*: he performs a covering (*saṃvaraṇa*), thus *vallabha* means "beloved" (*piya*).
*Vasabha*: by means of this they dwell, thus *vasabha* means "leader" (*puṅgava*).
125. *Gadārabha*.
From *gada* comes *rabha*. One who speaks (*gadati*) is a *gadrabha*, that is, a donkey (*khara*).
126. From *usa* and *rāsa* comes *kabha*.

With these two—*usa* in the sense of burning (*dāha*) and *rāsa* in the sense of sound (*sadda*)—the suffix *kabha* occurs. That which burns (*usati*) its adversaries is an *usabha*, meaning "excellent" (*seṭṭha*). That which cries out (*rāsati*) is a *rāsabha*, meaning a donkey (*gadrabha*).
127. *Ito bhaka*. After the word *iti*, the suffix *bhaka* occurs. [Example: It goes (*eti*) or moves (*gacchati*), thus it is an *ibha*—an elephant. 128. *Garāvā bho*.
[The suffix *bho* occurs after the word *garu*.]

Regarding *gabbha*, *ghara-secana*, and *ava-rakkhana*: by these [meanings] it becomes *bho* (a word). It "sinks" (*garati*) by way of exiting outside and it "sprinkles" (*siñcati*), thus *gabbha* means offspring and a room. It "protects" (*avati*) beings, thus *abbha* means a cloud. 129. *Sobbha* and others.
*Sobbha* and other words are derived from the root *bhant*. For Sadatissa, there is *otta*; they sink (*sīdanti*) therein, thus *sobbha* means a hollow or pit.
*Sobbha* is a particular type of water reservoir. *Kumbha*: that which is desired (*kāmīyati*) is a *kumbha*; it refers to a measure of ten *ambhas* and also to a jar (*ghaṭa*).
[Alternatively,] it is called a *kumbha* because it is filled (*umbhīyati*) or made full by water. *Kusumbha*: that which is called *kusuma* is *kusumbha*, namely the great dye (*mahārajana*).
*Kusumbha* also means gold; other such words are to be understood in the same way.
130. *Usa*, *kusa*, *pada*, *sukha*, and *kuma*. [The suffix] *ma* occurs after *usa* and others.

That which heats (*usati*) and burns (*dahati*) is *usuma* = heat (*uṇha*). That which calls out (*kusati*) or invites (*avhāyati*) is *sukuma* = flower (*puppha*). That which goes toward (*pajjati*) the worship of gods and so forth is *paduma* = lotus (*paṅkaja*). That which brings happiness (*sukhayati*) is *sukhuma* = subtle (*aṇu*).
131. *Vaṭuma* and others.

The suffixes *vaṭuma*, etc., are applied after verbal roots with the sense of "going" (*nipacca*). After the root *vaj* (to go), the suffix *ṭo* is added; since they go there, it is *vaṭumaṃ* = a path.

After the root *silis* (to adhere), *lissa* is substituted for *silissa*; since it adheres, it is *silesupaṃ* = phlegm. After the root *kam* (to desire), *kuṅka* is substituted; since it is desired, it is *kuṅkamaṃ* = saffron from Kashmir; other examples are similar. 132. After the root *guh* (to hide), the suffix *umo* is added.
The suffix *uma* occurs after the roots *gudh* and *pariveṭh*. Because it covers (*gudhati*) and envelops (*pariveṭhati*), *godhuma* is a specific kind of grain.
133. *Paṭha* and *cara* take the suffixes *ama* and *ima* respectively.

The suffixes *ama* and *ima* follow the roots *paṭh* and *car* in their respective order. That which is recited (*paṭhiyati*), uttered (*uccāriyati*), or placed in a superior state (*uttamabhāvena*) is *paṭhamam*, meaning "the best. That which moves toward inferiority (*hīnatta*) is *carimam*, meaning "the last."

134. The suffix *maka* occurs after the roots *hi* (in the sense of going) and *dhū* (in the sense of shaking). That which goes forth (*hinoti*) and proceeds is *hima*—namely, snow (*tuhina*). That which shakes (*dhunāti*) or trembles is *dhūma*—namely, the production of smoke (*aggipasava*). 135.
Also after the roots *bhī* (to fear) and *rīs* (to be angry).

From the root *bhī* (to fear), with the suffix *asana*, the word *bhīsana* is formed; it is a synonym for *makaca*. There is elision of the internal vowel and so forth (*antarasarādilopa*). That from which they fear is *bhīsana*, meaning "terrifying. *Bhīma* is the same. 136.
The roots *khī*, *su*, *vī*, *yā*, *gā*, *hi*, *sā*, *lū*, *khu*, *hu*, *mara*, *dhara*, *ghara*, *jamāma*, *samā*, and *mo*:

*Khī* means destruction (*khaye*). *Su* means hearing (*savane*). *Vī* means the continuity of a thread (*tantasantāne*). *Yā* means reaching (*pāpuṇane*). *Gā* means sound (*sadde*). *Hi* means motion (*gatiyam*). *Sā* [is used] in the senses of making thin and conclusion (*tanukaraṇāvasānesu*).

The suffix *mo* occurs after these verbal roots: *lū* (to cut), *khu* (the sound *khu*), *hu* (to invoke), *mara* (to abandon life), *dhara* (to hold), *kara* (to do), *ghara* (to sprinkle), *jama* (to eat), *ama* (to go), *gama* (to go), and *sama* (to compare).
*Khema* means "free from danger" because it causes the state of being free from calamity (*nirupaddavakaraṇatā*).
*Soma* is "that which presses out" (*sunoti*), namely the moon (*cando*). *Vema* is "that by which they weave" (*vāyanti etenāti*), namely the loom or weaving apparatus (*tantavāyopakaraṇaṃ*).
It goes (*yāti*), thus *yāma*—the sixth or eighth part of the day. They sing (*gāyanti*) there, thus *gāma*—a dwelling place. It flows (*hinoti*) and proceeds (*pavattati*), thus *hema*—gold.
It makes beautiful (*sundara*) and thin (*tanu*), thus *sāma*—dark. It is plucked (*lūyate*), thus *loma*—hair of the body. It is spun (*khūyate*) into a superior state, thus *khoma*—linen cloth.
Offering (*havana*), or that which is offered (*hūyate*), is *homa*—a burnt offering. By means of this they die (*maranti*), thus...

That which, when struck, does not live is *mamba*. That which sustains itself and prevents one from falling into the miserable states (*apāya*) and the suffering of the cycle of existence (*vaṭṭadukkha*) is *dhamma*, namely the scriptures (*pariyatti*) and so forth.
That by which something is done, or that which is done, is *kamma*, namely the fruits of pleasure and pain and so forth.
That by which sweat flows is *ghamma*, namely the heat of summer. One who eats what should not be eaten is *jammo*, namely a base person.
And one who acts without reflection. She moves (*ameti*) with affection toward her children; thus, *ammā* means mother. That by which they are brought together is *sammā*, meaning friendly conduct.

137. *Asma-ādayo*. Words such as *asma* are derived as mantras; the absence of subsequent forms (*pararūpa*) and so forth occurs by way of conventional rule (*nipātanā*). In the sense of throwing (*khepane*), one throws (*assateti*); thus, *asmā* means stone.
The root *bhas* means "to reduce to ashes"; that which "crumbles" (*pakkharati*) is *bhasman* (ashes). The root *us* means "to burn";
that which "burns" (*usati*) is *uṣman* (heat, the fire element). The root *vis* means "to enter"; that which they "enter" (*pavisanti*) is *veśman* (a house). The root *bhī* means "fear";
with the suffix *suñ*, that from which people "fear" (*bhāyanti*) is *bheṣman* (terrible). The root *as* takes the suffix *dhaṅ*; that by which people are "abandoned" (*cajīyati*) is *asman* (stone).
*Adhamo* means low or inferior. *Karoti* becomes *uttaṃ* for him; because he acts (*karoti*), he is a *kummo*, that is, a tortoise.
Other cases are similar. 138. *Nīto* becomes *mi*. After the root *nī*, *mi* occurs. Because it leads (*nayati*), it is a *nemi*, that is, the rim of a wheel.

139. *Ūmi*, *bhūmi*, *nimi*, *rasmi*. These words ending in *-i* are formed as nouns (*nipaccante*). In the root *ūh* (meaning "to reflect"), there is the elision of *h*: that by which they reflect or think is *ūmi* = a wave (*taraṅga*). In the root *bhū* (meaning "existence"), there is the absence of the suffix *-tta*:
that wherein beings exist is *bhūmi* = the earth (*mahī*). In the root *ni* (meaning "to lead down"), there is the absence of the suffix *-tta*: [that which leads] to a happy rebirth...
"He leads away from evil," thus [he is] King Nimi. "In the tasting of flavor, there is an absence of another form; beings taste by means of this," thus *rasmi* is a rope (*rajju*).
(Thus ends the section on the rules for the suffix -vaggapaccaya). 140. *Māchāhi yo*.

*Mā* means "to conceal" (*chādanē*). That which arises from these [roots] is *māyā*. It conceals one's own lack of virtue by means of some other superior quality; thus, *māyā* is characterized by the concealment of existing faults (*santadosa-paṭicchādana-lakkhaṇā*). *Chā* means "to cut" (*chindati*) or "to doubt" (*saṃsayati*);

hence *chāyā* is a reflection (*paṭibimbaṃ*). 141. *Janissa jā ca*: that which arises from *jan* (to be born) is *jā*; and the wife (*jāyā*) is she who gives birth (*janetīti*). Thus, *jāyā* means a wife (*bhariyā*).

142. *Hadaya-ādayo*. The suffixes beginning with *ya* are applied after the root *hṛ* and others. From the root *hṛ*, the suffix *daṅ* is added: that which carries (*harati*) is the heart (*hadayaṃ*), namely the mind-element (*manodhātu*), the mind-consciousness-element (*manoviññāṇadhātu*), and their support. From the root *tan*, the suffix *issaaka* is added:
that which extends affection toward oneself (*attani pemaṃ tanoti*) is a descendant (*tanayo*), meaning a son. From the root *sar*, the suffix *issa* is added: it remembers (*sarati*).
It goes, thus *sūriyo* = *ādicco*. It is the name for taking away (*harati*); it brings happiness, thus *hammiyaṃ* = a palace with a flat roof. *Kasa* means going;
the suffix *alaka* is added to *kasa*, and *i* is substituted for *assa*; it grows, thus *kisalayaṃ* = a sprout. Other [derivatives] are likewise. 143.
After the roots *khī*, *si*, *si*, *nī*, *sī*, *su*, *vī*, and *kus*, the suffix *raka* is applied.

The suffix *ra* occurs after these roots: *khī* (to destroy), *si* (to serve), *si* (to bind), *nī* (to lead), *sī* (to lie down), *su* (to hear), *vī* (to go), *ku* (sound), and *sū* (to give birth).
It destroys by milking, thus *khīraṃ* = milk (*payo*). It is served by flowers and the like, thus *siraṃ* = the head (*muddhā*).
It lies down and binds the body, thus *sirā* = a vessel that binds the body (*dehabandhanī*). It leads, or is led away by others, thus...
*Nīraṃ* means water (*jalaṃ*). It flows (*sayati*), thus *sīro* means a plough (*halaṃ*). It yields undesirable fruit (*aniṭṭhaphaladāyaka*), thus *surā* means liquor (*madirā*).
He hears (*suṇoti*) excellent songs and so forth, thus *suro* means a god (*devo*). He attains (*veti*) the supreme state (*uttamabhāvaṃ*), thus *vīro* means valiant (*vikkanto*).

It cries out (*kavati*) or roars (*nadati*), thus *kuraṃ* means food (*bhattaṃ*). It produces (*pasavati*) the heroism (*sūrattaṃ*) of those who were terrified at the beginning of the eon (*paṭhamakappiya*), thus *sūro* means the sun (*sūriyo*) and also valiant (*vikkanto*).

144. After *hi*, *ci*, *du*, and *mi*, the suffix *ra* is added, and the preceding vowel becomes long. In the sense of "going" (*gati*), after *hi*: that which moves or proceeds is *hīraṃ*, such as a palm-sickle (*tālahīrā*) and so forth.

In the sense of "accumulating" (*caya*), after *ci*: that which accumulates is *cīraṃ*, meaning bark (*vakkala*). In the sense of "distress" (*pakkhepana*), after *du*: that which is moved by suffering is *dūraṃ*.
*Dūram* means not near (*anāsannam*). It is measured and enclosed, thus *mīra* is the ocean (*samuddo*). 145. *Dhā*, *tā*, and *nī*:

from the roots *dhā* (to hold) and *tā* (to protect), the suffix *ra* is added, and the final vowel is replaced by *ī*. That which holds is *dhīra*, meaning one who possesses fortitude (*dhitimā*). That which protects the water is *tīra*, meaning the bank (*taṭam*).

146. Bhadrāyo. Words beginning with *bhadra* and ending in the suffix *-ra* are derived through the *nipātana* (irregular) process. From the root *bhad* in the sense of "auspiciousness," there is the elision of *da* and the absence of the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) sandhi; it is called *bhadraṃ* because it is "to be enjoyed" (*bhajīyati*), thus *bhadraṃ* = auspiciousness.

From the root *bhī* in the sense of "fear," the suffix *vī* is applied due to its inclusion in the *nadādi* group; it is called *bherī* (kettledrum) because "they fear it" (*bhāyanti etāya*). From the root *cit* in the sense of "perception."

*Vipubbo*: *vicintitabbaṃ* means "to be thought about" (*vicitraṃ*); *yā* means "to reach," with *tuṇ* as the suffix for the short vowel; *gamanam* (going) is *yātrā*, which becomes *yānaṃ*. *Gup* means "to protect";
with *o* as the suffix and the elision of *pa*, that which is protected is *gotraṃ*, meaning "lineage" and so forth. *Bhas* means "to reduce to ashes";

with *tuṇ* as the suffix for the short vowel, it consumes its food (*bhakṣaṃ karoti*), thus *bhastā* is a blacksmith's bellows. *Usa* means "to burn"; with the elision of *sa*, [it is] by sorrow (*sokena*).
In the phrase *tāḷite usati dahatīti uro*, *uro* refers to a part of the body, namely the chest;
the same applies to other [words]. 147. *Manda*, *aṅka*, *sasāsa*, *matha*, *catā*, *uro*.
*Manda* means dullness; *aṅka* means a mark or characteristic; *sasāsa* means going, harming, or living beings; *asa* means throwing; *matha* means churning or agitating.
In the case of *cata-yācana*, the vowel *u* arises from these [rules]. Because it is not beautiful (*amandī asundarattā*), it went to the state of being dull (*jaḷattha*);

thus, *mandurā* = a stable for horses. It is marked (*aṅkīyati*) or characterized; thus, *aṅkura* = the sprouting of a seed. It hisses (*sasati*) or harms (*hiṃsati*); thus, *sasura* = the father of a husband and wife. It was eaten (*asīyittha*); thus, *asura* = a Dānava.
It is crushed (*mathīyati*) or stirred up (*āloḷīyati*) by enemies; thus, *mathurā* = a city. It is measured (*catīyati*); thus, *caturo* = clever.

148. *Vidhurādayo*. Words beginning with *vidhura* ending in the suffix *-ura* are treated as *nipātas* (irregular formations). From the root *vidh* in the sense of "piercing" (*vedhane*), there is the elision of the vowel *e*; since it pierces or harms (*vedhati hiṃsati*), it is *vidhura*, meaning "opposed" (*viruddha*).

From the root *und* in the sense of "moistening" (*kiledane*), since it moistens or makes wet (*undati kiledati*), it is *undura*, meaning "mouse" (*ākhu*). From the root *maṅk* in the sense of "adornment" (*maṇḍane*), there is the elision of the nasal (*niggahīta*); since it adorns (*maṅkati*)...
That by which one adorns oneself is *makura*: a mirror, a chariot, a dice-box, and a fish. [The root] *kuka* and *vaka* mean "to take";

there is a doubling of the consonant in *kuk*. That which takes up saliva and so forth is *kukkura*: a dog. [The root] *maṅga* means "auspiciousness"; that which has gone to what is not inauspicious (*amaṅgi*)—that is praised—is *maṅgura*:
a particular kind of fish. In this way, others are also [to be understood].
149. *Tima*, *ruha*, *rudha*, *badha*, *mada*, *manda*, *vaja*, *aja*, *ruca*, *kasa*:

the suffix *-kira* occurs after these. *Tima* means "to be dark"; *ruha* means "to produce"; *rudha* means "to obstruct"; *badha* means "to afflict"; *mada* means "intoxication" (or madness); *manda* means "joy," "praise," or "sluggishness"; *vaja* means "to go swiftly";
*aja* means "to go"; *ruca* means "splendor"; *kasa* means "to go. That which makes one dark (*temeti*) is *timira*—namely, darkness (*andhakāra*).

*Āpa*: water. *Ruhiraṃ* = *lohitaṃ*: it grows and continues, thus "blood. *Rudhiraṃ*: that same thing; it obstructs life, thus "blood. *Badhiro*: one who is afflicted; one deficient in hearing. *Madirā*: *surā*;
people become intoxicated by this, thus "intoxicating liquor. *Mandiraṃ*: *gharaṃ*; they rejoice therein, thus "mansion" or "house.
*Vajiraṃ*: *kulisaṃ*; it pierces, thus "thunderbolt" or "diamond. *Ajiraṃ*: *aṅgaṇaṃ*; they go or move there, thus "courtyard"—the space within the precincts of a house.

*Rocati* means "it pleases," hence *ruciraṃ* = "agreeable. *Kasīyati* means "it is traversed with difficulty," hence *kasiraṃ* = "hardship. 150. *Thirādayo*: Words beginning with *thira* are derived from roots ending in *-ka*.
From the root *ṭhā*, meaning "to stand" or "to cease moving," there is the substitution of *tha* for *ṭha*; thus, *ṭhāti* means "it proceeds" or "it stands."
*Thiraṃ* means long-lasting. *Isa* is used in the sense of wishing; with the elision of the *niggahīta*, that which is wished for is *sisiro*, a particular season.
*Ada* and *khāda* mean to eat; for the sake of shortening the vowel *ā*, that which is eaten by small creatures is *khadiro*, a toothbrush tree, and so on for others as well.
151. *Dada* [means] difficult to support.

In *dada* (to give) and *gara* (to sprinkle), they are difficult to bear (*durabharā*) according to their respective order. One who gives to the ends (*antānaṃ*) is a *daddura*, meaning a frog. That which swallows (*garati*) or sprinkles (*siñcati*) is a *gabbhara*, meaning a cave.

152. By means of the roots *cara*, *dara*, *jara*, *gara*, and *mara*, those [terms] beginning with *cara* are formed respectively. From the root *cara*—which signifies moving and eating—one forms *carā* because they move (*caranti*) therein.

*Cañcara*: a crossroads (*vīthicatukka*) and a courtyard (*aṅgaṇa*). *Dara*: in the sense of tearing apart; it is torn open (*darīyati*), thus *daddara* is a musical instrument (*vāditta*) and a kettle-drum (*bherī*).
*Jara*: in the sense of the decline of age; one who has aged (*ajarī*) is *jajjara*, meaning "worn out" (*jiṇṇo*). *Gara* and *ghara*: in the sense of sprinkling;
it sprinkles (*garati*), thus *gaggaro* is a broken voice and the cry of a swan (*haṃsassaro*). *Mara*: in the sense of abandoning life; it dies (*marati*), thus *mammara* is a withered leaf.
And the sound of *pattha-pannānam*.
153. *Pī* takes the suffix *-kvara*.
The suffix *-kvara* occurs after the root *pī*, which means "to swell. Thus, *appiṇī* becomes *pīvara*, meaning "stout" or "thick."

154. *Cīvarādayo*. Words such as *cīvara* ending in the suffix *-ra* are derived from verbal roots. In *cināti*, there is a lengthening of the vowel. That which is gathered (*cīyati*) is called *cīvara*, i.e., the saffron robe (*kāsāva*). From the root *sam* (to calm) with the prefix *upa*, the suffix *vī* is added because it belongs to the *nadādi* group;
that which calms the fever of passion (*pariḷāha*) is *saṃvarī*, i.e., night. From the root *dhā*, the suffix *ī* is added; that which holds up nets, baskets, and so forth, is [called *dhārī*].
*Dhīvara* is a fisherman; *tāyatissa* is *ī*. Because one protects oneself by means of anything [else], it is *tīvara*, meaning one of low birth. *Nayatissī*:
because beings lead [themselves] here, it is *nīvaraṃ*, meaning a house; other such terms are also like this.
155. From where does *kriro* come?

The suffix *kura* is added after the word *ku*. Because it cries (*kavati*), it is a *kurara*—a bird; in the feminine, with the suffix *vī*, it is *kurarī*. 156. The suffix *chara* is added after the roots *vas* (to dwell) and *as* (to cast).

Because they dwell (*vasanti*) there, it is *vassacchara*—a year (*vassa*). Preceded by the prefix *saṃ*, because they dwell together (*saṃvasanti*) there, it is *saṃvacchara*—the same. Because she bestows (*asati*) [pleasure], she is *accharā*—a celestial maiden (*devakaññā*) and also the snapping of fingers.
157. *Masā chero ca*.
From the root *mas* (to grasp), *chero* and *charo* are formed. *Taṇhāya parāmasanaṃ maccheraṃ* = the hiding of one’s own prosperity; *maccharaṃ* is that very same thing. 158. *Dhū vāto saro*.
[The root] *dhū* [expresses] wind and sound.
*Dhunāti vātīhi saro hoti.* "Dhunāti" means *dhūsaro*, which is coarse (*lūkha*) and slightly pale (*īsaṃpaṇḍu*). "Vāti" means "goes," thus *vāsaro* is "day.
159. *Bhamādīhyaro*:

after *bham*, *tasa*, *manda*, *kanda*, and so forth, the suffix *-ara* occurs. "Bhamati" means "it wanders," thus *bhamaro* is "a bee" (*madhukaro*). "Tasati" means "it takes hold of the thread," thus...

*Tasara* is a shuttle for weaving thread. *Mandara* is a mountain; it is so called because they "revel" (*mandanti*) and "delight" (*modanti*) therein. *Kandara* is a cave; it is so called because it "cries out" (*kandati*) or "calls out" (*avhāyati*).
*Devara* is a brother-in-law; it is so called because one "plays" (*devanti*) with him for the duration of the day (*divassa ettam*).
160. From the root *vad*, the suffix *ca*.

In *vadatisma aro yo*, there is the substitution of *ba* for *va*. That by which they speak is *badara* = the fruit of the *kakkandhu* tree. With the prefix *vi-*, it is *badarī* = the *kakkandhu* tree. 161.
From the root *vada* [meaning] "to speak," the suffixes *ṭhaṅa* and *aca* are added.

In *vadati janehi*, *a* becomes *ra*, and *ṭhaṅa* is the final substitute. One who speaks [stiffly] is *vaṭharo* = one who is dull-witted; *vaṭharaṃ* = thick or stout. That which is born is *jaṭharaṃ* = the belly.
162. *Paci-īṭhaṅaca*.
After the root *paci*, the suffixes *īṭha* and *ṅac* occur, provided they do not end in *as*. That by which they cook is *piṭhara* = a cooking pot (*thālī*).
163. *Vakā araṇa*. [The suffix *araṇa* occurs] after the root *vac*.
Regarding *vaka*: it means "one who does not take" (*na ādāna*). From this comes *araṇa* (non-conflict). *Vaketi* means "she takes by means of this," thus *vākarā* = a snare for binding deer.
164. *Siṅgi*, *aṅga*, *aga*, *majja*, *kala*, *lāla*, *āro*.

*Siṅgi* is a verbal root (*nāmadhātu*) meaning "to go"; *aṅga* has the sense of "going"; *aga* has the sense of "crooked going"; *majja* has the sense of "purification"; *kala* has the sense of "counting."
In the sense of binding (*ala-bandhane*), the suffix *āra* occurs by means of these [prefixes]. In the sense of piercing (*vijjhanatthena*), it is like a horn (*siṅga*);

thus *siṅga* is the name for the "horn" of defilement (*kilesasiṅga*) known as urbanity (*nāgarikabhāva*). It either performs that [piercing], or it is engaged in that; or it arises among those possessed of passion (*rāgīsu*).

According to the rule “there is a variety of names in the sense of verbal roots” (*dhātvatthe nānāmasmī*, 5.12), the letter *i* is applied, with the elision of the preceding *sa* and *ra*. Thus: *siṅgi*; from that, the suffix *āra* is added, with the elision of *sa* and *ra*.
*sare* (1.26): there is elision (*ilopa*). Previously, *vippaṭisedhe* (1.22) referred to the negation of what is undesired;
here, however, it refers only to the elision of the preceding vowel when followed by *ārato* or elsewhere, and also in cases other than the suffix *i*.

*Siṅgāro* means "the making of the horn of defilement" (*kilesasiṅgakaraṇaṃ*), which is to say, "graceful charm" (*vilāsa*). *Aṅgāro* means that which goes to destruction (*vināsaṃ gacchati*), i.e., burnt wood. They go (*ganti*) toward fire (*agaṃ*).
*Ettha* means "in the house" (*agāraṃ = gharaṃ*). Because it cleanses its own body by licking and makes it stainless, it is called *majjāro*, that is, a cat (*biḷāro*).

By the rule of substitution, *la* becomes *ḷ*; thus, because its quality (*guṇa*) is measured (*kalīyati*) or delimited (*parimīyati*) by this [color], it is called *kaḷāro*, that is, tawny (*piṅgalo*).
Because it is long (*dīghattaṃ*) and it binds (*alati*), it is called *aḷāro*, meaning crooked (*vaṅko*) and wide (*visālo*).
165. *Kamissassu ca*.

The suffix *āra* is applied after the verbal root *kam*, and the letter *u* is substituted for *assa*. That which is desired (*kāmīyati*) is a *kumāro*—that is, a child. 166. *Bhiṅgārādayo*. [The words] beginning with *bhiṅgāra* [are formed by this rule].
Words beginning with *bhiṅgāra* are declined as *ārantā*. The root *bhṛ* means "to support" (*bharaṇe*); supporting includes both holding and nourishing.

For the root *bharati* in the sense of "holding," there is the substitution of *bhiṅga*. Since it holds or supports water, *bhiṅgāra* = a golden vessel. The roots *klid*, *klid*, and *alla* signify "moistening. There is the elision of *la*.
That which moistens is *kedāra* = a field (*khetta*). [The etymology is: when there is water (*ke*), there is a split (*dāra*).
Or, it is called *kedāra* because it is "that which tears" (*vidāraṇa*); the elision of the locative case ending does not occur here due to the rule of the frequentative suffix (*bahulādhikāra*).

From the root *vida* (to obtain), with the prefix *ku*, the suffix *ara* is added; the letter *da* becomes *ḷa*, the syllable *issa* becomes *etta*, and in the compound, the *ku* becomes *o*—thus, by way of derivation, *koviḷāra* means "that which finds the earth" (*kuṃ pathaviṃ vindati*) because it grows there, and it has double leaves.
167. *Karā* means Māra.
Because he performs deeds (*karoti*), he is called Māra. One who performs the work of iron is a blacksmith (*kammāro* = *lohakāro*).
168. After the vowel *u*, *kharo* [is substituted].

With the prefix *sa-*, [the root] *khar* becomes *kharo* (a donkey). That which is nourished by water is *pokkharaṃ* = *padumaṃ* (a lotus). That which remembers, i.e., undergoes transformation, is *sakkharā* = a product of sugarcane. 169.
With *sa-*, *vasa-*, *kala-*, *ki-*, *ro-*, *vassa-*, and *uṭa-*, these become *kīro*, *vassa-*, and *uṭa-*.

That which is remembered is *sarīraṃ* = the body. That by which they dwell or reside is *usīraṃ* = the root of the *bīraṇa* grass. By this, that which is thickened and measured is *kaliro* = a sprout.

170. *Gambhīrādayo*. Words beginning with *gambhīra* are derived by adding the suffix *kīra*. [The root] *gam* takes the suffix *bhuka*, or there is the elision (*lopa*) of *ma*. That which goes by breaking through the earth and proceeds is *gambhīra*; *gabhīra* means "bottomless. In *kulissa*, *la* becomes *ḷa*. That which spreads out at the feet is *pāde kulati*. By the rule "there is the substitution of *va* for the vowel of the first member," it becomes *poṅkava*. By the rule "there is the substitution of *ya* for the final vowel of the first member," it becomes *poṅkaya*. By the rule "there is the substitution of *e* for the vowel of the first member," it becomes *peṅkaya*. By the rule "there is the substitution of *i* for the vowel of the first member," it becomes *piṅkaya*. By the rule "there is the substitution of *a* for the vowel of the first member," it becomes *paṅkaya*. By the rule "there is the substitution of *ka* for the vowel of the first member," it becomes *paka*. 171. *Khajja*, *valla*, *masā*, and *ūro*.

With these—[namely] *khajja* in the sense of eating, *valla* and *valla* in the sense of covering, and *sama* in the sense of touching—the suffix *ūro* occurs. Thus, it is that which is eaten (*khajjīyati*).
Khajjūra is a date; *vīmhi* is a specific type of date palm tree. That which is dried (*vallīyati*) or shriveled (*saṃvarīyati*) is *vallūra*, meaning dried meat.
That which is ground (*masīyati*) is *masūra*, a specific type of grain.
172. Camphor and others.
Words ending in *-ūra* are derived as *nipātas*. Because it is suitable (*kappati*) or capable of producing satisfaction (*tuṭṭhi*), it is *kappūra*, that is, camphor (*ghanasāra*).
Because he commits evil (*assu*) deeds, he is a doer of evil; thus, one who commits wickedness is a *kurūra*, meaning an evildoer. The root *pasa* means to afflict;
because he afflicts or oppresses (*pīḷeti*), he is a *pasūra*, meaning a wicked person, a condiment, and also the name of a certain individual. Other such words are to be understood in the same way.
173. *Kaṭha* means "hard" (*oro*).

In the word *kaṭhora*, *kaṭha* means "living with difficulty" and *caka* means "reflection"; from these, *oro* arises. One who lives with difficulty (*kaṭhati*) is "hard" (*kaṭhora*); one who reflects (*cakati*) is a "cakra-vāka" (*cakora*), a specific kind of bird.
174. *Morādayo* ("Peacocks and others").

Words beginning with *mora* and ending with *oranta* are derived through grammatical transformation (*nipacca*). From the root *mī* in the sense of "to injure," there is the elision of *ī*; thus, *mayati* (he injures) becomes *morō*, i.e., *mayūro* (a peacock).

From the root *kas* in the sense of "going," with the suffix *assi*, *kasati* (he goes) becomes *kisorō*, i.e., a horse in its first stage of life. *Mahīyati* (it is honored) becomes *mahoro*, i.e., an anthill (*vammiko*); other examples are to be understood in the same way. 175. *Kuto eraka*.

From the word *ku*, the suffix *eraka* occurs. By the rule “for semi-vowels, *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* occur before vowels” (5.136), there is *uvaṅ*. Thus, *kuvati nadati* (“he cries out”) becomes *kuvero* = Vessavaṇa. 176. With the roots *bhū* and *sū*, the suffix *rika* occurs.

*Bhū* means existence; *sū* means procreation. With these [roots], *rika* occurs. *Bhavati* (“it exists”) becomes *bhūri* = abundant (*pahūta*); with the feminine suffix *ṅīm*, it is *bhūrī* = wisdom (*medhā*). *Savati hitam pasavati* (“he produces what is beneficial”) becomes *sūri* = wise (*vicakkhaṇo*).
177. *Mī*, *kasī*, *nīhi*, *ru*.
After the roots *mī* (in the sense of harming), *kas* preceded by *ka*, and *nay*, the suffix *ru* occurs. That which harms darkness with its rays is *meru* = *sireru*;
that which lies or moves in water (*ke*) is *kaseru* = a particular kind of grass. [Regarding] those dependent on oneself...
It leads to beauty and brings about evil; thus *neru* means a mountain (*pabbata*).
178. *Sinā eru*:
from the root *sinā*, meaning "to purify" (*soceyya*), the suffix *eru* occurs. Because it purifies—that is, makes pure—it is called *Sineru*, the king of mountains (*pabbatarāja*).
179. *Bhī* means fear; *ru* means sound.
With these [roots], the suffix *-ruka* occurs. That from which they fear is *bhīru*, meaning "fearful. It roars, thus it is *ruru*, meaning "deer.
180. *Tamā* means darkness; *būla* means a mass.
From the root *tama* meaning "to adorn," *būla* is the suffix. Since it adorns the mouth (*mukhaṃ tameti bhūseti*), *tambūla* means "mouth-adornment. 181.

From the root *si*, meaning "to serve" (*sevāyaṃ*), the suffixes *laka* and *vāla* occur. That which is served by beings (*sattehi sevīyati*) is *silā*, meaning "stone"; *selo*, meaning "mountain. That which serves water (*jalaṃ sevatīti*) is *sevālo*, meaning "aquatic grass."

182. *Maṅga*, in the sense of auspiciousness; *kama*, in the sense of desire; *samba*, in the sense of ornamentation; *sabai* is a designation for *asva* (horse) with the elision of the suffix *kata*; *saka*, in the sense of power; *vasa*, in the sense of dwelling; *pisa*, in the sense of going; *keva*, in the sense of service; *kala*, in the sense of counting; *palla*, in the sense of going. *Kaṭha*, *paṭa*, *kuṇḍa*, and *maṇḍā* are [names of] places. *Alo* [is a particle]. *Maṅga* means auspiciousness; *kama* means desire; *samba* means ornamentation;

The suffix *ala* occurs after these [roots]: *kaṭh* in the sense of a difficult life (*kicchajīvane*), *paṭ* in the sense of going (*gamanattho*), *kuṇḍ* in the sense of burning (*dāhe*), and *maṇḍ* in the sense of adorning (*bhūsane*).
*Maṅgala*: beings attain growth by means of this; thus it is *maṅgala*, meaning "praised" (*pasatthaṃ*). *Kamala*: it is desired; thus it is *kamala*, meaning "lotus" (*paṅkajaṃ*).

*Sambala*: it adorns thoroughly; thus it is *sambala*, meaning "provisions for a journey" (*pātheyyaṃ*). *Sabala*: having a variegated color; thus it is *sabala*, meaning "of diverse colors. [Sakala]: it is able to endure.

*Sakalaṃ* means "all. One who dwells (*vasati*) is a *vasala*, meaning a "low-caste person" (*sudda*). One who grinds away (*pisati*) or goes toward (*gacchati*) a state of being dear is a *pesala*, meaning "one of amiable character.
*Kevati* means "it proceeds," thus *kevalaṃ* means "entire. That by which water is measured (*kalīyati*) or delimited is *kalalaṃ*, meaning "mud" (*apatthinna*).
That from which water comes forth (*pallati*) or arrives is *pallalaṃ*, meaning "a shallow lake" (*appodako saro*). *Kaṭhaṃ* means "here [it is] with suffering."
*Yanti* means it goes; *kaṭhala* is a fragment of a skull. *Paṭati* means it increases or grows; *paṭala* is a collection or mass.
*Kuṇḍati* means it burns or consumes by friction; *kuṇḍala* is an ear-ornament. *Maṇḍīyati* means it is delimited or defined by way of making a boundary;
*maṇḍala* is that which is circumscribed on all sides.
183. *Musā* means "to lie.
That which lies is *musā*. That by which one lies is *musala*, meaning "unfit" (*ayogga*).
184. *Thalādayo* ("The sands, etc.").

Words beginning with *tha* and ending with *la* are derived as primary nouns (*nipātta*). By the rule *ṭhassa tho*, the substitution of *tha* for *ṭha* occurs, followed by the elision of the preceding vowel. That which stands there is *thalaṃ*—an elevated place. The root *pā* means "to drink.
With the prefix *upa*, and by doubling the root and eliding the preceding vowel, that which drinks water is *uppalaṃ*—the blue lotus (*kuvalaya*).

For the root *pat*, the substitution *pāṭaṃ* occurs. That which falls, moves, or ripens is *pāṭalaṃ*—a fruit, and also a flower of copper-colored hue. In the case of the root *baṃh*, there is the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra).

It is called *bahala* because it increases and grows; it is *ghana*. *Capala* refers to that which moves (*cupissa ussattaṃ*); it is called *capala* because it does not remain in one place (*cupati ekattha na tiṭṭhati*), thus it is unsteady.
Other [terms] are likewise [to be understood]. 185. *Kula* and *kāla*.

*Kulapatthāreti*: this is the time; it is the right time (*kālo*). One spreads out one’s own craft (*sippa*)—thus *kulālo* = a potter (*kumbhakāra*). One spreads out one’s wings (*pakkhe*)—thus *kulalo* = a species of bird. 186. *Muḷālādayo*.
Words beginning with *muḷāla* ending in *-āla* are derived [from roots] ending in *-anta*. From the root *mīla* (to close): *uttaḷatāni*, it closes as soon as they have been pulled up.

*Muḷālam* means *bhisaṃ* (lotus root). Regarding *biḷāla*: because it possesses strength (*bala*) through its life-force (*pāṇana*), and because it lives by eating mice and other creatures, it is called *biḷālo*, that is, a cat (*majjāro*).

Due to the elision of the initial conjunct in *kappi*, [it becomes] *kapālaṃ*; since one makes a livelihood (*jīvikaṃ*) by means of this, it is a fragment of a pot (*ghaṭādikhaṇḍaṃ*). Regarding *piyāla*:

from the root *pī* in the sense of "to satisfy" (*tappane*), the substitution *iyaṅ* occurs according to the rule "for semi-vowels, *iyaṅ* and *uvaṅ* before a vowel" (Pāṇini 6.4.77). Because it satisfies beings with its own fruit (*phalena*), it is the *piyālo* tree.
In the word *kuṇa*, "to sound," it is called *kuṇāla* because the rows of waves stirred up by the wind *kuṇanti*, meaning they resound there; it is one great lake.
In *visa*, "to enter," it is called *vissāla* because they enter (*pavisanti*) there; it means "extensive. In *pala*, "to go," it is called *palāla* because it moves or goes by the wind;
it refers to the stalks and leaves of the grain brought forth from the crops. In *sara*, "to remember" or "to injure," it is called *sara* because those such as hares (*sasādayo*) remember or injure.
*Sigāla* is *kotthu*; other [derivatives] are likewise. 187.
From *caṇḍa* and *pata*, the suffix *ṇāla* occurs.

With *caṇḍa* in the sense of "to afflict" and *pata* in the sense of "going," the suffix *ṇāla* is applied. He afflicts (*caṇḍeti*) or torments (*pīḷeti*), thus *caṇḍāla* = a Mātaṅga (outcaste). He falls (*patati*) or goes downward (*adhogacchati*), thus *pātāla* = Rasātala (the netherworld).
188. Regarding the suffix *lo*:

it occurs after roots such as *mā* (in the sense of measuring), *i* (in the sense of study and going), *pī* (in the sense of drinking), and *dū* (in the sense of burning). That which is measured or fully measured is *mālā*, meaning a row or series (*paṅkti*).
That which goes or moves is *elā*, meaning cardamom (*sukhumelā*). That wherein one drinks or satisfies oneself is *pelā*, meaning a drinking vessel or a water-pot stand (*āsittakūpadhāna*).
It causes distress and torments, thus it is a *dolā* (swing/plaything). In the sense of counting, *kalana* means *kalla*, which is "fit" (*yutta*).
189. The roots *ana*, *sala*, *kala*, *kuka*, *saṭha*, *maha*, and *ila*.

*Ana* is in the sense of breathing; *sala* is in the sense of going; *kala* is in the sense of counting; *kuka* is in the sense of eating; *saṭha* is in the sense of a rogue; *araha* is in the sense of worship; *maha* is in the sense of honor.

With these [prefixes], *ila* becomes [various words]. That which does not move (*anati*) or proceeds is *anilo*, meaning wind (*māluto*). That which flows (*salati*) or moves is *salilaṃ*, meaning water (*jalaṃ*). That which moves about (*kalati*) or proceeds is *kalilaṃ*, meaning a thicket (*gahanaṃ*).
That which cries out (*kukati*) and captivates the minds of beings with its own song is *kokilo*, meaning the cuckoo (*parapuṇḍo*).
That which moves crookedly (*saṭhati*) or deceives is *saṭhilo*, meaning a rogue (*saṭho*). That which is honored (*mahīyati*) or worshipped is *mayilā*, meaning a woman (*itthī*).
190. *Kuṭā kilo*.
From the root *kuṭ* (to bend), the suffix *kila* occurs. "The straight (*akuṭi*) has gone to a state of bending (*kuṭilatta*)"—thus, *kuṭila* means crooked (*vaṅka*). 191.
*Sithilādayo* (the group beginning with *sithila*).

*Śithila* and the others are declined in the *kila* sense. Together with *khamā* (patience): the state of being slack for one who endures, or that which is unable to endure, is *sithila*—that is, not firm.

From the root *kamp*, there is the elision of the *saṃyoga* and so forth; because he trembles when there is suffering in others, he is *kapila*—the sage. From the root *kab* in the sense of color (*vaṇṇa*), *ba* becomes *pa*;
because it has attained the state of blue and other colors, it is *kapila*—a particular color. From the root *math*, *math* becomes *mith*; it is that which is churned (*mathīyati*).
*Mithilā-purī*, and others as well. 192.
*Caṭa*, *kaṇḍa*, *vaṭṭa*, *putha* with the suffix *-kula*.
The suffix *-kula* occurs after these: *caṭa* in the sense of breaking, *kaṇḍa* in the sense of cutting, *vaṭṭa* in the sense of turning, and *putha* in the sense of spreading out on the path.
*Caṭula*: one who "breaks" or "divides" friends is *caṭula*, meaning a flatterer (*cāṭukārī*). *Kaṇḍula*: that which "is cut" or "is lopped off" is *kaṇḍula*, meaning a tree.
*Vaṭṭula*: that which "is round" is *vaṭṭula*, meaning circular (*parimaṇḍala*). *Puthula*: that which "is spread out" is *puthula*, meaning broad (*vitthāra*).
193. *Tumula* and others.

Words such as *tumula* and others are derived from verbal roots (*kulantā*). The root *tam* means "to distress. Because it has attained expansion (*vitthiṇṇatta*)—that is, it has spread—it is *tumula*, meaning "extended" or "vast.

The root *tamissa-ḍuka* means "to undergo transformation. That which undergoes transformation is *taṇḍula*, meaning "the essence of rice. In the word *nicula*, there is the elision of the suffix *i* from the root *ci* preceded by the prefix *ni*.
It is called *nicula* because it is gathered (*nicīyati*) by those who desire it; thus it is the *hijjala* tree. Other words are to be understood in the same way.
194. *Kalla*, *kapa*, *takka*, and *paṭa* [form] *olo*.
In the sense of "shouting" (*kalla*), "covering" (*kapa*), "thinking" (*takka*), and "going" (*paṭa*), the suffix *olo* occurs.
That which rises from the ocean with the force of the wind and "calls out" (*kallati*) is *kallola*—a great wave. That which "covers" (*kapati*) the teeth is... [the word for lip].
*Kapola* is a part of the face. It is called *takkola* because it is inferred (*takkīyati*); *kolaka* is a synonym. It is called *paṭola* because one goes toward disease (*byādhi*) by means of it;

*tittaka* (bitter) is a synonym. 195. *Aṅgula*: *aṅga* has the sense of "going"; from this, *ulaulī* occurs. They know [the measure] by means of this as *aṅga*, thus *aṅgula* is a measure. It goes up (*uggacchati*) from the body, thus *aṅgali* is a finger.
196. *Añjali*.

The root *añj* occurs in the senses of manifestation (*byatti*), anointing (*makkhana*), going (*gati*), and beauty (*kantī*); from this, the suffix *ali* is added. Because one manifests devotion (*bhatti*) by means of it, *añjali* is the hollowed palms joined together (*karapuṭa*). 197. *Chadā li*. [The suffix *li* follows the root *chad* (to cover)].
The suffix *li* occurs after the root *chad*, meaning "to cover. *Challī* means "bark" (*sakalikā*), as in "it covers" (*chādeti*). 198. *Alli-ādayo*:

Words beginning with *alli* ending in *li* are derived as nouns (*nipacca*). From the root *ar*, meaning "to go," *alli* is formed; it is a tree (*rukkha*) because movement (*arati*) proceeds within it. [This applies to] *nayati*.
The absence of *atta* [is indicated by the suffix] *ika*; it is led (*nīyati*) by means of *ika*, hence *nīli*. With the suffix *ṅī*, it becomes *nīlī*, which is a species of tree (*gacchajāti*).

According to the rule "after a short vowel, two" (1.34), when the *la* is doubled and the preceding vowel is shortened, there is also the form *nillī*. From *pāli* comes *pā*: it protects (*pāleti*), guards (*rakkhati*), hence *pāli*; with the suffix *ṅī*, it becomes *pālī*, meaning a row (*paṅkti*).

From *pāli* comes *palla*: it protects, guards, hence *palli*, meaning a hut (*kuṭi*). *Cuḍa* means to urge (*codane*); the absence of *otta* [is indicated by the suffix]; it is urged (*codīyati*), hence...
From *cull* (to cook), *uddhana* (a hearth);
likewise others. 199. *Avo* follows *pila*, etc.

From *pila* (to turn), *palla* (to go), and *paṇa* (in the sense of trade and praise), and so forth, the suffix *avo* occurs. *Pilyate* means *pelava* = light. *Pallati* means *pallava* = a sprout. *Paṇīyati* means *paṇava* = a small drum (*mudaṅga*). Likewise others.

200. *Sāḷavādayo*. Words beginning with *sāḷava* are derived from the root *avant*. [The word] *sala* has the sense of "going. By means of a grammatical anomaly (*nipātana*), the vowel of the prefix *upa* becomes long and the letter *l* is substituted for *v*.
It moves or proceeds, thus it is *sāḷa*. *Va* refers to prepared food such as jujube fruits and the like. [The root] *kit* means "dwelling"; there is the absence of the suffix *ettā*.

*Kitava* means a gambler; it is derived from the root *kit*, meaning "to play" (*ketati*), thus a gamester, as well as a thief. From the root *mū*, meaning "to bind," with the shortening of the vowel *ū* to *u* and the substitution of *tu* for *ta*, we have *mutava*, meaning one who binds or ties—namely, a *caṇḍāla*.
From the roots *vala* and *valla*, meaning "to cover" (*saṃvaraṇe*), with the change of *ḷ* to *l*, we have *vaḷavā*, which either covers or is covered—namely, a mare, the beloved of the horse.
From the root *mura*, meaning "to envelop" (*saṃveḷane*), we have *murava*, that which is enveloped—namely, a drum (*mudaṅga*). In this same manner, other words are also formed.
201. *Sarāvo*. From the root *sar* (to flow), *āva* is the suffix. That which flows or moves is a *sarāva*, a specific type of vessel.
202. *Ala*, *mala*, and *bila* take the suffix *ṇuva*.

The suffix *ṇvu* occurs after these roots: *ala* in the sense of binding (*bandhana*), *mala* in the sense of holding (*dhāraṇa*), and *bila* in the sense of breaking (*bheda*). One that hides by means of creepers is *āluva*, a species of shrub (*gaccha-jāti*). One that holds or supports is *māluva*, a leafy creeper (*patta-latā*). One that breaks or splits is *beluva*, a tree (*rukkha*).
203. After the root *gā*, the suffix *īva* occurs. From this root *gā* (meaning "to go"), *īva* is added. That by which they sing is *gīvā*, the neck (*gala*).
204. Having made [the word] *suta* [from the root] *śru*.
By means of this [rule], *su-savana* becomes *su-savaṇa*. That which hears is *suvaḥ* = *kīraḥ* (a parrot). *Suvā* = *suṇī* (a female dog).
205. *Vidvā*.

It should be understood that the absence of the subsequent form occurs when suffixes beginning with *a* are not applied. From the root *vid* (to know), in the sense of "he knows," we have *vidvā* = *vidū*.
206. *Thu* followed by *reva*.
From the root *thu* (in the sense of praising), *reva* is added. From *thavati* (he sprinkles), we have *thevo* = a drop.
207. *Sama* with the suffix *riva*.

From the roots *sama* (to be even) and *upa-sama* (to be tranquil), the suffix *riva* occurs. That which is even and tranquil is *siva*, namely Umāpati; *sivā* is a female jackal; *sivaṃ* is peace (*santi*). 208.
*Chada* with the suffix *ravi*.
From the root *chad* (in the sense of covering), *ravi* occurs.
Because it covers, *chavi* = radiance. 209. *Pūra*, *tima*, *kisa*, and *rassa*.

From *pūra* (in the sense of filling) and *tima* (in the sense of darkening), *kisa* and *rassa* [suffixes] occur. Because he fills, *puriso* = a man (*pumā*). Or, because he lies/sits (*seti*) in a high place (*pure*), he is called *puriso* = a man. Because it darkens (*temeti*), *timisaṃ* = darkness (*tamo*).
210. *Karā* becomes *īsa*.
From the root *karoti*, *īsa* is substituted. That which is made (*karīyati*) is *karīsaṃ* = excrement. 211. *Sirīsādayo*.
(The words beginning with *sirīsa* follow.)

Words beginning with *īs* are derived from the root *ī*. From the root *sar*, as in *saratissa* (of the one who flows) or *assi* (in the case of being bitten by a snake), we have *sirīso*—a tree—because it "flows" (*sarati*).
From *pūr*, there is the shortening of the vowel: *purīsaṃ*—excrement—because it "fills" (*pūreti*). From *tal*, there is lengthening:
*tālīsaṃ*—a specific medicinal herb—because it "becomes a support for beings" (*talati*). Other examples are to be understood in the same way.
212. *Karā* becomes *ribbiso*.
From the root *kṛ*, it becomes *ribbiso*. That which is done (*karīyati*) is *kibbisaṃ*—that is, evil.
213. After the suffixes *sa*, *āsa*, *va*, *sa*, *visa*, *hana*, *vana*, *mana*, *āna*, and *ka*, [the preceding vowel] becomes long (*so*).

The root *sas* means injury (*hiṃsā*), trust (*vissāsa*), and breathing (*pāṇanesu*); *as* means throwing (*khepana*); *vas* means dwelling (*nivāsa*); *vis* means entering (*pavisana*); *han* means killing (*hiṃsāyaṃ*);
*van* means acquisition (*sambhattiyaṃ*); *man* means knowledge (*ñāṇe*); *an* means breathing (*pāṇane*); and *kam* means desire (*icchāyaṃ*). Through these [roots], it becomes *sassaṃ*:
that by which beings (*sattā*) breathe and live is *sassaṃ*, such as rice (*kāla-mādi*); that which throws is *asso*, a horse (*hayo*); [and] they dwell... (*vasanti*).
*Ettha* means *vassa*, which is a year (*saṃvaccharo*). *Visati* means *vessa*, the third caste (*tatiyavaṇṇo*). *Haññate* means *haṃsa*, the white-winged bird (*sitacchado*).
*Vana* means it spreads out (*pattharati*), thus *vaṃsa* is a lineage (*santāno*) and also bamboo (*veḷu*). *Maññate* means *maṃsa*, flesh (*pisitaṃ*);
*aṃsa* means that by which one lives (*anati jīvati etena*), thus it is a portion (*ekāṭṭhāso*) and the shoulder (*bhujasiro*). *Kāmīyati* means *kaṃsa*, a measure (*parimāṇaṃ*).
214. *Āmi*, *thu*, *ku*, *sī*, and *ta* [are suffixes]. *Ā* is prefixed to *mi* in the sense of throwing (*pakkhepa*);

*thu* is used in praise (*abhitthava*); *ku* is used in the sense of sound (*sadde*); *sī* is used in the sense of lying down (*saye*). With these, *saka* occurs. That which is thrown inside (*āmīyati anto pakkhipīyati*) is *āmisaṃ* = food (*bhakkhaṃ*).
That which is praised (*thavīyati*) is *thuso* = the husk of rice (*vīhitaco*). That which cries out with the wind (*kavati vātena nadati*) is... [kavaḍa].
*Kuśa* is a specific kind of grass. *Sīsa* means head or top; it is also used for the end of a thread. 215. *Phassādayo*.

Words beginning with *phassa* are declined ending in *-anta*. From the root *phus* (to touch), with the suffix *-sa*, one who touches is *phassa*; it is the object of body-consciousness (*kāyaviññāṇa*).
*Phussa* is the name of a lunar mansion (*nakkhatta*). From the root *puṣ* (to nourish), that which is nourished is *pussa*; [with the suffix *a*,] it becomes *phussa*, meaning a specific fruit.

From the root *bhū* (existence), with the shortening of *bhū* to *bhu*, that which has come into being is *bhusa*, meaning empty grain. From the root *aṅk* (to mark), with the suffix *uka*, that by which one marks another is *aṅkusa*, meaning an elephant goad.
From the root *phā* (increase), preceded by *pa*, with the elision of *y*, that which goes to increase is *papphāsa*, meaning a specific part of the body (the lungs).
From *kali* (to measure): *māña*, *kulismā*, and *kammāsa*. It is called *kammāsa* because it is measured (*kalīyati*) or delimited; thus *kammāsa* means variegated (*sabala*) or evil (*pāpa*).

From *kula* (to spread out): *kummāsa*, a specific kind of food. From *man* (to think): *mañjūsā*. It is called *mañjūsā* because one thinks of wealth by means of it; thus it is a wooden box (*kaṭṭhapeḷā*). From *pi* (to drink): *pīyūsa*.
It is called *pīyūsa* because it is drunk (*piṇeti*); thus it is the nectar of immortality (*amata*). From *kula* (in the sense of covering/protecting), with the suffix *ika*: *kulīyati*.
It is called *kulisa* because it restrains (*saṃvarīyati*); [the root] *bala* means to restrain, with the suffix *ika*, and the substitution of *ḷ* for *l*.

It is called *baḷisa* because one catches fish with it; *baḷisa* is a fish-hook. *Mahesī* is derived from *mahissa eka*; she is called *mahesī* because she is honored (*mahīyati*); thus, *mahesī* refers to the principal woman who has received consecration.
Other words are to be understood in the same way.
216. *Suta* becomes *ṇisaka*. That which hears (*suṇāti*) is *ṇisaka*. "She who hears" (*suṇisā*) means the wife of a son (*puttabhariyā*).
217. After *vetā*, *yu* [is substituted] for *panāla*, *kala*, *camā*, and *aso*.

The suffix *aso* occurs after these [roots]: *veta-* in the sense of flowing (*suttī*), *ata-* in the sense of constant movement (*sātaccagamana*), *yu-* in the sense of mixing (*missaṇa*), *pana-* in the sense of praise (*thuti*), *ala-* in the sense of binding (*bandhana*), *kala-* in the sense of counting (*saṅkhyāna*), and *cama-* in the sense of eating (*adana*).
*Vetati* means "it flows" or "it moves," thus *vetaso* = the *vānīra* (cane).

*Atati* means "it constantly goes to a state of being shaken by the wind," thus *ataso* = a particular kind of forest tree; with the suffix *vī*, it becomes *abhasī* = a particular kind of shrub. *Yavīyati* means "it is mixed," thus...
*Yavasa* is fodder for cattle. That which is established and praised is *panasa*, the jackfruit tree. That which is clung to and bound is *alasa*, one who acts slowly.
That which is struck (*kalīyati*) is *kalasa*, a jar. That by which one chews or eats is *camasa*, a sacrificial vessel.
218. *Vaya*, *diva*, *kara*, *karehī*, *saṇa*, *saka*, *pāsaka*, *sā*.

From *vaya*, *ati*, and so forth, *aśana* and other words arise in their respective order. That which flies or goes is a *vāyasa*—a crow. That wherein they play is a *divasa*—a day. That which is spun is *karpāsa*—the source of thread. One who commits a foul deed (*kibbisa*) is *karkaśa*—harsh.

219. *Sasu*, *masa*, *daṃsāsa*: after these, *su* is added. After *sas* and the others, *su* occurs. One who breathes or lives is a *śvaśrū*—the mother of the husband and wife. That which is rubbed is *śmaśru*—the beard on a man’s face.
*Pavaddhalomāni*. "Lopa" means the elision of the *niggahīta* (anusvāra), as in *dassu*—a thief (*coro*)—because he is bound by this.
*Assu*—a father (*bappo*)—because he is thrown (*asīyati*) or cast down.
220. *Vidā dasuka*.
*Vidismā dasuka* becomes *dasuka*. One who sees (*vidati*) or knows (*jānāti*) is a *vidvasu*, [which becomes] *vidvā*.
221. *Sasā rīho*.
After *sasati*, *rīho* occurs. One who hisses (*sasati*) or injures (*hiṃsati*) is a *sīha*, [that is,] a lion (*kesarī*).
222. *Jīvāmā* and *ho vamā*.

In the sense of "living" (*jīva*) and "going" (*ama*), the suffix *ho* occurs after these roots, and *va* and *ma* respectively undergo substitution for the final letter. This rule of substitution is intended to supersede the application of the *pararūpa* (single-substitute) rule.
By the rule "long and short vowels [are substituted] before a consonant" (1.39), there is shortening; thus: "they live by means of this."
*Jivhā* means the tongue (*rasanā*). That which moves or proceeds is *amhaṃ*, meaning "we" (*asmā*). That which moves or proceeds with the prefix *pa-* is *pamhaṃ*, meaning the eyelash (*pakhumaṃ*).

223. *Taṇhā* and others. Words beginning with *taṇhā* are derived from the root *han*. *Tas* is used in the sense of thirst; the suffix *ṇa* is applied to *sas*, and so it is in the following cases as well: *tasati* means he desires to drink.
In *etāyati*, *taṇhā* [becomes] *lobho*. In *kasa-vilekhane*, from the root *kasati*, [it becomes] *kaṇho* = *kāḷo*.

In *jota-dittiyaṃ*, there is the substitution of *ṇa* for that [root], and the elision of *o*; from *joteti*, [it becomes] *juṇhā* = moonlight. In *mīlissa ḷo*, because one closes the eyes by means of it, *mīḷhaṃ* = excrement.
In *gāhissa ḷo*, because it is grasped, *gāḷhaṃ*. In *dahissa ḷo*, because it burns, *daḷhaṃ*. In *bahissa ḷo*, there is the substitution of *ḷa* and the lengthening [of the vowel].

It is called *bāḷha* because it carries (*bahati*) and increases (*vuddhiṃ vaḍḍhati*); these three [roots] have the sense of "firmness. *Gimha* (summer) is so called because it goes (*gacchati*) toward the end of the rainy season (*assi*). *Paṭaha* is a specific type of drum;

it is so called because it moves or travels (*paṭati yāti*), with the suffix *aka* added to the root *paṭ*. *Kalaha* (quarrel) is so called because by means of it one is measured or diminished (*kalīyati parimīyati*) in terms of courage;

thus it is a dispute. *Kaṭāha* is a specific kind of vessel; it is so called because medicinal herbs and the like are crushed there (*kaṭanti ettha osadhādiṃ maddanti*), with the suffix *āka* added to the roots *kaṭa* and *vara*.
It is called *varāha* because it covers (*varīyati*), that is, a boar. It is called *loha* because it cuts (*lunāti*) or that by which one cuts, such as iron and so forth;
other [derivatives] are to be understood in the same way. 224. *Paṇussa hā hihī ṇoḷaṅa ca*:

For the word *paṇu*, *hā* and *hihī* are substituted respectively, and *ṇa*, *o*, and *laṅ* are substitutes for the final letter. By the force of this rule prescribing the substitutes, there is no formation of a single resultant form (*pararūpa*). It is called *paṇhi* because it is used to denote (*voharīyati*), namely, the back part of the foot. It is called *ussāḷhī* because it exerts itself (*ussahati*), that is, energy (*vīriya*).

225. After the roots *khī* (to perish), *mī* (to throw), *pī* (to satisfy), *cu* (to fall away), *mā* (to measure), and *vī* or *vā* (to go), as well as *kā* (to sound), the suffix *ḷa* occurs, and the vowel *u* may optionally become long.

Because it perishes (*khīyati*), it is *khela* = saliva. Because it is measured (*mīyati*) or thrown (*pakkhipīyati*), [it is *mela*]. Because it satisfies (*pīyati*), [it is *pela*]. Because it falls away (*cuyati*), [it is *cela*]. Because it measures (*māyati*), [it is *mela*].

Because it goes (*vīyati* or *vāyati*), [it is *vela*]. Because it sounds (*kāyati*), [it is *kela*]. In these cases, *ḷa* is applied, and the vowel *u* may optionally be lengthened. *Mīyati pakkhipīyatīti* means "it is measured or thrown."
*Meḷā* = ink. *Piṇeti* (he presses together) thus *peḷā* = a particular kind of vessel. *Cavati* (it falls off) thus *cūḷā* = a crest. *Coḷo* = a rag.

*Mīyati* (it is measured) or *parimīyati* (it is measured around) thus *māḷo* = a particular type of dwelling consisting of many angles but covered by a single roof-peak. *Vāti* (it moves/goes) thus *vāḷo* = a wild beast.
*Kāyati* (he speaks harshly) thus *kāḷo* = black; with the prefix *vi-* it becomes *kāḷī* = a dark woman.
226. *Gu-to ḷaka ca*.

After the word *gu*, the suffix *ḷaka* occurs, and there is also the substitution of *ḷa* [for *u*]. That by which one moves about among cows is *guḷa* = a product of sugarcane. *Goḷa* = a ball. 227. *Paṅguḷādayo*. [The words] beginning with *paṅguḷa* [are formed in this manner].

Words such as *paṅguḷa* ending in *ḷa* are derived through grammatical substitution (*nipacca*). 1. *Paṅguḷa*: Due to a deficiency in the act of walking (*gati-vekalla*), there is the substitution of *paṅgu*. One who has reached a state of deficient walking without being lame (*akhañji*) is a *paṅguḷa*, namely a cripple who crawls on a board (*pīṭhasappī*).
2. *Kakkhaḷa*: From the root *karoti* (to do), there is the substitution of *khaña* for *ḷa*. One who performs evil deeds (*kibbisa*) is *kakkhaḷa*, meaning cruel or harsh (*kurūra*).

3. *Kukkuḷa*: From *kukata* (evil deed), there is the substitution of *kuka*. That which is seized by evildoers (*kukyati*) is *kukkuḷa*; it refers to a pit strewn with stakes (*saṅku-saṃkiṇṇa-sobbha*). *Kukkuḷa* also refers to a fire of chaff (*thusaggi*).
In the word *maṅkissa*, there is the elision of the vowel *u* and the substitution of *bindu* (anusvāra); thus, that which adorns (*maṇḍeti*) the forest is *makuḷa*—an unblown flower.
228. *Pāto ḷi*:
after *pāta*, *ḷi* occurs. That which protects (*pāti*) and guards the meaning is *pāḷi*—the tradition.
229. *Vīto ḷu*.
After the prefix *vī*, the suffix *ḷu* occurs. That which moves or proceeds is a *veḷu* = *veṇu* (bamboo).
(Thus ends the rule for the application of the *avagga* [guttural] suffixes.)
Thus ends the seventh chapter, the section on the *Ṇv-ādi* suffixes, in the commentary on the *Moggallāna-byākaraṇa*.
The rules (*sutta*), the verbal roots (*dhātu*), the groups (*gaṇa*), the *Ṇv-ādi* suffixes, and the instruction on nouns and genders (*nāmaliṅgānusāsana*).
He on whose tongue-tip this [grammar] abides is a lion among expounders.
This Moggallāna-vutti is completed in seven recitation sections (bhāṇavāra).
By the power of that king, this community of developed beings has become entirely free from confusion caused by wicked monks who have attained false gains; thus,
the teaching of the King of Sages in Laṅkā is well-established.
Like the ocean swelling at the conjunction with the full moon,
faith, wisdom, and virtue flourished while that Parakkamabhuja—
whose form was like the banner of the Manu lineage— ruled over the island of Laṅkā.
Composed by the wise Elder Moggallāna, whose speech is pure,
this work is easy to understand, free from ambiguity, and unconfused.
It pervades the entire range of its subject matter and relies upon the path of expression of the Victor.
This work, which increases wisdom and is easily mastered without effort through the *Saddhammasaṅgaha*,
has been composed once again by that same author, the illuminator of the Dispensation, as a concise exposition for the sake of clarifying its extensive meaning.
The Exposition of Moggallāna is finished.
